12842-a-fairy-tale-in-two-acts-taken-fro:
Printed in 1763 for performance at Drury Lane, this short play adapts Shakespeare's fairy scenes into two acts. Quince, Bottom, Snug, Flute, Snout, and Starveling, the rude mechanicals, rehearse their interlude for the Duke's wedding night, while Oberon, Titania, and Puck quarrel in a wood near Athens. The cast list names the original players.

Puck's songs and tricks, with his pinches and silver drops, give the piece its comic heart, and the fairy king and queen trade proud, jealous lines by moonlight. The adaptation trims Shakespeare to stage fairy magic alone. It interests readers of theatre history as an eighteenth-century taste of the Bard.
20928-three-months-in-the-southern-state:
A diary kept day by day through the Confederate States fills Three Months in the Southern States. Arthur Fremantle, a British officer, toured the South from April to June 1863. His Gettysburg section first ran in Blackwood's Magazine to wide notice.

Fremantle dined with generals, rode with troops, and watched a slave society at war. Lee, Longstreet, and Davis pass through his sharp, foreign eyes. He reached Gettysburg in time to see its vast fight unfold. Few outside views of the Confederacy match his for access, detail, and calm, curious tone at close range.
4139-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-20-jan:
January 1662 to 1663 finds Pepys lying with his wife at his lord's lodgings, talking with great pleasure till ten o'clock. Rising, he walks at Whitehall among the courtiers, and finds he can do so with growing confidence.

The volume follows a Navy man becoming a court man, at ease in rooms where favor is won by talk and presence. Pepys notes dress, company, and his own rising nerve with the same frank care. Readers see the Restoration court from inside, through a clerk learning to belong there. His frank notes keep the grandeur human.
4140-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-21-mar:
March 1662 to 1663, a Lord's day, walks Pepys to Whitehall Chapel, where Lewes preaches. Once famed as a great wit, Lewes now reads every word of his sermon. He reads so brokenly and so low that nobody far off can hear him.

The volume mixes chapel, office, and home, with Pepys judging sermons as sharply as ships. His ear for preaching, music, and talk gives these spring entries their life. Readers who enjoy Pepys the critic will find sermons, suppers, and Navy business in equal measure. Chapel, office, and home trade places through the spring.
4141-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-22-may:
May 1663 opens at home, with Pepys's father beside him and Will Stankes private in his wife's closet above, settling matters of the Brampton estate. After all debts are paid, Pepys reckons some fifty pounds a year clear toward his father's maintenance.

The volume pairs estate business with office days, dinners, and family talk, as a son provides for a father while building his own fortune. Pepys's care for sums runs through every entry, from land income to dinner bills. Readers get a warm, practical view of a rising man settling his family's affairs.
4142-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-23-jul:
July 1663 opens in hard rain, fair yesterday having raised hopes of fair weather wanted these three months. The rain wakes Creed, who lay with Pepys last night, and the two fall to discourse of Creed's accounts, now under question.

Wet summer, accounts, and talk fill the volume, with Pepys turning even a rainy morning into business. The diary's gift for making small days interesting shows at full strength here. Readers get high summer London in rain and reckoning, with friendship carrying the talk. Rain on the roof and talk of accounts make a complete Pepys morning.
4143-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-24-sep:
September 1663 sends Pepys betimes to his office, then by coach with Sir John Minnes to Whitehall. Sir William Batten meets them there, and they wait by the Council Chamber till the lords call them in.

The council wants an account of a riot among seamen some days before, a Navy matter with real heat behind it. Pepys records the waiting, the summons, and the hearing in his usual crisp style. The volume shows the Navy Office answering to power, with sailors' anger pressing on clerks and lords alike. Pepys never hides his own part in the hearing.
4144-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-25-nov:
November 1663, a Lord's day, brings Pepys's brother's man with a new black baize waistcoat faced with silk, which Pepys puts on that day, laying by half-shirts for winter. The man also brings a new gown of purple shag, trimmed with gold and very handsome.

Clothes, gifts, and winter dressing fill these entries, beside office and church. Pepys loves a new gown as he loves a balanced account, and notes both with pride. Readers who enjoy the diary's material world will find this volume rich in cloth, color, and cold-weather cheer.
agassiz-methods-of-study-natural-history:
Louis Agassiz published Methods of Study in Natural History in 1863, a book of popular lectures given in Boston. Agassiz taught teachers and general readers how to observe nature at first hand. The lectures drew on his years at Harvard's museum and his field trips.

Agassiz urged students to look at one fish until they truly saw it, a lesson his students retold for decades. He explained grouping, fossils, and the spread of animal life in plain terms. The book spread his influence far beyond his classroom. It also shows the warm, commanding teacher behind the famous name. Natural history was then America's most popular science.
arxiv-2509-00263:
Jared D. Fisher, working alone, proposes probit monotone BART in 2025, an extension of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees for binary outcomes. BART models a response as a sum of many small decision trees, with a Bayesian prior that keeps each tree weak. Monotone BART sharpens estimates when the true response is known to move in one direction as an input grows.

The probit form adapts that monotone frame to binary outcomes, where the response is a yes-or-no event. A probit link maps a hidden score to an event chance through the standard normal curve. The method aims for precise conditional mean estimates under a monotonicity constraint. Binary outcomes with a known direction arise in medicine, credit, and policy studies alike.
arxiv-2509-00663:
Binghang Lu, with two co-authors, proposes Morephy-Net for hard equation problems. The target equations describe change across space and time, with parameters that can be set per case. Data for training may be noisy or sparse. Physics-informed networks often fail to balance data loss and physics loss well. They can also lack sound estimates of their own uncertainty.

Morephy-Net treats data terms and physics terms as two separate goals. It searches the set of best trade-offs between those goals. A sampling-based training method improves exploration and stability during learning. Bayesian sampling then yields estimates of uncertainty in the outputs. Tests cover the Burgers equation and a time-fractional diffusion-wave equation. Results beat standard operator-learning baselines on accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2509-00763:
Karol Wawrzak, with three co-authors, Yiqing Li, Bernd R Noack, and Artur Tyliszczak, investigates pseudo-rotating spiral jets found through active flow control, a method that manipulates jets with added actuation. Machine learning optimization recently revealed this pattern, where separate branches leave the main jet along curved paths that seem to rotate around its axis.

Wawrzak and his co-authors show spiral jets belong to a family of multi-armed jets appearing only at specific control settings. The apparent rotation is an illusion: viewers connect neighboring moving vortices into continuous patterns. Through theory and three-dimensional simulations, they build a simple kinematic model that captures the vortical paths, reproduces the apparent jet shape, and identifies the true pattern.
arxiv-2509-00963:
Deepika Dash leads a team of five authors on disability inclusivity in large language models. Such models are used more and more for accessibility guidance. Yet many disability groups remain underserved by their advice. The team presents a taxonomy-aligned benchmark of accessibility questions. The questions are human-validated and general-purpose in scope.

Models are evaluated along three dimensions. They are breadth within answers, balance across nine disability categories, and depth of support. Seventeen proprietary and open-weight models are tested. Vision, hearing, and mobility are addressed often. Speech, genetic and developmental, sensory-cognitive, and mental health lag behind. Depth is also concentrated in a few categories. The findings highlight levers like taxonomy-aware prompting and training.
arxiv-2509-01263:
A price cut draws buyers, but it also changes what their choices tell later buyers about quality. Georgy Lukyanov and Arina Azova study that tension in a duopoly, two rival sellers facing shared doubt about quality. Buyers have a default seller and may pay to reach the rival and gain a private signal.

In a worked pricing case, a cut raises current revenue and pays over two buyer arrivals, but loses over three for patient enough firms. When quality is redrawn for each buyer, the same cut stays profitable. The pair then build steady equilibria on finite price menus where one informative purchase can lead to uninformative ones and uneven prices. Cheap comparison by a few buyers reshapes how fast beliefs move, tying information flow to market outcomes.
arxiv-2509-01663:
Tomoya Suzuguchi and Tatsuya Matsumoto study brief X-ray flares that repeat on a near steady beat from galaxy centers. These quasi-periodic eruptions, meaning flares that recur at almost regular gaps, seem tied to stars torn apart by giant black holes. One likely cause is a star that crosses a disk of gas left by such a tear. The authors work out what flares should look like soon after the disk forms.

Early disks feed at a very high rate and hold a slim, hot shape. A star crossing one should give flares that last only minutes and run far hotter than flares seen so far. Their small share of each cycle makes them hard to catch. Finding them would teach us how these disks first take shape.
arxiv-2509-01963:
Naval Shah uses a physics informed neural network to predict Formula 1 front wing performance far faster than classic simulation. New rules cut wind tunnel hours and cap team budgets, pushing demand for cheap design tools. Classic fluid simulations take many hours per wing shape. His network trains on simulation data for a dozen shape features while obeying fluid flow equations.

A hybrid loss keeps predictions close to data and to the governing flow laws at once. Fit scores for drag and lift coefficients both land near perfect in his tests. Compute time drops sharply versus full simulation runs. Teams could scan many wing designs quickly within budget and testing limits. Physical adherence guards against wild predictions off the training range.
arxiv-2509-02063:
S Avraham leads six co-authors in showing reentrant superconductivity in granular aluminum tuned by radio frequency power. Superconductivity normally fades as heat or magnetic field rises, but in rare cases it returns. Granular aluminum acts as a natural array of Josephson junctions, links that carry supercurrent across thin barriers. Radio power tunes the coupling energy between those junctions.

At low temperatures, giant Shapiro steps signal phase locking across the whole array like a single junction. Raising radio power can flip the system from coherent superconductivity to an insulating state. At higher temperatures, charge screening lowers charging energy and superconductivity reappears. That revival needs many body correlations beyond any single junction view. The system thus serves as a quantum simulator for competing order physics.
arxiv-2509-02163:
Wenxiao Zhang leads four co-authors in a unified framework that guards language model robots against both attacks and unsafe actions. Language models give robots flexible decision making, but prompt injection attacks can hijack their instructions. Safety in complex physical settings is a parallel concern. Their design combines prompt assembling, state management, and safety validation in one loop.

Experiments measure both task performance and security under adversarial conditions. Performance under injection attacks improves by a solid margin versus baselines. Gains in complex environments under attack are far larger still. Simulation and physical robot demos accompany the open source release. The framework offers actionable guidance for deploying mobile robots with language model control.
arxiv-2509-02363:
Gaurav Negi, Atul Kr. Ojha, Omnia Zayed, and Paul Buitelaar wrote a 2025 natural language processing paper on building a knowledge base of opinions that keeps track of time. Fine-grained opinion records, tied to dates, can support forecasting and trend studies.

Their method uses large language models as automatic annotators, guided by fixed data models drawn from sentiment research. Three schemas define how opinions get stored, so no hand-crafted prompts are needed. Human-labelled samples check the pipeline's quality. Two separate models produced the final labels, and agreement was scored label by label, much like human annotation studies. The finished base stores time-aligned opinions ready for search tools, temporal questions, and timeline summaries.
arxiv-2509-02463:
Thomas Burton, Sean Symon, and Davide Lasagna wrote a 2025 fluid mechanics paper. It hunts for invariant solutions in flows bounded by walls. These are steady or repeating flow states. Such states help organize how turbulence behaves. Getting them near walls is hard.

Their method puts the Navier-Stokes equations, the basic rules of fluid motion, into variational form. The method shrinks the error of the equations over a set time window. A Galerkin projection makes it work at walls. The modes used obey the no-slip wall rule and come from resolvent analysis. On rotating plane Couette flow, the method found exact steady and periodic states. The states matched direct simulations well. Speed of convergence tied to how stable each state is.
arxiv-2509-02763:
Shengjie Yu and fourteen co-authors wrote a 2025 nanophysics paper. It studies quantum transport in aligned carbon nanotube fibres. The fibres are made by solution spinning. They conduct extremely well. The team probes how quantum interference shapes that conduction at low heat.

Conductivity rose as samples cooled toward about thirty-six kelvin. Then it eased downward. That signals quantum corrections from localisation, where electrons get trapped by disorder. Magnetic field data showed the positive corrections expected for weak localisation. Models for one, two, and three dimensions were compared. A pure two-dimensional fit had flaws. A hybrid model mixing three- and one-dimensional behaviour matched field and heat data. It used realistic coherence lengths. The mix reflects fibre structure: quasi-one-dimensional bundles woven into a three-dimensional network.
arxiv-2509-02963:
Vladislav Pokidkin wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on discriminants of systems of polynomial equations. A discriminant marks the border where a system's behavior changes, such as where solutions merge or vanish. Classifying the parts of that border for one equation is classical work by Gelfand, Kapranov, and Zelevinsky.

Pokidkin builds combinatorial tools aimed at the harder case of whole systems. His setting uses arrangements of vector subspaces and their abstraction, polymatroids, which generalize the rank ideas behind matroids. He works out how bases, circuits, cycles, and rank functions behave for these objects. He also defines contraction operations and a new structure he calls BK-sets. A planned sequel applies the tools to finish the classification.
arxiv-2509-03663:
Rudi Brits and two co-authors prove a 2025 mathematics result extending the Kowalski-Słodkowski theorem to Hermitian algebras. The original theorem recognises characters, the well-behaved multiplicative functions on an algebra, using only a spectral condition. A Banach algebra is a complete space where members can be added, scaled, and multiplied.

Their setting adds the Hermitian property, a symmetry condition on the algebra's elements. Take any continuous complex-valued function whose product values always land inside the spectrum of the corresponding product. The theorem says that function, or its negative, must be a character of the algebra. The converse also holds, so the spectral test is exact. The proof leans on positive members and square roots, which Hermitian algebras are guaranteed to possess. The result sharpens a classic tool of functional analysis.
arxiv-2509-03763:
Catching magnetar giant flares with AXIS, a planned X-ray imaging satellite, is the focus of a 2025 feasibility study by Michela Negro and eight co-authors. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, and their giant flares rank among the brightest transients nearby. Each flare fires a short gamma-ray spike, then a softer X-ray tail that pulsates. Only three galactic events are firmly known.

Two detection routes are assessed. Serendipitous catches of the prompt spike inside the field of view are possible but unlikely, given the spikes' brevity and hard spectra. Rapid follow-up looks far more promising: with fast repointing, AXIS could record pulsating tails from galaxies out to about twenty megaparsecs. That would give the first extragalactic measurements of a magnetar's periodic modulation. Softer X-ray lines from radioactive element creation in flares prove extremely faint, detectable only at galactic distances.
arxiv-2509-04163:
Hiroki Wadati, writing alone, turns tomato juice into a teaching tool for light absorption in a 2025 physics education paper. The Beer-Lambert law says light fades exponentially, meaning by a fixed fraction per step, as it crosses a colored material. Students test that rule with diluted juice and a halogen lamp instead of costly chemicals. A small spectrometer, an instrument that splits light by color, records how much light survives at each shade.

The juice drank in green-blue light most strongly, matching its red pigment lycopene. Plotted results followed the law's straight-line pattern at weak dilutions, then bent away when the juice grew stronger. Classes get hands-on practice with data, ideal laws, and where those laws break down.
arxiv-2509-04563:
Balpreet Kaur and two co-authors image hydrogen gas in the host galaxy of a fast radio burst in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope in India mapped the 21-centimeter line of atomic hydrogen in galaxy NGC 4141, home of burst FRB 20250316A. Images reveal a companion galaxy nearby, a stray hydrogen cloud, and disturbed gas in both galaxies. The host's southwestern outskirts hold dense hydrogen, and optical spectra show metal-poor gas with rapid star formation there.

Fresh metal-poor gas, delivered by a merger or accretion, likely sparked the southwestern starburst. That burst may have forged the star whose remains produced the radio burst. No hydrogen glows at the burst site itself, suggesting it was ionized or turned molecular.
arxiv-2509-04663:
A quiet-Sun filament eruption created a coronal hole near the centre of the solar disk in June 2014. Stefan J. Hofmeister, lead author with eleven co-authors, reconstruct that event in a 2025 solar physics paper. They use images and magnetograms from two instruments aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory.

The hole formed in three stages: formation, migration, and stabilisation. Emission and temperature fell hours before the eruption, then a large dimming formed. The dimming later migrated to a region of open magnetic field lines, which marked the transition into a coronal hole. The authors link the drift to magnetic interchange reconnection at its boundaries.
arxiv-2509-05063: Lorenzo Barban, lead author with two co-authors, work out the Chow quotient for the complete flag variety in four complex dimensions, in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. They show the quotient is smooth and is a Mori Dream Space, a well-behaved class of varieties whose birational geometry can be described completely. The paper then describes that birational geometry in detail.
arxiv-2509-05663:
A handful of expert labels can fix the weakest point of unsupervised anomaly detection, its threshold, Lucas Correia and three co-authors show in a 2025 machine learning paper. Truly unsupervised detectors for time series exist, but a poorly set threshold cripples them, and many secretly calibrate on labelled data.

Their dissimilarity-based query strategy picks which samples an expert should label, maximising diversity by comparing anomaly scores with a time-warping distance. On small labelling budgets it beat rival query strategies, though rivals handled mislabelled answers more robustly. Every strategy beat the unsupervised threshold even with labelling errors. The choice, they conclude, depends on expert reliability and budget.
arxiv-2509-05763:
A tunable optical cavity on a chip is controlled through its mirrors rather than its length, in a 2025 photonics paper by Ayed Al Sayem and six co-authors. Fabry-Perot cavities trap light between two mirrors, and tuning usually shifts the cavity phase and thus its resonant frequency.

Their device sits on thin-film lithium niobate, a material whose optical properties respond to voltage. The mirrors are Mach-Zehnder interferometers tuned by the electro-optic effect. Full tuning of a low-finesse cavity is achieved with a low half-wave voltage and a mirror only a few millimetres long. Mirror-side tuning offers a compact control route for integrated photonics.
arxiv-2509-05863:
Keeping a speaker's voice while translating their speech into another language is the goal of LatinX, a 2025 text-to-speech model from Luis Felipe Chary and Miguel Arjona Ramirez. The model serves cascaded speech translation, where speech is recognized, translated, then spoken again. Losing the original voice in that chain makes output feel impersonal.

LatinX is a twelve-layer decoder-only transformer trained in three stages: text-to-audio pretraining, fine-tuning for zero-shot voice cloning, and preference alignment scored by word error rate and speaker similarity. Trained on English and Romance languages with emphasis on Portuguese, the aligned model lowered word errors and raised similarity scores over its fine-tuned base. Human listeners rated its speaker match above a strong rival system, even where objective scores disagreed, and the authors discuss faster, better-balanced versions as next steps.
arxiv-2509-05963:
Bloom is the soft glow around bright spots in a game scene. Rafal Karp and two co-authors draw it with a neural network, faster than classic filters can, in a 2025 paper. Traditional bloom stacks multiple blurs and texture samples, often with branching code, and eats a large share of frame time. Their methods, Neural Bloom Lighting and a fast variant, predict the brightness mask directly.

Both networks were tested across varied three-dimensional scenes for mask accuracy and inference speed. The fast variant ran about twenty-eight percent quicker than a standard state-of-the-art implementation, and the quality-focused one about twelve percent quicker, while keeping high-quality glow. The authors frame the savings as headroom for smoother, more realistic real-time rendering.
arxiv-2509-06263:
A light beam bouncing off a surface shifts sideways by a whisker, and Yahong Chen and Sergey A. Ponomarenko tie those shifts to coherence in a 2025 paper. The in-plane Goos-Hänchen and out-of-plane Imbert-Fedorov shifts displace reflected and refracted beams from geometric predictions. The authors discover a universal link between the shifts and the phase-space nonseparability of the incoming wave packet, at any degree of partial coherence.

Two new effects follow. A coherence Goos-Hänchen effect can strongly enhance the spatial shift. A coherence Hall effect can cancel or hugely amplify the other shift for nearly incoherent beams. The results span optical, X-ray, neutron, and matter waves.
arxiv-2509-06563:
Curvature bounds fail in a twisted geometric space, according to Samuël Borza and two co-authors in a 2025 geometry paper. Their space is the sub-Lorentzian Heisenberg group, a model where motion is restricted and time-like directions matter. Such synthetic curvature conditions are meant to capture, in rough form, how curved a space is.

Using a direct variational method, the authors give a new proof describing the longest paths in the space: they lift from hyperbolas tied to an area problem in the Minkowski plane. They show the space's Lorentzian Hausdorff dimension is four, with the natural measure matching that dimension. A ball-box style estimate compares causal diamonds, the regions reachable between two events, with stretched boxes. Finally, they prove the space satisfies neither of two standard timelike curvature conditions for any parameter values, unlike its better-behaved Riemannian cousin.
arxiv-2509-06863:
Value functions with adjustable internal computation are trained by flow matching in a 2025 reinforcement learning paper by Bhavya Agrawalla and three co-authors. Modern machine learning gets dense supervision at intermediate steps, as in next-token training or diffusion denoising. Value learning in reinforcement learning, by contrast, usually represents values in one monolithic block.

Their approach, floq, parameterizes the Q-function through a velocity field borrowed from flow-matching generative models. A temporal-difference objective trains that field, bootstrapping from a target field integrated over several steps. Turning the number of integration steps up or down scales the value function's capacity in a controlled way. Across hard offline reinforcement learning benchmarks and online fine-tuning tasks, performance improved by nearly twofold, and capacity scaled far better than with standard architectures.
arxiv-2509-06963:
Simulations built from small-scale interacting elements are given a chance-based structure by Jeffrey D. Picka in a solo 2025 statistics paper. Models of complex phenomena, from granular flow to convection patterns, often run in a fixed way: one set of starting conditions, one simulation. Real outcomes vary, though, and matching that spread needs random parts.

Random trajectory models add those parts, producing models that can be fitted to data and checked. Models enter the framework as computer code whose coefficients can be tuned, not as equations on paper. It states a simple basic condition for such code models to be easy to fit and verify, then argues the condition can almost never be checked. Uncheckable models are black boxes: they may mimic patterns in a few observed statistics but give weak evidence for any explanation. Useful, checked models may take many person-years of extra work.
arxiv-2509-07063:
Stellar flares reshaping the air of a brown dwarf companion are simulated by Aidan Gibbs and one co-author in a 2025 planetary science paper. Brown dwarfs on short orbits around active M dwarfs offer a chance to watch flare-driven chemistry in a planet-like atmosphere. The authors adapted two open-source codes, one for chemical kinetics and one for radiative transfer, to model the response.

Single strong superflares change the amounts of many chemical species by orders of magnitude, including major opacity sources like methane and carbon dioxide. Brown dwarf air is hot and dense, though, so chemistry resets fast and the changes last less than a day. High-resolution emission spectroscopy could plausibly catch them. The clearest short-term signs in hot, high-gravity, cloudless cases are water split by light and extra carbon dioxide, producing small spectral changes in the hours after a flare.
arxiv-2509-07363:
Qifei Wang and 5 co-authors combine semantic communication with multiple access for sending images in a 2025 paper. Semantic communication sends meaning rather than raw bits, which can save bandwidth, a key promise for 6G networks. Non-orthogonal multiple access, or NOMA, lets several users share the same channel at once, but interference makes image recovery harder.

Their system, KDD-SemNOMA, uses a ConvNeXt-based coding design that adapts to noise and channel state. A teacher model trained on clean, interference-free signals guides a student model through a two-stage distillation, improving recovery at no extra cost when running. A diffusion model, a generative method that refines images step by step, then polishes the output.
arxiv-2509-07563:
Aaron Daniel's 2025 paper, with 3 co-authors, rebuilds input-output theory on a path integral foundation. Input-output theory describes quantum systems probed by light and is a standard tool across quantum optics, circuit QED, and cavity QED. The new approach uses the Schwinger-Keldysh path integral formalism, a framework from non-equilibrium quantum field theory, which gives direct access to the full statistics of the output field.

Coherence functions of first and second order come out naturally, and the rich diagram toolbox of field theory becomes available. Nonlinear systems, awkward in older treatments, get a uniform perturbative route. As a showcase, the authors compute output statistics for a Kerr nonlinear oscillator at finite temperature using diagram summation. They find a drop in reflection caused not by photon leakage but by squeezing of the output light, a distinctly quantum signature.
arxiv-2509-07663:
Valerio Proietti's 2025 paper, joined by 1 co-author, builds a Chern character map for ample groupoids whose stabilizers have no torsion. The Chern character is a bridge between K-theory and homology. K-theory classifies vector-bundle-like objects. Homology counts holes and cycles. The domain here is the Baum-Connes assembly map. That map is a central object linking geometry to operator algebras.

The authors assume the rational Baum-Connes conjecture. Under it, the construction implies a match between two groups. The operator K-groups of the groupoid C*-algebra match the periodicized groupoid homology over the rationals. That confirms a variation of Matui's HK conjecture. The construction leans on the recent infinity-categorical viewpoint on bivariant K-theory. Applications reach the homology of hyperbolic dynamical systems. They also reach topological full groups and the Elliott invariant used to classify C*-algebras.
arxiv-2509-07763:
Mikel Robredo and 4 co-authors use large language models in 2025 to study why developers refactor code. Refactoring restructures code with no change in its behavior. It improves quality, at real cost in time and effort. Knowing the motivations behind it could encourage wider practice. It could also show which metrics capture those motivations. The test bed is open-source projects.

The large-scale study mines version control data. It asks language models to identify the motivation behind each refactoring. Results are compared with human judgment and with motivations reported in past literature. The models matched human judgment in 80 percent of cases. They aligned with literature categories in only 47 percent. They enriched 22 percent with more detailed rationale, often about readability and structural clarity. Most motivations proved pragmatic, centered on simpler, easier-to-keep code. Metric correlations with motivation categories stayed weak.
arxiv-2509-07863:
Hands-free control inside virtual reality is tested in a 2025 paper by Kyle Coutray and 3 co-authors. Their system, NeuroGaze, combines brain signals measured by electroencephalography with eye tracking. Twenty volunteers used it to pick cubes arranged in a full circle around them, inside an immersive headset scene.

Performance was compared against ordinary VR controllers and against gaze plus a pinch gesture. Brain-computer interfaces were once confined to clinics and labs, but cheaper consumer devices now invite everyday uses. People with limited hand movement could gain the most from control that needs neither hands nor controllers. The study measures speed and accuracy across the three methods, giving designers evidence about where thought-and-glance control already works well.
arxiv-2509-08963:
Alexander Binder and 2 co-authors analyze value bounds and convergence for averages of LRP attributions in a 2025 paper. LRP, layer-wise relevance propagation, explains a neural network prediction by assigning relevance scores. Users often average those scores over many augmented samples.

Attributions are written as products of modified gradient matrices, linking them to Jacobi matrices from calculus. Bounds on singular values and on each attribution value follow. Those bounds yield constants that govern how fast sample averages converge to expected values. For one LRP variant, constants do not depend on weight norms, unlike gradient methods. The results guide use of augmentation and smoothing explainers.
arxiv-2509-09263:
Chao Yuan and 3 co-authors present DATE for long video understanding in multimodal models in a 2025 paper. Long videos challenge models on precise time reasoning and event localization. Uniform frame sampling and implicit position codes lose critical information over long ranges.

A timestamp injection mechanism interleaves frame embeddings with textual timestamp tokens, building a continuous time reference. Sampling is reframed as a vision language retrieval task, with query enrichment and a greedy strategy balancing relevance and coverage. Results reach state of the art among large models on hour long benchmarks. Even the smaller model exceeds many far larger models on some tests.
arxiv-2509-09363:
Arnab Goswami and 1 co-author study endomorphisms of the cohomology algebra of the even orthogonal Grassmannian in a 2025 paper. An endomorphism is a map from an algebra to itself preserving its structure. The Grassmannian parametrizes planes in a space with an orthogonal symmetry.

If an endomorphism sends all Chern classes of the canonical bundle to zero, it must itself be zero. The same holds if it sends all Pontryagin classes of a related real bundle to zero. A second result concerns endomorphisms vanishing on degree two cohomology that admit a splitting. In that case the splitting must equal zero. The proofs use the special class structure of this space.
arxiv-2509-09463:
Jana Jovcheva and 2 co-authors study when the bond sizes of a tree tensor network are as small as they can be in a 2025 mathematics paper. A tuple counts as minimal when some tensor fits the network at those sizes but fits no version of the same tree with any size strictly lowered. Knowing the boundary helps users avoid wasted capacity.

The authors give conditions that are both necessary and sufficient for minimality, widening an older characterisation tied to multilinear rank. They also show the tensors that fail minimality form a closed algebraic set. Minimality is therefore the typical case, not a rare accident, within such a network.
arxiv-2509-09663:
Zhiyu Fan and 1 co-author challenge a popular route toward quantum computing in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Many designs hope to store information in Majorana zero modes inside superconductors and swap, or braid, those modes to compute. The plan rests on such modes being their own antiparticles. Fan and his co-author argue that picture breaks once particle number is properly conserved.

Their proof works from a Hamiltonian that conserves particle number, and shows one-body quasiparticles carry quantised charge and inertia matching the bare particles. On that basis they argue Bogoliubov zero modes cannot serve as self-antiparticles fit for braiding. The authors call for the Majorana programme to be reconsidered and for a theory of superconductivity that never fictitiously breaks the global symmetry.
arxiv-2509-09863:
Sarvan Gill and 1 co-author teach reinforcement learning agents to carry their own stability certificate in a 2025 control paper. Ordinary reinforcement learning offers no promise that a learned policy will keep a system steady. Newer methods learn a Lyapunov function beside the policy as proof of steadiness, but learning it only from the agent's own fresh behaviour wastes samples, since old data cannot be reused.

Their off-policy version learns that certificate from stored experience instead, then plugs into two popular algorithms, Soft Actor Critic and Proximal Policy Optimization. Simulations on an inverted pendulum and a quadrotor show both hosts performing better with the addition. Data hunger drops while the stability guarantee, the whole point of the exercise, stays in place.
arxiv-2509-10163:
Francisco Javier Esono Nkulu Andong and 1 co-author design a federated learning system for managing resources at the edge of future 6G networks in a 2025 telecommunications paper. Ultra-dense edge deployments must juggle task placement, spectrum, and processor energy for moving devices, without pooling private data centrally. Their framework lets each device run its own reinforcement learning agent while a federation quietly merges what the agents learn.

Each agent, a deep recurrent network, watches local queues, energy, processor load, and mobility before choosing. Model updates travel under an elliptic curve key exchange so semi-honest onlookers learn nothing raw. The shared reward balances delay, energy, spectrum use, fairness, and reliability across 6G service classes, and simulations beat centralised and hand-built rivals on success and efficiency.
arxiv-2509-10363:
Benjamin David Shaffer and four co-authors present a machine learning system for finding pollution sources and steering sensors toward them in this 2025 paper. Moving agents must plan paths and absorb streaming measurements in real time, guided by a digital twin of water flow coupled with transport of the substance being tracked.

Their twin is built from conditional neural Whitney forms, which marry the conservation guarantees of finite element methods with transformer-style learning. It keeps the discrete conservation laws intact while adapting to live sensor data, and it produces a reduced model stable enough to trust. The team alternates twin updates with a coverage algorithm that repositions sensors, proving conditions under which coverage keeps improving. Against transformers that ignore physics, their version locates sources more accurately in complex shapes.
arxiv-2509-10663:
When a document contradicts what a language model already believes, which side wins? Zineddine Tighidet and five co-authors investigate a special set of neurons that seem to referee that fight in this 2025 interpretability paper. These entropy neurons strongly affect how spread out the model's predictions are, while barely changing which tokens rank highest.

Across a range of large language models, the authors find entropy neurons suppress the copying of context. Remove them, and generation changes significantly, with the model leaning harder on the text in front of it over its stored knowledge. The result gives a concrete mechanism behind a familiar inconsistency: models sometimes parrot a misleading prompt and sometimes ignore it. Knowing which neurons hold the balance helps explain, and perhaps eventually steer, that behavior.
arxiv-2509-10763:
Md Tanvir Emrose and 3 co-authors design pixels that can switch their structural color in this 2025 paper. Structural color comes from a material's layered structure rather than from dyes. Their stacks use phase-change materials, which flip between states and hold each state without power. One pixel built this way can show several distinct colors in turn.

The team searched for layer materials and thicknesses that make the colors in a set as different from each other as possible, using an optimization algorithm paired with an electrical impedance method. Designs for two-color and four-color pixels both achieved strong contrast. Because the layers need no fine lithography, the approach suits large surfaces and slow-changing displays.
arxiv-2509-11363:
Noah Schlossberger and 3 co-authors receive ordinary radio broadcasts with atoms in this 2025 paper. Rydberg atoms, atoms excited to very large states, react strongly to electric fields, which makes them promising radio sensors. Earlier work fed them signals crafted in a laboratory. This team instead picked up a consumer handheld two-way radio, the kind anyone can buy, transmitting in the UHF band.

The radio's frequency-modulated audio shifted the atoms' energy levels, and the team recovered the sound with an offset oscillator and lock-in detection. They measured the audio response and working range, received every consumer channel at once, and pulled apart two neighboring channels with strong isolation. The result moves atomic receivers toward everyday signals.
arxiv-2509-11663:
Haisheng Wang, Dong Liu, and Weiming Zhi formalize a harder version of embodied question answering in a 2025 paper. In the classic setup, an agent explores a 3D setting to answer one question. Real deployments instead face many questions that arrive at random times with varied urgency.

Their scheme, ConEQsA, schedules and answers questions at once with urgency in mind. Shared group memory cuts repeated exploration across questions, and a priority-planning method orders the work on the fly. The authors also built a benchmark of indoor scenes, each with several questions, follow-ups that arrive later, and human-marked urgency labels. Two new metrics gauge direct answering and urgency-weighted delay. Tests showed ConEQsA beating strong step-by-step baselines throughout, backing concurrent, urgency-aware scheduling.
arxiv-2509-12263:
Big multimodal models can recite physics laws they saw in training, but can they learn a new law from a few examples on the spot? Gautam Sreekumar and one co-author test exactly that in 2025 with InPhyRe, a benchmark of synthetic collision videos paired with questions about what happens next.

More than thirteen open and commercial models were examined. The verdict is weak across the board: models fumble even familiar laws, reason poorly when the governing law was never in training, and often lean on language cues while ignoring the video. The authors frame the gap as a trust problem for safety-critical uses.
arxiv-2509-12663:
Turbulence in a pipe at modest speed organizes into puffs, patches of disorder that drift inside smooth flow and eventually calm back down. Basheer A. Khan and three co-authors watch that relaminarization in fine-grained direct simulations in 2025 at three Reynolds numbers just below two thousand.

The energy of the streamwise fluctuations decays exponentially, at a rate that barely depends on the Reynolds number. At the puff's trailing edge, streamline patterns form saddle-node pairs that drift together, collide, and vanish as calm returns. The shrinking distance between each pair follows a square-root law in time, the signature of a saddle-node bifurcation.
arxiv-2509-12763:
Yican Zhao, Ce Wang and three co-authors present DyGLNet in 2025, a new network for marking organs and lesions in medical scans. Medical scans are hard to split into regions because lesions vary in size, edges are faint, and heavy models run slowly.

DyGLNet joins wide context and fine detail in one block that mixes self-focus with filters at several scales. A second part rebuilds the feature maps with learned shifts so edges stay sharp. Tests on seven public data sets beat older methods, with the best gains on edges and small objects, while using less compute. That mix suits fast, careful help in clinics.
arxiv-2509-13063:
Simone Costa, Marco Dalai and two co-authors test in 2025 what monadic second-order logic can state about hash codes. Hash codes ask that any k rows split at some column. Size and test tasks matter for computing.

The k-hash link on k rows proves beyond that logic. That marks a clear limit for solver specs in the base tongue. Extensions that add equal-size links can state the trait. The result tells tool builders when to step up logic strength. It also maps a gap between use needs and base power.
arxiv-2509-13163:
The Euclid Collaboration tests in 2025 how well its Wide Survey will find faint dwarf galaxies near home. Dwarfs probe cosmos growth and mass build. Deep surveys now reach their faint, spread glow, but pipelines can lose them.

Fake dwarfs were planted in a real survey field and run through the merge pipeline. Found shares were high for brighter dwarfs and near half for the faintest band. Background clash cuts true shares further. Flux loss hits large dwarfs due to local sky cuts. A sky-restored image recovers sound measures below arcminute size. That product suits local dwarf study.
arxiv-2509-13363:
Jianlong Lu studies in 2025 basis-free structures in the canonical seesaw for light neutrino masses, with three heavy sterile partners. Seesaw matrices link light masses to heavy singlets with diagonal masses. Many right moves leave light masses fixed.

Those moves form a group built from the heavy masses and complex orthogonal maps. Oscillation data fix mixing and squared splits, but not the move class. Invariants split into class-blind and class-aware sets. Non-unitarity traces and CP-odd traces mark the aware set, with use for leptogenesis. Benchmarks at high and GeV scales show fingerprints and scaling. Hidden freedom becomes measurable.
arxiv-2509-13463:
Joseph Paat, Zach Walsh, and Luze Xu settle a combinatorics question in a 2025 paper about modular matrices, integer matrices whose square sub-blocks all have small determinants. For a matrix that is 3-modular, meaning every such determinant is at most three, they ask how many pairwise non-parallel columns it can have.

Exact answers were known only for tiny cases. The three authors prove that, once the rank is large enough, the maximum column count follows a clean formula in the rank, settling a conjecture by Lee, Paat, Stallknecht, and Xu. They also exhibit at least three different matrices reaching the bound, and show the number of such extreme examples grows fast for larger determinant limits.
arxiv-2509-13863:
Chu Chen and five co-authors present LamiGauss in a 2025 imaging paper, a reconstruction method for X-ray computed laminography. Laminography inspects flat objects such as microchips and battery materials that ordinary tomography cannot handle, but rebuilding a volume from very few viewing angles is an ill-posed puzzle.

LamiGauss renders the volume as a cloud of radiative Gaussians, adapting Gaussian splatting from computer graphics, with a dedicated transform that carries the laminography tilt angle from detector to world coordinates. Its initialization filters out the artifacts typical of quick preliminary reconstructions, so model capacity is spent on the real object instead of ghosts. Using only a tiny fraction of the usual views, it beat an iterative method that had been given the full dataset.
arxiv-2509-13963:
Qinxiu Sun and Min Wu introduce anti-pre-Poisson bialgebras in a 2025 algebra paper. The new structure mixes two operations, with fit rules loosened by sign changes. Bialgebras carry an algebra and a coalgebra that must fit together. Sorting the fitting patterns is a standard way to generate Yang-Baxter type equations and their solutions.

The authors show their new structures correspond exactly to two other objects. One is quadratic anti-pre-Poisson algebras. The other is matched pairs of Poisson algebras: three languages for one object. Coboundary cases lead to an anti-pre-Poisson Yang-Baxter equation. Its skew-symmetric solutions build them directly. Relaxing skew-symmetry forces two wider notions, quasi-triangular and factorizable bialgebras. Such solutions turn out to be relative Rota-Baxter operators in disguise. The match holds on the quadratic side too.
arxiv-2509-14363:
Sean Bryan and seventeen co-authors report detector work in 2025 for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a planned NASA mission. The observatory aims to image and study twenty five or more Earth like planets directly. Its coronagraph must count single photons with very low false counts.

Kinetic inductance detectors, called KIDs, are the team choice for large energy resolving arrays. How many planets the mission finds depends sharply on detector dark counts. The authors describe readout electronics built to run many KIDs at low power and high count. Status and goals for the electronics are set out in detail. The same readout path also serves future far infrared missions with large detector arrays.
arxiv-2509-14563:
Shiyuan Luo and seven co-authors put forward a retrieval frame in 2025 for field and nature modelling where labelled data are costly and sparse. Ecosystems vary by place and season, so a model trained in one spot often fails in odd or data poor spots. Borrowing apt past records could fill the gaps.

Their self taught frame learns how alike nature scenes are, at more than one level of closeness. Those scores drive retrieval of helpful records from other places or times for a target scene. Adaptive training that shifts with augmentation suits scenes that vary a lot. The aim is to reuse the record of past watches with care, rather than demand new field trips for each lake, forest or basin a model must cover.
arxiv-2509-14663:
Gaurav Bhandari and four co-authors derive shared geodesic equations in 2025 for paths in curved spacetime with three added effects. Geodesics are the free fall paths of masses. Safe keeping forces, drag like loss and quantum gravity tinged minimal length fixes are most often treated apart.

Outside vector fields add the safe keeping forces. An exponential rescaling of the particle Lagrangian, the action based maths of motion, adds the loss. A generalised uncertainty rule warps the Hamiltonian brackets for minimal length effects. Free fall paths stay the same at leading order, the authors show. With outside fields in play, speed linked fixes appear and may break the equivalence rule by a small amount. One shared frame lets theorists weigh rival effects side by side.
arxiv-2509-14763:
Stephen Jonathan Chapman studies what happens at high orders in perturbation theory in a solo 2025 applied mathematics paper. Perturbation methods expand an eigenvalue in powers of a small parameter. For many problems that series eventually diverges, and the pattern of divergence itself carries useful information about the problem.

Chapman develops a new technique for pinning down the precise nature of that divergence. The method is shown on four examples drawn from different areas. They include the anharmonic oscillator from quantum mechanics. They also include a simplified model of Rossby waves trapped near the equator. Two further models come from quasinormal modes of charged black holes with a cosmological constant. The examples show the technique applies well beyond a single field.
arxiv-2509-14863:
Gang Wu and Zhengwei Wang study how graph Transformers should combine global attention with local graph structure, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Graph Transformers mix graph neural networks, which pass messages between neighboring nodes, with attention, which links distant nodes. Common designs run both in parallel or put the graph network first, and local detail can get diluted by attention.

Their model, G2LFormer, reverses the order: shallow layers use attention to gather global context, and deeper layers use graph networks to refine local structure. A cross-layer fusion strategy carries useful global information into the local layers so it is not lost. The empirical study compares attention schemes across graph learning tasks. The results support global-to-local ordering as a way to keep neighborhood detail intact.
arxiv-2509-15063:
P. Z. Zhao and Lei Qiao protect three-level quantum systems from noise with dynamical decoupling in a 2025 quantum control paper. Three-level systems, or qutrits, are promising building blocks beside ordinary two-level qubits. They still suffer decoherence from their environment and crosstalk from neighboring qutrits, which corrupts stored information.

The authors construct a pulse sequence that is physically feasible for qutrits. The sequence attacks two error channels at once. One is phase drift between the ground and excited states. The other is population relaxation among the levels. Combined with Hamiltonian engineering, the sequence extends to protecting actual qutrit gates. It filters environmental noise so gate fidelity rises. Cleaner qutrit gates would widen the design space for quantum processors that use three levels per unit instead of two.
arxiv-2509-15163:
Saeed Tafazolian and Jaa Top construct error-correcting codes that can repair erased symbols locally, in a 2025 coding theory paper. A locally recoverable code lets a lost symbol be rebuilt from a small set of others instead of the whole file. Codes with several disjoint recovery sets per symbol offer backup options when some helpers are also missing, a property called availability.

Their construction draws on algebraic curves with many rational points, especially maximal curves, and on maps between smooth projective curves. By widening the family of curves beyond earlier work, they obtain better parameters and broader applicability. The paper also corrects inaccuracies in the existing literature on such constructions. The resulting codes combine strong local repair with large availability, suiting distributed storage systems.
arxiv-2509-15363:
Debasish Dutta and four co-authors survey deep learning methods for enhancing microscopy images in a 2025 review paper. Microscopy reveals cells and materials at scales the eye cannot reach, but raw images suffer noise, blur, and limited resolution. Deep learning has rapidly become the standard toolkit for cleaning them up.

The survey organizes the field around three core tasks: super-resolution, reconstruction, and denoising. Each domain is traced through its evolution, current trends, and practical uses, with attention to where the methods genuinely help working microscopists. Open challenges include scarce ground truth, models that hallucinate fine structure, and uneven validation across imaging modalities. Future directions close the snapshot, charting how learned enhancement might be made trustworthy enough for quantitative biology and materials measurement.
arxiv-2509-15463:
Dangka Shylla leads a team of ten that tests two ways to sense radio fields with atoms. Certain atoms, called Rydberg atoms, react strongly to electric fields. One way to read them is with light passing through a cesium vapor cell. Another way collects the charge freed when the atoms are ionized. The team compare both ways side by side in the same cell.

With a known radio field applied, the light based readout proves far more sensitive than the charge based one. Heat noise limits the charge method, and the team trace it to a thin cesium film on the cell walls. Removing or controlling that film could sharpen the charge method a lot. The work guides a new kind of radio sensor.
arxiv-2509-15863:
Malika Belrhazi and Tom Mestdag study when a constrained machine’s paths can be read as geodesics. Nonholonomic systems move under limits on their velocity, like a rolling wheel that cannot slide sideways. Their paths are not usually the shortest paths of any metric. A projective extension reparametrizes the paths so they can be seen as part of a metric’s geodesics.

The pair derive conditions that are both needed and enough for such extensions, when the energy is kept up to a conformal stretch. For systems with a symmetry group, they clarify how extensions relate to three near ideas: a simplicity trait, invariant measures, and Hamiltonization. Fresh examples mark the gaps between these notions.
arxiv-2509-15963:
Michail Kavousanakis leads a team that solves moving pattern equations by first removing their symmetries. Many nonlinear wave equations host self similar or traveling wave answers. If the drift from symmetry is factored out with a time varying change of frame, the answer stands still or moves slowly. Speeds and scaling rates then come out as part of the solution.

The change of frame adds algebraic constraints, giving stiff equation systems of a hard class. The team solve those systems with physics informed neural networks, which fold all terms into one loss. Both the pinned answer and the symmetry traits are inferred at once. The frame covers two kinds of self similarity.
arxiv-2509-16163:
Vision-language models can be fooled by tiny image tweaks that humans would never notice, and most fixes demand costly retraining. Het Patel and four co-authors offer a light defense that works on any trained model as-is. Their method splits the model's image features into compact parts and rebuilds them, which washes out attack noise while keeping the meaning.

Tests with a leading model on two photo sets show clear gains in accuracy under attack. A low-rank form of the split worked best, within a narrow range of settings. The defense is cheap to add and needs no change to the model's design.
arxiv-2509-16263:
A quantum method that lets wave amplitudes turn negative may dodge the stalls that trap standard quantum annealing. Vicky Choi analyzes such a method for the maximum independent set problem, a classic hard task. Under stated assumptions backed by math and numeric checks, the method is argued to run in polynomial time and beat both standard annealing and classic methods on a built family of cases.

The gain comes in two stages: smooth steering into the right region, then interference along a sign-flipped path. Shrunken models of the process could let today's quantum machines test the claimed edge. The anti-crossing test replaces the usual gap measure.
arxiv-2509-16563:
Joanna K. Kalaga and Jan Perina study linked light and matter states in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Their system holds three modes that share a small state space. Some of its states show true three-way entanglement, where all parts are linked at once. The pair ask how that linking relates to squeezing, a cut in quantum noise.

They compare two-mode and three-mode forms of both effects. Measures of entanglement are set beside measures of noise cut. The study picks out which linked states also show squeezing. It also maps how the two effects rise and fall together. Such links could guide work on quantum sensors and secure links.
arxiv-2509-17063:
Shuang Liang and co-authors dissect design choices in time-series forecasting in a 2025 paper. Deep models now lead at predicting multivariate series, from sales to sensors. Most studies judge a whole model at once, which hides which choices matter. Their testbed, TSGym, varies parts systematically so each choice can be credited or blamed.

Extensive tests show the gym beats top forecasting and automated machine learning methods. All code is shared in public. A shared gym for design choices could end wasteful folklore in forecasting, where teams copy full recipes without knowing which ingredients earn their keep. New models can be probed piece by piece.
arxiv-2509-17163:
Francesco Giacosa and six co-authors report a 2025 arXiv study of how unstable matter decays at very late times. Quantum theory says decay should stray from the classic exponential curve both very early and very late. Hard proof of the late-time effect has been scarce, so the team looked for it in glowing chemical compounds.

They found a slow power-law tail after about ten lifetimes in two fluorescent dyes. Two detectors, each watching a distinct color band, confirmed the tail but measured distinct strengths for it. The authors also prove a broad result: in decay with several channels, the lifetime is the same for all channels. The size of the late-time straying, by contrast, depends on the channel, which fits their data.
arxiv-2509-17263:
Colman McGuan and six co-authors wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on training cybersecurity staff who also grasp the law. Small and mid-size firms must guard their systems, yet the national NICE framework that maps the needed skills is hard to put into practice. The team set out to turn that framework into lessons a small firm can use.

First they list the attack routes small firms face most often. Then they map the tasks, knowledge, skills, and abilities in the NICE framework onto those attacks, in both technical and non-technical terms. On that base they build a scenario-based curriculum that drops learners into lifelike incidents. The course blends hands-on drills with real skill building. Firms can also use the model to judge their current staff or to guide hiring.
arxiv-2509-17363:
Yichao Huang and Youtao Liu continue a study of random measures from conformal field theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. It is the second part of a series on the tail profile of quotients of Gaussian multiplicative chaos measures. Such measures arise in boundary Liouville theory, and their tails govern how extreme values behave.

This part studies the right tail of a bulk chaos measure whose singularity sits evenly on the boundary, in the exact scale-invariant case. Rhodes, Vargas, and Wong handled the flat case before, with localization tricks or Tauberian theorems. The new twist is to localize not the bulk measure but a helper measure on the boundary, where the bulk measure is not even defined. The authors show this scheme captures the right tail correctly. The tail coefficient comes out through a variant of a known object.
arxiv-2509-17663:
Graeme N. Campbell, Lewis Hill, Pascal Del Haye, and Gian Luca Oppo map dark light pulses inside a Fabry-Perot resonator. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies cavity solitons, self-sustaining dips in a light field, in a Kerr nonlinear medium with two polarization components. The work sits in the normal dispersion regime, less explored than its anomalous cousin.

A Fabry-Perot cavity couples the field nonlocally: the round-trip average power shifts the cavity detuning. Against ring resonators, that coupling yields strongly detuned dark solitons that persist over a wide detuning range. The authors chart where these states exist and stay stable. They find a symmetry breaking between opposite circular polarizations at a special codimension-two point. Regular crystals of dark solitons can form on their own, spaced by Turing patterns of alternating polarization. Their frequency combs carry three distinct spacings at once.
arxiv-2509-17763:
Sudip Mukherjee, writing alone, shows how correlated noise can calm a driven system instead of roughening it. His 2025 arXiv paper revisits a coupled model he proposed in 2023. It holds two fields: one evolves on its own, and the second is driven by the first, a one-way street that creates a strong coupling phase.

Mukherjee asks what noise cross correlations do to that phase, in general dimensions. Coupling theories give the answer: the scaling laws of the driven field hinge on the strength of those correlations. As the correlation amplitude rises, the roughness exponent of the second field falls step by step. In other words, shared noise suppresses the driven field's fluctuations, the opposite of the usual intuition that noise adds disorder. The author closes with what that surprise could mean for real driven systems.
arxiv-2509-17963:
Rudra Biswas and 9 co-authors make a memory chip cell do logic on its own stored bits. Their 2025 paper uses a ferroelectric RAM design with two transistors and many capacitors per cell. Unlike common dynamic RAM, it needs no refresh and sips energy.

A gentle read mode lets one cell run a key logic step that standard RAM cannot do alone. That step yields the core NAND and NOR gates, checked in sims and lab data. Stacking cells in 3D lifts both storage and compute density. On eight real data-heavy tasks, the design ran faster and used far less energy than dynamic RAM.
arxiv-2509-18063:
Jan-Felix Klein and Lars Ohnemus build a simple agent that walks a knowledge graph to answer hard queries. Their 2025 system, ARK-V1, pairs a language model with a graph of linked facts. Model memory alone can be stale or wrong, while graph facts are firm but hard to search across many hops.

The agent steps through the graph bit by bit, guided by common sense as well as graph links. Backbones tested were large models with no extra tuning. On a bench that needs both graph facts and common sense, scores beat step-by-step text prompts by a wide margin. Bigger backbones gave broader and steadier answers.
arxiv-2509-18263:
Hanna Linn and 8 co-authors fold proteins on quantum gear with a circuit that needs no task-built form. Their 2025 paper deals with a classic hard task: guess a protein's shape from its chain of amino acids. Past quantum tries built a full energy operator first, which cost extra qubits and deep circuits.

Their flow trains a generic circuit to cut an energy score that a classic computer can sum. That skips the operator build and lets higher links enter the score. Tests span many proteins on three lattice types, in noise-free sims and more. Shapes with up to a few dozen units were handled.
arxiv-2509-18663:
Plastics that conduct electricity power a growing class of lights, transistors, and solar cells. Miguel Lagos, Miguel Kiwi, and Rodrigo Paredes argue that the standard theory of such solids does not fit these materials. Their 2025 paper notes that Bloch's theory treats electrons as spread out and nearly free. In conjugated polymers, electrons stay tightly bound and interact strongly with the atomic cores.

Their model adds electron-electron interactions, both on one site and between the alternating sites along the chain. That yields a many-body picture of conduction and explains why the pure material acts as a semiconductor. A striking prediction follows: two flat bands of excited bonding states that obey Bose-Einstein statistics and help carry charge. The model also fits measured light absorption and emission spectra well. The authors offer it as a blueprint for organic electronics theory.
arxiv-2509-18763:
Vision-language models are powerful but heavy, and shrinking them to two bits per weight or less is hard. Xijun Wang and five co-authors present Bi-VLM, a quantization method that pushes that low-precision frontier. Their 2025 paper splits weights by a bell-curve rule into outliers and several inlier groups. Each group keeps a share matched to its place in the distribution.

A saliency-aware hybrid scheme then compresses each group under its own constraints. On the language side of the models, the method beat the prior best by wide margins on visual question answering. Across whole models the gains were similar. The team also found most image tokens in the compressed models are redundant. Pruning them lifted efficiency further. The work targets vision-language models on hardware with tight memory.
arxiv-2509-18863:
Axion-like particles are candidate dark matter messengers that could live inside neutron stars. Prashant Thakur and four co-authors constrain such a model with telescope and gravitational wave data in this 2025 paper. Dark matter inside a star would change its size at a given mass. The team builds that effect into relativistic models of dense matter.

They generate over thirty thousand candidate equations of state across dark matter masses and momenta, for one stiff and one soft matter model. A layered statistical filter weighs them against pulsar, X-ray, and merger data. The stiff model yields a lower bound on the particle mass, with a preferred range stated. The soft model sets no firm floor but disfavors heavy, dense cases. A machine learning model then reads parameters back off mass-radius curves with high accuracy. Each observable, they find, constrains a different knob.
arxiv-2509-18963:
Andrius Grigutis and Lukas Turčinskas study a quantity built from the Riemann xi function, a completed form of the famous zeta function. They look at the real part of its logarithmic derivative in a thin strip just right of the critical line, for large heights up the complex plane. The question is whether that real part stays positive there.

The authors give an explicit lower bound for a sum over the zeta zeros that lie on the critical line. They also explore what would follow if some zeros sat off the line, the case the Riemann hypothesis says never happens. Work of this kind links the pattern of zeros to the smooth behavior of related functions. That link sits at the heart of analytic number theory.
arxiv-2509-19063:
Przemysław Spyra, writing alone, asks whether neural networks can be trained without backpropagation, the standard method that sends errors backward through a network. Backpropagation drives most of the rising energy and computing cost of deep learning. Spyra compares three methods that avoid it: Forward-Forward, Cascaded-Forward, and Mono-Forward. Each was tuned carefully and trained on the kind of network it was designed for, then matched against a backpropagation baseline.

Mono-Forward not only matched the baseline but beat it on accuracy for its native networks. It also used up to about forty percent less energy and trained about a third faster, measured at the hardware level. Its wins come from settling into a better spot in the error landscape, not from global optimization. The study also exposes wasteful spots in the Forward-Forward design, giving a data-driven roadmap for leaner training.
arxiv-2509-19163:
People increasingly call low-quality AI-written text slop, but nobody agrees on what counts as slop. Chantal Shaib and three co-authors set out to measure it. They interviewed experts in language technology, writing, and philosophy to build a taxonomy of the term. From those talks they propose readable dimensions along which a text can be judged, such as coherence and relevance.

Annotators then marked spans of text, and the team compared their calls. Simple yes-or-no slop judgments proved somewhat subjective from person to person. Still, those judgments lined up with the underlying dimensions the experts had named. The resulting framework can be used in detection tasks and in head-to-head preference tests. Fully automatic, scalable measurement, the authors note, remains an open challenge for the field.
arxiv-2509-19463:
Robots that explore together must merge their separate views into one map, and Doncey Albin and eight co-authors supply a benchmark dataset for that problem. Existing multi-robot datasets are scarce, and many evaluations cheat by slicing one robot's path into fake teammates. Available sets also tend to be short, with little overlap between robots and few loop closures. CU-Multi was collected over several days at two large outdoor sites on the University of Colorado Boulder campus.

Four synchronized runs start together with controlled overlap, imitating a real team's distinct viewpoints. Sensors include color-and-depth cameras, precision GPS, and semantic laser scanning, with refined ground-truth odometry. Dense semantic annotations ride along with the overlap variation. The authors offer the dataset as a foundation for reproducible comparison of collaborative perception methods, a field that badly needs shared yardsticks.
arxiv-2509-19563:
Some language models read text as patches of pixels rather than as words from a fixed list. Stefania Radu, Marco Zullich, and Matias Valdenegro-Toro ask how well such models know their own uncertainty. They test pixel models across eighteen languages and seven writing systems. Three tasks probe meaning: naming entities, answering questions, and one more text task.

The models tended to understate their uncertainty when rebuilding patches. Writing system mattered too: languages in Latin script showed lower uncertainty than others. Ensembles of models helped most after careful tuning of their settings. The study is an early map of trust for a young model family. Builders of multilingual tools need that map before pixel models can be used where errors carry real cost.
arxiv-2509-19663:
Prices in markets remember the distant past more than simple models allow, a trait called long-range dependence. Yifan He and Svetlozar Rachev measure that memory in equities, farm goods, and energy assets. Daily data span stock indexes on three continents plus wheat, corn, soybeans, and oil funds. Several statistical lenses agree on where the memory sits.

Average returns showed weak persistence, but volatility remembered strongly in most assets. Equity scaling traits also shifted after the pandemic shock of 2020. The authors then test whether a generative AI model can fake data with the same memory. It struggles against classic statistical benchmarks. Fake market data that lacks true memory can mislead risk tools. The study sets a bar that financial generators must clear.
arxiv-2509-19763:
Near Earth's magnetopause, broad slow waves in the plasma can coexist with tiny, rapid ion sound waves. Xiaofei Shi, Xin An, and Vassilis Angelopoulos test whether the big waves create the small ones. Satellite readings show the small waves grow strongest near the magnetic peaks of the slow waves. That pattern suggests a direct energy hand-off across scales.

A hybrid simulation built from observed values confirms the chain. The slow wave spawns two ion beams streaming through each other. Those beams excite ion acoustic waves and then relax. Energy thus flows from magnetohydrodynamic scales down to kinetic scales in a clear channel. Cross-scale transfer shapes how the boundary between Earth's field and the solar wind behaves. The result links two wave families long observed side by side.
arxiv-2509-19863:
A classic partial differential equation problem, named for Brezis and Nirenberg, sits at the critical exponent where standard methods break. Fengliu Li and three co-authors survey its history and open questions, then add new results in dimension six. The equation couples a linear term with a critical power term on a bounded domain, with zero boundary values. Existence of solutions hinges on the parameter and the dimension in delicate ways.

Dimension six has resisted several standard attacks, which makes progress there notable. The paper mixes review, new theorems, and a list of open problems for the community. Critical problems act as benchmarks for nonlinear analysis as a whole. A clear map of what is known, plus fresh ground in a hard dimension, serves both specialists and newcomers.
arxiv-2509-20063: Stefania Demaria and Fernando Mazzone wrote this short 2025 arXiv paper in pure math. It proves that a class of systems with set-valued terms has solutions that repeat in time. The systems use a phi-Laplacian term, a kind of spread whose strength changes with direction. Their proof uses the direct method from the calculus of variations, which finds solutions by making an energy-like quantity as small as it can be.
arxiv-2509-20163:
Aifei Zhang and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on graphene physics. They study the quantum Hall effect, where electrical conduction in a flat material changes in steps. Theory predicts that the size of localized states near each step follows one universal scaling law. Clean experiments, though, often break that prediction.

The team measured the localization length across broken-symmetry quantum Hall states in graphene. The smallest length they found varied up to tenfold depending on the state and its energy gap. Clear departures from universal scaling appeared as well. A simple picture explains the pattern: localized states from two neighboring energy levels coexist and mix. The same picture also accounts for the older puzzling results from other groups.
arxiv-2509-20363:
Neutrinos left a fingerprint on the cosmic microwave background, and Gabriele Montefalcone and four co-authors use it to test neutrino interactions in a 2025 arXiv paper. Free-streaming neutrinos shift the phase of sound waves in the early universe. That shift is stamped on the microwave sky. Interactions would change how and when neutrinos decoupled.

The authors study scattering rates that vary with temperature, covering self-interactions and couplings to dark matter. Even with gradual decoupling, the phase shift keeps the free-streaming shape; only its final size shrinks as interactions strengthen. That simple pattern lets data speak directly. Combining Planck, Atacama, and South Pole telescope data, they bound the decoupling epoch tightly. Neutrinos, the analysis finds, have streamed freely since deep in the radiation era. Flavor-specific cases are also explored.
arxiv-2509-20463:
Scores that rate how strongly a model memorized a training example can themselves be gamed. Tue Do, Varun Chandrasekaran, and Daniel Alabi demonstrate the attack in a 2025 arXiv paper. Memorization scores guide data attribution and dataset curation. If the scores bend under pressure, decisions built on them bend too.

The attack crafts inputs that look highly memorized while being highly sensitive queries. It needs only black-box access to model outputs and modest computing power, using a pseudoinverse calculation at its core. Across a wide suite of image classification tasks, even state-of-the-art proxy scores fell to targeted manipulation. The authors back the experiments with theory on when influence estimates are inherently fragile. Their findings argue that attribution tools need defenses of their own before high-stakes use.
arxiv-2509-20563:
Science runs make more data than disks can hold, so Skyler Ruiter, Jiannan Tian, and Fengguang Song build made-to-order squeeze pipelines in a 2025 conference paper. Lossy squeezing trades a small, bounded error for a much smaller file. The best pipeline shifts with each dataset and goal, yet chip-based squeezers hard-code their design and block quick trials. Their framework, FZModules, takes the other path.

Pipelines snap together from fast modules through a short, open interface. A task engine works out which stage needs what, moves memory, and runs stages side by side where it can. The team built three pipelines and tried them on four real science datasets. Speed matched the fused chip-based squeezers end to end. At the same time, size-versus-error quality matched higher-grade CPU and hybrid tools. The aim is fast, field-tuned design with no kernel rewrites.
arxiv-2509-20663:
Quantum circuits must be shrunk and simplified before noisy present-day machines can run them well. Tobias Fischbach, Pierre Talbot, and Pascal Bouvry review one tool for that job in a 2025 survey paper. The tool is ZX-calculus, a diagram language that rewrites circuits while keeping their meaning intact.

The survey sorts ZX-based optimization methods by technique, by target measure, and by machine type. Target measures include qubit count, gate count, and circuit depth. The authors also set out open problems. These include optimizing several goals at once, scaling the methods to larger circuits, and pulling circuits back out of diagrams more cleanly. The review serves researchers in quantum computing and combinatorial optimization.
arxiv-2509-20763:
Yair Caro and three co-authors introduce a new graph parameter in a 2025 mathematics paper, the first in a series. The parameter is the odd independence number of a graph. It builds on the recently introduced strong odd coloring concept.

An odd independent set is a set of vertices with no edges among them, where every outside vertex touches the set zero times or an odd number of times. The largest such set size is the new number.
