The authors lay foundations for the parameter and work out its values for classical families of graphs. They also relate it to strong odd coloring numbers. A later revision added a proof that computing the parameter is computationally hard.
arxiv-2509-21063:
SS 433 is a microquasar, a stellar system whose jets mimic a quasar's on a small scale, sitting inside a supernova remnant. Tobias Kleiner, writing for the VERITAS Collaboration, reports gamma-ray observations of it in a 2025 conference paper for the International Cosmic Ray Conference. The system is prized as a laboratory for particle acceleration.

VERITAS collected more than one hundred hours of observations over more than a decade. Its sharp angular resolution separates the eastern and western jet lobes. The team studies the lobes' shapes and spectra in very-high-energy gamma rays. Recent detections at the highest energies have strengthened SS 433's role in explaining cosmic rays. The paper adds long-baseline measurements to that picture, tracing where jets dump energy into their surroundings.
arxiv-2509-21163:
Rare words matter most in specialized fields, yet language models handle them worst. Jing Liu, Haozheng Wang, and Yueheng Li look for the neurons responsible in a 2025 interpretability paper. They ask whether rare-token handling lives in a dedicated module or spreads across the network.

Analyzing final-layer neurons across several model families, the authors find distributed specialization. Coordinated but scattered subnetworks process rare tokens. Their influence follows three regimes: a plateau of highly influential rare-token neurons, a power-law decay group, and a long tail. The organization is reproducible across models. No single discrete module exists to patch; the skill is woven through the parameters. The finding shapes how engineers might improve rare-token performance, from names and codes to technical vocabulary.
arxiv-2509-21363:
Salient object maps from deep networks still come out incomplete, with blurred boundaries. The 2025 paper is by Runmin Wu and 5 co-authors. Salient object detection finds the most prominent object in a scene. Deep models still give incomplete maps and blurry boundaries. Pooling and strided convolution blur fine edges. The authors train networks with help from related tasks to fix those flaws.

Their method intertwines salient object detection with foreground contour detection. That pairing yields maps with uniform highlight. Contour and edge detection tasks also guide each other at the same time. That leads to precise contour prediction and less local noise in edges. A novel mutual learning module serves as the building block of the network. Tests support the design.
arxiv-2509-21663:
Neurosymbolic systems split between hand written rules injected into networks and rules learned from data. Davide Bizzaro and Alessandro Daniele propose a language unifying both strands in a 2025 paper. Logic of Hypotheses extends propositional logic with a choice operator. The operator has learnable parameters and selects a subformula from a pool of options. Expert knowledge and data driven learning meet in one syntax.

Using fuzzy logic, formulas compile directly into a differentiable computational graph. Optimal choices are learned by backpropagation. The framework subsumes some existing neurosymbolic models. Arbitrary degrees of knowledge specification become possible, from zero to full knowledge. Gödel fuzzy logic and the Gödel trick yield models with useful properties, the authors show.
arxiv-2509-21963:
Approximating a huge matrix by a smaller one of low rank is a workhorse of machine learning and control. Nathaniel Pritchard, Taejun Park, Yuji Nakatsukasa, and Per-Gunnar Martinsson present IterativeCUR in this 2025 paper. The CUR approach builds the approximation from actual rows and columns of the original matrix. That keeps useful structure, like sparsity or non-negativity, that decomposition methods based on singular values can blur.

Earlier CUR methods need the rank guessed in advance. IterativeCUR instead takes a target error and finds the rank itself, with error at or below the target, with high probability. It works from a single small random sketch of the matrix, updating that sketch as it goes. In broad experiments, it ran several times faster than the best sketch-based rivals at no loss of accuracy. Against rank-adaptive randomized methods, the speedups were far larger still.
arxiv-2509-22063:
Separating one sound from a mixture, using the matching video as a guide, is the task of audio-visual sound separation. Chao Huang, Susan Liang, Yapeng Tian, Anurag Kumar, and Chenliang Xu present DAVIS in this 2025 paper, accepted by a leading computer vision journal. Most existing methods treat separation as filling in a mask over the mixed sound. That framing works, but it struggles to capture the full variety of real sounds across many categories.

DAVIS instead generates the separated sound directly, using generative diffusion modeling. Starting from noise, it synthesizes the target sound's spectrogram, guided at once by the mixed audio and the visual information. The team built two variants, one on classic denoising diffusion and one on the newer flow matching approach, inside a purpose-built separation network. On the standard AVE and MUSIC data sets, both variants beat leading methods on separation quality.
arxiv-2509-22563:
Simone Di Gregorio and 3 co-authors study how a broker should learn to profit from trade between strangers. In bilateral trade, a seller and buyer each hold a private value for a good. Each round, a new pair arrives and the broker must offer a mechanism that is honest-proof and worth joining. The goal is profit, judged against the best such mechanism in hindsight.

Their learning algorithm keeps regret near the square-root rate over time when values come from a fixed unknown distribution. They also prove sublinear regret is impossible when an adversary sets values in advance. A chaining analysis handles the fact that profits cannot converge uniformly over all mechanisms. The tools extend to a joint ads problem.
arxiv-2509-22963:
Reinforcement learning breaks down when each step offers a huge mix of possible actions. Haitong Ma and 9 co-authors train discrete diffusion models to act as policies in such spaces. Diffusion models build outputs step by step, which suits rich action mixes. Their key move is a stable online training loop. A mirror descent step first sets an ideal, regularized target policy.

Training then becomes a matching task: the diffusion model learns to copy that target. Splitting the two steps keeps learning steady and boosts results. Tests covered DNA sequence design, macro-actions, and multi-agent setups. The method set new best scores and used fewer samples than rivals.
arxiv-2509-23063:
Plasma instabilities in fusion devices need control that reacts at once and lasts. Jingcheng Lu, Li Wang, and Jeff Calder design feedback control for the Vlasov-Poisson system. Their first route learns an operator that maps state disturbances to a control field. A low-rank neural operator keeps the design lean. Training uses the adjoint state method from optimal control theory.

The learned controller suppressed instabilities far past its training horizon. A second route needs no training at all. It cancels the destabilizing part of the electric field outright. That route promises decay over infinite time and shrugs off noisy feedback. Numeric tests in one and more dimensions support both routes.
arxiv-2509-23363:
Debates about AI in universities tangle teaching, operations, and the future of work into one knot. Tian Zheng offers a taxonomy to sort the narratives of AI education. The frame is the mission of knowledge that universities carry. That mission covers deep expertise plus meta-knowledge like judgment and ethics. Curriculum, Zheng argues, is where the deepest stakes sit.

AI speeds inquiry while unsettling what expertise means. Disciplines evolve through research, curriculum, teaching, and faculty skill in interplay. Teaching innovation is the practical entry point for reform. Structured faculty paths can build toward deeper curricular renewal. The paper is a first attempt at the taxonomy, by its own account.
arxiv-2509-23463:
Chips that steer light need wires of an exact length, not the shortest path. Xiaoke Wang and Dirk Stroobandt study that routing task for programmable photonic circuits, where parts such as ring resonators and delay lines depend on precise lengths. They present length-matching strategies built on best-first search, guided by a new scoring rule that never overstates the cost left. A pruning step trims dead ends from the search.

For two-pin routes, the pair prove their methods complete when the scoring rule stays consistent. Multi-pin routes get a pin-ordering trick based on detour room, which lowers the chance of blocking a workable route early. Tests on varied layouts show how run time and search quality trade off.
arxiv-2509-23563:
A drone hunting for a lost object outdoors cannot rely on room layouts or fixed maps. Seungchan Kim and 7 co-authors present RAVEN, a navigation system for aerial robots in open, unstructured places. It keeps a 3D semantic memory built from voxels and rays, so the robot plans over long horizons instead of reacting to each view. Short-range voxel search and long-range ray search let it scale to big areas.

A vision-language model suggests extra cues when targets are scarce. A behavior tree switches strategies to keep the search robust. Across ten simulated outdoor scenes and one hundred tasks, RAVEN beat baselines by a wide margin, and field tests on a real drone followed.
arxiv-2509-23763:
An electron in graphene, treated as massless, behaves oddly when space itself is made noncommutative. Aslam Halder, the sole author, studies that Landau problem under a constant magnetic field. Gauge invariance is the technical hurdle. Halder handles it with an effective noncommutative Dirac field theory that uses the Seiberg-Witten map and the Moyal star product, yielding a plainly gauge-invariant Hamiltonian.

From that Hamiltonian he computes the energy spectrum of the noncommutative Landau system. The shifted levels then feed a study of the system's heat response. At low temperature, spatial noncommutativity produces spontaneous magnetization, which Halder flags as a distinct signature of the geometry in relativistic condensed matter.
arxiv-2509-23963:
The Chinchilla scaling rules steer how the field sizes its models, so doubts about them matter. Rylan Schaeffer and 6 co-authors stress-test those rules and conclude they hold up. First they show the original model parameters were ambiguous, with three readings differing by up to about fifteen percent. Surprisingly, the choice barely moves the scaling estimates or the optimal tokens-to-parameter ratio; one reading makes that ratio even steadier.

Then they deliberately distort the parameters four ways. The key results bend mainly under additive or systematic errors, yet withstand sizable perturbations overall. The field, they argue, can keep trusting Chinchilla.
arxiv-2509-24063:
Simulating a living organ cell by cell can need billions of small agents that act and react. Lukas Breitwieser and 5 co-authors built TeraAgent, an engine that spreads such simulations across many servers. The prior leading tool, BioDynaMo, ran on one server only, which capped its size.

TeraAgent packs agent data so it can be read and changed right in the receive buffer. It also sends only what changed between steps, which cuts traffic a lot. The engine ran a simulation with half a trillion agents on tens of thousands of cores. It packed data far faster than a standard baseline and sped up live viewing many times over.
arxiv-2510-00063:
Jinghang Shi and a team of co-authors published this 2025 paper introducing AstroMMBench, a test for AI models in astronomy. The test checks how well large models that read images and text can interpret space pictures. General tests miss the hard parts of astronomy data, so the team built one for this field alone. Fifteen experts in the field reviewed every question for quality.

The test holds 621 multiple-choice questions spread across six branches of astrophysics. The team ran it on 25 models, both open and closed, and compared the scores. An open model, Ovis2-34B, scored highest, at about seventy percent correct overall. Cosmology and high-energy topics proved hardest, while tools and solar topics went better. The results show why field-specific tests matter when judging AI for science work.
arxiv-2510-00363:
Michael Heisel, Rahul Deshpande, and Gabriel Katul published this 2025 fluid dynamics paper on turbulence near walls. They study the wall-normal velocity, the up-and-down motion in channel, pipe, and boundary layer flows. Direct numerical simulations spanning a decade of friction Reynolds numbers supply the data. One spectral feature stands out across every flow case they examined.

The spanwise spectrum peaks at mid-range wavenumbers through the lower half of each flow. That peak scales with the dissipation rate and the cube of the local shear stress. Scaling by local stress, rather than the surface friction velocity, explains quirks in earlier boundary layer data. The authors trace the pattern to Townsend's attached eddy hypothesis, where wall-normal motions are mostly active eddies. A semi-empirical fit for the variance matches values reported across the literature well. The findings matter for modeling atmospheric flow over land and water.
arxiv-2510-01163:
Azizian and Hasan ask why language models can learn a new task from a few examples shown in the prompt. This in-context learning feels like magic, yet its reliability varies wildly across tasks. The authors trace the behavior back to the statistical shape of the data used in pretraining.

Their theory unifies two error sources, picking the wrong task and generalizing badly within the right one. Heavy-tailed data and dependent sequences, both realistic for text, fit inside the new bounds. Experiments on equation-driven and memory-laden processes show the distribution steering performance directly. Designers can shape the training mix deliberately to buy robustness where it counts. Bayesian consistency results, long confined to tidy settings, anchor the analysis. Sample efficiency becomes a design variable rather than a mystery. Robustness follows the same dial as accuracy here. Pretraining curation deserves theory, not folklore.
arxiv-2510-01363:
Garza and co-authors ground a prescribing assistant in real past cases so its suggestions follow clinical precedent. Emergency decisions must sift sprawling records quickly, and unsupported model advice is dangerous. Their framework finds similar past cases and lets a language model reason over them.

Structured codes and free-text notes merge into one format for retrieval. The generator then proposes treatments matched to the patient's own pattern. Tests across tens of thousands of emergency visits did as well as classic predictors. Augmenting judgment, never replacing it, is the stated design ethic. Federated sources extend retrieval where local archives run thin. Age, sex, complaints, symptoms, and histories all feed the patient picture. Case-based answers carry their evidence visibly. Context-sensitive output is the goal, since generic advice harms. Emergency care supplied the test arena. Support that cites its cases builds trust with doctors.
arxiv-2510-01463:
Anczarski and co-authors model and calibrate a cryogenic amplifier quiet enough to count handfuls of electrons for a dark matter detector. Low-mass dark matter deposits mere milli-electron-volts, demanding extraordinary charge sensitivity. Their two-stage design pairs commercial transistors across temperature stages inside a dilution refrigerator.

A source-follower sits at base temperature, with voltage amplification at four kelvin. Measured noise matches the model closely at the reference frequency. Photon calibration confirms a resolution near nineteen electrons, plus or minus four. The modular platform serves rare-event searches beyond its home experiment. Narrow-gap semiconductors form the detector substrate the amplifier serves. Low capacitance is engineered alongside low noise throughout. Single-electron sensitivity remains the longer-term quantum-device goal. Substrate agnosticism lets one readout serve many candidate materials. Rare-event physics lives or dies on readout noise. Calibration against photons grounds the electron count honestly.
arxiv-2510-01863:
Cococcioni, Pagani, and Rossi test a compact number format for large language models in this 2025 paper. Ordinary floating-point values each carry their own scale, which costs memory and computing effort. Microscaling instead shares one scale across a whole block of values. That sharing squeezes each value into a single byte while keeping a wide dynamic range.

The authors built the format into the GPT-2 architecture and tried several configurations. Their eight-bit microscaling variants reached accuracy competitive with standard formats in both training and inference runs. The savings in memory footprint and compute cost were the point of the exercise. Open-source code accompanies the work for other teams to reproduce. The study supports microscaling as a practical route to deploying large models more cheaply. It also runs on modern C++ tooling for software-defined number formats.
arxiv-2510-01963:
Solak, Grötschla, Lanzendörfer, and Wattenhofer audit global bias in AI music generators in this 2025 paper. Music models have improved fast, but nobody had mapped how unevenly they treat the world's traditions. The team built GlobalDISCO, a dataset of seventy-three thousand generated tracks. Prompts came from artist profiles spanning seventy-nine countries, five continents, and one hundred forty-seven languages, with ninety-three thousand real reference tracks linked alongside.

Commercial generators performed markedly worse for low-resource regions than for wealthy ones. Quality and closeness to the reference music both dropped for Northern Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Southern Asia. Genre gaps appeared too, even inside well-served regions. For some regional genres, models drifted toward mainstream styles instead of the requested sound. The authors release the dataset as a benchmark for fairer music generation. Their results warn that generative music may amplify global cultural inequality.
arxiv-2510-02263:
Qu and co-authors introduce RLAD, a method that trains language models to reason with reusable abstractions. Their 2025 machine learning paper targets hard reasoning problems. Standard training produces one long chain of thought per problem. Those chains often wander and repeat weak steps. An abstraction is a short summary of which steps worked. RLAD teaches the model to write such summaries first. The model then reuses them while solving new problems.

The team trained the system with reinforcement learning. They tested it on math benchmarks, including AIME 2025 problems. Under an equal compute budget, abstraction-guided sampling beat plain repeated sampling. At one setting the scores rose from sixty five percent to seventy one percent correct. The gain supports a clear claim. Once basic errors are fixed, varied strategies help more than longer chains alone.
arxiv-2510-02363:
Abedi and co-authors design a 6G vehicle network that sends only safety critical data first. Their 2025 telecommunications paper joins sensing and communication in one system. Future cars must locate themselves precisely to avoid crashes. They must also share warnings with nearby traffic. Radio resources stay limited and interference grows in dense streets. The authors rank messages by value of information. A safety aware filter passes only high value updates. Positioning, messaging, and control become one decision problem. A multi-agent learning method solves that problem over two time scales.

Simulations showed clear safety gains from the design. Time to collision improved by up to sixty six percent. Collision risk fell to the lowest level among compared methods. A compact state design kept the learning tractable. Dense mixed traffic stayed manageable in the tests. The frame suits future intelligent transport systems.
arxiv-2510-02463:
Shaposhnikov and co-authors deploy an AI clinical assistant that routes patients to the right specialist. Their 2025 health informatics paper presents a platform called CLARITY. The system blends two control styles for safety. A finite state machine runs structured dialogue flows. Language model agents analyze symptoms and judge severity together. Modular microservices keep the platform flexible and scalable. The assistant was integrated into a large national interhospital platform. Real patients used it from the first day of deployment.

More than fifty five thousand rich dialogues arrived within two months. Experts annotated twenty five hundred of them for validation. Routing precision on the first attempt beat human performance. The result held on the annotated validation subset. Severity triage guides urgent cases toward faster care. Hospital networks need exactly this kind of front door. Structured control keeps free model chat in check.
arxiv-2510-02763:
LaHaye, Luis, and Gierach fuse many satellite sensors to map harmful algal blooms without labeled training data. Their 2025 remote sensing paper presents a framework called SIT-FUSE. Blooms poison fisheries and drinking water worldwide. Each satellite sees only part of the needed signal. The framework blends reflectance from four operational instruments. Fluorescence data from another sensor adds a fifth view. Self-supervised learning builds shared representations across sensors. Hierarchical clustering then groups plankton types and concentrations. The classes stay interpretable for human analysts.

Validation used field data from two coastlines. The Gulf of Mexico and Southern California supplied the checks. Maps matched measured plankton totals closely. Three harmful species groups matched well too. Labeled data is scarce exactly where blooms matter most. A sensor web sidesteps the labeling bottleneck. Global bloom monitoring could run on this pattern.
arxiv-2510-03063:
Chandramouli and co-authors hunt rogue waves inside quantum droplets. Droplets form in ultracold atom mixtures with competing forces. A mean-field push fights a quantum correction named for Lee, Huang, and Yang. The extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation governs that balance. The team solved it with a fixed-point scheme over space and time. They mapped where its rogue waves differ from textbook ones.

Familiar shapes appeared across wide zones of the map. The Peregrine soliton, a single tall spike, led the list. Its periodic cousins, the Akhmediev breathers, showed up too. Higher-order rogue forms joined them in some regions. Two recipes proved able to summon the waves on demand. Smashing dam-break flows together was one recipe. Letting a smooth hump steepen into catastrophe was the other. Droplet waves run wider than their textbook kin. Broken integrability and the force fight explain the change.
arxiv-2510-03263:
Polowczyk and co-authors show that image models made to forget a concept can often remember it with a nudge. Machine unlearning scrubs specific knowledge from trained models. Harmful or unlawful concepts are the usual targets. Adversarial prompts already hinted that erasure is shallow. This work defines a Memory Self-Regeneration task to measure recovery. Their MemoRa strategy then attempts the recovery deliberately. A small adapter and inversion technique do the heavy lifting.

Only a few images of the forgotten content are needed. The adapter steers the model back toward the erased concept. Forgotten knowledge returned readily in the shallow cases. The authors distinguish two modes of forgetting in models. Short-term forgetting yields to quick recall attempts. Long-term forgetting resists, with recovery slower and harder. Retrieval robustness, they argue, belongs in unlearning evaluations. Compliance claims are shaky without such stress tests.
arxiv-2510-03763:
Deng and Pang present a 2025 arXiv paper cutting the cost of Sharpness Aware Minimization, a training method that generalizes but runs twice as slowly as training. That optimizer seeks flat minima by computing gradients twice per step. The authors show its gradient splits into the gradient plus a second order correction projected onto it, which they call the PSF term. Because that correction changes, their method, ARSAM, samples it adaptively and reuses it across steps, mixing values.

On the CIFAR benchmarks, ARSAM matched the method's accuracy while running forty percent faster. It sped up human pose estimation and model quantization without losing performance. In some cases it reached flatter minima and higher accuracy than the method. The correction term grows important, which the adaptive sampling exploits. Flat minimum methods have been a luxury for training runs. A forty percent discount widens the set of teams that can afford them.
arxiv-2510-03963:
Kurama and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper asking how often a key genericity assumption in geometric invariant theory actually holds. For a representation of a reductive group, a character selects a semistable locus, and quotient constructions need a maximal torus to act there with finite stabilizers. The authors call representations with such a Weyl-invariant choice Weyl-generic and investigate when they occur.

They give necessary and sufficient conditions, sometimes equivalent ones, for the required character to exist. The proof exploits the combinatorics of weights of irreducible representations of semisimple groups. Their classification shows Weyl-genericity is the exception rather than the rule, hence the paper's title. As an application, they generalize the Grassmannian flop example of Donovan and Segal. The moral for geometers and physicists is blunt: genericity assumptions in quotient constructions deserve verification, because the Weyl-invariant subspaces they need are usually absent.
arxiv-2510-04063:
Pandey and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on improving solar flare forecasts by respecting the ordering of flare sizes. Forecasters usually split flares into just two classes, flare or no flare, at a chosen strength threshold. That split ignores the ladder of subclasses inside each side, from weak A-class up to extreme X-class events. Most mistakes happen right at the boundary, where near-identical events fall on opposite sides.

The authors modify the training loss to encode this ordinal structure. Errors near the threshold now cost more than errors far from it, because borderline confusion is the dominant failure mode. In their tests the gains over ordinary binary loss were modest, especially with data limited to part of the solar disk. Still, the approach shows how ordered severity scales can inform binary prediction more broadly. Better flare warnings help protect satellites and power grids from space weather.
arxiv-2510-04163:
Yu and Yuen present this 2025 arXiv paper proving White's conjecture for the class of paving matroids. The conjecture says any two collections of bases with the same multiset union can be morphed into each other through symmetric exchanges. It also implies matroid toric ideals are generated by the corresponding binomials, linking combinatorics to algebra. The conjecture has resisted general proof for decades.

The authors settle it for paving matroids, a broad and important class. Their strategy generalizes a recent inductive argument by Han and coauthors. That argument used circuit-hyperplane relaxations, which simplify a matroid in a controlled way. Yu and Yuen extend the induction to stressed hyperplane relaxations, reaching the paving class. Progress on White's conjecture matters because toric generation controls how matroid ideals can be computed with. Paving matroids cover most matroids encountered in practice, so the result has wide reach.
arxiv-2510-04363:
Hyunjun Kim and Sejong Kim, researchers at KAIST in South Korea, wrote this 2025 paper on testing web automation. They built MacroBench, a benchmark that asks a large language model to write a reusable browser program from a stated goal. The program reads page code and acts through Python and Selenium tools. The test runs on seven self hosted copies of well known sites, modeled on Airbnb, TikTok, Reddit, and others.

The benchmark holds 681 tasks, sorted by how hard each step is and how hard targets are to find. Graders check the code, run it in a sandbox, and verify the final page and data state. Across many runs, the best model reached about 97 percent success overall. Simple tasks went well, but every model scored zero on the hardest multi step workflows. A safety suite also probed scraping, spam, and credential prompts. The test kit was released in public.
arxiv-2510-04663:
Mihai Pavel, Julius Ross, and Matei Toma wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on generalizing a classic inequality. The inequality bounds the geometry of stable bundles on a complex surface. Behind it sit the Hodge Riemann relations, a positivity statement about forms on the manifold. The authors define two new notions of pairs of cohomology classes. One pair type extends the Hodge Riemann pattern, and the other extends the Bogomolov pattern.

Their central conjecture says every pair of the first kind is also a pair of the second kind. That claim would carry the classical inequality into far wider terrain. The paper proves the conjecture in a range of cases rather than in full. Schur polynomials supply natural examples of the new pair types along the way. As an application, they win fresh boundedness results for semistable sheaves. The work gives algebraic geometers new tests for when positivity forces the Bogomolov bound.
arxiv-2510-04763:
Shammi Malhotra, Sarika Goyal, and K. Sreenadh wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on equations that mix two kinds of diffusion. The model blends the ordinary Laplacian with a fractional one that feels distant points. A Hardy potential, singular at one point, adds pull toward the center. Two growth terms, one tunable and one at the critical power, shape the solutions. The authors first pin down how solutions behave near the boundary and the singularity.

Uniform estimates come from a change of variables suited to the problem. With behavior controlled, they split analysis by the size of the tunable exponent. In each of three regimes they prove a positive solution exists. In the gentle growth regime, small tweaks of the fractional part yield several positive solutions. Existence and multiplicity results guide where such mixed models can be trusted. Equations arise in physics where both local and long range effects act at once.
arxiv-2510-05163:
Abdelilah Ganmati, Karim Afdel, and Lahcen Koutti survey how deep learning is reshaping login security in this 2025 arXiv paper. Passwords alone fail against phishing, leaks, and brute force. Multi-factor authentication stacks independent proofs: something known, something held, and something inherent like a fingerprint. Smart cards now carry chips that verify biometrics on the device itself.

The survey reviews work from 2019 to 2025 across face, fingerprint, iris, and voice recognition. It compares hardware routes such as smart cards, NFC tokens, and secure enclaves. Real deployments in banking, healthcare devices, and critical infrastructure anchor the discussion. Open problems include the usability-security trade-off and adversarial attacks on the learning models. Privacy of stored biometric data and missing standards round out the roadmap.
arxiv-2510-05263:
J. Michael Shull and three co-authors identify what ionizes the gas clouds drifting past the Sun in this 2025 arXiv paper. The local interstellar clouds are oddly ionized: about 40 percent of their helium but only 20 percent of their hydrogen. Candidate light sources include two nearby B-type stars, three hot white dwarfs, and the local hot bubble.

The authors update the second B star's temperature and ionizing output after correcting for intervening gas. Together the two stars bathe the clouds in a strong hydrogen-ionizing flux. The million-degree hot bubble may contribute a comparable share through metal line emission. That extra source can explain why helium is more ionized than hydrogen. Both stars also passed within ten parsecs of the Sun about 4.4 million years ago, with far stronger effects then.
arxiv-2510-05463:
Guo and Obłój work on pricing American options without trusting one market model. An American option lets its holder sell or buy an asset at any time before a set date. Classic pricing picks one model for price moves and derives a fair price. Their 2025 paper asks what price stays safe across many possible models.

The authors allow wide uncertainty about volatility, the size of price swings. They prove that the cheapest safe hedging plan costs exactly the worst-case model price. That match, called duality, also holds when European options trade at known prices. Their proof uses randomized stopping times and optimal transport methods. Earlier work had settled this question only for step-by-step discrete time. Continuous time had resisted a complete answer until now. The result gives traders a firm base for pricing under deep model doubt.
arxiv-2510-05663:
Senthamizhan and colleagues add frequency weighting to a model of swarming oscillators. Swarmalators both move and synchronize, like flocking units with internal clocks. In their one-dimensional ring model, each agent's natural frequency scales its couplings. Their 2025 study maps the collective states this heterogeneity creates.

Three states appear across the simulations. The asynchronous state shows no correlation between position and phase. The phase-wave state aligns the two along a diagonal. A bistrip mixed state splits antipodal clusters into frequency-dependent sub-strips. Self-consistency analysis pins down the transition conditions between these states. Abrupt transitions arise precisely from the heterogeneous coupling. Numerical simulations agree well with the analytical transition conditions. The bistrip state emerges even for unimodal frequencies, unlike its Kuramoto cousin. The work extends swarmalator theory to more realistic, nonuniform interaction rules. Natural systems from bacterial colonies to robot swarms motivate the model.
arxiv-2510-05863:
Caravelli and Delvenne recast how systems compute, in Koopman operator language. Which dynamic systems truly compute stays debated across analog and symbolic models. The Koopman operator lifts nonlinear motion into a linear form on observables. Their 2025 lens defines halting through its resolvent.

The Koopman halting problem is recursively enumerable in general. For equicontinuous systems, the same problem becomes decidable, ruling out universality. On Cantor-space symbolic systems, the framing captures which clopen sets reach which. Absorbing halting states appear as eigenfunctions with eigenvalue one. The count of such states tallies the distinct sink basins. Cycles in the state graph impose algebraic constraints on the spectrum. Turing's model reads, in this view, as a discrete dynamic process. Polynomial and analog models fit the same lens. Hardness may thus leave dynamic signs in the spectrum.
arxiv-2510-05963:
Hafner and colleagues teach machine learning only the cloudy part of radiation physics. Earth system models cannot resolve clouds at their coarse hundred-kilometer grids. Subgrid cloud assumptions inject large uncertainties into radiative fluxes. Their 2025 MLe-radiation scheme learns cloud effects from storm-resolving simulations.

Training data come from five-kilometer simulations coarse-grained to coarse resolution. The learned target is the cloud radiative impact alone. That impact is the difference between all-sky and clear-sky fluxes. Clear-sky tendencies stay with the conventional physics-based scheme. No assumptions about horizontal or vertical cloud distributions are needed. The hybrid therefore responds correctly to greenhouse gas or aerosol changes. Stochastic column approaches can err by a hundred watts per square meter. Offline tests cut radiation errors by a factor of four to ten. Next-generation climate models are the intended deployment.
arxiv-2510-06163:
Diaz, Pagonabarraga, and Calero work out how surface reactions propel colloids in a 2025 soft matter study. Janus particles swim when reactions on one face push against the surrounding fluid. Whether direct momentum transfer alone drives that motion has stayed unclear.

They solve the exact unsteady Stokes equation for a colloid with a localized reaction. They model the reaction as a force dipole on the fluid, or as a pair force on particle and fluid. After one reaction, the velocity decays with a distinctive two-stage power-law tail. That tail differs from a kicked particle's because the mechanism is force-free overall. The reaction's distance from the surface strongly controls speed and transient response. With periodic reactions, the predicted steady speed matches experiments and earlier simulations. Fluid compressibility proves unnecessary for the mechanism. Momentum exchange alone stands as a relevant engine for self-propelled colloids.
arxiv-2510-06263:
Wu and six co-authors build a dual-stage chart summarizer running entirely on embedded devices in a 2025 medical informatics paper. Emergency physicians drown in unstructured health record text while hunting critical facts. Sending records to cloud models would endanger privacy, so the system works offline.

Two Jetson Nano devices split the job over a lightweight socket link. The first retrieves relevant record sections for a clinician's query, splitting long notes into coherent parts. The second runs a small local language model that writes the summary. Output comes as a fixed-format list of critical findings plus a narrative tailored to the query. The team benchmarked six open small models under seven billion parameters. An LLM-as-judge scored summaries for accuracy, completeness, and clarity. On MIMIC-IV and de-identified real records, the system produced useful summaries in under thirty seconds.
arxiv-2510-06363:
Babatunde, Ayodabo, and Raqibul evaluate a Git-based assignment submission system in a real university in a 2025 software engineering case study. Traditional submission workflows burden instructors and students with tracking friction. Version control is standard in industry, so the team rebuilt submission around Git.

The system was developed iteratively with user-centered design and deployed live. Usability testing and feedback showed gains in tracking, collaboration, and efficiency. About eighty-five percent of instructors found the Git system easier to use. About eighty-four percent of students preferred it over traditional methods. Submission and review took about thirty-eight percent less time, and storage fell by about forty-eight percent. Adoption hurdles and the learning curve eased through iterative improvements. Students also reported better learning outcomes from working in a professional workflow. The study offers practical guidance for bringing version control into classrooms.
arxiv-2510-06563:
Swathi Chandrasekhar, Shiva Raj Pokhrel, and Navneet Singh test whether quantum machine learning can predict how much energy a chemical bond holds. Their 2025 paper is a careful benchmark study. Bond dissociation energies guide the design of new molecules and materials. The team built features from atomic properties, bond types, and the local setting around each bond.

Five quantum model types were trained on six qubits in a simulator. They included quantum regressors, support vector models, neural networks, and random forests. Strong classical models, such as random forests and multilayer perceptrons, served as baselines. The best quantum models matched the classical ones in accuracy and robustness. They did especially well in the middle range of bond energies. Both kinds of models struggled at the extremes of the data. The study gives a clear, repeatable baseline for quantum chemistry with machine learning.
arxiv-2510-06863:
Jiheon Seong and four co-authors extend a tool for detecting quantum entanglement in bigger systems. Their 2025 paper works with entanglement witnesses, which are measurements that flag entangled states. A witness returns a nonnegative value on every unentangled state. A negative value therefore proves entanglement is present.

Recent work showed that witnesses also have an upper bound on such states. That bound implies a partner measurement, called a mirrored witness. Using both bounds together lets one device detect more entangled states. The authors build mirrored witnesses for systems with many parties and for high-dimensional systems. They work out examples for famous GHZ states, graph states, and bound entangled states. For three-qubit systems they exhibit a mirrored pair of optimal witnesses. Such pairs provably do not exist for two qubits alone. They appear once the system grows, which is the paper's neat dividing line.
arxiv-2510-06963:
Riccardo Ferrazzoli leads a collaboration reporting how the IXPE telescopes have performed in orbit. Their 2025 paper characterizes the imaging of the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer. IXPE carries three telescopes that measure X-ray polarization, a first for astrophysics. Each pairs a Wolter-I mirror with a gas pixel detector.

The team analyzed observations of point-like X-ray sources gathered over thirty months. They fitted a model of the point spread function, the blur pattern of a point source. Comparing with ground calibrations showed the behavior matches expectations. The angular resolution, measured as half-power diameter, showed no drift over time. Bright sources behaved the same, with no rate-driven broadening of the image tails. Those checks cover the energy bands used for science. Stable optics mean polarization maps stay trustworthy for point-like and extended sources. The telescopes look ready to serve the mission's lifetime into 2030.
arxiv-2510-07063:
Francesca Cocchella, Nilay Choudhury, Eric Chen, and Patrícia Alves-Oliveira ask painters how it feels to create alongside a robot arm. Their 2025 paper reports one of the first empirical studies of artists co-creating with a painting robot. Eight abstract artists painted in six sessions. Three sessions paired them with a human partner, and three with the robot.

Interviews after the sessions were analyzed thematically. Painting with a human felt intuitive, dialogic, and emotionally engaging. Painting with the robot felt more playful and reflective instead. Artists reported greater autonomy with the machine partner. Its limits even pushed them toward novel strategies and improvisation. Several described creative breakthroughs that arose because the robot was repetitive. The robot could not match the emotional reciprocity of a human collaborator. Still, artists built meaning around its gestures and imagined uses. The study argues for long-term, multidisciplinary engagement when designing robots.
arxiv-2510-07163:
Rodrigues and co-authors count disks around free-floating objects of planetary mass. Their 2025 study focuses on Upper Scorpius, a young group of stars. Some objects there drift alone, too light to be stars. A disk of gas and dust around one hints at how it formed. Past disk surveys stopped at heavier objects because samples were small. This team pushed the census down to far lighter bodies.

The survey used infrared data to spot the warm glow of disks. A Bayesian method judged which objects truly showed extra glow beyond their own light. The sample reached objects near six times the mass of Jupiter. Disk shares were traced across a fine grid of masses. Results rest on between seventeen and forty free-floating objects, depending on the assumed age. How many loners keep disks helps test whether they formed like planets or like stars.
arxiv-2510-07263:
Bagchi and Sen recast the Kiselev black hole in coordinates designed for observers falling into it. Their 2025 paper uses Painlevé-Gullstrand coordinates, which keep time tied to a falling watch. The Kiselev solution describes a black hole surrounded by quintessence, a candidate form of dark energy. The authors add a deformation term that marks departures from the standard coordinate form. They study two cases for the surrounding matter, radiation and dust.

Closed-form expressions give the Hawking temperature and the entropy of the hole. Entropy grows with mass in a pattern that shifts with the deformation. As charge approaches a limiting value, the radiation case shows entropy approaching the square of the mass. A remnant mass survives even when the temperature falls to zero. Such studies refine how exotic matter might imprint on black hole thermodynamics.
arxiv-2510-07463:
Lin and a large collaboration present a machine-learning method for recycling simulated neutrino events instead of regenerating them. Their 2025 paper addresses a cost of cross-section measurements at gigaelectronvolt energies. Experiments compare data against event generators, and each generator version demands fresh, expensive simulation. A boosted decision tree learns weights in a high-dimensional space of detector observables. Applying those weights reshapes one generator's events until their reconstructed particle content, kinematics, and detector efficiency match a target model's output.

The demonstration reweights a MINERvA experiment sample from an old generator version to a newer one. The physics target is the sideways momentum imbalance between the muon and proton in quasielastic-like events on carbon. Events are split by observable particle count to keep the reweighting dimensions manageable. Reusing legacy samples saves the heavy computing of full regeneration.
arxiv-2510-07563:
Van Luijk's doctoral dissertation asks whether infinite entanglement comes in kinds, and answers with a classification theorem. The 2025 thesis, from Leibniz University Hannover, works in von Neumann algebra theory, the rigorous language for quantum systems with infinitely many degrees of freedom.

One instance makes the correspondence concrete: Connes' classification of type III factors matches the smallest achievable error when embezzling entanglement from a system. That protocol extracts entanglement while barely disturbing the source. The work promotes a taxonomy long treated as pure structure theory into a classification of quantum resources. In quantum information science, which meets infinite systems in field theory and gravity, the kind of infinite entanglement held determines which protocols are possible and how well they can ever work.
arxiv-2510-07663:
Wang wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on predicting long-term loan defaults. Borrowers change their habits over time, and economic conditions shift too. Models trained once tend to decay as those patterns drift. Wang presents HYDRA-EI, a hybrid ensemble system built to keep learning. The system refreshes itself weekly using fresh data and needs manual care only rarely.

HYDRA-EI builds several kinds of features before it predicts. It adds relationship features through graph attention, interaction features, and frequency-domain features that expose cycles. Three model types then vote as an ensemble, and their weights shift with recent performance. Tests under shifting data showed strong stability and accuracy for long-horizon default prediction. The author argues the modular design transfers well to other risk tasks. Defaults carry heavy costs for lenders. Such steady updating matters for lenders who must trust scores over many years.
arxiv-2510-07963:
Hoang, Pham, Hoang, and Zimányi wrote this 2025 database paper on managing movement data inside a lightweight analytics engine. Trajectory data powers transport planning and mobility services. Research systems for such data exist, but few feel production-ready or light. MobilityDB extends a full server database and inherits its heaviness. The authors instead extend DuckDB, an embedded columnar database prized for quick analytics.

Their extension, MobilityDuck, plugs in the MEOS library for spatiotemporal types and trajectory operators. Queries keep the expressive power of dedicated moving-object systems. The engine's in-memory, columnar design speeds the work. Tests on the BerlinMOD-Hanoi benchmark compared runtimes against MobilityDB. MobilityDuck won most queries, with and without indexes. A notebook-based use case showed fast visualization through the Python interface. The authors claim the first embedded analytical system with native spatiotemporal types, aimed at data scientists rather than database administrators.
arxiv-2510-08063:
Buendía, Pura, Giannini, and Sánchez-Gil wrote this 2025 nanophotonics paper on how a finite grid of metal nanoparticles radiates light mode by mode. The array follows the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger pattern, famous for protected edge and corner states. Instead of watching the total response, the authors decompose it. A coupled-dipole eigenmode analysis isolates what each mode contributes to the far field.

Antisymmetric modes proved darker and longer-lived than symmetric ones, with higher quality factors. The out-of-plane resonances force all bulk modes at the zone center to be dark. Edge and corner states need extra in-plane symmetries before their radiation cancels. As the array grows, radiation patterns grow more complex and concentrate along the array plane. Breaking symmetries inside multi-part cells mixes multipoles and reshapes the patterns. The results give designers a mode-level map for metasurfaces that emit exactly where intended.
arxiv-2510-08263:
The Co-TAP Team proposes a shared rulebook for AI agents in a 2025 arXiv technical report. Groups of agents from different makers often cannot talk to each other well. This silo problem raises costs and blocks teamwork between agents. Human-agent chats also lack standard forms, so context gets sent again and again. Agent experience, once gained, is hard to store and share.

Co-TAP answers with three stacked protocols, each handling one layer of the problem. The Human-Agent Interaction Protocol sets event-driven rules for chats between users, screens, and agents. The Unified Agent Protocol breaks down barriers between unlike agents through shared services. The third protocol, MEK, extracts and stores agent memories as shareable knowledge. Together, the layers aim to cut repeated context, speed joint work, and let groups of agents build shared skill over time.
arxiv-2510-08563:
El Houcine Bergou and co-authors track where randomized Kaczmarz iterates end up on noisy problems in a 2025 arXiv paper. The randomized Kaczmarz algorithm solves large linear systems by repeatedly projecting onto single equations. It is among the most memory- and compute-efficient iterative solvers known. For clean, consistent systems its convergence is well understood, but real systems carry noise and inconsistency.

The team studies the asymptotic behavior of the iterates in expectation for noisy, inconsistent systems. Singular vectors of the noisy coefficient matrix play a central role in locating the limit points. They derive bounds on the convergence horizon that depend on noise levels and system traits. Extensive numerical experiments validate the theoretical predictions in detail. The results clarify both the robustness and the limits of the algorithm under realistic conditions. Practical guidance for scientific and engineering users follows from the bounds.
arxiv-2510-08963:
Iser and Luna revisit a disagreement between two flagship particle physics measurements, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When protons collide at the highest energies, the total chance of interaction keeps rising slowly. Their model, inspired by quantum chromodynamics, blames that rise on semihard processes: glancing gluon exchanges that spawn tiny jets. They track the total cross section and a ratio describing the scattering wave's shape, for proton and antiproton beams alike.

Two detector teams at the LHC, ATLAS with ALFA and TOTEM, report values that appear to clash, especially for that ratio at the top energy. The authors show that fitting each dataset on its own can still yield descriptions consistent with all the data taken together. The small remaining offset from the measured central values hints at something extra: a possible odd component in the semihard scattering amplitude. Resolving it would refine extrapolations to even higher energies.
arxiv-2510-09563:
Andrea Rubiola, Matteo Zennaro, Carlos García-García, David Alonso, and Raul Angulo measure how cosmic structure grows nearby, in a 2025 arXiv paper. They combine galaxy clustering with gravitational lensing of the cosmic microwave background, which maps the matter between us and the early universe. They focus on low redshifts, the recent universe, where departures from a perfect cosmological constant might show first.

Galaxy data come from the 2MASS photometric survey and the WISC survey, and lensing data from the Planck satellite. A hybrid effective field theory model handles how galaxies trace matter. With a prior from DESI oscillation measurements, they find the clumpiness measure S8 near zero point seven nine, in reasonable agreement with microwave background results. Without that prior, the data favour a lower matter fraction, nearly three standard deviations below the Planck value. Reconstructed growth history still matches Planck predictions and earlier lensing studies.
arxiv-2510-09663:
Raju Dhakal, Prashant Shekhar, and Laxima Niure Kandel defend radio fingerprinting against imitation attacks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Radio frequency fingerprinting authenticates devices by the unique imperfections of their hardware, visible in the signals they emit. An attacker, though, might train a generative model to mimic a genuine device's fingerprint and sneak a rogue transmitter onto the network.

The authors build that attack themselves to test the defence. A generative adversarial network learns from the in-phase and quadrature samples of genuine devices and tries to forge their characteristics. Their detector is a convolutional neural network that uses softmax probability thresholding to separate genuine devices from rogues. The setup uses ten ADALM-PLUTO software-defined radios: seven genuine, two rogue, and one reserved for validation to set the threshold. The paper frames the arms race between mimicry and detection in device authentication.
arxiv-2510-09863:
Gündüz studies 2-absorbing submodules in this 2025 arXiv paper in commutative algebra. A submodule is a part of a module, the algebraic structure that generalizes vector spaces over a ring. The 2-absorbing notion weakens the classical prime submodule idea: a product landing inside the submodule forces a weaker, two-factor conclusion.

The paper sets up two rings linked by a ring map, with a module over each ring and a matching map between the modules. Within that setup, Gündüz studies 2-absorbing submodules and their amalgamations, which glue a submodule of one module to data from the other. The work extends prime-like concepts to this joined setting, where results from each side must fit together.
arxiv-2510-10063:
Yang presents CLMN in this 2025 arXiv paper on interpretable language models. Deep learning leads natural language processing, but its opacity is a real problem in high-stakes fields like healthcare and finance, where decisions must be explained. Concept bottleneck models helped in vision by routing predictions through human-understandable concepts.

Their move to language is understudied and still limited. CLMN ties predictions to named concepts and reasons over them with symbolic rules. The design aims for transparency that survives contact with real text tasks. A model whose steps can be inspected is easier to audit before it is trusted with consequential calls.
arxiv-2510-10163:
Plou, Borja, Martínez-Cantín, and Murillo present SparseUWSeg in this 2025 arXiv paper on underwater image analysis. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel of an image by category, automating the study of underwater scenes for ecology monitoring. Even top models struggle with fine-grained underwater analysis.

The bottleneck is supervision: dense expert labels for underwater scenes are costly to produce. SparseUWSeg uses active sparse point-label augmentation, starting from a few labeled points and growing them into training signal. The method asks for labels only where they add the most value. Cheaper supervision could unlock segmentation for marine surveys that cannot afford full annotation of every frame.
arxiv-2510-10263:
Kanwal, Muhammad Sami Siddiqui, and Syed Anael Ali profile gamer archetypes in this 2025 arXiv paper on gaming analytics. Video games have grown from a niche pastime into a global entertainment and social medium. Knowing what kinds of players exist helps designers and platforms serve them.

The authors use multimodal feature correlations and unsupervised learning to uncover archetypes from gaming behavior. Unsupervised means the groups emerge from the data rather than from preset labels. Correlating features across modes of play sharpens the clusters. And a knowledge graph links the resulting archetypes to their traits. The work offers a data-driven map of player types for an industry that often segments its audience by intuition.
arxiv-2510-10863:
Aleksander Skenderi shows that discrete subgroups of Lie groups always contain large free semigroups, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is a connected real Lie group that is semisimple, has finite center, and has no compact factors. Inside it sits a Zariski dense discrete subgroup, a discrete set of symmetries spread through the group. A subsemigroup's growth is measured by its critical exponent. The natural question is whether these exponents must stay below the whole group's exponent by some gap.

Skenderi proves there is no gap. Inside it sit free, finitely generated subsemigroups whose critical exponents come arbitrarily close to the group's own exponent. These subsemigroups are themselves Zariski dense and satisfy a strong property called P-Anosov. The contrast is with a 2003 gap theorem of Leuzinger for certain subgroups with property (T). As an application, the critical exponent is lower semicontinuous when subgroups converge in the Chabauty topology.
arxiv-2510-10963:
Zhuo Li and five co-authors sharpen reward models, the scorers that steer language models toward human preferences, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard reward models train on pairwise preferences with the Bradley-Terry objective. They struggle to separate similar responses, overfit easy examples, and generalize poorly to new distributions. The team's APLOT method adds an adaptive margin: pairs that are hard to tell apart get extra separation pressure.

The margins are set from both semantic similarity and the model's own predicted reward differences. Choosing them is framed as a distribution matching problem and solved with optimal transport, which computes the cheapest way to morph one distribution into another. Across multiple benchmarks, APLOT beat several existing reward modeling techniques in distribution and out of distribution. It also converged faster. Follow up reinforcement learning experiments confirmed the practical payoff: models aligned with APLOT reward models matched human preferences better.
arxiv-2510-11063:
Chang Liu, Henghui Ding, and a large group of organizers report on the 2025 edition of a major video segmentation contest, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The LSVOS challenge, now in its seventh year and held with ICCV 2025, tests how well algorithms track objects through video. It keeps two classic tracks: standard video object segmentation and the referring variant, where a text description picks the target. A new third track, Complex VOS, built on the MOSEv2 dataset, raises the difficulty sharply.

The new track packs in denser small objects, frequent disappearances and reappearances, severe occlusions, and bad weather and lighting. Its ranking metric is adapted to credit performance across object scales and disappearance cases. The report summarizes datasets and protocols, highlights the top performing solutions, and distills trends: language model components are entering pipelines, and memory aware propagation is becoming central.
arxiv-2510-11363:
Recent cosmic surveys hint the standard cosmology is incomplete; one fix is an interaction in which dark energy and dark matter exchange energy. Tian-Nuo Li and co-authors test that idea in this 2025 arXiv cosmology paper. They combine the latest DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation data with cosmic microwave background data and two supernova compilations.

The team analyzed four interacting dark energy models with different forms of the coupling term, using data from Planck, ACT, SPT, and WMAP plus PantheonPlus and DESY5. Microwave background experiments beyond Planck strengthened the evidence for an interaction in models where the coupling scales with the dark energy density. With SPT, DESI, and DESY5 data, the best-supported model gave a coupling deviating from zero at the 3.4 sigma level, weakening to 2.1 sigma with PantheonPlus instead. Bayes factors favored the interacting models over the standard model in all cases.
arxiv-2510-11463:
The ALICE experiment at CERN is upgrading its inner tracking system with sensors bent into true cylinders, which demands silicon chips the size of a whole wafer. Omar Abdelrahman and a large collaboration report the characterization of the prototype in this 2025 arXiv instrumentation paper. The device, called MOSS, is a monolithic stitched sensor fabricated by joining reticles across a wafer into one continuous pixel matrix.

The stitched sensors measure 1.4 by 25.9 centimeters and are thinned to fifty micrometers so they can be bent around the beam pipe. The paper describes the chip architecture and in-pixel front-end electronics, then reports laboratory and in-beam characterization, tests of susceptibility to single-event radiation effects, and series testing. The campaign validates the wafer-scale stitched design, with pixel matrix performance inside the upgrade's requirements. The authors conclude the prototype demonstrates the feasibility of the ITS3 detector concept.
arxiv-2510-11563:
A chatbot can ace cultural trivia yet converse in a style that feels wrong to users from that culture. Shreya Havaldar, Sunny Rai, Young-Min Cho, and Lyle Ungar build the first benchmark aimed at that conversational gap in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their framework, grounded in sociocultural theory, formalizes how linguistic style is shaped by three forces at once: the situation, the relationship between speakers, and the cultural context.

From the framework they construct a benchmark dataset annotated by culturally diverse raters. They propose three criteria for cross-cultural evaluation in natural language processing: conversational framing, stylistic sensitivity, and subjective correctness. The last one recognizes that more than one response style can be right. Evaluating today's top large language models on the benchmark, they show the models struggle with cultural adaptation in conversation. The authors argue trivia-style evaluations are misaligned with real conversational challenges.
arxiv-2510-11763:
Virgile Troude and Didier Sornette offer a new origin story for power laws, behind wealth inequality and market crashes. Such heavy-tailed patterns are usually blamed on systems sitting near a critical point. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies multidimensional Kesten processes, where a vector of coupled components is multiplied by random matrices again and again and topped up with noise.

Even when every random matrix is stable on its own, trouble can grow because the matrices' eigenvectors are not perpendicular. That non-normality lets disturbances swell for a while before decaying, and the swelling changes the system's long-run behavior. Troude and Sornette derive explicit formulas linking the growth rate and the tail exponent to the statistics of a quantity called the condition number. Computer runs confirm the links. The picture unifies cases as unlike as polymer stretching in turbulence, magnetic dynamos, and clustered market swings, all with no true instability.
arxiv-2510-11963:
Aditya Gupta, Kirandeep Kaur, and Vinayak Gupta propose reading a language model the way physicists read a quantum system. Tools that peek at transformers today offer diagnostic checkpoints: intermediate guesses at the final answer. What is missing is a mathematical story of how each layer moves the model from one state to the next. Their 2025 arXiv paper, QLens, borrows that story from quantum mechanics.

Under QLens, a transformer's activations become a state vector in a Hilbert space built from its output units. Each hidden layer acts as a unitary operator, with an associated Hamiltonian describing the evolution it drives. The final probability distribution emerges by the Born rule, quantum theory's way of turning states into odds. The authors stress the framework is preliminary. As a proof of concept, they probe a toy transformer to trace how individual layers steer its prediction trajectory. The hope is a foundation for mechanistic interpretability.
arxiv-2510-12063:
Sunzhu Li and four colleagues steer reasoning models by evolving the instructions tucked before their thoughts. Large reasoning models often wander or overthink. Training-free fixes rely on rigid heuristics, while analyses describe problems without fixing them. ThinkPilot, their 2025 arXiv paper, runs an evolutionary search over think-prefixes, guided by a taxonomy of reasoning behaviors.

The gains are broad. Accuracy per token improves across benchmarks; on one math test, two iterations raised accuracy by over three percent while cutting token use by a fifth. Safety improves dramatically: one model's harmful-response score on a jailbreak benchmark fell from twenty-seven percent to under one percent. Instruction following improves too, and the method stacks with training-based techniques. The analysis shows prefixes reliably control behavior, and that tasks strongly prefer particular behavior mixes. ThinkPilot finds and elicits those mixes automatically. Steering, it turns out, can be evolved rather than hand-written.
arxiv-2510-12263:
Aditya and Kataria examine whether Milky Way like galaxies stay stable against local disc instabilities, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. They use the TNG50 simulation of galaxy formation in a large cosmic volume. Their sample covers ten barred and ten unbarred galaxies like our own, traced from cosmic noon to today.

Their stability criterion accounts for stars, gas, and the dark matter halo's gravity. The galaxies stayed stable against axisymmetric instabilities at every epoch, with the stability measure always above the critical range. Stability grew at higher redshift, where faster gas motions offset the weakening effect of larger gas fractions. Barred galaxies were always less stable than unbarred ones, though still stable. Gas density stayed below the critical value everywhere, so these instabilities are not the main trigger of star formation. Growth timescales ran from a few million years at galactic centers to billions of years in outer discs.
arxiv-2510-12763:
Sihag, Mateos, and Ribeiro offer a tutorial on brain age gap models, which estimate how much older a brain looks than its owner's age, in a 2025 arXiv paper. They explain the models through graph signal processing. The brain age gap is a compact summary of brain health: models predict it from magnetic resonance imaging, and larger gaps track neurodegeneration and disease severity. Clinicians, however, have struggled to deploy these models because their inner workings are opaque.

The tutorial surveys the algorithm family and the evidence for its clinical relevance, then names the roadblocks to adoption. The central problem is conceptual: nothing guarantees that a model accurate at predicting age yields a meaningful gap measure, and heterogeneous patient populations strain generalization. The authors identify mathematical principles from graph signal processing to ground what these models compute. Their aim is to disentangle genuine neurodegeneration signals from the statistical structure of neuroimaging data.
arxiv-2510-13063:
Mitchel, Ryu, and Sitzmann argue that transferable poses define true novel view synthesis in this 2025 arXiv paper. Novel view synthesis re-renders a scene from new camera angles, and self-supervised methods try to learn it from video without known camera poses. The authors propose a sharp test: a pose extracted from one video should drive the same camera trajectory in a different scene.

Auditing prior self-supervised methods, they found predicted poses fail that test, producing different trajectories in different scenes. Their model, XFactor, is the first geometry-free self-supervised system passing it, combining pairwise pose estimation with a simple input-output augmentation that disentangles camera pose from scene content. It uses no explicit three-dimensional pose parameterization. Large-scale experiments with a new transferability metric showed XFactor far ahead of earlier pose-free transformers, and probing found its latent poses correlate strongly with real camera poses.
arxiv-2510-13163:
Iskandar, Bedri, and Tsen explore graph-based code generation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models write raw sequential code well, but visual programming systems represent logic as nodes wired by edges, where big chunks of behavior live inside predefined blocks. That graph form matters when source code is inaccessible to users or missing from training data.

The authors propose and evaluate JSON representations of such graphs, testing them on ScratchTest, a mini-benchmark built on their own Python re-implementation of the Scratch programming environment. Models were asked to generate code graphs in a single pass. The findings show language models can indeed perform this generation without specialized pipelines, provided the graph representation is right. Different representations induced significantly different accuracies, which the authors read as evidence that representation choice is instrumental, and a first step toward representation learning for graph-based code generation.
arxiv-2510-13263:
Collier, Gozzard, Wallis, and Dix-Matthews stabilize the phase of a very long optical interferometer in this 2025 arXiv paper, published in Optica. Astronomical interferometers gain resolution from long baselines between apertures, but attenuation, phase noise in the optical path, and delay line limits cap practical baselines at a few hundred meters. The authors push far beyond that with fiber links.

They implemented off-band phase stabilization on two fiber links of eighty-five kilometers each, creating a total baseline of one hundred seventy kilometers, and fed the interferometer an incoherent pseudo-thermal source. The system cut phase noise by four to five orders of magnitude across the relevant frequency band and could track an applied phase sweep continuously. With stabilization active, the interferometer recovered both first-order and second-order photon correlations, showing feasibility for long-baseline optical and quantum astronomy, limited mainly by chromatic dispersion.
arxiv-2510-13663:
Demir proves a fragmentation property for relative Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms on symplectic manifolds. This 2025 arXiv paper studies smooth maps that preserve a symplectic form and also fix a Lagrangian submanifold. Such maps form the group Ham(M,L), a relative version of a classic object. Fragmentation means each map splits into pieces supported on small regions.

The proof adapts relative versions of techniques built by Thurston and Banyaga. Those tools were first made for ordinary Hamiltonian diffeomorphism groups. Carrying them into the relative setting takes care, since the Lagrangian must stay invariant throughout. The result adds the relative group to the list of transformation groups with this splitting trait. Such traits feed into questions about group structure and simplicity in symplectic topology. The paper sets out the needed flux and covering-space background along the way. It is a short, focused contribution to the area.
arxiv-2510-13763:
Yang and co-authors let users swap the prior of a trained diffusion-based inference model at test time, with no retraining. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves simulation-based inference, where neural models learn to invert simulators. Amortized models answer new datasets instantly after one expensive training phase. The catch: training bakes in one prior over the unknown parameters.

Real users often gain new knowledge after training, or disagree with the original prior. PriorGuide answers with a guidance approximation that steers the diffusion sampler. The trained model bends toward the new prior while sampling posteriors. No simulator calls or gradient updates are needed for the switch. The technique targets diffusion-based amortized methods specifically. It preserves their speed advantage while removing the prior lock-in. Fields like engineering and neuroscience, where priors evolve with experiments, benefit most directly.
arxiv-2510-14063:
Nan Li and co-authors present OATH, a framework for assigning tasks to teams of different kinds of robots working in obstacle-filled spaces, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multi-agent task assignment and planning struggles with scale, spatial reasoning, and adapting as the environment changes, especially when robots have different capabilities.

OATH introduces an adaptive Halton sequence map, which spreads sampling points across space but adjusts their density according to where obstacles sit, the first use of obstacle-aware sampling in this problem. A cluster-auction-selection scheme groups tasks with obstacle-aware clustering, lets robots bid in weighted auctions, and finalizes selections inside each cluster, keeping coordination effective and scalable. A large language model interprets human instructions and steers the planner in real time. Validated in the NVIDIA Isaac simulator and on TurtleBot hardware, OATH improved assignment quality, scalability, and adaptability over state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2510-14163:
Mohammadsajad Alipour and Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri propose reversible model merging, a take on combining fine-tuned models into one artifact, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Merging usually collapses all task-specific models into a single set of weights. But the authors show a problem. Applying standard merging to low-rank weights, the compressed form produced by adapters or by singular value decomposition, badly degrades performance.

Their reframing keeps a basis from which each specialist model can be recovered by linear combination, so merging becomes building a reconstruction-capable model space rather than one compromised average. This allows reverting to the specialist model when a task demands it, since no merged model always beats one. Their method, RMM, is efficient, needs no data, and computes the mixing coefficients by formula. Experiments across data sets and model scales show RMM outperforms approaches for low-rank models by a wide margin.
arxiv-2510-14263:
Mary Graveman and co-authors settle a question in noncommutative geometry about how many distinct holomorphic structures can live on line bundles over the quantum projective line, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The quantum projective line is a deformed version of the ordinary sphere-like projective line, where coordinates no longer commute. A holomorphic structure is the extra data that lets one speak of holomorphic sections, central to complex geometry.

The authors show that there exist infinitely many holomorphic structures on these line bundles that are not gauge equivalent, meaning no change of trivialization can turn one into another. This answers no to a 2011 question from Khalkhali, Landi, and Van Suijlekom. They had asked whether exotic structures exist, or whether the quantum geometry forces uniqueness, as in some classical settings. The result shows the noncommutative projective line is richer in holomorphic structures than its classical counterpart.
arxiv-2510-14363:
Lachlan Passenger and co-authors ask whether GW231123, the most massive black hole merger yet heard by gravitational-wave detectors, was built from earlier mergers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The event's black holes are both heavy and spinning near the maximum, a combination stellar evolution struggles to produce, prompting a flurry of explanations.

Hierarchical assembly is the suspect: in dense star clusters, merger remnants can pair up and merge again, stacking mass and spin across generations. The authors test whether GW231123 could be the merger of two second-generation black holes in such a cluster. Taking the inferred spins at face value, they find it is possible, with probability around five percent, that a binary with spins like those observed forms this way in a cluster. The answer is 'not ruled out, but not favored either,' sharpening what future events must show to prove hierarchical assembly happens.
arxiv-2510-14763:
The M-A-P group and 2077AI present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a dataset meant to teach language models creative writing in Chinese, thought processes included. Models write far worse creatively in Chinese than in English, because training data is scarce and rarely shows how a text was composed. The authors reverse-engineered high-quality texts: for each, they reconstructed the prompt, wrote out the creative reasoning step by step, and kept the final piece.

The result, COIG-Writer, holds 1,665 such triplets across fifty-one genres. Experiments suggest creative writing has two separable parts: narrative logic, from process supervision, and linguistic expression, from general data. Process data works only when diluted, at least one creative sample per twelve general ones; below that ratio, win rates fell steadily in their tests. Creative skill also proved culture-bound, with no transfer between Chinese and English. Paradoxically, higher word diversity tracked lower quality.
arxiv-2510-15463:
Otto A. Hannuksela and six colleagues settle how to judge claims that a gravitational wave was seen twice through a cosmic lens. Their 2025 arXiv paper explains that massive galaxies can split a gravitational wave into repeated copies, differing in loudness, arrival time, and phase. Searches by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration now hunt for such pairs in a growing event catalog.

A statistical trap lurks, since more events mean more chance look-alike pairs, much like shared birthdays in a crowd. Two camps, frequentist and Bayesian, had developed separate detection methods. The team recasts both in Bayesian language and derives the posterior odds for strong lensing. Their key finding is that while the Bayes factor and prior odds shift with catalog size, the posterior odds stay stable once lensing time delays are included. A normalization tied to selection effects cancels out of the final odds, simplifying future searches.
arxiv-2510-15563:
Edward Tansley, Estelle Massart, and Coralia Cartis test a proposed law about how deep networks organize their first layer during training.
