Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns the neural feature ansatz, which says the Gram matrix of first-layer weights ends up proportional to a power of the average gradient outer product. Earlier work proved this for two-layer linear networks under balanced starting weights.

The team extends the proof to any depth of at least two layers, and the exponent changes with depth in a simple reciprocal pattern. With lopsided starting weights, the law still holds in the long run if weight decay is applied. They also give counterexamples where the ansatz fails for some nonlinear architectures, even when those networks fit the training data perfectly. Simulations across optimizers, decay rates, and initializations backed the theory. The work sharpens when feature learning can be predicted from gradients alone.
arxiv-2510-15663:
Counting periodic orbits in chaotic systems relies on pressure, a quantity weighting orbits by their behavior. Richard Sharp proves equidistribution results for a broad class of such systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. The systems are skew products over countable-state Markov shifts, extended by amenable groups. Amenable groups are those tame enough to admit averaging, like abelian groups. Earlier pressure equality results required the base system to have finitely many states.

Sharp shows the Gurevič pressure of the extension equals that of its abelianized version, without extra hypotheses. He also proves a weighted equidistribution theorem when the base has the BIP property. The pressure equality is the key step behind the equidistribution result.
arxiv-2510-15763:
Qihao Peng, Jiuyu Liu, Qu Luo, and Yi Ma propose a simpler receiver in a 2025 paper. The receiver is for future wireless systems. It senses signals with atoms. Many antennas work at once in this atomic MIMO design. A programmable panel helps steer the radio waves. The design uses pulse amplitude modulation to line up signal phases.

Lining up the phases removes phase ambiguity. That ambiguity is what makes atomic receivers complex. Removing it cuts detection complexity sharply. The team reshaped the remaining design problem into a tractable form. They solved it with a gradient descent method built on Adam. The receiver settings rest on that solution. The goal is a practical, low-complexity quantum sensing receiver.
arxiv-2510-15963:
Jiani Huang leads eight co-authors with a framework that grounds embodied agents in scene graphs of what they see. Multimodal models aim to serve as general embodied agents, but they often miss fine links between low-level visual detail and high-level meaning, which weakens perception. ESCA answers by describing each scene as a spatial-temporal graph of objects and relations.

At its core sits SGCLIP, an open-domain model that generates scene graphs on request, built on CLIP. It trains on a large set of open videos through a neurosymbolic pipeline that aligns automatic captions with graphs the model itself produces, needing no human labels. SGCLIP leads on scene graph and action localisation benchmarks, in both prompt and fine-tuned use. Plugged into open and commercial agents, ESCA cuts perception errors and lets open models pass proprietary baselines, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16063:
Muhy Eddin Za'ter and Bri-Mathias Hodge estimate substation voltages across whole distribution networks with a hierarchical graph neural network. Accurate voltage knowledge underpins real-time monitoring and grid reliability. As rooftop solar and other distributed resources make distribution voltages swing more, state estimation grows more essential, yet classic methods buckle under sparse measurements and modern feeder scale.

Their network exploits both electrical topology and physical features and stays robust at the low observability typical of real feeders. Trained and tested on the public SMART-DS data sets, it covers thousands of buses across many substations and solar penetration levels. Error runs up to twofold lower than rival data-driven models, and accuracy stays high with as little as one percent of buses measured. The pair present graph networks as a scalable, reproducible path to distribution monitoring.
arxiv-2510-16763:
Victor Barroso-Nascimento, Maria Osório, and Elaine Pimentel present a bilateral logic in which proving and refuting are separate acts that can never both succeed on the same claim. Most logics treat denial as a by-product of proof. Bilateralism instead gives assertion and denial equal standing, an idea first used to defend classical logic.

Their system is written as a natural deduction calculus with strong proof-theoretic behavior, including normalization. A base-extension semantics demands explicit constructions of proofs and refutations while blocking both for one formula. The authors prove the semantics sound and complete for the calculus. They also show their refutation matches David Nelson's notion of constructive falsity, so the system extends intuitionistic logic rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2510-16863:
Shujian Gao, Yuan Wang, and Zekuan Yu target cheaper medical image labeling in a 2025 paper. Their task is segmentation, marking which pixels in a scan belong to disease. Full labeling of three-dimensional scans is slow and costly. Semi-supervised methods learn from a few labeled scans plus many unlabeled ones.

Their framework, called BARL, aligns two model branches in two ways. One way keeps the predicted labels of both branches consistent. The other way matches their inner features, region by region and lesion by lesion. That second alignment had been mostly ignored before. Tests on four public datasets and one hospital dataset beat earlier methods. Separate checks confirmed each added part helped the final score.
arxiv-2510-16963:
Donggu Lee, Sung Joon Maeng, and Ismail Guvenc model drone interference over cities in a 2025 paper. Drones can cover disaster zones and watch over crowded areas. In dense cities, though, their control links face heavy interference. Signals traveling upward suffer more than signals traveling downward.

The authors build a random-geometry framework for this lopsided interference. Their model captures how interference clusters across city space. It tracks both altitude and horizontal distance to the controller. They define a ratio measuring the uplink-downlink interference gap. Simulations show the gap grows with altitude and distance. Higher drones see more interfering signals along clear sight lines. The results warn planners that uplink links need extra protection.
arxiv-2510-17063:
Shunan Sheng, Bohan Wu, and Alberto González-Sanz explain a failure of a common approximation method in a 2025 paper. Mean-field variational inference approximates complex probability distributions with simpler ones. It replaces tangled distributions by products of independent pieces. Users often see its answers collapse onto one mode.

Mode collapse means the approximation hugs one peak and ignores others. The authors give the first theoretical explanation of this behavior. They measure component separation with a new separateness notion. Explicit bounds then limit the mass placed on each component. The analysis extends from two components to many. Collapse turns out to depend on the components' relative positions. Their fix adds a rotation to the approximation family. Numerical tests support both the theory and the remedy.
arxiv-2510-17263:
Avishek Lahiri, Yufang Hou, and Debarshi Kumar Sanyal build survey outlines with language models in this 2025 paper. Outlines, called taxonomies, sort a field into a tree of topics. Good outlines help scholars map and scan a whole field. Past auto survey tools never checked tree match with expert trees.

Their bench holds four hundred sixty outlines drawn from expert surveys. A held-out set adds eighty trees from meeting surveys. Their three-step method guides topic picks with model prompts. Strict scores grade both tree shape match and sense match. Their method beats baselines on near all scores, by machine and by hand.
arxiv-2510-17463:
Court records look like solid ground truth for training legal prediction models, but Cor Steging and Tadeusz Zbiegień warn that the labels hide human choices. A recorded outcome may reflect a settlement, an appeal, or another step that could easily have gone the other way. They call that gap label indeterminacy: the same case could carry a different label if an intervention had or had not happened.

Methods exist to fill in such uncertain labels, yet all of them rest on assumptions that cannot be checked. Using cases from the European Court of Human Rights, Steging and Zbiegień show that how labels are built during training can strongly change model behaviour. They urge legal machine learning to treat label indeterminacy as a core concern, not a footnote.
arxiv-2510-17563:
Helium atoms drift into the solar system from interstellar space, and counting how many get ionised by sunlight helps map the neighbourhood around the Sun. Małgorzata Antonik and four co-authors use data from the SWAP instrument aboard the New Horizons spacecraft, which catches the pickup ions created when those helium atoms gain a charge. A recent analysis of a different mission had suggested that sunlight ionises this helium far faster than models predicted.

Antonik and her co-authors built a new fitting method for a decade of SWAP data gathered far beyond Earth orbit, accounting for the spacecraft rotation and the instrument response. Their measured photoionisation rate came out well over forty percent above the model values, confirming the earlier hint. The result forces a revision of how interstellar helium is tracked through the heliosphere.
arxiv-2510-17663:
Faqiang Yuan, with Haida Li and two co-authors, quantizes a modified gravity theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. In scalar-tensor gravity, an extra scalar field joins the usual metric in describing gravity. The theory's Hamiltonian constraint, an equation linking energy terms, normally blocks a clear notion of time. The authors use the scalar field itself as the clock to remove that block.

With time defined this way, they quantize the system nonperturbatively using loop quantum gravity methods. Physical states then evolve in discrete steps with respect to the gravitational degree of freedom. They work out the physical solutions for the Brans-Dicke cosmological model, a classic scalar-tensor case. The quantum dynamics replaces the classical big bang singularity with a quantum bounce.
arxiv-2510-17963:
Matthias Fabry and Andrej Prša model how close double stars evolve when heat flows between them and magnetic braking weakens at high strength. These contact binaries circle each other in under a day. Their slow spiral inward is thought to be driven by magnetic braking, the loss linked to stellar winds and spin.

Evidence from detached pairs already hints that braking saturates rather than growing by the classic law. The new models add support for that weaker braking. They also show that energy transfer is needed across a wide range to explain the very uneven masses seen in such pairs.
arxiv-2510-18363:
Zhen Zhang and Bingsheng He tackle a learning problem on graphs, where data points are linked in a network. A model trained on a fully labeled source graph often must work on a target graph with no labels. Standard methods assume both graphs use the same set of classes, yet real target graphs may hold node types the source never showed, and those new types still need to be spotted.

Their framework, called GraphRTA, reprograms both sides of the problem. It reshapes the target graph so known and unknown classes separate more clearly, and it trims source-specific parts of the model while keeping parts that transfer well. An extra output slot handles the unknown class, removing the need to pick a cutoff by hand. Experiments on public data sets showed solid results against recent leading methods.
arxiv-2510-18963:
Zekun Zhuang and three co-authors study superconducting diode effects in materials that lack a center of symmetry. When a magnetic field lies in the plane and spin-orbit coupling is present, current can flow more easily one way than the other, in both bulk samples and Josephson junctions.

Using a quasiclassical method, the team maps helical phases where Cooper pairs carry finite motion, along with related Fermi surfaces. They find diode efficiency can approach its highest allowed value near a transition between weak and strong helical phases. The results guide searches for controllable nonreciprocal superconductors.
arxiv-2510-19363:
Siyuan Wang and six co-authors introduce LoongRL, a reinforcement learning method that teaches language models to reason over very long contexts. Reinforcement learning sharpened short reasoning by rewarding step-by-step breakthroughs, but long documents pose harder problems, and good training tasks for them are scarce.

Their KeyChain synthesis hides a true question inside large piles of distracting documents, linked by chains of identifiers the model must trace in order. Solving such tasks forces the model to find the real question, pull the right facts, and reason across them. The approach builds advanced long-context thinking from ordinary multi-hop questions.
arxiv-2510-19563:
Asaf Nachmias and Yuval Peled determine the local limit of a broad family of determinantal processes. These random processes arise from orthogonal projections and include uniform spanning trees, determinantal hypertrees, and related structures in combinatorics. The authors look at projections onto row spaces of signed adjacency matrices of certain bipartite graphs with no four-cycles.

As the graph grows, one side's degree rises without bound while the other side's stays fixed. Nachmias and Peled show the local limit is a variant of a branching process with Poisson-distributed offspring, conditioned to survive forever. The single result covers spanning trees, hyperforests, discrete Grassmannians, and incidence matroids whenever their degree tends to infinity.
arxiv-2510-19663:
Vojtěch Vrba and three co-authors speed up the marker detection that lets drone swarms locate each other visually. In agile unmanned aerial vehicle swarms, each craft finds its teammates by spotting ultraviolet markers in camera frames, and that detection has to run onboard in real time. The team re-engineered the detector three ways: an optimized CPU routine, a GPU shader, and an FPGA streaming design.

The CPU and GPU versions cut the average processing time per pixel by two to three orders of magnitude compared with the unoptimized state of the art. The FPGA version minimized the total delay from camera exposure to detection result. Tests on several embedded platforms showed the approach works even on low-end drones.
arxiv-2510-19763:
Max Dupré la Tour, Manuel Lafond, and Ndiamé Ndiaye prove that recognizing two graph classes invented to model family trees is NP-complete. Both classes date back more than twenty years, built as stripped-down stand-ins for the trees that show how species relate. Much research followed, but their recognition problems stayed open. NP-completeness means no fast general algorithm is likely to exist.

The hardness result reaches beyond the two original classes. It covers a broader hierarchy, including pairwise compatibility graphs and their multi-interval generalizations. For biologists and computer scientists who hoped to test fast whether data fit these tree-based models, the answer is discouraging but clear. The task sits in the same hard family as classic intractable problems.
arxiv-2510-19863:
K. El Bourakadi and four co-authors trace how features stamped by cosmic inflation would show up in the first stars and galaxies. Working in the transfer function formalism, they follow primordial perturbations into the matter power spectrum. Then they use the spread of smoothed density fields, with the Press-Schechter framework, to predict how many dark matter halos collapse. The analysis then turns to gas falling into small halos.

Molecular hydrogen cooling governs that collapse and leads toward the first, Population III stars. The authors also examine primordial black holes as seeds whose accretion could grow early galaxies. Wavy features from inflation, they conclude, can measurably alter halo counts and early galaxy traits. That gives the James Webb Space Telescope a possible test of high-energy physics.
arxiv-2510-20063:
Alec Dektor and three co-authors introduce a subspace iteration method for finding low-lying excited states of quantum many-body systems on two-dimensional lattices. Their approach rests on a new block isometric projected entangled pair state form, which extends the block matrix product state idea from one-dimensional chains to two dimensions.

The new form allows exact block orthogonalization, controlled local truncation through singular value decompositions, and efficient measurement of observables. The authors test the inexact iteration on the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising and Heisenberg models and compare with existing pair state methods. Their results show that block isometric tensor networks offer a scalable way to study excitations beyond one dimension.
arxiv-2510-20263:
Tahir Boudjeriou and Prosenjit Roy study how weak solutions act far out in long tube domains for a fractional p-Laplacian task. The tubes grow without bound in one sense. The op is non-local, which brings hard points that local work does not face. Their study sits in a non-local frame built for such tasks.

The main results tell how solutions act as the tube stretches. They stretch and round out like facts known in the local case. The pair frame the work as the non-local twin of the known local view for long tubes. In that way, readers gain a broad tool set for far-out asks on fractional tasks in stretched domains.
arxiv-2510-20363:
András Rácz and three co-authors build AttDet, a MIMO receiver shaped by the transformer plan. MIMO links send and catch waves on many paths at once. Their method treats each sent layer as a token and learns cross-stream clash with a light self-attention step. Query and key parts come straight from the gauged channel grid, so scores map channel links.

Value parts start from matched-filter reads and are honed step by step. The design joins model-based clarity with learned give. Link sim tests use real 5G channel forms and high mixed code schemes. Scores land near the best error rates for both bits and blocks. Cost stays in a known poly form, which aids real use.
arxiv-2510-20963:
Yongqiang Chen leads four co-authors on when and why multi agent debate among language models fails, and whether it truly underperforms a single agent. Debate was promoted as a way to pool model wisdom and even supervise stronger systems, yet mounting results show it often loses to simpler setups.

Two popular forms are analyzed by their incentives, competitive debate where agents hold opposing sides, and consensus seeking debate where agents are pushed to agree. Both forms carry structural flaws in the analysis, such as pressure that rewards winning or agreeing over being right. The findings guide when debate helps, when it hurts, and how protocols might be repaired.
arxiv-2510-21363:
Zihao Fu and five co-authors tackle bias in text-to-image models, which often copy and even strengthen social stereotypes about groups such as gender and race groups. Their tool, FairImagen, debiases a model after training, working only on the numerical form of the prompt, so the image model itself stays untouched.

A fair version of principal component analysis projects prompt codes into a space that keeps the prompt's meaning while stripping out group-specific signals. Added noise strengthens the effect, and a single unified projection can debias several traits at once, including combined settings. Across gender, race, and combined tests, fairness improves clearly while picture quality and faithfulness to the prompt dip only moderately, beating other after-the-fact methods.
arxiv-2510-21663:
Aarav Shetty and Gary B. Huang sort synapses into types without being shown any labeled examples, reading only electron microscope images of fly brains. Knowing a synapse's type can hint at its chemical messenger or at whether its strength can be tuned, yet hand-labeling enough examples to train a classifier is slow. The true number of types is unknown beforehand.

Their unsupervised trick leans on biology: synapses sitting near each other on the same neuron probably resemble each other more than random pairs drawn across cells. Learning from that neighborhood signal alone, the method separates synapses into classes whose count it discovers rather than assumes. Beyond the immediate sorting, the classes can help experts choose ground-truth examples that span the real range of synapse shapes for future studies.
arxiv-2510-21763:
Julien Boudier and Hugo Caselles-Dupré give artists two missing dials for AI image generation: proportion and perspective. Text-to-image models render beautifully but place objects at whatever size and geometry they please, leaving illustrators and designers without the spatial authority they have in every traditional medium.

Two specialized ControlNet modules add that authority. One reads bounding boxes and honors the position and scale they dictate for each object; the other reads vanishing lines and bends the scene's three-dimensional geometry to match. Vision-language models help annotate the training data, and custom algorithms synthesize the conditioning images. Experiments show both dials work, though complex combined constraints still strain them, and both modules are released publicly for others to build on.
arxiv-2510-21863:
Max Nguyen and Vardan Adibekyan ask how the metal content of a star shapes the planets that form around it. The standard core accretion picture explains small and mid-sized planets well. The heaviest planets are often credited to a different route, gravitational collapse, which might not care about metals at all.

Using the total heavy-element share of each star as a stand-in for the raw material in its planet-forming disk, the pair find that even the most massive planets favor metal-rich homes. Metal content also tracks with how many planets a system holds and their combined mass, though the clear link to individual planet mass appears at the top of the mass range. Disk chemistry, they conclude, steers planet formation at every size.
arxiv-2510-21963:
Vincent Flynn and Benedetta Flebus report an unusual state of matter assembled inside an ordinary ferromagnetic multilayer, a stack of magnetic films. By balancing an electric drive against the natural damping of the magnet, they stabilize a self-organized, current-carrying state that keeps cycling in time rather than settling down.

That swirling state, a spin superfluid, breaks the symmetry between directions. Ripples traveling one way along it move differently from ripples traveling the other way. The material acts like a one-way valve, or diode, for spin waves, with no structural asymmetry or finely tuned gain and loss required. The mathematics of the flow even maps onto waves moving in curved spacetime, and shaping the drive can create sonic horizons, raising the prospect of tabletop gravity analogues.
arxiv-2510-22363:
Jan Simson and four co-authors argue that fairness research in machine learning often rests on a narrow and messy set of data. Studies pick few datasets, handle them in unlike ways, and then claim broad results. To fix that base, they built FairGround, a shared corpus and software package for fair classification work.

FairGround holds forty four tabular datasets, each with notes on traits that matter for fairness checks. The package gives one standard way to load, clean, split, and change the data. Readers get a clear case for starting fairness work with better, shared data.
arxiv-2510-22563:
Patrick Erik Bradley, writing alone in 2025, builds diffusion operators on p-adic analytic manifolds, spaces from a number system where closeness is measured differently from ordinary geometry. Kernel functions, the weights inside such operators, are assembled from local charts stitched together across the space.

In the compact case, Bradley defines an operator of Vladimirov-Taibleson type, tuned by a real parameter. He establishes its spectrum, meaning its set of vibration like values, and shows it generates a well behaved heat flow. Heat and Green functions exist when the parameter is large enough. An application counts points on certain elliptic curves over finite fields.
arxiv-2510-22763:
Large models can translate well, but they are costly to run. Yasmin Moslem, Muhammad Hazim Al Farouq, and John D Kelleher tackle that cost in 2025. Their entry targets a model compression track. The method cuts model layers one step at a time. Layer importance guides each cut.

They test on the Aya-Expanse-8B model. One task is Czech to German. The other is English to Egyptian Arabic. Cutting layers shrinks the model a lot. Inference also runs faster. Translation quality stays near the baseline level. The work shows pruning can suit real translation use.
arxiv-2510-23163:
Hang Lei and five co-authors argue that screenplays should not be written by a language model in one direct pass. A screenplay sets story structure, character growth, and dialogue for a production. Forcing one model to master creative storytelling and strict format at once, they say, yields scripts that mimic style but lack substance.

Their decomposed approach splits the work so each capability gets focused handling. Narrative construction and format adherence are treated as separate jobs that are later joined. The method aims for scripts with real structural integrity, a practical direction for AI tools in television and film writing rooms.
arxiv-2510-23363:
Sean Fletcher and five co-authors classify exposure to the drug paclitaxel from microscope images of glioma cells using an interpretable tile-based method. Scalable, objective readouts speed drug discovery and preclinical testing. Dose differences here are subtle, and full-image models struggle with them in phase-contrast images of C6 glioma cells.

Their pipeline cuts images into tiles, classifies each patch, and aggregates tile outputs into an image label. It beats the published baseline by about twenty percentage points on the benchmark. Because decisions rest on visible tiles, biologists can inspect which regions drove the call.
arxiv-2510-23863:
Pritom Mozumdar and three co-authors present MAGNUS I, a sample of 213 early-type galaxies at intermediate distances, seen as they were several billion years ago. The team combines integral-field spectroscopy from the MUSE-DEEP survey with Hubble imaging. With those data they measure each galaxy's structure, the motion of its stars, and the makeup of its populations.

Galaxies are classed as fast or slow rotators using a proxy for specific angular momentum. The slow rotator share matches local samples, suggesting the early-type population has changed little over the span covered. Fast rotators show well-aligned kinematic and photometric axes, like their nearby counterparts. Age, metal content, and mass-to-light ratio all track the central velocity dispersion, following local trends. Slow rotators are heavier, hotter, and more metal-rich. The authors conclude the scaling relations of these galaxies were already set seven billion years ago.
arxiv-2510-23963:
Hiroki Ishikawa and two co-authors build a soft robot finger that twists as it bends, so it can wrap around objects and lift them out of clutter. Picking one item from a dense bin demands a finger that slips into narrow gaps, which requires twisting both in its plane and out of it. After insertion, the finger must press with the right normal force while holding the twisted shape — a combination the authors call grasping by wrapping.

Both abilities run off a single actuation source, thanks to a variable stiffness mechanism whose stiffness rises with pressure. The team ran finite element analysis on the design and fixed its parameters from the results. A built prototype then demonstrated the idea in basic experiments, grasping a variety of objects. The work targets the messy case that defeats rigid grippers: mixed piles where the target is wedged between neighbors.
arxiv-2510-24063:
Yicheng Chen and three co-authors test fast machine learning tools for guessing the redox potential of molecules. This value shows how easily a molecule gains or loses electrons, and it matters for uses like capturing carbon with electricity. Exact quantum chemistry is accurate but slow and costly for screening many molecules at once.

The team compares two foundation potentials, MACE-OMol-0 and UMA, against a range of quantum methods and lab data. Both tools do very well for reactions that move protons and electrons together, close to their target method. They do less well for pure electron transfer, most of all when several electrons move at once.
arxiv-2510-24263:
Maksymilian Manko studies the module theory of a new family of ribbon Hopf algebras, working alone. These algebras do not split into tensor parts. They were first built in recent work that used a method due to Nenciu. This paper is a sequel. It asks how the modules of these algebras behave and how their module classes are put together.

Manko sorts the basic blocks that cannot be split further. He treats both the projective blocks and the simple ones. He also breaks the adjoint module into its parts and proves the rules for how those parts fuse. He then looks at the centers of these classes and notes they can fail to be semisimple. A new family over fields of prime characteristic is also treated, with links to four dimensional field theories.
arxiv-2510-24363:
Maxim N. Chernodub and three co-authors describe a one quark state bound to a reflective boundary in the confinement phase of quantum chromodynamics. Using lattice Yang-Mills simulations at finite and zero temperature, they place a test quark near a chromometallic mirror. The quark is attracted to its neutral mirror image by a Cornell type potential, forming a state they call a quarkiton.

Surprisingly, the string between the quark and the mirror has lower tension than the fundamental string. The quark is confined near the mirror yet can still travel freely along it, a partial confinement like surface excitons in metals. The finding suggests new bound states at QCD boundaries.
arxiv-2510-24463:
Hao Jia leads a team of twelve authors on electric circuits and physics. Topolectrical circuits use wired boards to mimic quantum materials. Such boards let labs test exotic states with cheap, safe parts. Past boards were hard to retune and poor at guessing new states. The team add deep learning and full tuning to one platform.

Each site term and link term on the board tunes on its own. A physics-aware AI design tool proposes states to build and test. The board showed edge states, slow phase shifts, and flat energy bands. It also placed Anderson localization, wave trapping by disorder, at chosen spots. That control beats the random trapping seen in older setups. They even hid full text messages with the trapping patterns.
arxiv-2510-24663:
Yifu Lu, Shengjie Liu, and Li Dong build a test set for agents that call tools over many turns. Most past work looks at one call or a short chain, not a web of steps. Their pipe, OrchDAG, lays tool steps out as a graph with no loops, where each step can feed later ones.

They can set how hard each graph is, then score how well a model runs it. A new graph based prize helps train models with trial based learning. Tests show the set is hard but can be solved. Their point is that graph shape and task depth should guide training.
arxiv-2510-25063:
Nikki Xu and Hien Tran show that a trial based controller is just as good as the model it was trained on. Such controllers learn in a fake world, then must run on real gear. When the fake model is off, the learned controller can shine in the fake world yet fail on the real rig.

With a true model, by contrast, the controller held up to shakes and small gaps with the real rig. A sense check helps show why the two cases split. A map of the zone where the controller can pull the rig back helps draw its strength. The lesson is blunt: model care comes first, or the learned gains are at risk.
arxiv-2510-25463:
Hongjie Zhang, Gideon Billings, and Stefan B Williams present SPADE. Their 2025 paper values depth underwater from one camera. Underwater infrastructure needs frequent inspection and maintenance. Harsh marine settings damage forms over time. Human divers and remotely operated vehicles face limits. Turbid water and complex forms challenge perception greatly.

SPADE stands for Sparsity Changing Depth Estimator here. It mixes a pretrained relative depth estimator first. Sparse depth priors supply metric scale information. A two-stage method scales the relative map first. Cascade transformer blocks then refine the final prediction. Those blocks use convolution and deformable attention ideas. The system produces dense, metric-scale depth maps. Quality and generalization beat leading rivals, they report. It runs over fifteen frames per second quickly. Embedded hardware can run it in real time. Useful underwater inspection and intervention may benefit. Greater vehicle autonomy could reduce piloting risks.
arxiv-2510-25563:
Victor Medina, Giovanny A Cuervo-Londono, and Javier Sanchez forecast sea surface temperature. Their 2025 paper adapts an atmospheric foundation model. Classic numeric forecasting faces computational cost limits. Scalability is another limitation of numeric methods.

Fine-tuning uses high-resolution oceanographic reanalysis data. The target region is the Canary Upwelling System. Staged fine-tuning incorporates latitude-weighted error metrics. Hyperparameters were optimized for quick learning during tuning. The model reached low root-mean-square error overall. Anomaly correlation stayed very high in tests. Finer coastal details proved harder to capture accurately. Data-driven ocean forecasting feasibility is showed here. Models pretrained in other domains can transfer. Future work may add variables and physics-informed networks.
arxiv-2510-25863:
Ken Huang leads ten co-authors in presenting a governance platform for autonomous AI agents used in real workplaces. Agents that act at machine speed and improvise can break the assumptions behind standard software security tools. Their platform, AAGATE, is built to run on Kubernetes, a system for managing container software, and it follows the national AI risk framework from NIST.

Huang and the team attach a specialized method to each risk step, from threat modeling to red team testing. The platform adds a zero trust service mesh, a policy engine that can explain its choices, behavior tracking, and accountability hooks. Extra modules cover identity rights, logic layer attacks, and signs of cognitive decline in agents.
arxiv-2510-25963:
Izzy Grosof and Daniela Hurtado-Lange introduce a scheduling rule that beats a famous benchmark at every load. The setting is a queue with several servers, where jobs of known size arrive over time. SRPT, short for shortest remaining processing time, serves the job closest to done. It is known to be near optimal when the system is almost full. Yet no rule had beaten its multi server version anywhere.

Grosof and Hurtado-Lange propose a variant that, in specific cases, serves large jobs before small ones to keep servers better used. That counterintuitive move lowers the mean response time for later jobs. They prove the gain for all loads and job size patterns, then test a simpler practical version in simulation.
arxiv-2510-26263:
Duaa Abdullah and Jasem Hamoud study whether popular mathematical puzzles improve the thinking of Syrian schoolchildren. The paper first gives an overview of problems and background in mathematics education in Syrian schools. Puzzles are widely believed to build problem solving skill and flexible thinking, but classroom evidence in this setting is limited.

Abdullah and Hamoud run a paired experimental study with a pre test and post test control group design. Their sample is sixth grade primary students at the Lady Mary School in Syria. Skills were measured before and after the puzzle work, and results were analyzed with a t test, a standard statistical tool for comparing group means. The study evaluates how far puzzles shift problem solving and mathematical skills.
arxiv-2510-26363:
Ilya Kurinov, with Miroslav Ivanov, Grzegorz Orzechowski, and Aki Mikkola, tackles a hard job in forestry: loading cut logs onto a forwarder, the truck that hauls timber out of the woods. Driving one is tiring work done far from help for long hours. The team asks if a learning program could take over the loading task.

Kurinov and his three co-authors train their program by trial and error inside a simulator built in NVIDIA Isaac Gym. The program learns step by step, from finding and gripping a log to carrying it to the truck bed. Its best run finished the full task in ninety-four cases out of a hundred. The work points toward machines that ease the load on human operators.
arxiv-2510-27063:
Shairoz Sohail and Taher Ali ask a basic question in their 2025 paper: when do two programs count as truly alike? An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. Two recipes can look quite different yet do the same job. The pair note that no test can settle this in full. Still, fields like clone hunting and program writing need a workable score.

They first review older ways of judging sameness. Then they set out EMOC, a scheme that scores a program on four traits: how it runs, memory use, step counts, and growth of cost. They also built PACD, a checked set of Python programs for three problems. Tests show the scores group like programs, spot near copies, and gauge variety in code written by AI models. Code and data are shared openly.
arxiv-2510-27563:
Volodymyr Vasylkovskyi and seven co-authors report a clean way to make tiny crystals called perovskites in 2025. These crystals respond strongly to light and suit solar cells, lights, and sensors. Past ways to make them use liquid mixes and added coats. The new way uses very short laser pulses in open air, with no liquid and no added coats.

Crystals form with high purity and sizes that vary by recipe. One hybrid kind forms larger cubes near ninety units across, while a lead-free kind forms small rounds near ten units. Light tests show color shifts tied to size, an effect of small scale. The method could ease work on new light-based tools.
arxiv-2511-00663:
Alex Dobra and eight co-authors make sensitivity analysis cheap for climate science. Asking how a storm or a feedback responds to sea surface temperature usually means weeks on a supercomputer with a physical model. Generative AI weather models evaluate in a blink, but extracting sensitivities from them stayed a bottleneck. The authors apply the adjoint state method, a classic gradient technique, to generative flow models.

Working with the cBottle generative model, trained on ERA5 and ICON data, they compute how any atmospheric variable responds to sea surface temperatures. The gradients check out quantitatively against the model's own outputs. What took weeks on a supercomputer now takes hours on a GPU. The speedup simplifies a core climate workflow and widens who can afford to ask sensitivity questions.
arxiv-2511-00763:
Wanda Hou and five co-authors measure how long language models can stay focused on repetitive, deterministic tasks. The tasks apply one rule again and again: letter replacement, integer addition, and string operator multiplication drawn from quantum mechanics. If a model simply repeated a fixed procedure, its success rate should decay exponentially with output length, each step adding an independent chance to slip.

Experiments on leading models reject that picture completely. Accuracy falls off a cliff: the negative log of the success rate grows faster than linearly, and performance collapses near a characteristic length. A double-exponential accumulation law fits the crossover, and its scale is stable across fitting choices. A minimal model of interacting step-correctness variables, solved by direct enumeration, reproduces the cliff and assigns each model-task pair an intrinsic error rate and an accumulation factor.
arxiv-2511-01563:
Jakob Stoye, Simon Mataigne, Pierre-Antoine Absil, and Ralf Zimmermann measure shortest closed geodesics on the Stiefel manifold. These are the tightest loops that start and end at the same point, heading the same way. That space, the set of orthonormal frames in a larger space, underlies problems from computer vision to quantum chemistry, and its geometry depends on the metric chosen.

Working across a one-parameter family of metrics that includes the standard canonical and Euclidean choices, the authors determine the exact length of the shortest nontrivial geodesic loop. Combining older and new bounds on sectional curvature, they then pin down the injectivity radius. That is the largest distance over which shortest paths stay unique. They pin it down exactly, for a wide range of the metric family.
arxiv-2511-01663:
Louis Bradshaw, Alexander Spangher, Stella Biderman, and Simon Colton built a piano that duets with an artificial intelligence. Generative music models are capable, they note, but musicians must usually prompt them with text and wait, a workflow far from the give-and-take of playing an instrument. Their system, Aria-Duet, uses a Yamaha Disklavier self-playing piano as the shared instrument.

The pianist plays, signals a handover, and the generative model Aria continues the piece, performed acoustically on the same piano in real time. Analyzing the output musicologically, the authors find the model maintains stylistic character and develops coherent phrasal ideas across the exchanges. They present the system as evidence that embodied, turn-taking setups can support genuine musical dialogue between people and models.
arxiv-2511-02163:
L. F. Melo, János Bergou, and Alexandre Tacla improve how receivers in quantum communication tell apart signals made of laser light. Coherent states must be distinguished to share secret keys, and one strategy, unambiguous discrimination, sometimes answers with certainty and sometimes gives up. The failure outcomes are normally thrown away. The authors show those failures still carry usable information about which state was sent, at least when more than two states are in play.

Their scheme recycles the failure states into a second, minimum-error discrimination step, so every trial ends with a definite answer, and a flagged subset of answers is guaranteed error-free. They quantify the disturbance the first step causes and show that at the low light levels used for long-distance key distribution, the separation succeeds often while disturbing the states only slightly.
arxiv-2511-02263:
Jaeyeon Lee, Lin Yao, Hyun-Hwan Jeong, and Zhandong Liu speed up the hunt for the gene behind a rare disease. Clinicians must match a patient's symptoms against genes carrying suspicious variants, across sprawling and inconsistent evidence sources, which makes interpretation slow. Their system, LA-MARRVEL, adds a language-model reranking layer on top of an existing prioritisation pipeline rather than replacing it.

The framework improved top-rank accuracy by twelve to fifteen percentage points over established approaches across three real-world patient cohorts, including cases where the true gene had initially been ranked low. The biggest contributor was prompt construction: giving the model rich, structured phenotype descriptions beat using disease labels alone. For each candidate gene the system also writes an auditable explanation aligned with clinical guidelines, weighing how well symptoms fit, the inheritance pattern, and the variant evidence.
arxiv-2511-02363:
Jie Sheng, Tsutomu Yanagida, Bo Gao, and Hong Ding propose a tabletop test of an unobserved prediction of gauge theory: electromagnetic memory. The idea is that a passing electromagnetic disturbance can leave a permanent phase imprint on charged quantum states, long after the field itself has vanished. The effect is tied to soft photons and large gauge transformations. It has never been verified in an experiment.

The authors point out that gravity itself can write the imprint. The electric field and gauge potential induced inside a usual conductor by gravitational acceleration provide a clean source of the phase. A superconducting measurement protocol can then read the stored phase back out. For representative experimental parameters, the predicted signal falls within the reach of present-day sensitivities, which would make this subtle infrared effect testable on a bench rather than only in theory.
arxiv-2511-02663:
Simone Formentin asks whether politicians change the tone of their posts in response to how the public reacts. The 2025 study draws on more than 1.5 million tweets posted in 2021 by members of parliament in the United Kingdom, Spain, and Greece. A simple linear model tracks how the mood of one post relates to feedback on earlier posts.

The analysis finds a closed loop: cheers and jeers both shape the tone of later posts. Roles matter too. Opposition members reacted most to negative feedback, while government officials responded more to praise. Formentin frames the result in control theory terms, showing how feedback rules can explain self-reinforcing spirals in online political talk.
arxiv-2511-02763:
Guy Katriel studies a classic selling puzzle: a seller must accept one offer before a deadline, and each rejected offer is gone. In his 2025 version of the Cayley-Moser problem, offers arrive at random times set by a Poisson process, rather than in neat rounds. Each offer is an independent draw from a known distribution.

The continuous-time setup proves far easier to solve than the usual discrete one. It yields a simple differential equation whose explicit solution gives the best selling rule. Katriel then derives exact formulas for the spread of the final sale price and of the sale time itself. He uses those results to probe how the rule behaves, and tests the theory on several concrete offer distributions.
arxiv-2511-02863: David LeBlond reframes the electron double-slit experiment, where single electrons build up an interference pattern, through indivisible stochastic processes. That view treats each event as a whole that cannot be split into steps. It gives a statistical reading of quantum probability and coherence rather than a purely wave-based one. His 2025 paper presents the model as a teaching tool and supplies R code so readers can run it. The aim is a fresh lens on what the experiment says about nature at small scales.
arxiv-2511-02963:
Walner Mendonca, Meysam Miralaei, and Guilherme Mota prove a new result in Ramsey theory, the study of patterns forced by coloring. Color every edge of a graph red or blue. Some graphs force either a red complete group of one size or a blue complete group of another. Their 2025 paper builds a graph with an asymmetric pair of such guarantees, tuned close to the classic Ramsey threshold.

Their graph avoids forcing the symmetric pair at size k, yet it does force a mixed pair: a near-maximal red clique or a slightly smaller blue one. The proof uses probabilistic methods and hypergraph containers, tools for taming huge families of sets. The result varies a classical theorem of Nesetril and Rodl from the nineteen seventies.
arxiv-2511-03063:
Margarita Geleta, Daniel Mas Montserrat, and Alexander Ioannidis generalize a classic genetics statistic that measures how populations differ. The fixation index compares variation within groups to the whole. Their 2025 paper defines a Tsallis-entropy version with a tuning order q. At q equal to two it matches the classic index, and at q equal to one it becomes a Shannon entropy form tied to mutual information between alleles and population labels.

Turning q down weights rare variants more, while higher q stresses common ones, giving a finer view when variant frequencies are skewed. On 865 Oceanian genomes and on simulated genealogies, the statistic pinpointed which groups drive regional structure. It also dated isolation, migration, and founder events with good sensitivity, in two comparison modes.
arxiv-2511-03263:
Ruizhe Zheng and co-authors build FAPEX, a system meant to warn of epileptic seizures across people it has never seen. Brain signals differ a lot from person to person and across recording setups, which makes a single warning model hard to trust. FAPEX uses a learnable frame that splits signals by both time and pitch, with fractional math that keeps high and low parts in balance.

From that split, the system reads instant strength and phase patterns that may mark the lead-up to a seizure. Scores rose by about a tenth over strong rivals on standard tests. The design also aims to hold up on new kinds of recordings. Better cross-person warnings could give patients and carers precious minutes to prepare.
arxiv-2511-03363:
Xiaocai Zhang and colleagues propose DMTC, a pipeline that reads traveler intent without any hand-labeled training data. Sorting transport queries by intent is hard when one message carries several aims at once. Hiring people to label thousands of examples is slow and costly, so the team skips that step entirely.

First, language models invent varied fake queries for many travel scenes. Next, a sentence encoder packs each query into a compact meaning code. Last, a light classifier trains on the fake set with a loss that stresses hard cases and pushes classes apart. Tests show the data-free route can still split fine-grained intents well. Transport assistants could adopt it where labeled data are scarce.
arxiv-2511-03663:
Prashin Jethwa, Simon Hubmer, Ronny Ramlau, and Glenn Van de Ven compare two algorithms that fit galaxy light in full three dimensions at once. Integral field data give a spectrum at every sky pixel, and fitting stars jointly across space and wavelength promises cleaner motion and population maps than slicing spectra one by one. The cost is heavy computation.

One contender adapts a projected fast reconstruction method, the other extends a Bayesian velocity tool to honor spatial correlation. Both are run on the same test data to expose strengths and weak spots. Three-dimensional fitting should cut noise-driven wiggles that plague pixel-by-pixel work. Better stellar maps sharpen stories of how galaxies formed their disks and bulges.
arxiv-2511-03863:
Olha Silina, writing alone, studies the perfect matching lattice of a matching covered graph, the lattice generated by incidence vectors of all its perfect matchings. Building on work by Lovasz and by de Carvalho, Lucchesi, and Murty, Silina gives a polynomial-time, polyhedral method to build a lattice basis made of perfect matchings.

Decomposition along certain odd cuts reduces the graph to pieces whose perfect matching polytopes match their bipartite relaxations, known as Birkhoff-von Neumann graphs. That reduction yields a constructive proof that such bases exist. It also exposes fresh links between combinatorial structure and geometry in the theory of perfect matchings.
arxiv-2511-04263:
Zeinab Bakhshipour and Mir Vahid Hosseini study the helical edge of a 2D topological insulator when disorder, a Zeeman field, and superconductivity act together. Bosonization and renormalization-group analysis track how impurity potentials reshape charge and spin density waves and pairs along that edge.

The Zeeman field steers the contest. In the attractive regime it widens the superconducting gap, while in the repulsive regime it keeps disorder active for longer. Disorder cuts transverse density waves by a log factor yet adds positive corrections that strengthen pairing. Spin conductance scaling changes with it, giving lab tests clear signatures of how the two interact in such channels.
arxiv-2511-04563:
Vincent Gierisch and his co-author introduce QEF, a framework for quantum software experiments. Today's noisy quantum devices allow small hybrid experiments, but tools often hide settings or demand ad hoc scripts. That makes results hard to repeat or compare.

QEF supports systematic, hypothesis-driven study of quantum algorithms on real hardware. It favors step-by-step exploration of evolving strategies over one fixed score run. A literature review shaped which parameters and measurements the framework records. By capturing the full setup of each run, QEF aims to make quantum software claims checkable by other teams.
arxiv-2511-04663:
Ryan Golant and three colleagues examine intermittency in collisionless, large-amplitude plasma turbulence. Here the wobbling magnetic field outweighs the steady one, and sharp bends and reversals appear. Magnetohydrodynamic models cannot describe most cosmic plasma, where collisions are negligible.

Fully kinetic three-dimensional simulations of electron-positron plasma supply the evidence. The team varies the field ratio and the gap between driving and small scales. They track how the intense, localized structures form and behave in this regime. Such structures may drive particle transport and acceleration across astrophysical settings, from solar wind to distant jets.
arxiv-2511-04763:
Chris Kouvaris and his co-author calculate millicharged particle production inside pulsars. Such particles carry a tiny fraction of an electron's charge and could form dark matter. Strong electric fields can create them through the Schwinger effect.

The polar gap of a pulsar supplies the needed field strength. Once made, particles accelerate past megaelectronvolt energies in the local field. Some would reach Earth, where low-threshold detectors could catch them. Current XENONnT data already limits charges for particles from the Crab pulsar. The pulsar route turns nearby neutron stars into natural factories for testing dark sector ideas.
arxiv-2511-04963:
Xiongri Shen and co-authors propose PDS, a diffusion method that can create one kind of brain scan from another. Clinics use both functional and diffusion MRI to study brain disease, but one type is often missing for a patient.

PDS learns across the two modes with a pattern-aware design, then refines tissue and fine structure to keep scans true. The signal styles of the two modes differ a lot, which made past attempts weak. On three data sets, the method tops prior work on both scan types, with clear gains in standard quality scores.
arxiv-2511-05363:
Aparna Maya Warrier and co-authors study how community college instructors judge no-code, scenario-based tools for teaching AI literacy to non-STEM students. AI literacy now matters across fields, yet good, scalable ways to teach it outside STEM are scarce.

The team built AI U, a set of hands-on projects with no coding, set in real-world scenes. Instructors tried the tools and rated their fit for class use. Their views show what helps non-expert learners grasp how AI works and where it can mislead, which guides design of such courses very well.
arxiv-2511-05463:
Manan Vyas and co-authors shrink the correlation matrix of S&P 500 stock returns down to a two-by-two matrix, the most extreme coarse view that still keeps mean correlation as a parameter. A full matrix has far too many values to read as a market gauge.

They split stocks into two sets, average the matrix over the blocks that split creates, and keep that block structure. Sector-based views sit between the full matrix and this bare form. The aim is a tiny set of numbers that still tracks how stocks move together in stress and calm.
arxiv-2511-05563:
Sanghyun Lee, Seungryong Kim, Jongho Park, and Dongmin Park improve how diffusion language models choose the order in which they reveal words. These models start from masked text and uncover tokens step by step. Common rules pick the most confident token next, a greedy habit that can lock in early mistakes.

Their method, Lookahead Unmasking, treats decoding as picking a full path rather than single steps. It proposes several unmasking orders, scores each by its uncertainty, and keeps the safest paths. Only two or three paths were needed for peak scores. Across six benchmarks in math, planning, and coding, the method lifted results for two versions of the LLaDA model.
arxiv-2511-05863:
Yuning Chen, Sha Zhao, Shijian Li, and Gang Pan unify how brain-wave data from many studies can teach one emotion-recognition model. EEG emotion data sets differ wildly in labels and formats, so models trained on one rarely transfer. The team maps every label scheme into one shared space of valence and arousal, the two axes that describe feeling pleasantness and intensity.

A soft-weighted contrastive loss then pulls emotionally similar samples together in that space. A flexible backbone reads time, frequency, and spatial features from varied EEG formats. Pretrained on eight public data sets, the model reached state-of-the-art scores on three benchmarks. The authors argue the shared emotion space is what lets knowledge move between studies.
arxiv-2511-05963:
Jayden Teoh leads a team adding a training signal that pushes transformers to build compact inner world models. A transformer remembers by keeping every past token available, so it has no pressure to compress history into a tidy state with steady rules. That habit, the authors argue, hurts generalization.

Their method, NextLat, also trains the model to predict its own next inner state, given the next token. Theory shows those inner states converge toward belief states: the compressed facts about the past that matter for the future. Architecture, training speed, and inference stay unchanged. Across world modeling, reasoning, planning, and language benchmarks, NextLat beat plain next-token training on accuracy, compression, and lookahead planning.
arxiv-2511-06063:
Wentao Tang and Xiuzhen Ye choose a special function space so that the Koopman operator, a linear lens on nonlinear dynamics, can certify stability. The operator lifts a nonlinear system into a linear one on a space of observables. For stability work that space should reflect both local behavior near an equilibrium and global smoothness.

They build the space from a product kernel: a linear kernel times a Wendland radial kernel. Under smoothness conditions the space is invariant under the operator. When the equilibrium is stable, the operator's spectrum provably sits inside the unit circle, and escapes when a bifurcation hits. Learned from data with a proven error bound, the operator thus becomes a stability certificate for control use.
arxiv-2511-06763:
Nicy Scaria, Silvester John Joseph Kennedy, and Deepak Subramani test how sensitive small language models are to corrupted training data. They instruction-tuned 23 models, ranging from 270 million to 4 billion parameters, on data mixed with controlled amounts of damage. The damage came in syntactic forms, like reversed characters or words, and semantic forms, like irrelevant or false answers.

Syntactic damage proved devastating: character reversal caused near-total failure in every model, whatever its size or family. Semantic damage hurt less and showed threshold behavior, but larger and more capable models were paradoxically easier to corrupt, following harmful instructions more readily. The authors argue that small models need contamination-aware training, since the usual assumptions about robustness do not hold.
arxiv-2511-07063:
Alexander B Shick and Evgenia A Tereshina-Chitrova model the permanent magnet CeCo5, whose cerium atoms fluctuate between valence states and defeat standard electronic structure methods. Plain density functional theory, even with a static correction, cannot reproduce its magnetism. The authors combine that fix with exact diagonalization of an Anderson impurity model for the cerium f shell, capturing the fast fluctuations.

The fluctuations greatly shrink the cerium spin and orbital moments, matching more expensive dynamical mean-field results. The computed total moment of 6.70 Bohr magnetons agrees with experiment, the f-electron spectrum reproduces photoemission readings. The magnetic anisotropy energy reaches 4.8 millielectronvolts per formula unit, in very good accord with data. The work offers guidance toward high-performance magnets using less rare-earth substance.
arxiv-2511-07163:
Ruiqi Lyu, Alistair Turcan, and Bryan Wilder detect disease outbreaks in real time by fusing noisy data streams that individually would mislead. Case counts alone are erratic, and aggregation tricks that denoise other fields are underexplored in epidemiology. Their system, LRTrend, is an interpretable machine learning system that combines diverse health and behavioral signals within each region and learns disease-certain epidemic networks to share information across regions.

The learned networks reveal clusters and connections across the United States that human mobility networks do not explain, a finding with coordination implications for public health agencies. Applied to two years of COVID-19 data across 305 hospital referral regions, LRTrend frequently flagged the Delta and Omicron waves within two weeks of their start. At that point cases were still a small fraction of the eventual peak.
arxiv-2511-07263:
Saba Latif, Huma Latif, Touseef Ur Rehman, and Muhammad Rameez Ur Rahman verify object-centric event data formally before it ever reaches a database. Process mining traditionally flattens event logs, losing relationships among the interacting objects, while object-centric data keeps them native. Their system specifies temporal features and structural relationships between objects and events in the Alloy modeling language. It then checks them against constraints such as cross-object cardinality bounds and time-aware consistency rules.

Verification catches data integrity problems early and exposes implicit dependencies among objects in event logs. That matters when importing data into graph databases like Neo4j, where flaws can make data effectively invisible. Automatically generated Python bindings expose the verified system, called FOCED, to industrial users without formal methods expertise, and the code is public.
arxiv-2511-07663:
Paweł Liskowski and colleagues at Snowflake describe Cortex AISQL, a database engine that answers questions about messy data with plain SQL. Users can mix normal relational queries with semantic operations that read text and other unstructured content. Production scale makes that blend hard, since semantic steps cost more and behave unlike joins or filters.

Costs and selectivity stay unknown while a query is compiled, so classic optimizers stumble. The engine redesigns planning and execution around those unknowns. Companies sit on mountains of documents beside their tables; a system that queries both together, declaratively, removes piles of glue code and custom pipelines.
arxiv-2511-07963:
Franc Forstneric proves that the universal family of punctured Riemann surfaces is a Stein manifold. The surfaces are compact, have a fixed genus, and carry at least one puncture. The family gathers all such surfaces into one larger space, and the paper studies that total space directly.

Along the way, fibrewise algebraic functions are shown to be dense among holomorphic functions on the family. A fibrewise algebraic map also embeds each fibre properly into Euclidean space. The paper adds a relative Oka principle for maps into flexible algebraic manifolds, describes basic function theory, and poses several open questions.
arxiv-2511-08063:
Bitap Raj Thakuria and co-authors study a cavity coupled quantum battery whose useful work is shaped by noise and leakage. Ergotropy measures the work that can be extracted from a quantum system. Their battery gains coherence from noise, and a storage station exchanges quanta with measurable higher order fluctuations.

Full counting statistics tracks those fluctuations beyond simple averages. Machine learning models, both supervised and unsupervised, then predict which operating settings give high ergotropy. Usual quantum and thermodynamic variables alone predict poorly. Instead, the kurtosis of exchange at storage and coherence in the leakage mode emerge as the controlling features.
arxiv-2511-08263:
Yue Min and co-authors introduce ImageBindDC, a method for condensing multimodal data into a tiny synthetic set that still trains models well. Data condensation works for single data types, yet paired data such as image and text must keep delicate cross links, which ordinary distribution matching loses. Their framework works inside the unified feature space of ImageBind, a model that embeds several modalities together.

A characteristic function loss aligns real and synthetic statistics through exact matching of infinitely many moments. Alignment is enforced within each modality, across hybrid real synthetic pairs, and jointly over full pairs. On one benchmark, five condensed points per class train a model matching full data performance.
arxiv-2511-08463:
Erika Palmerio argues, in a commentary, for measuring the solar wind upstream of the L1 Lagrange point before it reaches Earth monitors. Space weather forecasts start from remote images of the Sun and gain ground truth only when plasma reaches L1, typically tens of minutes before impact, and less for fast streams. The severe geomagnetic storm of May 2024 offered a natural test of an earlier vantage point.

Real time data from the STEREO-A spacecraft, sitting slightly closer to the Sun and west of Earth, were used to build predictions for that storm. Palmero contextualizes those results, weighing benefits for both basic interplanetary physics and practical forecasting. Earlier in situ sampling could meaningfully extend warning lead times.
arxiv-2511-08763:
Jerry Huang and Stefan Radev model how people move together inside immersive rooms, augmented reality spaces where several agents share one virtual world. Content and hardware have raced ahead, but the social physics of how users drift, gather, and avoid each other in these rooms is barely understood.

Their agent-based model treats each person as simple geometry that relocates and turns toward salient virtual objects. Motion mixes outside pushes, modeled as diffusion from the environment, with inside drives from agent-to-agent interaction. Simulation-based inference then recovers the model's governing parameters from simple observations of the motion. The fit captures action-related traits well but reveals spots where the data cannot pin down environmental awareness. The authors aim at rooms that adapt their interfaces to collective movement.
arxiv-2511-08963:
Moustapha Diallo and Brian McDonald connect a learning theory measure, VC-dimension, to the geometry of structured point sets over finite fields. For a family of shapes such as spheres or hyperplanes, lower-bounding the VC-dimension of the classes they define on a set amounts to building intricate geometric configurations inside that set.

The sets in question are Salem sets, which balance randomness and structure in a precise Fourier sense. The authors show that many techniques developed for distance problems over finite fields extend to a far broader setting that does not depend on the special geometry of circles and spheres. Their unified framework handles highly structured sets like algebraic curves and random sets within the same argument. The work ties the Erdős distance problem and its Falconer cousin to modern questions about the complexity of geometric hypothesis classes.
arxiv-2511-09163:
Xuyao Yu, Zijun Gong, and Zhilu Lai examine interference in integrated sensing and communication systems, which share hardware between radar-like sensing and data links. In channels that spread signals in both delay and Doppler shift, symbols and carriers interfere with each other. The paper compares four ways of handling that mixed interference.

The four options are explicit estimation and compensation, ignoring the interference, treating it as uncorrelated colored noise, or modeling the noise as correlated. Within a generalized OFDM framework, the authors derive channel estimators and their errors as sensing measures. They also bound communication capacity when channel knowledge is imperfect. The results expose clear trade-offs between performance and complexity for practical receiver design.
arxiv-2511-09263:
Stefano Balietti, Pietro Saggese, Stefan Kitzler, and Bernhard Haslhofer review whether decentralized autonomous organizations can govern democratically. DAOs run blockchain-based projects in finance, science, and digital communities through coded, open voting. Their promise is to spread decision power instead of concentrating it.

The chapter weighs that promise against familiar failure modes: token concentration, low turnout, and quiet recentralization. It also examines DAOs meeting artificial intelligence, where automation could help coordination yet weaken human oversight and openness. The authors ask when DAOs can keep their democratic aims. Without the right setup, they warn, DAOs may rebuild the very power asymmetries they set out to escape.
arxiv-2511-09663:
Cumi Oyemike and two co-authors name and measure 'alignment debt'. It is the extra work users in the Global South must do to make frontier AI systems usable. Big models assume high-resource languages, devices, knowledge, and connectivity, and misfit other contexts. A survey of 411 AI users in Kenya and Nigeria grounds the concept.

Their four-part taxonomy covers cultural and linguistic debt, reported by about half of measurable respondents. Infrastructural debt follows at about 43 percent, then epistemic debt near 34 percent and interaction debt at 14 percent. Country patterns diverge, undermining one-size-fits-Africa assumptions. Users with epistemic debt verify outputs far more often, tying fairness to user burden, not just model metrics.
arxiv-2511-09763:
Guy Blanc, Yizhi Huang, Tal Malkin, and Rocco A. Servedio compare two harsh noise models for machine learning. Under malicious noise, an adversary corrupts a random subset of training examples. Under nasty noise, the adversary picks which examples to corrupt, which sounds strictly worse for the learner. The paper asks whether efficient algorithms really find nasty noise harder.

For learning that must work across any distribution, the authors prove the two models are strongly equivalent: tolerating one rate of malicious noise means tolerating the same rate of nasty noise. For a fixed distribution, though, they show an arbitrarily large gap, under a standard cryptographic assumption. A broad class of algorithms that ignore contradictory examples recovers equivalence up to a factor of two.
arxiv-2511-10063:
Yiwen Wang, Vivek Shah, Marcos Antonio Vaz Salles, Claudia Bauzer Medeiros, Julio Cesar Dos Reis, and Yongluan Zhou present Dolphin, a database system for data about moving objects that must also react. Applications from traffic to logistics need objects that sense, move, and trigger responses, yet reactive behavior is usually hand-built by each application on top of spatio-temporal storage. Their answer is a moving actor abstraction with reaction built in.

Moving actors extend the actor model with reactive sensing, movement, and spatial querying, plus defined concurrency semantics. Dolphin layers this design, non-intrusively, on Microsoft's Orleans distributed actor framework. Experiments with realistic reactive scenarios showed the system scaling across machines while keeping reaction latency near real time, sparing developers from balancing performance and consistency by hand.
arxiv-2511-10163:
Yixin Ma, Chao Xu, and Shenghan Jiang set out a test for a class of materials whose edge states are shielded by symmetry. The hard case is where the parts inside interact strongly. Such states are on their way in quantum simulators, but the transport tests used on real samples do not fit those platforms. The team studies two cases: a boson case with a paired symmetry, and the fermion quantum spin Hall case.

Their test reads one quantity: a phase tied to the total charge in a large patch of the system. For these states, that read-out bends sharply as its angle is swept, a mark that holds up even with noise and loss. Math proofs and computer runs both back the claim, and the team says near-term quantum hardware can run the test.
arxiv-2511-10663:
Raymond Puzio and Sam McCrosson offer a new description of the renormalization transform in terms of algebra, the operation at the heart of the Kadanoff-Wilson-Fisher approach to renormalization in physics. The transform is usually computed by working with path integrals or perturbation series, routes that can be technically heavy.

In their new version, the space of interactions is treated as a semigroup under convolution, a structure that encodes how interactions combine. The renormalization transform then acts through a Lie group associated with the quantum harmonic oscillator. The authors present this as a replacement for the standard analytic machinery, recasting a central tool of renormalization theory in purely algebraic terms.
arxiv-2511-10763:
Abdul Saboor and Evgenii Vinogradov model the radio channel between drones and the ground for future 6G networks. Drones acting as aerial base stations could extend millimeter-wave coverage over cities, but the air-to-ground channel depends strongly on height and on how the city is laid out.

Using ray tracing at 26 gigahertz, they simulated about ten thousand city realizations across four urban layouts that share the same standard built-up parameters but differ in spatial organization. Line-of-sight probability and path loss both improve with altitude, and shadow fading weakens. Even with identical built-up parameters, the geometric layout shifted path-loss exponents modestly but consistently. Their unified height-dependent model matches the ray-tracing statistics and is offered as a planning tool for aerial base stations.
arxiv-2511-10863:
Yiping Ma, Yue Guo, Harish Karthikeyan, and Antigoni Polychroniadou present Armadillo, a secure aggregation system for federated learning that refuses to be disrupted by cheating clients. In this setting one powerful server trains a model with many weak clients holding private data, and the server must learn only the aggregate, never single inputs.

Armadillo guarantees that any coalition of malicious clients below the tolerated threshold can sway the result only in one way. They must lie about their own inputs within a predefined legitimate range. Two designs keep it efficient: a two-layer grouping protocol needing only simple arithmetic, and an agreement protocol that strips out malicious influence with few communication rounds. Each aggregation completes in three rounds while keeping both server and clients computationally light, improving on earlier systems' costs.
arxiv-2511-11063:
Rahul Dalal, Mathilde Gerbelli-Gauthier, and Simon Marshall prove two results on how representations of the p-adic general linear group grow. Representations are ways a group can act on a space, and fixed vectors count the parts left still by deep subgroups. How fast that still part grows is a basic measure of a representation's size.

First, they bound that growth evenly across all cases by the representation's own dimension measure, and extend the bound to key coefficient sets. Second, for unitary cases, they link that dimension to how fast matrix values fade. Both results rest on the Langlands and Zelevinsky sorting of representations.
arxiv-2511-11163:
Thomas Pethick, Kimon Antonakopoulos, and their colleagues review modern optimization methods for training neural networks, with a focus on efficiency at large scale. Training cost grows with model and data size, so the choice of optimizer shapes what is practical to build. The review is written as an introduction for both practitioners and researchers entering the area.

State-of-the-art algorithms are set under one shared template, which brings out how each adapts to structure in the problem at hand. A second thread covers how to make those algorithms indifferent to problem scale, so settings transfer across sizes. The survey maps a fast-moving field in a unified way.
arxiv-2511-11263:
Anton Talkachov, Paul Leask, and Egor Babaev show that even a seemingly single-component superconductor can carry several correlation lengths, the scales over which its order fades. A superconductor's state is usually summed up by one coherence length, but multi-part systems are known to hold several. The authors study nearest-neighbor pairing on a square lattice, which yields both s-wave and d-wave forms of the order parameter.

Even when the weaker form is fully suppressed in the ground state, its hidden rivalry leaves multiple lengths with a nontrivial ordering. Under stated conditions that ordering yields type-1.5 superconductivity, where the magnetic penetration depth falls between two coherence lengths and vortices cluster in a field.
arxiv-2511-11563:
Sylvia Yuan and five co-authors introduce LARM, a feedforward model that rebuilds three-dimensional articulated objects, things with moving joints, from just a few images. Older reconstruction methods needed dense multi-view photos and slow per-object fitting, while recent fast methods often gave coarse shapes, no surface texture, and fragile pipelines.

LARM recovers detailed geometry, realistic textures, and joint structure in one unified pass. It extends a recent view-synthesis method for static objects by reasoning jointly about camera position and joint movement inside a transformer design. Faster, cleaner articulated models would help animation, robotics simulation, and product visualization, where hinged and jointed objects are everywhere.
arxiv-2511-11863:
Ole König and seven co-authors teach a model to undo photon pile-up in X-ray data. Pile-up strikes when photons arrive too fast and the detector merges them. Bright sources suffer most. Spectra warp, inferred physics is biased, and the signal can vanish. Archives of piled-up data sit largely unused as a result.

A simulation based inference frame with a normalizing flow does the repair. It estimates posterior ranges for source values straight from piled-up eROSITA data. The intractable likelihood is sidestepped. Rescuing discarded data expands the usable X-ray archive at no new telescope cost. The approach also suits other detectors where saturation corrupts the brightest targets.
arxiv-2511-11963:
Nikola Janjušević and three co-authors rebuild noisy, accelerated MRI reconstruction on a firm statistical base. Scans speed up through undersampling. Diffusion models reconstruct well from such data. But many ignore the true acquisition noise model. They wobble when noise changes, a reliability problem in clinics.

Their method, Implicit-MAP, puts the noise model inside a maximum a posteriori frame. A stochastic ascent method is generalized to MRI encoding operators. Realistic measurement noise is handled directly. Across simulated and real noisy datasets, the method beats leading rivals. A prior that knows the physics and the noise is what hospitals need. Only then can learned reconstruction be trusted on patients.
arxiv-2511-12063:
Enoch Hyunwook Kang and Hema Yoganarasimhan present TextBO, a method for self-improving language models when checking results costs far more than making them.
