Prompt-based self-improvement can beat fine-tuning, yet most work counts how many tries are made, not how much costly feedback is used. Their aim is to gain the most from each evaluation.

TextBO extends a Bayesian optimization method with known efficiency guarantees into language space, where prompts are text and normal gradients do not apply. The authors show that simple text edits proposed by the model, paired with picking the best of several tries, mimic the right search direction. The result works purely in language, without extra training.
arxiv-2511-12163:
Vlad-Matei Angheluţă and four co-authors design controllers that keep a group of agents in a tight formation despite bounded disturbances, mainly measurement noise. Much past work treats such noise with chance-based methods. This team instead uses a deterministic, set-based approach.

Their method rests on set invariance, the idea that once a state enters a safe set it stays there, adapted to formation dynamics based on relative positions. That framework lets them tune the control law so performance bounds set in advance are guaranteed. They test the controller on the hard case of holding a tight formation while moving through a space with many obstacles.
arxiv-2511-12463:
Adham M. Alkhadrawi, Kyungsu Kim, Arif M. Rahman and Fahad Mushabbab G. Alotaibi build an explainable deep learning system to rank genes as targets for cancer therapy. The method joins two views of a protein interaction network: centrality scores that mark how connected and influential a protein is, and learned embeddings that capture the network's hidden topology.

Classifiers are trained against CRISPR essentiality scores that show which genes cancer cells need to survive. A gradient-based explanation tool then measures how much each feature drove the predictions, and a blended score mixes model probability with explanation strength. The framework reports state-of-the-art ranking of the most essential genes, with degree centrality the strongest single signal.
arxiv-2511-12563:
Eljas Linna, Kestutis Baltakys, Alexandros Iosifidis and Juho Kanniainen introduce LOBERT, a foundation model for the stream of messages that make up a financial limit order book. Order book dynamics are hard to model: events arrive at irregular times, regimes shift fast, and high-frequency traders react to visible order flow. Older models need awkward data forms and adapt poorly to new tasks.

LOBERT adapts the BERT architecture with a token scheme that treats each complete multi-dimensional order message as a single token, while keeping price, volume and time as continuous values. The encoder model is built for fine-tuning on downstream tasks. It reports leading results on predicting mid-price moves and next messages, with shorter context than prior methods.
arxiv-2511-12763:
Harrison Katz turns a research article about hotel booking lead times into a ready-to-use handbook written in R. The original study measured how the full distribution of booking lead times changes over time, using a normalized distance between distributions. It tracked that change month by month, against both the previous year and a fixed 2018 baseline. Proved a bound linking the measured change and the remaining booking horizon to the error of pickup forecasts used in revenue management.

Katz's commentary rebuilds those ideas end to end as runnable code. It uses a minimal data schema, scripted examples, and an evaluation plan fixed in advance. Every result runs on synthetic data, so readers can reproduce the whole workflow without any proprietary hotel records. The piece is a translation exercise: it takes methods published for specialists and packages them so practitioners can apply, check, and adapt them directly.
arxiv-2511-12863:
Xi Zheng and four co-authors rework a standard tool for valuing data. Data Shapley assigns each data source a fair share of a model's value, but it treats all sources as interchangeable. Modern pipelines break that symmetry: augmented data depends on originals, and stages of federated learning or fine-tuning happen in a set order. Their Asymmetric Data Shapley averages each source's contribution only over orderings that respect a given structure, keeping efficiency and linearity while honoring which sources came first.

They give two ways to compute it: a Monte Carlo estimator with accuracy guarantees, and an exact, efficient surrogate for nearest-neighbor predictors. In settings with directional and temporal dependence, the method beat benchmarks by telling novel contributions from redundant ones and by respecting training order. The goal is practical fairness in data markets: paying for what data actually added.
arxiv-2511-12963:
Crystal Su has withdrawn MedRule-KG from arXiv, and the record no longer offers a PDF, so the work should be read as a retracted proposal rather than a standing result. What it proposed was a scaffold for making large language models reason inside the rules of a domain. A compact knowledge graph would inject curated symbolic facts into prompts for mathematical and biomedical tasks. A lightweight verifier would then check each output against those rules, rejecting generations that violated them.

The preprint framed generation as constrained inference and reported, across ninety tasks in reaction feasibility, metabolic compatibility, and toxicity screening, far fewer rule violations than a chain-of-thought baseline, with little added latency. Those numbers are the author's own and, given the withdrawal, carry no current standing. The entry remains useful mainly as a record of an approach its author chose not to stand behind.
arxiv-2511-13863:
Kranti Kumar Parida, Omar Emara, Hazel Doughty, and Dima Damen define a new computer vision task: finding which objects made a collision sound in a first-person video. A crash or clatter comes from two objects meeting, so its sound depends on both, and head-mounted footage is cluttered with small, brief events. Their method learns with weak supervision, guided by the audio.

The approach builds on the CLIP and SAM2 foundation models and adds a first-person cue: objects held in the hands are likely actors in any collision. It beats rival methods by three to nearly five times on the overlap score across two new test sets drawn from EPIC and Ego4D videos.
arxiv-2511-14163:
Yuchen Zhang, Yang Liu, Hongwei Yu, and one co-author set the tightest fast-radio-burst limits yet on whether photons have any rest mass. Photons are assumed massless, but the claim needs testing, and bursts from far across the universe are ideal probes because a tiny mass would slow their radio waves measurably. The team first improved the model for how extragalactic gas spreads burst signals.

With that distribution fitting mock data well, they applied it under three cosmological models, including the evolving dark energy model favored by recent DESI results. The upper limits cluster tightly across models, showing cosmology barely matters here. The results give strong empirical backing to the massless photon.
arxiv-2511-14263:
Pietro Sittoni and Francesco Tudisco teach a transformer net to solve sets of linear equations head-on. The classic solvers for ill-posed sets need care, tuning, or expert tricks to stay exact and stable. Their model, Algebraformer, learns the task end to end. A new code scheme lets it write down a matrix and a vector with memory that grows as the square of the size.

The model stays close to the true answer even when the set is badly ill-posed. Tests cover curve-fit tasks from spectral methods for edge-value problems and speed-ups for Newton steps. It matched the accuracy of classic tools at much lower cost in use, a hint that plain neural nets can take over parts of the old science-computing stack.
arxiv-2511-14863:
S. D. von Fellenberg, R. Arcodia, and seven co-authors report new radio observations of a galaxy whose center erupts in repeating X-ray flares. These quasi-periodic eruptions are a newly found behavior of galactic nuclei, and their accretion flows look young and unlike ordinary active nuclei. A prior star-shredding event may have set the stage in some cases.

With a continent-scale radio array, the team confirms a very compact radio source at the heart of the galaxy RXJ1301.9+2747, smaller than a parsec across. Older lower-frequency data fit a falling spectrum toward higher frequencies. A source this small and steady helps narrow down what powers the eruptions, whether a compact jet or something else.
arxiv-2511-14963:
Adrian Shuai Li and Elisa Bertino present LFreeDA, a way to keep Windows malware detectors current without any new hand labels. Detectors decay as malware families drift, and relabeling fresh samples by hand or sandbox runs is slow and costly. Earlier self-training tricks label new data with the old model but waste the information already inside the unlabeled samples.

LFreeDA folds unlabeled data into training itself, so the model adapts to drift end to end with no manual labels at all. The framework is built to use the drifted samples as signal rather than as mere inputs for guesses. Label-free adaptation could let security teams refresh detectors at the speed malware actually changes.
arxiv-2511-15063:
Donggyun Seo studies twisting symmetries of free groups and the groups those twists generate together. Dehn twists are basic automorphisms modeled on twisting a surface along a curve, and they act inside the outer automorphism group of a free group. The question is what structure large powers of several twists create when they are compatible in a precise sense.

Seo proves that high enough powers of finitely many such twists generate a right-angled Artin group, a well-understood family built from commutation rules. Along the way come a criterion for when two twists commute and a compact space where combined twists act with a tame parabolic style. Fully irreducible elements, by contrast, act on that space with clean north-south dynamics.
arxiv-2511-15163:
Yang Wu, Rujing Yao, and five co-authors build TASA, a tutoring system that adapts mathematics teaching to each student's changing grasp. Language model tutors can sound human and flexible, but most ignore how a student's mastery rises, stalls, and decays through forgetting. In mathematics, where each skill builds on the last, that blindness wastes the tutoring advantage.

TASA keeps a structured persona for each student, recording proficiency across concepts, plus an event memory of past learning episodes. A forgetting model fades old mastery over time, so review arrives when it is actually needed. Scaffolding is then pitched at the student's current level, skill by skill, rather than at a class average.
arxiv-2511-15463:
Minh Trung Tran, Nasrin Sohrabi, Zahir Tari, and Qin Wang name and measure a slow crypto scam that earlier detectors miss. In a normal rug pull, a token creator holds pool tokens and sells at once, crashing the price. In the fragmented form, the exit is split across time and across many wallets, so each sale looks too small to flag.

Three tactic groups define the pattern: keep control of the pool, sell in thin slices, and pass sales to other wallets. Checking a huge set of liquidity pools, the authors label many as fragmented rug pulls and find serial scam wallets active across pools. Owner wallets now join the selling far less often, which helps the scam hide.
arxiv-2511-15563:
Shehbaz Tariq and Symeon Chatzinotas design a reliability scheme for quantum channels with many inputs and outputs, a setting expected in a future quantum internet. Noise, crosstalk, and mixing across subchannels make faithful transmission hard. Their adaptive diversity plan makes near copies of an input qubit at the sender and purifies the result at the receiver, guided by known channel information.

For fixed cloning settings, they derive a formula for the best end fidelity that can be tuned without repeated heavy optimization. A numerical program builds the purification step for a chosen success chance. Gains are largest where crosstalk dominates, and the scheme adapts on its own to channel symmetry and conditions.
arxiv-2511-16163:
Zhi Luo and four co-authors propose a verbose text induction attack that forces vision language models to generate extremely long, low value outputs. Token consumption drives energy use, latency, and cost for these models. Prior attacks merely delayed the end token, giving unstable and uncontrollable lengthening. Their two stage framework instead optimizes output token length directly as an explicit objective.

Imperceptible perturbations are injected into benign images to trigger the behavior. A malicious prompt embedding is identified first, then used to guide the perturbation. Stability and controllability improve over implicit methods. The attack exposes an efficiency vulnerability distinct from classic content jailbreaks. Defenders must guard output length, not only output content, when vision language models are deployed at scale.
arxiv-2511-16563:
Akash Deep, Svetlozar Rachev, and Frank Fabozzi build an econometric approach that joins behavioral probability weighting with heavy tailed asset returns. Investors distort probabilities in known behavioral ways, while returns show far heavier tails than Gaussian models allow. Their approach uses Student distributions with a weighting transform that preserves infinite divisibility. Dynamic pricing traits survive that combination by building.

Hundreds of thousands of records across dozens of assets over two decades test the model. Heavy tailed specifications beat Gaussian ones in most cases. Risk underestimation at extreme levels shrinks dramatically versus Gaussian practice. Joint estimation identifies tail and behavioral parameters with established asymptotic theory. Risk managers gain inference that respects both market tails and investor psychology.
arxiv-2511-17063:
Samaël Mackowiak proves that a rough version of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, a model of quantum fluids and condensates, behaves well in two dimensions, at least for short times. The roughness comes from the potential term, which can be as wild as spatial white noise. With such noise, the equation needs renormalization before it even makes sense, and standard methods fail.

Mackowiak first builds the associated Schrödinger operator from its quadratic form, then studies how smooth the functions in its domain are. Those facts feed a paracontrolled approach, a technique for taming rough equations, which yields Strichartz estimates. A contraction argument then gives local wellposedness: solutions exist, are unique, and depend sensibly on their starting data. The result widens the class of noisy quantum models on firm mathematical ground.
arxiv-2511-17263:
Ibtsam A R Alroily and Brahim Chaourar prove an inequality about counting topologies, the abstract structures that say which sets count as open on a finite set of points. Let f of n be the number of distinct such structures on n points, ignoring mere renaming of the points. The authors show that the count for a combined set is at least the product of the counts for its two parts.

The same product bound is proved for the labelled count, where points are kept distinct, and for the narrower class of T-zero topologies, in both labelled and unlabelled forms. Results of this shape matter because exact counts are known only for small sets. So bounds that link sizes give one of the few handles on how fast the numbers grow.
arxiv-2511-17763:
P. Frank Winkler, Joseph Putko, and William Blair track how the Tycho supernova remnant has changed in visible light over thirty years. They gathered images at eight times from the mid nineteen eighties to twenty sixteen, using matched background images to reveal faint knots and filaments.

Measurements of motion for dozens of filaments are far more precise than earlier work. Filaments at the outer rim expand in line with a classic blast wave value, while inner ones move more slowly. Combined with shock speeds, the motions could sharpen the distance estimate to this famous remnant.
arxiv-2511-17963:
Jun Kevin and Pujianto Yugopuspito combine two machine learning tools for managing an investment portfolio. One tool is a memory network that forecasts from past patterns, and the other is a reinforcement learning agent that adjusts holdings over time. Each tool alone misses something, forecasting without adapting or adapting without foresight.

Tested on United States and Indonesian stocks, United States Treasury bonds, and major cryptocurrencies over seven years, the hybrid is compared with equal weight, index style, and single model baselines. After transaction costs, it earns higher returns and holds up better when markets shift regime. Scores include return, volatility, risk adjusted return, and worst drawdown.
arxiv-2511-18063:
Gabriela Fernandes builds a lightweight deep learning system to flag cervical adenocarcinoma in situ, an early lesion that can progress to invasive cervical cancer if missed. Reading these tissue slides is hard, and early detection matters. The system trains on a data set of over two thousand expert-labelled tissue images, split between normal glands and the lesion, after stain normalisation and patch-based preparation.

A compact convolutional network is trained with balanced sampling and a loss that stresses hard examples. Overall accuracy lands near seventy-three percent, with balanced scores for the two classes. Heat maps show which tissue areas drive each call, and Fernandes checked those areas against known biology. The work is a step toward a virtual assistant for pathologists, not yet a clinical tool.
arxiv-2511-18163:
Pasquale De Marinis and four co-authors introduce the first dedicated method for explaining matching based few shot segmentation models. These models outline objects from new classes given only a few labeled support examples. Such models perform well, but how they decide has stayed opaque, and interpretability work had not addressed this setting.

Their Affinity Explainer uses the model's own matching scores between support and query features, at several levels, to map which support pixels drive a prediction. On standard benchmarks it beats adapted general attribution methods, and its explanations show coherent patterns that help diagnose models and choose support sets wisely.
arxiv-2511-18263:
Yuhang Bai, Kristof Berczi, and Johanna Siemelink study a combinatorial problem. In a graph whose edges are colored, the goal is to find a forest with as many edges as possible such that no two edges sharing a vertex share a color. They approach it through a broader problem about independent sets in matroids with limits on how many elements each group may contribute.

They give approximation algorithms whose guarantees depend only on the maximum degree of the grouping structure. Applied to the colored forest problem on multigraphs, the method guarantees two thirds of the optimum, improving a previously known factor. The broader framing may help other constrained selection problems.
arxiv-2511-18563:
Cem Bilaloglu, Tobias Löw, and Sylvain Calinon move robot skills across curved objects that share no global frame. On a curved skin, words like toward or along shift sense with place, so a task taught on one shape resists transfer to the next. A flat frame cannot fix that twist.

Their tool, Diffused Orientation Fields, spreads local frames smooth across the surface. A task written in those frames then needs just a few key point matches to port to a new object. The field is computed live from raw point cloud data by a diffusion solve tied to the key points. Tests vary shape, topology, and key point noise. Smooth local frames turn a hard geometry gap into a sparse match task.
arxiv-2511-18663:
J. D. Vega-Sanchez, V. H. Garzon Pacheco, N. V. Orozco Garzon, H. R. Carvajal Mora, and F. J. Lopez-Martinez ask where the gains of fluid reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, wireless surfaces whose elements can move, really come from. Is it the spatial flexibility itself, or just differences in size and phase design compared with fixed surfaces?

Benchmarking against a conventional surface of the same size and a compact surface with tighter spacing, they find position optimization helps notably only when phase design is absent. With optimal beamforming and phase shifts, that advantage vanishes against the conventional surface. The fluid surface still beats the compact one, thanks to lower spatial correlation.
arxiv-2511-18963:
Adéla Hladká and Patrícia Martinková detect biased test items by a direct, model free comparison of response curves. A biased item favors one group over another at the same skill level, a flaw called differential item functioning. Their method smooths each group's item response curve with a kernel and compares the curves head on.

The work extends past curve comparison methods to binary answers, the norm in psychometrics. A new estimator gives the test statistic's long run variance, and weight functions are tuned to lift local power. Since the limit law is unknown, a wild bootstrap drives inference. Simulations show sound error control and power on par with the standard logistic method, with gains when curves cross more than once.
arxiv-2511-19063:
Hayami Takahashi and Kensuke Takahashi propose a logic of montage as a form to express emotion beside natural language. Words can state a feeling, yet some emotional states call for a proxy or window of another kind. Their base form is the Effect of Contradictory Structure, a dynamic unit whose effect can be pleasant or unpleasant.

The push to avoid the unpleasant side acts, in their frame, as a pseudo expression of will. Such units can overlap; that overlap operation is montage. A broader Structure gathers linked units and their effects, and montage yields an Effect of Structure. A notion of strength, borrowed in the word intensity from Deleuze and Guattari, tunes the overlaps.
arxiv-2511-19163:
Wanqin Nie, Kai Tu, Minglu Ye, and Shuqin Sun propose an algorithm for group sparse optimization, where solutions should switch on only a few whole groups of variables at once. Their target problems are both nonconvex and nonsmooth, with concave parts in the goal and the constraints that encourage that grouped pattern. Such models are hard to solve directly.

The method reweights twice over: each step builds a convex stand-in problem from first-order information, then solves it with the alternating direction method of multipliers. The authors prove each step stays feasible and that limit points are stationary. Early numerical tests support the method's efficiency, including for constrained grouped models.
arxiv-2511-19563:
The CMS Collaboration searches Large Hadron Collider data for the Higgs boson decaying into a pair of light pseudoscalar bosons. Each such boson would decay into a tight electron-positron pair, giving a four-electron final state. Data come from proton collisions collected with the CMS detector from 2016 to 2018.

A new multivariate method using tracks and calorimeter data picks out the merged electron pairs. No excess above Standard Model background appears. The team sets upper limits on the decay rate for boson masses from ten to one hundred MeV, reaching sensitivities near one part in a hundred thousand. The search is the first of its kind at the LHC.
arxiv-2511-19763:
Bat-Od Battseren and Bayarmagnai Gombodorj give a short number theory proof about which prime numbers can be written as a certain quadratic form in two whole numbers. The form combines the square of one number, the product of the two, and the square of the other. They follow the strategy of Zagier's famous one-sentence proof for a kindred result about sums of two squares. They show a prime has such a representation exactly when it equals three or leaves remainder one when divided by three.

Results of this type classify primes by the forms that can build them, a theme running from Fermat onward. The proof's brevity is part of its interest: a deep-looking classification settled with a single clever involution argument, in the spirit Zagier made famous. The note adds one more prime family to the list with an elegant elementary proof.
arxiv-2511-19963:
Changho Choi, Minho Kim, and Jinkyu Kim build MambaEye, an image encoder that accepts any input size. Human vision handles changing sizes naturally, but most encoders cannot, a gap the authors aim to close. Their design uses a pure Mamba2 backbone that processes patches in strict causal order, unlike earlier Mamba vision models that look both ways.

A relative move embedding records the shift between consecutive patches, giving translation invariance and freedom in resolution and scan pattern. A diffusion-inspired loss gives step-by-step supervision, training the model to grow confident as more of the image arrives. MambaEye stays robust across resolutions, above all at large sizes on ImageNet-1K classification, while time and memory grow only linearly with patch count.
arxiv-2511-20263:
Belhasin, Golan, El-Yaniv, and Elad classify images by diffusing over the labels themselves. Their 2025 paper introduces Discrete Diffusion Classification Modeling, called DiDiCM. Standard classifiers spit out one label directly. When images are corrupted or data scarce, that directness hurts. Uncertainty deserves an explicit modeling role.

DiDiCM models the likely spread of labels for an image. Diffusion steps refine label beliefs gradually. The process can run on class scores directly. Or it can run on discrete label tokens instead. That choice trades compute against memory flexibly. A few rounds already beat standard baselines. ImageNet tests showed the edge across uncertainty levels. Gains grew as tasks got harder. Corrupted inputs benefited most from the procedure. A ResNet-50-scale variant led the comparisons shown. Code is released for other researchers. Clinics and driving face the same issue. Stepwise label polishing offers them a new lever.
arxiv-2511-20663:
Barak Or adapts a classic engineering measure to multi-agent AI systems in 2025, asking how fast a team of software agents gets its reasoning back on track after it drifts. Factory engineers time repairs with mean time to recovery; Or argues that fleets of language-model agents need the same kind of clock for thinking failures, not just crashes. His measure, MTTR-A, times the gap between reasoning going wrong and the system working coherently again.

Or tested the idea in a simulation built on the AG News corpus and the LangGraph framework, running the setup 200 times across different recovery styles. Automatic reflexes, such as rolling back or replanning, restored stability in about 6 seconds on average, while fixes needing human approval took about 12 seconds. The median recovery time across all runs was 6.21 seconds, give or take 2.14 seconds, and the companion reliability ratio came out near 0.08 on his normalised scale.
arxiv-2511-20763:
Chi-kwan Chan and colleagues introduce in 2025 a direct calibration algorithm for time-interleaved analogue-to-digital converters, the chips that digitise signals at extreme speeds by taking turns sampling. Each converter in the array has its own small errors: phase delay, gain, and offset mismatches. Together they distort the rebuilt signal and inject spurious tones, a known headache in radio astronomy, where the Event Horizon Telescope's backend suffers spectral artefacts from this cause.

The algorithm feeds the system a sinusoidal reference signal and uses Fourier analysis to isolate each mismatch type, then corrects them. Because the reference is a pure tone, each error leaves a distinct fingerprint in the frequency domain, making the diagnosis direct. Simulations validate the method and show clear gains in reconstruction accuracy. The authors stress low cost, aiming at high-speed acquisition systems.
arxiv-2511-20963:
Jerry Lin and a large team report in 2025 what happened when competition-winning climate emulators were plugged into a real climate model. Machine-learning parameterisations promise fine-scale physics at coarse-model cost, but they often blow up once coupled, a failure called online instability. The ClimSim Kaggle competition drew about 700 teams and over 10,000 submissions chasing a 50,000 dollar prize pool in summer 2024. The authors coupled architectures inspired by the winners into a model with full cloud microphysics.

The headline result: stability, once coupled, proved reproducible across diverse architectures in the low-resolution, real-geography setting, a milestone for the field. All designs shared similar biases offline and online, though they reacted differently to choices like expanding the input variable list. Several Kaggle-inspired models set state-of-the-art marks on zonal-mean bias patterns and global error. Crowdsourcing the offline problem, the authors conclude, improves online hybrid simulation.
arxiv-2511-21863:
Yeats and colleagues improve image-generating AI with a guidance trick needing no labels or extra training. Generative diffusion models produce better samples when steered, but the standard steering method, classifier-free guidance, requires labelled data and a second trained model. The team noticed the positive curvature of the model's learned density in saddle regions provides a strong steering signal.

Their method, Saddle-Free Guidance, tracks that positive curvature during sampling and uses it to push generation away from saddle regions, at the same computing cost as classifier-free guidance. It works with existing models. On unconditional ImageNet-512 generation it reached state-of-the-art scores for a single model on two quality metrics, FID and FD-DINOv2. Combined with Auto-Guidance it cut the FD-DINOv2 score by a further 10 percent in the reported experiments. Tests on two text-to-image models showed more diverse outputs.
arxiv-2511-22263:
Won, Lee, Kim, and Lee, information retrieval researchers in Korea, benchmark learned sparse search at web scale. BM25, the classic keyword ranker, is cheap but semantically shallow; SPLADE models learn sparse lexical expansions that retrieve better, especially on complex queries, at higher computational cost. The team compares BM25, SPLADE, and Expanded-SPLADE on datasets growing from tens of millions to billions of web document titles, measuring both retrieval quality and efficiency in latency and operations.

The learned models win on effectiveness; pruning strategies then claw back their cost without significantly hurting quality. Expanded-SPLADE emerges with the best effectiveness-efficiency balance, particularly on the largest collections. The authors offer the study as deployment guidance for search engines weighing sparse neural retrieval against its infrastructure bill. All three pruning strategies are simple enough to retrofit into existing sparse-retrieval deployments, which is the audience the study aims at.
arxiv-2511-22763:
Garcia-Montero and colleagues ask how gluon saturation changes proton-structure probing. In exclusive vector meson production in deep inelastic scattering, a virtual photon splits into a quark-antiquark dipole scattering off the proton and recombining into a meson, imaging its gluon distribution. At high energies the gluon density grows until gluons recombine, the saturation regime of the Color Glass Condensate. They model the proton's colour charge as localised hot spots, computing coherent and incoherent cross sections versus momentum transfer.

The verdict is measured: within the ranges studied, saturation is mild, suppressing cross sections only modestly. But suppression grows clearly as the proton's colour-charge density increases, so hotter, denser protons show stronger signatures. Comparing coherent scattering, imaging the average shape, with incoherent scattering, sensitive to fluctuations, also tests the hot spot model itself. The work calibrates what future electron-ion collider measurements should expect when hunting for saturation signs.
arxiv-2511-22963:
Liu and colleagues aim to let a humanoid robot obey free-form spoken or written commands with its whole body, not just simple preset instructions. That is hard because a humanoid has many joints and complex balance. And training data of physically possible robot motion paired with language is scarce. So earlier systems traded natural movement against staying upright.

Their model, Humanoid-LLA, first builds a shared motion vocabulary from 26,846 motion sequences, each paired with three or four written descriptions. So human and robot moves become tokens a language model can pick. A controller distilled from a privileged teacher policy then executes the chosen tokens, and physics-based fine-tuning rewards motions that respect real dynamics. Tested in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 robot, it beat earlier language-controlled systems on naturalness, stability, and how often commands were carried out successfully.
arxiv-2511-23163:
Tan and colleagues explain the wild brightness swings of VHS 1256B, a planetary-mass companion with a mass under 20 Jupiter masses and the most variable object of its kind known. Its near-infrared flux changes by nearly 40 percent as it rotates roughly every 22 hours. Recent JWST spectra showed red colors and silicate features that existing theories of patchy clouds and banded flow could not account for.

Running a general circulation model, the team finds the atmosphere is dominated by giant planet-scale dust storms that persist for tens of days. Large patchy clouds are carried by equatorial waves rather than the tidy bands of Jupiter or Neptune. That single weather pattern reproduces the observed spectra and the light curves' large amplitude, irregular evolution, and wavelength dependence at once. It also matches variability trends across dusty substellar atmospheres in near-infrared color-magnitude diagrams.
arxiv-2511-23263:
Jiang and colleagues besiege Fermi-balls, a macroscopic form of dark matter made of many dark particles bound together like an atom, from two sides. These objects are too rare for Earth-based detectors to catch. A Fermi-ball crossing a white dwarf can deposit energy to ignite runaway fusion and blow the star up as a Type Ia supernova. Surviving white dwarfs already limit how strongly these objects can interact.

With more rigorous envelope modeling and expanded white dwarf data, their updated bound on the interaction strength per unit mass tightens previous estimates by orders of magnitude. It tightens in the conservative direction they report. They then show that space gravitational-wave observatories LISA and TianQin could register passing Fermi-balls of 1 to 10^14 grams through the kicks given to their test masses. Fisher forecasts reach percent-level precision on the object's parameters.
arxiv-2511-23363:
Kelman and colleagues make property testing survive an adversary, asking whether a function between groups preserves the group operation. A homomorphism, when an online adversary can erase or corrupt answers as the test proceeds. Classical homomorphism tests assume clean query access, but in dynamic or hostile settings responses can change based on the tester's own past queries, which breaks the usual analysis completely.

Their Random Signs Test checks the homomorphism condition on sums of random group elements where each element is randomly added or subtracted. And it is provably optimal, using a number of queries that grows like one over the distance parameter plus the logarithm of the per-query corruption budget. When the adversary is powerless the bound recovers the celebrated classic query count. And the authors add improved bounds for specific group families plus a general framework for proving testers resilient.
arxiv-2512-00363:
Detecting objects in remote sensing images often means combining several kinds of sensor data at once. Jianhong Han and co-authors present MM-DETR in 2025, a multimodal detection transformer designed for efficiency. Earlier fusion blocks based on attention or deformable convolution struggle to balance accuracy with lightweight design.

MM-DETR uses Mamba-driven fusion at two granularities and frequency-aware adapters for each modality. The point is sharper, more robust perception under hard conditions, without a heavy model. Earth observation and disaster work need detectors that run fast on fused imagery from satellites and drones. Dual-granularity fusion mixes fine local detail with broad scene context. Frequency-aware adapters tune each sensor stream to what it captures best. For field teams, the gain is a tool that runs on small kit near where shots are taken. It still gives sharp, clear maps of the land.
arxiv-2512-00563:
Doctors listening to lungs with a stethoscope face subjectivity, background noise, and disagreement between clinicians. Asiful Islam Saky and co-authors present an explainable multimodal deep learning framework for detecting lung diseases from respiratory audio in 2025. Respiratory diseases remain major global health challenges.

The framework aims for automatic detection that clinicians can inspect, not just trust. Explainability is the point: a model that highlights why it flagged a recording earns a place beside the stethoscope. Reliable audio screening could extend specialist-level listening to clinics that have no respiratory expert on site. Respiratory sounds are cheap to record with ordinary microphones or digital stethoscopes. Multimodal inputs let the model combine sound types that clinicians weigh together. For clinics with no lung staff on site, the gain is a first read they can act on. Flag the sick, pass the well, and send the hard cases up the line.
arxiv-2512-00663:
Language models hallucinate, and enterprise users need those fabrications caught automatically. Tanmay Agrawal presents structured visualizations for automated hallucination detection in 2025, under the banner of graphing the truth. In enterprise settings, models are augmented with closed-source domain knowledge to give informed answers.

Grounding answers in private documents helps only if unsupported claims are still detected. Turning model statements into structured graphs makes claims checkable against sources, claim by claim. Visual detection tools could let compliance and support teams audit AI answers at scale, rather than sampling them by hand and hoping. Closed-source knowledge makes verification harder, since auditors cannot inspect the whole corpus. Structured graphs also make disagreements between model and source easy to point at.
arxiv-2512-00763:
Robin Yadav, Shuo Xie, Tianhao Wang, and Zhiyuan Li analyze a simple training method in a 2025 machine learning paper. Adaptive methods like Adam train large language models far better than plain gradient descent. Newer work explains that gap with fresh ideas about how smooth the loss surface really is.

Sign descent is a minimal method that uses only the sign of each gradient step. The authors build a small model with heavy-tail class imbalance, where rare classes carry outsized weight. In that setting, they prove sign descent has a real benefit. A clean minimal case helps show why adaptive training works.
arxiv-2512-00963:
Emmanuel Fonseca wrote a 2025 paper on measuring how neutron stars resist spinning in their orbits. A binary radio pulsar is a spinning neutron star whose radio beam sweeps Earth as it orbits a companion. A future measurement of Lense-Thirring precession in such a system could yield the pulsar's moment of inertia, a key clue to its inner matter.

The catch is confusion. In most promising systems, Lense-Thirring precession makes orbital elements drift in a straight-line fashion. Other mechanisms cause similar drifts, and they are hard to separate. Fonseca studies the nonlinear orbital variations that might set the effect apart.
arxiv-2512-01063:
Hikmatullo Ismatov wrote a 2025 teaching note on maximal monotone operators. These operators are a core tool in functional analysis and the theory of differential equations. They are also hard for beginners, since the definitions pile up quickly.

Ismatov gives a stand-alone account of the basic tools a reader needs first. The note reviews domains, including unbounded ones, plus closed sets and closed operators. Concrete examples appear in both finite and infinite dimensions. Worked examples do much of the teaching here, in both small and large settings. A friendly on-ramp matters because monotone operators underlie modern work on optimization, fluid models, and nonlinear equations.
arxiv-2512-01163:
Soumyadeep Chandra, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury, and Kaushik Roy present 2D-ThermAl in a 2025 paper on chip heat. Thermal analysis matters more and more in modern integrated circuits. Uneven power use and tightly packed parts can cause rapid temperature spikes and reliability problems.

Traditional finite element simulations are accurate but far too costly for early-stage design. Thermal failures are then found late, forcing costly redesign cycles. Their physics-informed framework uses generative AI guided by physics to analyze circuit temperatures faster. Fast, trustworthy thermal checks early in design could stop hot spots before they are baked into silicon.
arxiv-2512-01463:
Jan-Frederik Schulte and co-authors present hls4ml, a free platform for fast AI hardware. It turns trained models into code for chip design. The target chips are FPGAs and custom ASICs. Such chips run models fast with low power at the edge.

Hand porting a model to a chip is slow expert work. The platform does that port on its own. It takes models from standard deep learning tools as input. Open code lets any team use and extend it. Fast ports help put AI in scopes, clinics, cars, and other tight spots.
arxiv-2512-01663:
Lin-Xing Zeng and co-authors predict a very fast proton emission from a lutetium isotope. The isotope 148Lu is odd-odd and triaxially deformed. It can emit a proton from its nucleus. Its half-life was not well known due to its odd shape.

Their WKB estimate gives a half-life in the hundreds of nanoseconds range, with wide bounds. The potential comes from a relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in the continuum. A sharp energy value drives the tight central call. Such fast emitters test nuclear theory at its edge. Nanosecond half-lives sit at the edge of what detectors can time, so a firm prior helps beam teams set their gear before a run.
arxiv-2512-01863:
Ahmed Abouelkomsan, Max Geier, and Liang Fu study topological order through deep quantum states. Topologically ordered phases host quasiparticles with fractional charge and statistics. Their strong coupling blocks mean-field treatment. Theory for them has thus lagged their interest.

The deep state view offers a new handle on that coupling. Representing states with deep structures may capture long-range entanglement well. Progress would help design materials and codes that use topological protection for quantum memory, a key step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. Deep states can be sampled on today's hardware, which lets the theory meet numeric tests while exact methods stay out of reach.
arxiv-2512-02063:
Atoms can be located and their surroundings sensed by how they absorb light, but a quantum trick called electromagnetically induced transparency may do it better. Mahboob Ul Haq's 2025 paper compares the two approaches head to head for atomic localization and gradient sensing.

Both methods are tested in a four-level tripod atom system, under identical and optimized conditions, using beams with a super-Gaussian profile. The title gives the verdict: dispersion, the transparency-based route, outperforms plain absorption. Careful comparisons like this guide the design of precision sensors built on quantum optics, from magnetometers to imaging tools.
arxiv-2512-02163:
A team of robots spreading out to watch an area should rearrange itself as the interesting regions move. Brandon Bao, Jorge Cortés, and Sonia Martínez present in 2025 a dynamic coverage control algorithm that lets robots track the best deployment pattern for any time-varying density.

The design uses singular perturbation theory, splitting the system into two time scales: fast communication between robots and slow physical motion. That separation makes the tracking provable rather than merely plausible in tests. Coverage control underlies environmental monitoring, search and rescue, and precision agriculture, all settings where the map of importance refuses to sit still.
arxiv-2512-02263:
Designers love 2.5D effects in flat art. Shading and overlap make a flat scene feel deep, but making them by hand is slow. Xia Su and three co-authors built DepthScape in 2025. The tool lets a user drop art straight into a 3D rebuild of a scene.

The tool reads depth, sorts what each thing is, and pulls out shapes. Then art can be placed so it sits in the scene in a natural way. The user works with the AI, not against it. Such tools aim to give flat design the feel of depth, without the need for full 3D craft from each artist.
arxiv-2512-02363:
Question-answering systems for services like health policy and welfare must blend many knowledge sources without inventing facts or leaking unsafe advice. Lei Fu and four co-authors build in 2025 a domain-adaptive system that fuses knowledge into memory and decodes its answers with safety in mind.

Large language models alone struggle with factual consistency and context alignment in such sensitive domains. Augmenting their memory with curated knowledge, and steering generation with safety-aware decoding, addresses accuracy and safety together. Service chatbots that citizens must trust are a natural proving ground for the design.
arxiv-2512-02463:
Social scientists increasingly need data infrastructure they can use without being engineers: datasets arrive in inconsistent formats and access is patchy. Puneet Arya and four co-authors present in 2025 a datalake designed for interdisciplinary, data-driven social science research.

A datalake stores raw data in its native form and organizes it for later analysis, lowering the technical barrier to entry. Tailoring that infrastructure to social science means serving many disciplines with shared tools. Better access to reliable datasets could widen who gets to do quantitative research on society's pressing questions.
arxiv-2512-02563:
Xiaotong Zhao and five co-authors work on aiming radio beams for low flying wireless networks. Drones and other low altitude links move fast, so a beam must be predicted ahead of time to stay locked on. Good prediction keeps links reliable and uses spectrum well.

Past methods often miss the deep links between different sensing inputs, such as position, motion, and signal data. The team's cross attention approach lets those inputs inform each other directly. In complex three dimensional settings, richer fusion could help low altitude networks adapt as conditions change around them. Links that hold lock while drones weave and climb would serve farms, ports, and rescue work as well.
arxiv-2512-02663:
Joachim Gudmundsson and five co-authors analyze simple routing rules for wireless networks with no beacons. In beaconless geocast, each node knows only its own location, yet messages must reach a target region. Nodes decide locally, using the source, the destination, and their own position.

Their theoretical analysis covers one dimensional settings, where nodes lie along a line. Even simple settings reveal how local rules succeed or stall. Clean guarantees matter for mobile ad hoc networks in disasters or battlefields, where no infrastructure exists to guide messages along their way. Line tests look toy like, but they strip a rule down to the part that can break in the field.
arxiv-2512-03163:
Matrices can stand in for whole quantum worlds. Jackson Fliss and Alexander Frenkel review entanglement entropy in matrix quantum mechanics in this 2025 work. They focus on systems of large matrices, where rich behavior emerges.

The review covers standard models and their links to string theory and D-brane physics. It also covers emergent non-commutative geometries, where space itself arises from matrices. Entanglement entropy shows how parts of such systems share information. The review gives newcomers a map of a deep and active field. Large matrices simplify some string models, which is why their entropy draws wide interest.
arxiv-2512-03263:
When a Higgs boson decays, the spray of particles carries clues. Elliot Fox and co-authors compute precise predictions for that spray in this 2025 work. They study decays of the Higgs to quarks and gluons.

The team works at very high accuracy, called NNLO plus NNLL, for two measures: heavy-jet mass and the C-parameter. Large logarithmic terms near the two-particle limit are resummed. Precise predictions let collider experiments test the standard model sharply. Any mismatch could hint at new physics. Higgs decays to quarks and gluons are common, so precise shapes guide many collider tests.
arxiv-2512-03363:
Federated learning over quantum links faces uneven quality. Shanika Nanayakkara and Shiva Raj Pokhrel propose A2G-QFL to handle that in this 2025 work. Clients differ in quality, teleportation fidelity varies, and devices can be unstable.

Classic aggregation rules assume flat geometry and uniform communication, which quantum systems break. Their adaptive method uses two gains to weight updates from each client. Smarter weighting could keep training stable on mixed classical and quantum networks. The work prepares learning methods for future quantum internet settings. Two gains let the method reward good clients while damping noisy or unstable ones.
arxiv-2512-03563:
Animal sounds can identify species and track wildlife health. Chengyu Tang and Sanjeev Baskiyar compare model types for bioacoustics in this 2025 work. They evaluate the Mamba model, a state space design, against Transformer baselines.

They pretrain a Mamba-based audio model on a large corpus with self-supervised learning. Then they fine-tune it, called BioMamba, on the BEANS benchmark of bioacoustic tasks. They compare performance and efficiency with models like AVES. Efficient models could run on field recorders with little power. Efficiency matters in the field, where recorders run on batteries far from labs.
arxiv-2512-03663:
Salim Khazem adapts a prompting trick from giant vision models to the small images used in classrooms and prototypes. Visual prompting teaches frozen models new tasks through learnable patterns pasted onto inputs. His 2025 module, MSVP, learns prompt maps at three scales at once for tiny benchmarks like MNIST and CIFAR-10.

Global, mid-scale, and local prompts merge with the image through a single lightweight convolution. The addition costs a negligible sliver of extra parameters and works with plain CNNs, ResNet-18, and small Vision Transformers alike. Every backbone improved consistently across the three datasets. Ablations and visualizations show which scales carry the benefit at this resolution.
arxiv-2512-03863:
Graphene conducts electrons in ways that magnetic barriers and laser light can each reshape. Rachid El Aitouni and colleagues combine both controls in one device in a 2025 condensed matter preprint. Electrons crossing a graphene sheet meet two magnetic barriers, and the region between them is bathed continuously in laser light.

That lit middle section acts as a Floquet cavity, opening new transport channels as electrons absorb or emit photons. Combining Floquet theory with a transfer matrix method, the authors track transmission through the main band and its photon-assisted sidebands. The device shows effects neither double magnetic nor double laser barriers produce alone, including sharp Fano resonances and angles where transmission vanishes. Barrier spacing tunes the coupling between channels, sometimes allowing perfect transmission despite strong magnetic confinement. Low-energy carriers stay blocked while conductance climbs with energy toward a plateau.
arxiv-2512-04063:
Magnetic topological insulators promise a quantum anomalous Hall effect, where current flows along one-way edge channels with no applied magnetic field. Michael Wissmann and a large team hunt for the related surface states in a 2025 condensed matter preprint. Their material is manganese bismuth telluride, grown thicker than the ultra-thin films where quantisation is usually studied.

In thick samples, edge states hide among bulk-like carriers, and disorder blurs electrical fingerprints. The team pushed magneto-transport measurements to very high fields, up to fifty-five tesla. Above forty tesla, Shubnikov-de-Haas oscillations appeared, the rhythmic resistance wiggles that betray Landau levels. Careful analysis confirmed the oscillations come from a two-dimensional system, the surface states themselves. The authors present Landau level spectroscopy this way as an alternative to photoemission for studying topological surface states, one that works with contacts and wires rather than light.
arxiv-2512-04163:
Bars of stars across spiral galaxies were once thought to dissolve quickly in the young universe. Boris S. Kalita and colleagues find them already grown up at cosmic noon, in a 2025 preprint. They study nine massive barred galaxies as they were when the universe was a fraction of its current age, using Webb telescope imaging.

Ellipse fitting and morphological modelling measure each bar's profile directly. Five of the nine show flat brightness profiles, the signature of mature bars. Only two show the exponential profiles of youth, and those bars are shorter. The strength of the bars, gauged by a force ratio, matches or trails local-universe bars. Oddly, two flat bars are the weakest in the sample, hinting that mature bars may weaken in phases fed by gas inflows or minor mergers.
arxiv-2512-04663:
Jannes Nys and Juan Carrasquilla introduce fermionic neural Gibbs states, a method for computing how strongly interacting fermions behave at real, nonzero temperatures. Warm quantum matter is far harder to model than cold ground states. Exact methods collapse as systems grow. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a variational frame that starts from a simple mean-field state, doubled in the thermofield style, and then sharpens it with neural network transformations plus imaginary-time evolution.

The test case is the doped Fermi-Hubbard model, the standard lattice sketch of strong electron correlations behind high-temperature superconductors. The method matched thermal energies across wide ranges of temperature and interaction strength. It stayed accurate even at large doping and for sizes past exact reach. A scalable route to warm fermionic matter could guide the design of quantum materials, where heat is not a detail but the operating condition.
arxiv-2512-04963:
Yupu Yao and Bowen Yang tackle a weakness in how vision transformers read images. These models chop a picture into patches and line them up in a row, which loses the true layout. Patches at the ends of different rows end up treated as close neighbors, even when they sit far apart in the image. Earlier fixes handled the two directions of the grid separately and never fully repaired the damage.

Their method, called GeoPE, marks each patch's position with rotations in three-dimensional space, using a branch of math built for turning objects. A single combined rotation keeps the two directions linked, so the model can tell real distance from false closeness. In tests on sorting images, finding objects, and labeling three-dimensional scenes, GeoPE beat earlier methods and pushed the models to judge images more by shape than by surface texture.
arxiv-2512-05063:
Silvia Montagnani, Barnabe Ledoux, and David Lacoste argue that debt is a hidden engine of the world's stubborn carbon emissions. Energy efficiency keeps improving and climate policies keep multiplying, yet global carbon dioxide output keeps rising. The authors build a stochastic model that ties credit, growth, bankruptcy risk, and cumulative emissions together. They use it to test whether borrowing itself locks economies onto high-carbon paths.

In the model, debt-financed growth inflates emissions even while each unit of output gets cleaner, because repaying debt demands growth and growth still runs on energy. Push leverage far enough and instability and emissions climb while real wealth gains fade — a frontier beyond which extra credit mostly buys risk. Fitted to decades of data from the United States, China, France, and Denmark, the debt-growth-emissions coupling holds across different economies, implying that net-zero plans must steer credit itself.
arxiv-2512-05263:
Mateusz Łełyk and James Walsh work on a delicate question in mathematical logic about towers of ever-stronger theories. A known theorem says there is no computably listable sequence of sufficiently strong, doubly consistent theories where each one proves the double consistency of the next — reflection cannot climb forever. Montalbán and Shavrukov independently asked whether the result survives when the sequence is allowed a stronger, oracle-assisted form of listing.

The authors take up the general problem: for each level of consistency and each complexity class, which definable sequences of theories can each prove the next one's consistency? The answer depends not only on the level and the class but on how sequences are encoded in arithmetic, a subtlety that decides the outcome. For certain encodings the answer is positive, for others negative. The paper maps that boundary, clarifying what self-reference can and cannot certify about itself.
arxiv-2512-05463:
Inkee Jung, Wonwoo Kang, and Heehyun Park turn the spectral fingerprint of a shape into a picture a computer can learn from. Topological data analysis summarizes shapes with persistence diagrams, and a newer tool, the persistent Laplacian, adds geometric and spectral information beyond topology alone. The challenge is turning that spectral information into stable, finite feature vectors without losing what makes it predictive.

Following the playbook of persistence images, the authors build a diagram from a scalar signature of the persistent Laplacian and smooth it into an image. They prove the images are stable — small changes in the input produce proportionally small changes in the features, measured properly — under a mild condition on the signature. On handwriting and molecular benchmarks, the new features, above all those from the trace signature, beat current persistent-Laplacian vector forms. The work makes a rich but unwieldy invariant usable by standard machine learning.
arxiv-2512-05863:
Tasnimul Hassan and five co-authors build a medical question answering system designed to answer from evidence, not from memory alone. Language models applied raw to medicine risk confident errors. Their system pairs open models with retrieval, fetching medical literature to ground each reply. Two open models were specialized by low rank fine tuning, which trains only a small added piece.

On standard benchmarks built from research abstracts and medical exams, retrieval improved accuracy over the models alone. The fine tuned model reached about seventy two percent accuracy on the abstract based benchmark, up from about fifty five percent without tuning. Unsupported content in answers fell by roughly three fifths when retrieval grounded them, with source references supplied. With retrieval and light specialization, open models can serve biomedical questions reliably, while showing their work. Transparency, in medicine, is not decoration but part of the answer.
arxiv-2512-06463:
Antoni Marcinek reports fresh results from the NA61/SHINE experiment at CERN on a short lived particle called the phi meson. The experiment fires beams at fixed targets and tracks what flies out, covering ground that collider setups miss, including the full forward spray of each collision. The phi meson is a sharp probe of strangeness in hot matter. It carries no net strangeness, yet it is built from a strange quark and its mirror. Its yield can betray whether matter melted into a quark soup.

Marcinek presents the first phi results for mid sized systems from this experiment, from central collisions of argon and scandium nuclei at three beam energies. The results map how phi output spreads over speed and sideways motion, give average yields, and set phi counts against other particles. Placed beside older data, they help trace how strangeness grows as collisions get bigger and hotter.
arxiv-2512-06563:
Max Ma and Gen-Hua Shi recast neural networks as geometry in motion. In their account, a network is a stack of piecewise manifolds, surfaces bent into facets, and learning is an iteration that hunts for fixed points under boundary conditions. Strip away fixed coordinates and operators, they argue, and what remains is a learnable computation shaped by the complexity of those manifolds and by strong nonlinearity.

Real data add their own burden: huge scope and scale, chopped into minibatches. Training adds more, as node covers shift, curvature piles up, and plasticity rises and fades. Capability, in this view, appears only when fixed point regions settle and hold. Networks do not start with such regions; they build them, driven by their own errors. The authors close by favoring designs that spread manifold complexity across many elastic models, joined in federated systems, over single monoliths.
arxiv-2512-06663:
Yu Qi and six co authors teach big vision language models to do the seeing tasks they are worst at. These models answer questions about images and read text in them well. Yet they lag specialist tools at finding objects, outlining regions, and judging depth. That gap is worst in crowded scenes with small objects. Their fix, CoT4Det, breaks perception into a chain of three steps that suits how such models reason.

First the model classifies what is present, then it counts the instances, then it grounds each one in the image. On a standard detection benchmark the chain lifted a mid sized open model's score from poor to respectable. Gains also appeared on referring expression tests, where a phrase must be matched to the right object, and on entity grounding in photo captions. The method needs no special training and leaves the model's general vision language skills intact.
arxiv-2512-06863:
Juntao Sun, Shuai Yao, and He Zhang study a coupled equation that links a quantum wave to its own electric field, posed on a flat two-dimensional region. They look for solutions whose total mass is fixed in advance, while a key multiplier in the equation stays unknown. The interaction here repels rather than attracts, and the growth rate sits in a regime specialists call mass supercritical, where standard methods strain.

First the authors show why the problem is hard: on the natural constraint surface, the energy runs off to both extremes, so the usual target level is slippery. Then, inside a large bounded region, they prove that two positive-energy solutions exist, one of lowest energy and one of high energy. That settles part of an open problem posed by earlier researchers. A final part tracks what happens to the solutions as the region grows toward the whole plane.
arxiv-2512-06963:
Yichao Shen and co-authors turn a video generator into a robot controller. Modern video models can imagine what a scene will look like next, and the team bets that such imagination is exactly what a robot arm needs. Their system, VideoVLA, takes a camera image plus a spoken-style instruction. It then predicts both the arm's action sequence and the future frames those actions should produce, in one joint model.

Built on a multimodal diffusion transformer, the system leans on skills the video model already learned from vast footage. Experiments support the bet: when the imagined future looks good, the predicted actions tend to succeed. The controller also carried skills across different robot bodies and handled objects it had not been trained on. The authors frame paired prediction as a route to robots that cope with new tasks.
arxiv-2512-07663:
Hendrik Schrautzer, Tim Drevelow, Hannes Jónsson, and Pavel Bessarab wrote this 2025 physics paper on magnetic textures. Tiny swirls like skyrmions can sit in a magnet as stable states. Knowing how one state turns into another decides their use in devices.

Transitions pass over saddle points, the mountain passes of an energy landscape. The authors present a framework that hunts those passes in a systematic way. First, symmetry defines useful deformation directions. Those directions push the system toward the rim around its energy valley. A following method then settles precisely onto each saddle point. The passes join a network that maps how all the states connect. Transition rates can then be estimated from theory. The test case is a two-dimensional chiral magnet on a lattice. The method uncovers how skyrmions, antiskyrmions, bags, and droplets form and vanish. Some routes preserve topological charge; others change it mid-flight.
arxiv-2512-07863:
Jianling Gao and Shuai Ma wrote this 2025 machine learning paper with Chongyang Tao, Xuelian Lin, and Junfeng Liu. Anomaly detection finds the odd cases hiding in mostly normal data. Semi-supervised versions learn from a few labeled examples plus mountains of raw data.

Most methods score one point at a time, or simple pairs of points. Anomalies, though, are defined against the crowd they sit inside. A point is strange because the group around it behaves differently. The authors reframe the whole task at the level of sets. Their framework, SetAD, encodes an entire set with an attention mechanism. A graded objective teaches it to rate a set's overall anomalousness.  A second mechanism calibrates each point's score against its peers. Deviations are normalized across many diverse contextual sets before judging. On ten real-world datasets, SetAD beats the leading rivals clearly. Bigger sets make it better still.
arxiv-2512-08363:
The BaBar Collaboration, a large international team of particle physicists, posted a measurement paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study rare decays among bottomonium states, the bound states of a bottom quark and its antiquark. Their data come from the BaBar detector at the SLAC PEP II collider, a large sample of upsilon three S decays.

The chain they follow starts with an upsilon three S emitting a photon to become a chi b state, which then decays into an omega meson plus an upsilon one S. Signals for the two chi b states stood out over negligible background. The team measured the branching fractions of these transitions with improved precision. They also measured the decay angular distributions for the first time, testing how the spins line up through the chain. No sign appeared of the third sibling state, chi b zero, taking the same path.
arxiv-2512-08463:
Antonio Terpin and Raffaello D Andrea, control researchers in Switzerland, posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. They train a reinforcement learning agent directly in the physical world, steering a cylinder in a tabletop water channel to raise or lower its drag. The flow is chaotic, hard to simulate, and good control strategies are not obvious in advance.

Classic experiments decades ago found simple periodic recipes with strong effects. With dense observations of the cylinder wake, the agent matched or beat those recipes within tens of minutes of real training. Its learned action sequences even kept working when replayed blindly, with no feedback. The twist came when flow observations were withheld during training. The agent still learned to cut drag well, but no run ever learned to raise it. Privileged information, it seems, can decide whether a policy is discoverable at all.
arxiv-2512-08663:
G A C Rijkers and coauthors identify known radio pulsars in a large low frequency sky survey. The survey, from the LOFAR telescope, covers a large part of the northern sky at a frequency well below most pulsar work. The team matches survey sources to pulsars and measures their positions and brightness at that frequency.

Most pulsars expected in the survey area were found, and their brightness values agree well with past work, with only two clear exceptions. Those gaps are linked to known pulsar behavior, such as nulling. Many detections were also found again using polarization alone, which suggests a good way to pick pulsar candidates in future releases. Adding data at an even lower frequency can help confirm candidates through their spectra.
arxiv-2512-08763:
Jinfeng Xu and coauthors strengthen the theory of universal graph prompt tuning and propose a new model that learns and edits such prompts. Prompt tuning adapts pretrained graph neural networks by adding small prompts. Universal prompts act in the input feature space and, in theory, can match the effect of any prompting method, without tying the result to one pretraining strategy.

Recent selective methods add prompts only to chosen nodes, which the authors argue breaks that universality. They prove that adding prompts to all nodes is necessary for the universal property. Their model, LEAP, first builds full universal prompts to keep the theory intact. It then uses actor critic reinforcement learning to select nodes and edit prompts toward better ones. Tests on graph and node level tasks, in full and few shot settings, show consistent gains over fine tuning and other prompt methods.
arxiv-2512-08863:
Yairon Cid Ruiz studies Segre classes, a central tool in algebraic geometry, and their link to integral dependence of ideals. A fundamental property of Segre classes is birational invariance. That invariance implies the class of a closed subscheme depends only on the integral closure of its defining ideal sheaf.

The author proves the converse direction in a precise form. The Segre class for a closed subscheme encodes a criterion for integral dependence of its defining ideal sheaf. As an application, Aluffi Segre zeta function is shown to provide such a criterion for homogeneous ideals in polynomial rings. That result ties a generating function built from Segre classes to a concrete algebraic test. The work deepens the understanding of what geometric data Segre classes carry, moving from invariance alone to a full characterization of dependence through those classes.
arxiv-2512-08963:
S Hariharan, R Suresh, and V K Chandrasekar propose clustered echo state networks for predicting multivariate time series, such as stock prices, solar wind measures, and chaotic systems. Forecasting several linked variables at once is hard because of noise and strong interdependence among the series. Echo state networks offer a light alternative to standard recurrent networks, since only output weights are trained.

Their clustered design organizes reservoir nodes into groups, with each group tied to one input variable. Connections stay dense inside a group and sparse between groups, mimicking the modular layout of biological neural networks. That structure limits interference across variables and allows each cluster to be trained independently with a standard regression method. The authors test ring, random, and scale free reservoir topologies. Across diverse real data sets, clustered networks beat conventional echo state networks in accuracy and noise robustness, especially with random and scale free layouts.
arxiv-2512-09063:
Gonzalo Benitez Irarrrazabal and coauthors propose an extension where neutrino masses arise from a two loop inverse seesaw process. That radiative origin explains naturally why neutrino masses are so small, while keeping the new mediator particles near the TeV scale,. The model adds four neutral leptons and two real singlet scalars.

Two global symmetries organize the setup, one continuous and one discrete. The discrete symmetry survives symmetry breaking, forbids tree level and one loop neutrino masses, and stabilizes dark matter candidates. The model fits neutrino oscillation data and yields two heavy pseudo Dirac pairs with small mixing to active neutrinos. Predictions include a narrow range for an effective Majorana mass and suppressed but testable charged lepton flavor violation. Viable parameter space for dark matter, is identified against the observed relic abundance. Flavor, collider, and dark matter signals are linked in one method.
arxiv-2512-09163:
Gabrielle Rives, Olivier Lopez, and Nicolas Bousquet build survival models, tools that predict how long equipment lasts before failing. Their work is motivated by a fleet of military vehicles used in harsh, changing conditions. Often the true wear is not measured directly; only proxy signs and incomplete, cut-off observations are available.

Their framework, WTNN, pairs a neural network with the Weibull distribution, a standard choice for lifetimes of maintained systems. The network lets the Weibull parameters depend on changing readings over time, going beyond older regression models. Its design also builds in expert knowledge about which measurements matter most, in a form that matches the Weibull shape. In numerical experiments, the model trained reliably on proxy and right-censored data. It produced survival forecasts that were both sturdy and interpretable, improving on existing methods.
arxiv-2512-09363:
Ke Xing leads a large team presenting StereoWorld, a system that turns ordinary single-camera video into stereo video for extended reality headsets. Stereo content is in demand, but filming it is costly and often produces artifacts. Their approach reuses a pretrained video generator rather than training a new model from scratch.

StereoWorld conditions the generator on the monocular input video and supervises it with a geometry-aware penalty, so the invented second view keeps the scene's 3D structure. A spatio-temporal tiling scheme makes high-resolution synthesis efficient. To train and test at scale, the team curated a high-definition stereo dataset of more than eleven million frames, aligned to natural human eye spacing. In experiments, StereoWorld produced stereo videos with better visual quality and geometric consistency than prior methods. The authors offer it as a practical route to more immersive content from ordinary footage.
arxiv-2512-09663:
Tao Zhang leads a team presenting IF-Bench, the first benchmark for how well multimodal language models understand infrared images. Such models have advanced quickly on photographs, but infrared imagery, vital for night vision, surveillance, and industry, has statistics of its own, and their ability there was unexplored. The benchmark draws nearly five hundred images from twenty-three infrared datasets.

Around those images the team curated six hundred eighty visual question-answer pairs spanning ten dimensions of image understanding. They evaluated more than forty open and closed models using cyclic evaluation, bilingual assessment, and hybrid judging to keep results reliable. They analyze how model scale, architecture, and inference style affect infrared comprehension. They also propose GenViP, a training-free prompting method that uses image editing models to translate an infrared image into a color counterpart, reducing the domain gap. Across many models, GenViP improved performance.
arxiv-2512-09863:
Zeyuan Zhou, Shaun Pexton, Aleksander Kubica, and Yongshan Ding argue that error mitigation still matters after fault tolerant quantum computers arrive. It is usually seen as a toolkit for today's noisy machines, of little use once quantum error correction takes over. The authors instead run it at the logical level, on already corrected qubits. Their key resource is soft information: the decoders used in error correction naturally report how confident each correction was. That information costs nothing extra to use.

Inside this framework they develop three techniques: discarding or aborting suspicious runs, probabilistic error cancellation, and zero noise extrapolation. Together these cut logical error rates more than a hundredfold while discarding few runs. Benchmarks on a surface code design covered random circuits and molecular simulations. Compared with correction alone or earlier combinations, the approach saved a large share of spacetime overhead, showing the two work better together than apart.
arxiv-2512-09963:
Phuong Tran leads a team presenting GoodSpeed, a system for running large language models across many edge servers fairly. Speculative decoding speeds up generation: small draft models propose tokens, and a big model verifies them. The system should maximize goodput, the rate of accepted tokens, while treating servers fairly. GoodSpeed coordinates the draft servers from a central verifier and processes their proposals in parallel.

A gradient based scheduling algorithm assigns verification work dynamically. It maximizes a logarithmic utility, a standard way to enforce proportional fairness among competing servers. Using fluid sample path analysis, the authors prove the system settles at the optimal goodput allocation in steady state. Under changing workloads it stays near optimal with provably bounded error. The framework targets real time inference in resource constrained, multi user settings, where raw speed alone would let strong servers starve weak ones. The work was accepted at INFOCOM 2026.
arxiv-2512-10363:
Mingyu Jeon and colleagues find moments inside hour long videos without any task specific training. Given a sentence like the part where she opens the letter, moment retrieval systems must return the right time span. Hour long video cannot be processed in one pass, so the field uses search then refine: cheaply shortlist candidate spans, then verify a few. Existing zero shot methods explode the candidate set and verify expensively. Their framework, Point to Span, attacks both stages.

An adaptive span generator restrains the candidate explosion, producing spans at scales matched to the content. Query decomposition then refines candidates by breaking the request into checkable parts, avoiding costly model verification. The authors claim the first zero shot framework able to ground language in hour long video. It beat supervised state of the art systems on a standard long video benchmark by a clear margin on an early retrieval measure.
arxiv-2512-10463:
Suman Panja and Vishnu Rajagopal compute the Casimir effect, the attraction between two close plates in empty space, at finite temperature inside a deformed space-time. Their setting is kappa-Minkowski space-time, where coordinates fail to commute, a feature many quantum gravity ideas predict. They ask how that deformation changes the thermal force and whether the physics stays consistent.

Using the Matsubara formalism with fixed boundary conditions on a massless deformed field, they derive corrected formulas for free energy, pressure, entropy, and internal energy. Non-commutativity strengthens the attraction, yet the system still obeys the Nernst theorem and the laws of thermodynamics. Their analysis also caps the deformation scale at an extremely small length, states when the effect could become visible in experiments, and gives the deformed version of the Stefan-Boltzmann law.
arxiv-2512-10563:
Xin Guan and co-authors present NormCode, a semi-formal language that makes artificial intelligence workflows auditable by design. As language model systems move into law, medicine, and finance, regulators want to trace exactly what each step saw and did.
