Their 2026 arXiv text explains state preparation, the encoding of data into a quantum state. Without a good encoding, no quantum learning method can even start.

The chapter presents the matrix product state description of quantum systems. It then shows how that description can be turned into circuits that build a desired state. Matrix product states keep large systems compact when their entanglement stays limited. Readers get a practical route from classical data to a working quantum circuit.
arxiv-2601-09663:
Xuyang Fang, Sion Hannuna, Edwin Simpson, and Neill Campbell teach software to tell animals apart in very long videos. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses self-supervised learning for animal identification. Knowing which individual is which matters for ecology, wildlife monitoring, and farm management.

Older methods need heavy manual labeling. Existing self-supervised ones demand much compute and strain on long sequences, where memory limits and drifting errors bite. The authors aim for a method that scales to long footage. Reliable IDs over hours of video would turn raw camera traps into behavioral data.
arxiv-2601-09763:
Ashish Kumar Patra and Saikumar Krithivasan revisit wave packets that fall apart and then rebuild. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies fractional revival dynamics in Kerr-type systems. Revivals are a hallmark quantum effect in systems with nonlinear energy spectra.

Earlier work tracked revival signatures in expectation values of observables. The authors extend that analysis in two directions. One focus is angular momentum moments, which capture the packet's rotation in detail. Classical analogs provide the other lens. Revival patterns are used in quantum optics and in control work, so sharper theory has real practical reach.
arxiv-2601-09863:
Ali Taani calculates the gravitational-wave strain of known binary pulsars across present and future detectors. His 2026 arXiv paper sums up the state of the art for these systems. It uses data from ground-based LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA, and from the planned space mission LISA.

Characteristic strain values run from about 3 to 73 in units of ten to the minus twenty-two. The frequencies span the bands the detectors cover. Binary pulsars are precise clocks whose orbits decay exactly as relativity predicts. Knowing their strain tells planners which systems LISA should hear clearly.
arxiv-2601-10063:
Shuta Kosuge and Teruyuki Kitabayashi study why neutrinos have such tiny mass. One lead idea is the type I seesaw. It adds heavy right handed neutrinos that no test has yet seen. Their mass scale is still free. That free scale sets much of what the idea can say.

The pair tie that scale to the form of the Dirac mass grid. Some grid forms are named textures. Each form has set zero and non zero slots. The team asks which forms fit known facts. They also ask what scale each form needs for the birth of matter over anti matter via leptogenesis.
arxiv-2601-10563:
Aradhya Gaonkar and co authors set two net kinds side by side: KANs and MLPs. MLPs are the base net form, with fixed curve steps at each node. KANs swap those steps for spline curves that learn. They rest on a known theorem of Kolmogorov. The team test both on base tasks.

Tasks span curve fits, time based calls, and class calls with many inputs. The paper weighs which form wins on each. KANs bring a new shape to the task. Their grid based curves can fit hard bends with fewer nodes. The work is a guide for when to pick each form.
arxiv-2601-11363:
Haocheng Zhong gives an algebraic account of the Page transition in this work. His 2026 preprint deals with black hole evaporation. The Page transition is a key mark in that process. Hawking radiation entropy first grows as the hole sheds mass.

In a unitary picture, that entropy must turn and fall. The full path is called the Page curve in the field. Zhong frames the turn as a phase transition in recovery. The tools come from approximate quantum error correction. Complementary recovery, a paired fix-up idea, does the key work. The algebraic view may unify how the curve is derived. It ties black hole physics to quantum information theory.
arxiv-2601-11463:
Marek Cuth, Jonas Havelka, Jakub Rondos, and Bunyamin Sari classify function spaces. Their 2026 preprint studies C of K spaces for compacta. Such a space holds all continuous functions on a compact set. Positive linear maps are the lens for the classification.

The compacta in scope are infinite and countable. The team shows a neat fact for isomorphic pairs. If C of K and C of L are isomorphic at all, a nice one exists. Either the isomorphism can be taken nonnegative in full. Or its inverse can be taken nonnegative instead. Positive maps respect order, so the result is strong. It sharpens how these classic spaces can be sorted.
arxiv-2601-11663:
Bruce Changlong Xu unifies post-training quantization under one principle. The 2026 preprint names that principle activation sensitivity. Quantization shrinks LLM weights to fewer bits for cheap runs. Post-training methods must guess which weight channels matter most.

Two paradigms dominate the field's heuristics today. Activation-aware methods like AWQ favor channels with large activations. Second-order methods like GPTQ use input covariance structure. They spread quantization error by that structure instead. Xu argues both rest on one shared idea. Sensitivity of activations is what each method estimates. A unifying view could yield simpler, stronger quantizers. Smaller models with less quality loss are the prize.
arxiv-2601-11863:
Raquib Bin Yousuf, Shengzhe Xu, Mandar Sharma, and their co-authors improve search for retrieval-augmented generation. In such systems, a model draws on text chunks to ground its reply. In neat, repeat-heavy files such as rule filings, chunk text alone can match the wrong file.

They use metadata, the tags and fields round each chunk, to sort hits with more care. Good tags can split files that read near the same. Better picks mean fewer wrong cites in the reply. The work is aimed at dense, formal corpora where terms repeat a lot.
arxiv-2601-11963:
Congpei An and Xiaosheng Zhuang survey spherical designs and their uses, with a stress on numerical analysis. A spherical design is a set of points on a sphere. The mean of any low degree polynomial over the set must equal its mean over the whole sphere.

The survey covers when such sets exist and how to build them by computer. It also covers where they are used. Good point sets help compute integrals on spheres with care. They show up in weather maths, graphics, and signal work.  The survey also lists open gaps for new point sets.
arxiv-2601-12363: V. V. Voytik takes up a problem in the physics of motion. The work deals with a frame that speeds up along a curved path. Voytik works out the key values for this kind of motion as seen from a lab frame. The abstract notes that the same values can be found in three ways that agree with each other.
arxiv-2601-12563:
Ismat Jarin, Olivia Figueira, Yu Duan, Tu Le, and Athina Markopoulou study privacy risks in consumer virtual reality apps. VR platforms and apps gather rich sensor data from users. The data can cover motion, face, eyes, and hands, though often in abstracted form. Even abstract data may expose users to profiling risks they do not know about.

The team present a tool and study named VR ProfiLens. It probes how apps could build user profiles from such sensor streams. The work was set for a 2026 symposium on usable security and privacy. Findings here matter as VR moves into homes and schools. Users deserve to know what their movements can reveal about them.
arxiv-2601-12663:
Yan-Chen Chen and four co authors work on energy prediction in textile factories. Traditional textile plants consume substantial energy, so efficient production matters for cost and sustainability. Deep neural networks can predict factory output and guide operations. The catch is that they need extensive historical data to train well.

Gathering that data is costly, since sensors must be deployed and records kept. The team use ensemble deep transfer learning to ease the data burden. Transfer learning reuses knowledge from related data, and ensembles average many models. Their title claims gains in both accuracy and data efficiency. The work was published in an open access engineering journal.
arxiv-2601-13363:
Oleksiy Dovgoshey marks the centre of distances for a class of ultrametric spaces. In such a space, all triangles are sharp in a set way, with the two long sides matched. The centre of distances is the set of spans that can be hit from each point by some mate at just that span.

Dovgoshey treats spaces grown from labelled trees, a stock build for such spaces. He proves the centre is just zero alone, or zero plus the full width of the space. No mid span can serve all points. Such a stark split shows how rigid tree grown spaces are. For metric staff, the result is a clean test of tree origin.
arxiv-2601-13463:
D. Keller sorts when quantum nets beat classic nets in hadron physics by a score called a quantum qualifier. Quantum machine learning builds fast. The hard ask now is not how to build such nets. It is where they help in real use and where they do not.

Keller's frame gives tools to call that line in data led hadron tasks. The qualifier is a number based mark of quantum gain. It guides the pick of classic or quantum net for each task. For physics teams with thin quantum time, a sound pick tool saves runs on tasks a classic net would win.
arxiv-2601-13563:
Aryan Karmore packs mixture of experts nets into far less memory by a butterfly plan for ternary experts. A mixture of experts net holds many expert weight sets. In plain form each set is stored in full, so memory grows as the count times the square of the width. Edge gear cannot hold that growth.

Old squeeze tools cut the per set cost but leave the growth form. Karmore's experts share a butterfly orbit plan, a set of fixed swap paths. Expert weights are ternary, in three states. Shared paths plus three state weights cut the growth to sub linear. For edge AI teams, that form may let big expert nets run on small gear.
arxiv-2601-13663:
Daniel Kalmanovich and Yaar Solomon study what happens when a triangle is cut again and again in 2026. Each cut joins the midpoint of the longest edge to the vertex across from it. Repeating the cut makes an endless family of new triangles. A result by Stynes from 1980 showed a surprise here.

For any start triangle, the endless family falls into just finitely many similarity classes. Shapes in one class are the same form at a new scale. The team studies the stability, complexity, and spread of these classes. Finite classes make the long-run pattern of cuts far more tractable.
arxiv-2601-13763:
Meijing Zhang and Ying Xu use large language models to model how travelers choose transport in 2026. Travel mode choice sits at the heart of transport planning and policy. Classic stats and machine learning tools miss much context in human choices. Each choice rests on habits, costs, time, and local facts.

Their method, TransMode-LLM, feeds feature data into natural language prompts. Domain-enhanced prompting adds transport know-how to the model's base knowledge. The goal is richer forecasts of which mode a traveler will pick. Better forecasts lead to bus, road, and rail plans that fit real life.
arxiv-2601-13863:
Rohit Das, Parthasarathi Majumdar, and Debadrita Mukherjee study fixes to the black hole entropy formula in 2026. The Bekenstein-Hawking formula ties entropy to horizon area. Their focus is corrections with inverse powers of area, key for very large horizons. The setting is F(R) gravity, a modified theory of gravity.

They use the Wald formula for entropy, with tweaks by Jacobson, Kang, and Myers. The holes in view are classical, spherically symmetric solutions. They also weigh gravitational wave observations as a check. Precise entropy rules test if modified gravity can match real data.
arxiv-2601-14163:
Mohammed Latif Siddiq and co-authors study code execution risks on model-sharing platforms in 2026. Platforms like Hugging Face, ModelScope, and OpenCSG are central to modern machine learning. Developers share, load, and fine-tune pre-trained models with minimal effort. That flexibility introduces a critical security concern.

Untrusted code can run during model loading, via flags like trust_remote_code. Their empirical study covers remote code execution in these hosting ecosystems. A single bad model file could compromise every user who loads it. The work maps how widespread the risky practice has become. Load-time code is a soft spot that many users never see. The study gives platform teams hard counts to act on.
arxiv-2601-14263:
Alex Echeverria, Sávio Salvarino Teles de Oliveira, and Fernando Marques Federson present Call2Instruct in this 2026 paper. Their goal is to fine-tune large language models for one domain. Fine-tuning works best with training sets in instruction form, such as question-and-answer pairs. Call center audio holds rich domain facts, but it is an untapped source for such sets.

The hard part is the state of the raw calls. Recordings are noisy and messy, with loose talk and no clear structure. Call2Instruct is an automated pipeline for that gap. It takes call center recordings as input. From them, it builds Q&A datasets fit for fine-tuning a model.
arxiv-2601-14363:
Luca Sciarini, Sophie Rosu, Sylvia Ekström, and three co-authors study close pairs of massive stars in this 2026 paper. Internal transport, the slow churn inside a star, is a top source of error in stellar models. In close binaries, tides between the two stars were thought to boost chemical mixing. Past theory said the boost is steady.

Observations tell a less clear story. They show no firm trend that links orbital period to nitrogen enrichment, the mark mixing would leave. That clash drives the paper's question. Do tides enhance mixing, or suppress it? Readers get a test of a long-held claim against what telescopes see.
arxiv-2601-14663:
Yogesh Pipada Sunil Kumar, S. Ali Pourmousavi, Jon A.R. Liisberg, and Julian Lesmos-Vinasco study energy markets in this 2026 paper. Reliable forecasting of prosumer flexibility is critical for demand response aggregators. Prosumers both use and produce power, for example with rooftop solar. Aggregators bid their flexibility into frequency controlled ancillary service markets. Those markets enforce strict reliability requirements, such as the P90 standard.

Forecasting is hard for three reasons the authors name. Historical data are limited. Forecasts depend on exogenous inputs. Prosumer behavior is heterogeneous. These factors create significant epistemic uncertainty. The stakes are cash. A bid that is too bold can fail the test and cost the firm a fee. A range you can trust beats a point you can not. That is the heart of the bid plan here. The paper builds calibrated uncertainty quantification for flexibility aggregation, so bids rest on honest confidence ranges.
arxiv-2601-14963:
Devashish Pandey, Corné Koks, Martijn Wubs, Nicolas Stenger, and Jake Iles-Smith predict a new twist in the light from a quantum emitter. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Mollow triplet, a three-peak pattern in emitted light. That pattern is the hallmark of an emitter dressed by strong light.

Emitters tied to local phonons, packets of vibration, show extra sidebands. The team predicts the triplet is not confined to the main line. Under a strong resonant drive, the triplet is copied onto the phonon sidebands. That is a surprise, since sidebands are usually seen as messy, incoherent paths.
arxiv-2601-15063:
Vipul Upadhyay and Amikam Levy test a claim about how electrons move through twisted molecules. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with chiral-induced spin selectivity, an effect where a helical molecule favors one electron spin. The open question is what drives it.

Some hope that weak coupling to vibrations is enough. The authors check that hope in a two-terminal setup. They run a self-consistent Green's function calculation on a helical chain model. The model adds spin-orbit coupling and electron-phonon links. Their answer is in the title: weak coupling alone is not nearly enough.
arxiv-2601-15263:
Amrapali Sen and Flavio Del Santo ask whether faster-than-light frames breed quantum-style chance. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with indeterminism, the idea that the future is not fixed by the past. Quantum theory is widely seen as indeterministic at its core.

Classical frames can show the same trait once infinite information is dropped. Relativity is usually read as banning superluminal signals. Yet Lorentz symmetry formally allows superluminal transformations. Dragan and Ekert argued these bring indeterminism like the quantum kind. The authors examine that striking claim in depth and in full detail.
arxiv-2601-15463:
Achilleas Karras computes determinants for a family of number-theory graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. The graphs encode two classic functions on classes of integers. One is the Collatz 3n+1 function, famous for its still-open problem. The other is Conway's amusical permutation function. Each graph is finite and directed. Its arrows show how the function moves between congruence classes.

Karras finds the determinants of the modular Collatz graphs. He does the same for the modular Conway amusical permutation graph. Along the way he describes number-theoretic traits of interest. Determinants are a compact summary of a graph's structure. For fans of the Collatz problem, the paper adds exact algebra to a topic often explored by computer search.
arxiv-2601-15863:
Faruk Pasic and four co-authors measure fading in vehicle radio channels in a 2026 arXiv paper. Future vehicle systems will use millimeter-wave links for high data rates. Designers need to know how those links behave on the road. The team compares propagation at centimeter-wave and millimeter-wave bands. Multi-band channel measurements supply the data. One key parameter is the Rician K-factor. It gauges how much of the signal travels a direct path.

The K-factor here varies with time, per the title. Moving vehicles make channels change fast. A time-varying measure captures that motion honestly. Small-scale fading differs between the two bands, and the K-factor summarizes much of it. Car makers and network designers use such numbers to plan antennas and protocols for connected driving.
arxiv-2601-16163:
Moo Jin Kim and coauthors tune video models to act as robot plans. Their 2026 preprint uses the rich time sense of video models. Video models learn how scenes shift and how touch plays out. Past robot work adds long post steps and new parts to use that sense. Those adds raise cost and slow the path to use.

The team tunes the video model in a plain, direct way. The tuned model then serves for both acts and plans. One model for both cuts the need for split tools. It also keeps the time sense the video model learned. The work, named Cosmos Policy, targets real robot tasks.
arxiv-2601-16463:
Wenbo Guo and coauthors mine facts to flag bad PyPI packs with low false rates. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Python pack store, PyPI. Bad packs in the store can harm all who pull them. Past tools flag a share of good packs as bad. That share runs from near one in six to near one in three.

High false rates stem from thin rule sets for flag calls. Fact mine pulls rich signs from pack code and past hits. Rich signs aim to split bad packs from good with care. Low false rates let teams trust and act on flags. The work seeks guards that wards can use each day.
arxiv-2601-16563:
Vasileios Sevetlidis and George Pavlidis view SGD train as a process tensor. Their 2026 preprint deals with how nets train step by step. SGD is the main train rule for nets in wide use. A process tensor maps a chain of acts to a read out. Here acts span batch picks, tweaks and step parts of the rule.

That view lets them sum past pull in the train path. Past pull is read by how clear past states stay in time. Clear pull marks mean train has a long past tail. Such tails shape how nets learn and what they keep. The work gives a new lens on train acts.
arxiv-2601-16663:
Zoltan Nagy, Ryan Wisnesky, Kevin Carlson, Eswaran Subrahmanian, and Gioele Zardini tackle a mess in building data. Homes and work sites spawn data at each life stage. Plans, builds, sales, and repairs each spawn their own files. More than forty file schemes now crowd the field. Their 2026 preprint seeks a clean way to link them.

Old fixes map each scheme to each next one by hand. That work grows fast as schemes pile up. Grand single schemes grow too bulky to use. The authors turn to category theory, a math of links. Their frame aims to join data with less strain. Smooth data flow could cut waste in the trade.
arxiv-2601-16763:
Cuong Le, Pavló Melnyk, Bastian Wandt, and Mårten Wadenbäck guess body poses from a single camera view. One flat shot hides how deep each joint sits. Past tools oft gave one pose, firm but wrong. Their 2026 preprint gives a spread of poses in place of one. The spread shows how sure the tool is at each joint.

Their tool learns flows that morph noise into pose sets. Each run can yield a fresh pose from the spread. Users can see doubt where the shot is vague. Such doubt maps aid sports, health, and robot work. They keep tools from bold claims on thin proof.
arxiv-2601-17263:
Sanyukta Deshpande and Sheldon H. Jacobson test how language models act in markets. They place the models in Cournot markets. In that setup, firms pick output amounts and price follows from total supply. It is a classic test of rival firm choice. The authors ask if model agents grasp that contest.

The study looks at choice from many sides, not just price. Fair market rules are part of the concern. As AI takes on more market choice, its habits matter for all users. Poor habits could skew prices or shut out rivals. This work gives an early map of how model agents behave. It can help shape guards for AI in trade.
arxiv-2601-17563:
Nathan Gavenski, Matteo Leonetti, and Odinaldo Rodrigues improve imitation learning from observation. In that setup, a learner watches a teacher act. It sees states, not the teacher's actions. Top methods have made real gains. They still lean on action-based fine tuning. They also assume one best action per state. And they copy teacher acts without full regard for the live state.

The authors add conditioned transition estimation and online behavior alignment. Those steps tie learning to what the world does next. Better imitation matters for robots that learn by watching. It cuts the need for hand-set reward rules. The work aims at learners that generalize past their teacher's exact path.
arxiv-2601-17663:
Jie Dou and co-authors probe density waves in the trilayer nickelate La4Ni3O10. Nickelates drew wide interest when related compounds superconducted under pressure. Density wave orders may hold the key to that state. The team uses lanthanum-139 nuclear quadrupole resonance. That probe reads local charge and spin order with care. They find charge and spin density waves intertwined.

Intertwined orders shape how superconductivity emerges. Knowing their form narrows theories of nickelate physics. NQR gives a local view that bulk tools miss. The trilayer compound is a key case in the family. This work adds a firm fact to a fast-moving field. It guides the next round of pressure tests.
arxiv-2601-17863: Alexandre Alouadi, Pierre Henry-Labordère, Grégoire Loeper, Othmane Mazhar, Huyên Pham, and Nizar Touzi give a direct PDE route to the Schrödinger-Bass Bridge problem. Their 2026 preprint is a short note that announces results proven in full in a companion work. In one dimension, they show how the bridge system, an optimal coupling problem, comes out of partial differential equations step by step.
arxiv-2601-18963:
The Fauna Robotics Team presents Sprout, a humanoid robot built to be light and easy to use. Learned control, large scale sims, and generative models have sped up work on general robot control. Yet the field lacks robots that are safe and warm enough for long use around people at home or at work.

Most humanoids today are shut factory systems or lab prototypes that are hard to run near people. Sprout aims at that gap: a developer ready robot people can live and work beside. The team frames it as a base for expressive, long term use in human spaces.
arxiv-2601-19263:
Aybars Yunusoglu and four co-authors wire AI agents to FPGA chips in a framework that can be reshaped on demand. AI now runs in real time, tight energy settings, where general chips waste power. FPGAs, whose circuits can be rewired, promise speed per watt that fixed chips cannot match.

Their framework joins the agent layer to the chip layer and speeds the pair together. A reconfigurable base lets the same system adapt as models and tasks change. Such links matter for drones, cameras, and factory gear that must think fast on a small battery.
arxiv-2601-19463:
Richard A. Battye and three co-authors work out how cosmic strings shine and what that says about dark matter. Global strings are line like relics that may have formed in the early universe, and they shed energy as radiation. That radiation includes axions, candidate particles for dark matter, so the spectrum of the glow sets how many axions survive today.

With a simple model, the team shows how the relic axion count leans on the spectrum's shape. They then study radiation from wiggled straight strings, watching the split between forms. The count of axions today is a key target for dark matter hunts.
arxiv-2601-19763:
Michael Pilipchuk, Chaitali Patil, and Veera Sundararaghavan compare ways to count defects inside crystals. When a metal deforms, line defects called dislocations appear. Some are geometrically necessary, arising where the deformation bends. Their density measures how much strain varies across a polycrystal.

Crystal plasticity simulations can estimate this density in several ways. All the methods start from the Nye tensor, computed as the curl of the plastic deformation gradient. The authors compare plasticity-based estimation methods against each other. Knowing which method is trustworthy matters for predicting strength and failure. The study gives modelers a firmer basis for choosing.
arxiv-2601-19863:
A study of dark matter halos asks how much dense leftovers boost annihilation signals. Simulations have found prompt cusps, compact remnants of the earliest density peaks. Their inner density rises steeply toward the centre. These cusps can survive as halos merge and grow, and they may brighten the glow expected if dark matter particles annihilate.

The authors fold prompt cusps into SASHIMI, a semi-analytic framework for halo substructure. That allows a hierarchical, environment-dependent calculation of the total annihilation luminosity. Earlier estimates often treated the boost in a rough, averaged way. A sharper boost changes how strongly telescope data constrain dark matter models. The work links small-scale structure to observable signals.
arxiv-2601-19963:
Canyang Zhao and four colleagues tackle a core problem for brain-computer interfaces: recordings change between sessions. Electrodes implanted in the brain pick up spiking activity that decoders turn into commands. Activity recorded in one session drifts by the next, so trained decoders often fail. Retraining is hard when new-session data is scarce.

Their method aligns latent representations across sessions, conditioned on the task. Task-conditioned alignment uses what the user is doing to stabilise the decoding space. The goal is a decoder that survives days and weeks without full retraining. Reliable long-term decoding is essential for assistive devices people depend on daily. The work targets exactly the nonstationarity that limits real implants. The need is not in doubt.
arxiv-2601-20063: A search at the LHC looks for heavy particles that live long enough to cross the detector before decaying. Such long-lived charged particles would interact with the CMS muon system over several bunch crossings, leaving an unusual trail. The search uses a new data stream from the level-one trigger scouting system, which saves events that normal triggers discard. The data come from proton-proton collisions recorded by CMS in 2024. Finding or excluding these particles tests theories where new states decay slowly.
arxiv-2601-20263:
Jesua Epequin, Pascale Bendotti, and Joseph Mikael bring quantum photonics to the graph coloring problem. The task asks how to color a map or schedule so that neighbors differ. Their tool is Gaussian boson sampling, a quantum model that uses light to sample outcomes thought to be hard for classical machines. Recent experiments have shown quantum advantage with this model.

The authors recast graph coloring as an integer programming problem built on independent sets. That reformulation lets the sampling hardware attack a classic optimization task. Work like this tests whether near-term quantum devices can help with real scheduling and network problems.
arxiv-2601-20363:
Mariia Drozdova asks whether continuous-time diffusion models can generate and solve discrete problems with global constraints. Diffusion models work in continuous spaces, while a Sudoku grid is a sparse, tightly constrained discrete set. She uses completed Sudoku grids as a controlled testbed, viewing them inside a continuous relaxation space.

The question is whether a standard generative model can put its mass on such a thin, rule-bound set at all. Sudoku is a clean stand-in for many real tasks with hard global rules, from scheduling to code. The answer would mark a limit, or a new strength, of continuous generative modeling.
arxiv-2601-20563:
Dinesh Kumar analyzes how to harvest a fishery sustainably when part of the habitat is a marine protected area. The model has two patches: a harvestable zone and a reserve. Within each season, fish die, are harvested, and disperse between patches continuously; reproduction then follows a discrete Beverton-Holt map.

The study seeks optimal harvesting under this hybrid system, including bang-bang and singular control strategies. Reserves are widely used to protect stocks, but their value depends on how fishing is tuned outside them. The model gives managers a principled way to set that tuning.
arxiv-2601-20863:
Gabriel Sasseville and five co-authors fill the gaps in a famous black hole's flicker. Their 2026 paper studies Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of the Milky Way. Understanding its variability needs coordinated observations across the spectrum. Four observatories anchor the dataset. Chandra watches in X-rays. GRAVITY, on the Very Large Telescope, watches in near-infrared. Spitzer adds infrared coverage. The light curves from these eyes rarely align in time.

The authors use diffusion models to interpolate between observations. Their approach is probabilistic, so each filled gap carries honest uncertainty. A flare seen by one telescope can then be matched against the others. Timing across wavelengths reveals how matter heats and cools near the hole. The work turns sparse, staggered data into one coherent movie. It sharpens the study of our nearest supermassive black hole.
arxiv-2601-20963:
Seongjun Park and four co-authors revisit a common belief about frustrated magnets. Their 2026 paper studies a triangular-lattice supersolid. Geometrically frustrated magnets, on triangular grids, host rich quantum phases. Spin supersolids are among the most intriguing. Spin-orbit coupling breaks continuous spin symmetry. The common expectation is that it destabilizes supersolids by gapping their soft modes. The authors question that assumption.

They map the phase diagram across coupling strength and magnetic field. Their tools are spin-wave theory and infinite density-matrix renormalization group simulations. The title reports what they find: instability induced by spin-orbit coupling, then stabilization at finite temperature. Heat, usually a spoiler, here rescues the phase. The result reshapes how researchers hunt for supersolids. It suggests warm samples may show what cold ones hide.
arxiv-2601-21363:
Weidong Huang, Zhehan Li, Hangxin Liu, Biao Hou, Yao Su, and Jingwen Zhang bridge large-scale pretraining and cheap fine-tuning for humanoid robots. Trial-and-error training in huge parallel simulations can produce sturdy control. Some policies even move to real robots without extra work.

The catch is that the standard methods learn slowly from each trial. Slow learning makes it risky and costly to adapt a robot to a new setting. The authors aim to keep the strengths of big pretraining while adapting with far fewer trials. That balance is key to humanoids that can adjust safely outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-21563:
Stanisław M. S. Halkiewicz tests a long-standing conjecture about directed graphs on the smallest cases. The conjecture, from Seymour, concerns the second neighborhood of a vertex: the nodes two steps out along arrows. It claims some vertex always has at least as many nodes two steps out as one step out.

The author settles the claim for oriented graphs with up to seven vertices. Split-twin extensions then carry the result further. Small-case proofs matter because they expose the patterns a general proof must use. They also give computers and humans firm ground at the base of a hard problem.
arxiv-2601-21763:
Shuigen Liu and Xin Tong study how fast a classic sampling method settles down. Metropolis algorithms draw samples from a target distribution and are used across statistics and science computing. Their speed is governed by a quantity called the spectral gap, which measures how quickly the underlying chain forgets its starting point.

Recent work gave the first clear bounds on that gap for smooth target distributions. Many real targets, though, are not smooth. The 2026 preprint turns to those harder cases, working under a condition known as isoperimetry. Which links the shape of a distribution to how well a chain can move through it. Sharp gap bounds tell users how long they must run a sampler before its output can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-21963:
Alexander Loth, Martin Kappes, and Marc-Oliver Pahl update their picture of machine-made misinformation. Since their 2024 survey, generative systems have improved sharply, and language models now produce text, images. And audio that are hard to tell from human work. The threat landscape has shifted with them.

Their 2026 preprint moves from reviewing literature to practical countermeasures. It reports how model output pollutes digital ecosystems as a side effect. This is an industrialized form of deception. It spills onto platforms, search results, and public debate. The authors focus on what defenders can actually do. Their perspective helps policymakers separate measures with real effect from security theater.
arxiv-2601-22063:
Kevin Hall and Hai Fu look for faint glowing gas around distant quasars. Quasars hosted by dusty starburst galaxies may mark a transitional stage. At that stage, a growing black hole is still wrapped in gas and dust. That material is what fed it. The gas around such galaxies, the circumgalactic medium, glows faintly in Lyman-alpha light.

That faint glow is drowned by the quasar's own brilliance. The authors introduce CubeCarve, a dual-channel deconvolution algorithm that separates the unresolved quasar light from the extended emission. Their 2026 preprint maps the Lyman-alpha halos of four such quasars. Those maps show how gas flows around young quasars, feeding stars and black holes alike.
arxiv-2601-22363:
Meng-Yuan Li builds quantum error-correcting codes by a bootstrap product method. Good codes shield fragile quantum states from noise. His 2026 preprint notes that product builds have yielded famed codes, from toric codes to sparse-check codes with strong rates.

Past product tools rest on chain complexes, a bookkeeping frame for the code's checks. The new work extends that line with a bootstrap twist. Stronger code families would let quantum machines run longer and deeper tasks. The work is a math step toward that goal. It gives code builders a fresh pattern to try.
arxiv-2601-22863:
Walter F. Wreszinski strengthens a proof of the second law of thermodynamics for quantum spin systems. The law says that in a closed system, entropy grows toward its maximum. His earlier version stated this as a strict theorem for a class of quantum systems.

The new work improves the statement in two basic ways, covering both the general claim and its details. Treating the second law as a theorem, not just a rule of thumb, firms up the base of physics. Spin systems are a clean test bed for such deep claims.
arxiv-2601-22963:
Kegan Dougal tackles a clash between rival admins in shared, replicated group data. The data type, a CRDT, lets many copies merge without a central server, favoring availability when networks split. Group management adds a hard case: two admins may duel over the same membership change.

The proposal, ERA, resolves such clashes by epoch, giving each era a clear order of authority. Predictable conflict rules keep shared rosters and channels consistent after a split heals. The design fits chat, documents, and other tools that must work offline. Epoch-resolved arbitration gives group systems a deterministic answer when two admins issue conflicting changes during a network partition.
arxiv-2601-23063:
Maddalena Amendola and four co-authors examine gender gaps on Stack Overflow, the programmer question-and-answer site. Such platforms rate answers and expertise, ideally without bias. Yet earlier research keeps finding gender biases, raising doubts about fairness and inclusion.

Their study frames the gap as a matter of quantity versus quality. It asks whether differences lie in how much users contribute, or in how their work is judged. Knowing which side drives the gap points to the right fix for community platforms. The platform's own answer ratings frame the study, since those mechanisms claim to reward expertise regardless of who contributes.
arxiv-2602-02463:
Sakthi Priya Amirtharaj and 9 co-authors use optical gating to read the history of light pulses reshaped by Raman scattering, in a 2026 arXiv paper. When two chirped pump pulses drive Raman scattering at many frequencies, the anti-Stokes orders broaden unevenly toward lower frequencies. Each order takes on a double-peaked spectrum.

Frequency-resolved optical gating, or FROG, tracks how the spectrum of the first anti-Stokes part changes over time. To read the traces, the team built a double-pulse interference model plus a learning-based algorithm using the Adam optimizer. The algorithm recovers how the field changed over time from the readings. Modeled results agreed well with the measured ones. The analysis ties the red-shifted spectral part to linear Raman effects in a two-photon dressed-state picture.
arxiv-2602-02663:
Preethi Gopalakrishnan and 2 co-authors show in a 2026 arXiv paper that measuring a quantum system again and again can dial its chaos up or down. Their probe is a generalized spectral form factor, computed as the chance that a thermal coherent state survives while its energy is measured again and again. The length of the form factor's ramp is a standard fingerprint of chaotic dynamics.

Changing how strongly and how efficiently the system is monitored stretches or shrinks that ramp. One fully monitored trajectory looks more chaotic than both the averaged monitored evolution and the same system left unmeasured. The pattern repeats across symmetry classes and across independent chaos diagnostics, including out-of-time-order correlators and Liouvillian spectra. Measurement, usually fought as a disturbance, becomes a deliberate control for quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2602-02763:
Bohan Wang and 6 co-authors show that a time series classifier's explanation can look fully steady while its prediction has been hijacked in secret, in a 2026 paper. Interpretable systems are often judged robust when explanations stay steady over time. That assumption, the authors show, is unsafe.

Their attack, TSEF, targets prediction and explanation jointly. It forces a chosen wrong class while keeping the explanation consistent with a reference rationale the attacker picks. Single-objective attacks, by contrast, scatter blame broadly and disrupt the explanation, giving themselves away. Across multiple data sets and explainer backbones, the dual-target attack succeeded again and again. The lesson cuts at testing practice: explanation stability is a poor proxy for choice robustness. Trustworthy time series systems need coupling-aware robustness tests that check prediction and explanation jointly, not one at a time.
arxiv-2602-02863:
Jinkun Chen and 3 co-authors ask whether a language model's reasoning breakdown can be spotted while it happens, in a 2026 paper. Most checks only grade the final answer. Yet many failures begin mid-answer, when the model loses the thread of its own argument.

The authors build a simple instability signal from token probabilities available in standard interfaces. It combines sudden shifts between steps with uncertainty at each step. Peak instability predicted wrong answers on math and multi-step question datasets. Timing mattered too. Early instability often recovered and ended correctly. Late instability more often led to failure. The method needs no training and works across model sizes.
arxiv-2602-02963:
Comparing chest X-rays over time is automated in a second 2026 paper by OFM Riaz Rahman Aranya and 1 co-author. Radiologists compare a prior and current scan to spot progression, response to treatment, or new findings. Earlier vision-language models handled single images, but none combined comparison, change classification, and localization together.

Their model, TRACE, takes both scans as input. It writes natural-language descriptions of interval changes, labeling each as worsened, improved, or stable. Each finding comes with box coordinates locating it in the image. Grounding score exceeded ninety percent. Ablation tests revealed something striking. Change finding emerged only when comparison and grounding were learned jointly, suggesting grounding supplies the spatial focus time thinking needs.
arxiv-2602-03063:
Matthew Dominique Mitchell's solo 2026 paper analyzes a wave equation in the limit where dispersion becomes very small. The intermediate long wave equation describes certain internal waves. Mitchell studies well-behaved starting profiles for which the number of solitons, isolated wave packets, in the solution grows without bound as the limit is approached in the analysis.

A WKB-style analysis of the scattering problem gives approximate eigenvalues and norming constants. Those define a modified set of scattering data for rigorous study of the inverse problem. The main results show convergence at time zero to the original profile. For a window of later times, solutions converge to those of the inviscid Burgers equation, up to the time of gradient catastrophe.
arxiv-2602-03263:
Safety failures that only appear when image and text combine are targeted by Yuxuan Liu, leading a team of 4 others, in a benchmark called CSR-Bench. Multimodal models can be driven by single-modality shortcuts instead of true joint understanding of intent. Each benchmark instance therefore requires integrated image-text interpretation, with paired text-only controls to diagnose shifts caused by adding the image to the prompt.

Four stress patterns span safety, over-rejection, bias, and hallucination across many fine-grained types. Sixteen leading models were evaluated. Systematic gaps appeared, including weak safety awareness, strong language dominance under interference, and consistent degradation from text-only to multimodal inputs. A trade-off also emerged between reducing over-rejection and maintaining safe, non-discriminatory behavior, suggesting some gains come from refusal habits.
arxiv-2602-03463:
Lidia Gargyants and 2 co-authors study a free boundary problem for the equations of cold plasma. Those equations describe electrons moving in the field of fixed ions. Their 2026 paper poses a Riemann problem at an impenetrable interface separating two media. The media differ only in the strength of their constant ion field, and the interface itself is allowed to move.

The position of the free interface is determined from generalized Rankine-Hugoniot conditions, the jump rules that any sharp front must obey. A stability condition also enters: Lagrangian particle trajectories must intersect at the interface. The work gives a precise mathematical formulation for how such a plasma boundary evolves. It is a building block for sharper models of plasma behavior at material interfaces.
arxiv-2602-03563:
Contrastive learning helps models pull similar examples together, but in supervised fine-tuning it can fight the main classification loss. Liz Li and Wei Zhu investigate that conflict in a 2026 paper on BERT, the classic language encoder. Their pilot experiments show the cross-entropy objective and the contrastive objective often pull in opposite directions.

Their framework, Aligned Contrastive Learning, turns label embeddings into extra augmented samples and aligns them with the matching examples. A gradient rule drops the contrastive term whenever the two objectives clash. A cross-layer version lets a strong deep exit teach the shallow exits of multi-exit BERT. On the GLUE benchmark the approach matches or beats plain fine-tuning and clearly improves multi-exit models' speed-quality trade-off.
arxiv-2602-03763:
Graphs capture pairwise links, but simplicial complexes also record group interactions through triangles and higher shapes. Mathias Hudoba de Badyn and Tyler Summers study flows on such complexes in a 2026 paper. They use weighted Hodge Laplacians, the natural extension of the graph Laplacian. Their goal is consensus dynamics, where interacting agents converge toward agreement.

The authors build a scheme for weighted consensus and prove decomposition results for the weighted operators. Two key spectral quantities, the trace of the pseudoinverse and the smallest nonzero eigenvalue, turn out to be jointly convex in the simplex weights. That convexity lets both be optimized through semidefinite programs, yielding globally optimal weights. Numerical tests show optimal weights far outperform uniform ones.
arxiv-2602-04063:
Pathologists grade protein stains by eye; Jacob S. Leiby and colleagues built an AI partner to help. Their 2026 paper introduces HPA10M, a dataset of over ten million immunohistochemistry images from the Human Protein Atlas. It spans forty-five normal tissue types and twenty major cancers, with rich metadata.

On that data they trained iSight, which jointly predicts staining intensity, location, quantity, tissue type, and malignancy. Attention links slide images with tissue metadata at token level. Held-out accuracy beat fine-tuned foundation models by several points, and predictions were well calibrated. The aim is expert-AI co-assessment, speeding triage without replacing pathologist judgment.
arxiv-2602-04163:
Two-bit language models usually fall apart; Junyu Chen and colleagues keep one standing. Their 2026 paper presents BPDQ, a quantization method that replaces the fixed grid of earlier schemes with a variable one built from bit-planes and scalar coefficients. Second-order information guides iterative refinement while errors are progressively compensated.

Theory shows the variable grid strictly enlarges the feasible set. In practice, a seventy-two-billion-parameter model served on a single consumer graphics card retained most of its math accuracy at two bits. Memory footprint and bandwidth, the true bottlenecks of local deployment, shrink several-fold.
arxiv-2602-04263:
Answering a question may require hopping between text, tables, and images across documents. Joohyung Yun and 2 co-authors built LILaC for that open-domain multimodal multihop retrieval in a 2026 paper. Fixed retrieval units drag in irrelevant content, and single-pass search cannot chain evidence.

Their layered component graph represents document parts at coarse and fine granularity together. Retrieval first finds coarse nodes cheaply, then reasons over edges with late interaction at fine granularity. Experiments show state-of-the-art results. Layered graphs let retrievers stay precise without scanning everything at maximum detail, a balance document-heavy assistants need.
arxiv-2602-04463:
Florian Adriaens and Nikolaj Tatti study a graph problem in a 2026 paper on bad triangles. In a signed graph, edges can be positive or negative. A bad triangle has exactly one negative edge, and the task is to remove as few edges as possible to eliminate all such triangles.

The authors give several simple methods that come within a factor of two of the best possible answer. They also prove the problem is hard to approximate beyond a very small margin. Their hardness result extends to related problems, including correlation clustering. They further show that the optima for two of these problems stay within a modest factor on complete graphs.
arxiv-2602-04563:
Duaa Abdullah and Marwa Abdullah propose a combined method for judging the risk in company accounts of manufacturing firms, in a 2026 paper that joins regression with multi-criteria decision making. Single discounting methods can miss how economic, workplace, and managerial factors interact.

Their scheme first converts costs and benefits at varied times into present values using compound interest. It handles one-time spending, costs that grow with time, and complex costs during development and setup. Linear regression then serves as the fitting method for judging how discounted results respond to several criteria. The paper is mainly about theory, setting out the model and its parts. It aims at richer risk checks than discounting alone.
arxiv-2602-04663:
Jaemoo Choi and 8 co-authors dissect how reinforcement learning should be applied to diffusion models in a 2026 paper. These image generators lack tractable likelihoods, the probabilities needed by standard policy-gradient methods, so practitioners rely on engineered objectives and rough estimates.

The authors separate three design factors: the objective, the likelihood estimator, and the sampling scheme. A likelihood estimate based on an evidence lower bound, computed only from the final sample, proved dominant. It outweighed the choice of loss function for effective, stable training. Tests on a mid-sized image model confirmed the pattern across reward benchmarks. Their method improved one score dramatically with far less computing than rivals.
arxiv-2602-04863:
Ishaq Aden-Ali and 5 co-authors uncover a mechanism by which training data can transmit hidden behaviors to language models in a 2026 paper. Recent experiments showed datasets conveying signals not visible in any single example, which challenges how researchers reason about training data.

Inspired by the linear structure inside language models, the authors introduce Logit-Linear-Selection, a method for choosing subsets of an ordinary preference dataset to elicit hidden effects. Models trained on selected subsets exhibited specific preferences, answered in a language absent from the data, or adopted a different persona. Crucially, the effect persisted for the selected subset across models with different architectures. That persistence supports the mechanism's generality. The work gives dataset curation a new, sharper risk to watch.
arxiv-2602-05163:
Underwater photos come back dull: contrast fades, colors shift, and fine detail blurs with depth. Andreas Mentzelopoulos and Keith Ellenbogen built LOBSTgER-enhance to undo that damage in this 2026 computer vision paper. Ellenbogen is an awareness photographer whose marine images supply the project's small, high-quality dataset.

Instead of collecting paired before-and-after shots, the team synthesized the damage. A corruption pipeline degrades clean images in realistic underwater ways, and a compact diffusion model, about eleven million parameters, learns to reverse the process. Training from scratch on roughly two and a half thousand images, the system produced enhanced pictures at 512 by 768 resolution with high perceptual consistency. The authors report strong generalization beyond the training set, which matters for photographers who cannot afford heavy manual post-processing.
arxiv-2602-05563:
Simulating turbulent airflow around cars and aircraft is costly, and fine grids that resolve every swirl are often out of reach. Diego Escobar, Douglas Pacheco, and 2 co-authors propose a variational multiscale method that handles the unresolved scales without a problem-specific turbulence model. Their version uses dynamic subscales applied term by term, inside a fractional-step solver that separates pressure from velocity.

Orthogonal projections keep the scheme stable while letting it use equal-order interpolation for velocity and pressure. The team validates it on the Ahmed body, a standard car-like test shape, across meshes of up to tens of millions of elements. A realistic Formula 1 configuration at highway-plus speed provides a second, harder test. Results show the method stays robust at scale and captures separated flow and wake structure. The work targets engineers who simulate external aerodynamics.
arxiv-2602-05863:
Adding safety constraints to GRPO, the dominant critic free method for fine tuning language models, exposes a subtle failure in how rewards are combined. Roger Girgis, Rodrigue de Schaetzen, and 4 co-authors introduce Constrained GRPO, a Lagrangian based extension for constrained policy optimization. The standard practice scalarizes rewards before normalization, mixing reward and constraint signals into one number.

That order creates a coupling problem: because normalization is shared, changing one constraint multiplier also reshuffles the relative weight of the reward and the other constraints. The fix is simple but crucial: scalarize the standardized advantages instead of the raw rewards. The update becomes better conditioned, multiplier dynamics behave, and constraint enforcement stabilizes. Experiments span a controlled gridworld, a real autonomous driving benchmark, and a math reasoning task. Across all three, the constrained method adhered better to the stated constraints. The paper targets safety critical fine tuning, where constraints are the point.
arxiv-2602-06863:
Elliot Gathercole works on the shape of spaces left after a divisor is cut out of a complex variety. Inside such a cut-out space sits a core shape called a Lagrangian skeleton. Gathercole gives rules for when that core acts as a barrier, in Biran's sense, blocking certain paths through the space.

He also bounds the Gromov width of what remains once the core is removed, a size gauge for the largest ball that can fit in a symplectic sense. The sharpest results come for line patterns in flat projective space. In two dimensions, with a generic set of at least three lines, the bounds are tight. The work links divisor shapes to the symplectic size of the spaces around them.
arxiv-2602-07263:
As low-rank adaptation becomes the standard way to fine-tune large models, clusters run many LoRA jobs at once on the same frozen backbone, and naive batching creates stalls and slowdowns.  Kevin Li and three co-authors present tLoRA, a method for training many heterogeneous LoRA jobs efficiently.

tLoRA fuses adapters sharing a base model into an elastic shared super-model and derives parallelism plans that share resources well. Kernel-level support covers the mixed ranks and batch sizes.  The payoff is higher cluster throughput without per-job slowdowns.  Teams fine-tuning fleets of adapters get a system-level answer to a problem that grows with every new adapter.
arxiv-2602-07563:
In a random model of minimum-cost bipartite matching with exponential edge costs, the optimal cost's spread turns out to be computable.  Johan Wästlund shows that spread is captured by its moment generating function, which in this model is always rational.

The complex zeros of that function matter: no zeros near the origin signals regularity of the spread.  The paper conjectures those functions never have complex zeros of smaller modulus than their first pole, which for the assignment problem would imply a Gaussian scaling limit.  Combinatorial optimizers get an efficient distributional computation plus a precise claim linking zeros to limit laws.
arxiv-2602-07663:
Serving language models and scheduling GPUs both involve picking a configuration and then deciding whether to accept each incoming request, a two-layer online problem.  Owen Shen and four co-authors build a method for joint online configuration choice and admission control over a planning horizon.

Each period, a configuration choice induces a reward-resource spread for the next request, which is then accepted or rejected.  Benchmarking needs care, so the paper presents a switching-aware fluid oracle that values mixing configurations over time and upper-bounds any online policy, with a max-min form and saddle-point characterization.  Operations teams get a principled benchmark and policy method for a ubiquitous serving problem.
arxiv-2602-07963:
Safety tests for language models mostly run in English, but harm does not always survive translation intact. Vaibhav Shukla and five co-authors build CompositeHarm, a benchmark that extends two English harm datasets into Hindi, Assamese, Marathi, Kannada, and Gujarati, to see how alignment holds as syntax and semantics shift.

Across three large models, harmful prompts succeed far more often in Indic languages, most of all when the wording is twisted against the model, while harms tied to context spread moderately. The study uses lightweight inference strategies to keep the evaluation scalable and energy-efficient. Multilingual safety teams gain evidence that English-only testing overstates safety, and a benchmark for measuring the gap in languages spoken by hundreds of millions.
arxiv-2602-08063:
Learning an unknown probability distribution from samples is fundamental, but users also need a trustworthy bound on how far their approximation sits from the truth. Eduardo Figueiredo and two co-authors build a method that approximates a distribution by a discrete one while bounding the Wasserstein distance between them with high confidence.

Their approach combines optimal transport, nonlinear optimization, and concentration inequalities, reducing the bound to a tractable optimization problem even though the true distribution is unknown. The method matters across machine learning, control, decision theory, and biology, wherever a distribution must be learned with a certificate, not just a point estimate. Statisticians gain error bounds they can actually compute.
arxiv-2602-08263:
Language-model program repair usually rewrites code directly, risking fixes that look plausible but behave inconsistently. Taohong Zhu and three co-authors propose VibeRepair, a specification-centric alternative that treats repair as fixing a behavior specification rather than editing code ad hoc.

The method first translates buggy code into a structured specification of intended runtime behavior, then finds and repairs misalignments in that specification, and finally synthesizes code strictly guided by the corrected specification. An on-demand reasoning component adds program analysis and historical fix evidence for hard cases while controlling cost. Across Defects4J and real-world benchmarks, the approach competes strongly. Software engineers gain repair grounded in stated behavior, not just plausible text.
arxiv-2602-08663:
Platinum ditelluride hosts tilted Dirac fermions that promise tunable non-linear optics, but its third-harmonic response needed a clear theory. Leone Di Mauro Villari and five co-authors calculate the non-linear conductivity from a low-energy model fitted to density-functional band structures. Their arXiv paper focuses on type-II Dirac cones along a high-symmetry direction.

Cone tilting efficiently modulates third-order non-linearities, producing a large boost in non-linear response strength. The results illuminate topological transitions in the material and point toward nanophotonic devices exploiting tunable non-linear traits of tilted Dirac fermions. Readers get an analytic account linking band topology to measurable optical response.
arxiv-2602-08763:
The Sun's middle layer sits between surface and corona, where light drives energy transfer and drift from balance matters greatly. W. Ruan and three co-authors extend the MURaM code with light transfer for Lyman lines, the strong hydrogen lines that rule energy exchange there. Their arXiv paper targets accurate H level counts and heat change in this layer.

A one-tone shortcut per line keeps costs down while solving level and heat rules self-consistently. Results match the Lightweaver benchmark well, capturing Lyman-line light physics. Deep-layer levels move closer to detailed balance, while upper layers remain far from it, as in the real Sun. Readers get a cheaper, checked route to motion in the Sun's middle layer.
arxiv-2602-08863:
A practical source of entangled light is a building block for quantum networks, and Tess Troisi and six co-authors report one built entirely from standard fiber parts. Their Sagnac interferometer source works at telecom wavelengths and needs no bulk optics, making it compact, sturdy, and ready for field use. It supports both polarization and energy-time entanglement without changes.

Broadband generation allows dense wavelength multiplexing across the telecom C and L bands. On a standard 100 gigahertz channel pair, brightness reaches 10.3 thousand pairs per second per nanometer per milliwatt squared. Fidelities, purities, and visibilities top 96 percent across channels, and long runs confirm stable operation in a network setting.
arxiv-2602-09063:
Frontier AI agents shine at coding, but can they extract biology from messy single-cell data? Kenny Workman and four co-authors introduce scBench, a benchmark of 394 verifiable problems drawn from real single-cell RNA-sequencing workflows across six platforms and seven task types. Each problem freezes experimental data just before an analysis step, with a deterministic grader checking recovery of a key biological result.

Eight leading models score only 29 to 53 percent, with strong interactions between model, task, and platform. Platform choice matters as much as model choice, with accuracy dropping over forty points on less-documented technologies. Paired with SpatialBench, scBench offers a diagnostic lens for building agents that analyze single-cell data faithfully and reproducibly.
arxiv-2602-09163:
Curating a scientific knowledge base means searching papers, weighing evidence, and writing ontology-grounded annotations, expert work that isolated benchmarks do not capture. Xingjian Zhang and five co-authors present FlyAOC, which tests AI agents on end-to-end ontology curation for Drosophila genetics. Given a gene symbol, a short FlyBase description, a 16,898-paper corpus, and ontology resources, agents must recover as many curator-relevant annotations as possible.

The benchmark holds 7,397 expert annotations across 100 genes, spanning function terms, expression patterns, and historical synonyms from decades of naming. Four baseline harnesses, from memorization to multi-agent teams, show the task reacts to harness design, model family, and tool trust, exposing system-level failures that model-only tests miss. FlyAOC gives curation research a reproducible test bed.
arxiv-2602-09263:
Cloud-linked Internet-of-Things devices prove who they are through vendor silos, creating lag and uptime choke points for device-to-device talks. Sanket Goutam and two co-authors present Atlas, a setup stretching the web public-key base to IoT. Vendor-run ACME clients hand X.509 papers to devices under vendor-run DNS name zones, giving each device a world-wide checkable ID without hardware changes.

Devices then open joint TLS lines straight across office zones, cutting runtime proof-of-identity from cloud reach. Test builds on ESP32 and Raspberry Pi, joined with an MQTT stack and an Atlas-aware cloud, hand out papers in under six seconds per device. They add only about 17 milliseconds of TLS lag, and keep low, steady lag in smart-home and smart-city jobs. Since major vendors already use ACME-compatible paper issuers, rollout needs tiny new base.
arxiv-2602-09563:
Steering tiny swimmers along target paths is a core tiny-robot challenge, since low-Reynolds-number fluid physics tangles control design. Lucas Palazzolo and two co-authors frame path tracking as an optimal control problem in their 2026 paper, solving it with B-spline curve fitting plus Bayesian tuning. The mix handles high compute costs without needing complex math.

Applied to a tailed magnet swimmer, the method copies varied target paths, including life-like routes seen in tests. Tests on a three-sphere swimmer model show it bending to and partly easing wall-induced fluid effects. The plan works evenly across model detail levels, from low-size rule-based models to high-detail sim runs, showing Bayesian tuning as a handy tool for tiny-scale motion under complex fluid-structure play.
arxiv-2602-09663:
David Elbaz defines a global entropy for dissipative systems such as stars and galaxies in his 2026 paper. Emitted photons decouple from matter particles, so photons plus matter form a closed system to which the Second Law of Thermodynamics applies. His statistical definition counts contributions from both matter particles and photons, with radiation treated as a photon gas.

Rising global entropy can foster structure formation rather than disorder, because structures like stars and galaxies dissipate energy efficiently as photons and thus produce entropy. Stars generate nearly equal specific entropy, and comparable photons per unit mass, over their lifetimes on the Hertzsprung-Russell main sequence, suggesting the main sequence marks convergence toward a universal specific entropy production. A similar result holds for the star-formation main sequence in galaxies, and low-frequency photons dominate the extragalactic background light.
arxiv-2602-10163:
Agentic systems now plan syntheses, mine literature, and design molecules on their own, but how far do they generalize? A 2026 paper by Edward Wijaya tests six frameworks against fifteen task classes spanning peptide therapeutics, in vivo pharmacology, and tight-resource settings. The verdict is five capability gaps, not one.

The frameworks lack protein language models and peptide-specific prediction, bridge nothing between in vivo and in silico data, and rely on language-model inference with no path to training or reinforcement learning. They assume large-pharma resources and optimize single objectives, ignoring safety-efficacy-stability trade-offs. A paired probing experiment suggests the bottleneck is architectural: frontier models reason about peptides well, but no framework exposes that ability.
arxiv-2602-10263:
Nonlinear Schrödinger equations with log nonlinearity admit exact localized Gaussian solutions called Gaussons, but a broader family has remained open. A 2026 paper by Hadi Susanto, sole author, introduces a new set of nonlinear Schrödinger equations with a log-power nonlinearity admitting exact localized super-Gaussian solutions. The steady states show flat-top profiles with crisp edges and are named super-Gaussons.

The model, called logp-NLS, carries an exponent of at least one controlling flatness of the soliton core and sharpness of its decay. The exponent bridges the standard log-NLS and ever flatter profiles, while setting stiffness of an underlying log-power squeeze law. Computer runs in one spatial dimension show how the parameter shapes inner structure and collision behavior, widening log-NLS toward flat-top wave uses.
arxiv-2602-10363:
Transonic buffet over aircraft wings cuts handling through unsteady air loads from shock-layer interactions. A 2026 paper led by Tea Vojković, with five co-authors, presents a reduced-order model tracking nonlinear change in the full flow field by using an attracting two-dimensional invariant manifold. Current data-driven frameworks for finding invariant manifolds and reduced dynamics are adapted for large-scale fluid dynamics work.

The manifold is found as a graph over its tangent space through iterative encoder updates, with reduced dynamics from least-squares regression. A normal-form transformation then makes the model readable through a modal decomposition. That gives engineers a compact model of a classic global instability with nonlinearity, sharp spatial gradients, and coexisting shaky equilibrium and attracting limit cycle.
arxiv-2602-10863:
Cong Pang and ten co-authors improve credit assignment for web information-seeking agents in a 2026 paper. Long-horizon reward-based learning struggles because terminal rewards say whether the final answer is right, not which acquired information enabled it. Text-derived webpage views worsen the problem, as parsing and summarization produce unstable content models across paths.

Their evidence-centric system represents acquired information as identifiable units comparable across paths. Fetched webpages become rendered snapshots, keeping layout and mixed content as stable views. On those units, information-aware credit assignment propagates rewards post hoc, estimating turn-level utility from rollout success rates. The method tells agents not just that they succeeded, but what they found that mattered.
arxiv-2602-10963:
A slender rod that bends, twists, and changes its cross-section needs a careful model. Srishti Siddharth and two co-authors first write the full space-time motion rules for a 3D Cosserat rod with flat cross-section change. They then turn those rules into a discrete model with a Lie group variational integrator.

The discrete model keeps the volume of its small pieces by tracking local stretch, keeps the rod's spin setup intact, and keeps energy error bounded. A wide set of test runs under varied starts shows the model reproduces the rod's physics well. The work suits readers who need rod models that stay true to shape and energy over long runs.
arxiv-2602-11163:
Plasma physics papers hide entities that ordinary tools miss. Muhammad Haris and three co-authors apply nested named entity recognition to plasma physics articles, where entities nest inside one another and context runs dense. Their approach pairs encoder models with conditional random fields.

They annotate a plasma corpus with sixteen entity classes built for nesting, train separate models per entity type, and tune hyperparameters in a systematic sweep. The result is a lightweight pipeline for advanced search and literature navigation in plasma science. The paper also lays a foundation for researchers who need to find and compare specialized entities across many papers.
arxiv-2602-11263:
A small excess of electron-positron pairs may hint at a new particle. Max H. Fieg and three co-authors examine the X17 anomaly, where excited nuclei emit more pairs at wide angles than the Standard Model predicts. The hypothetical particle sits near seventeen megaelectronvolts, with a recent accelerator hint adding weight.

Prior spin-one studies used vector or axial-vector couplings alone, but realistic theories give both, chiral couplings like the weak force. The authors map the setting space that can explain the nuclear signals under chiral couplings. A fit is possible, yet the favoured region tensions with null results from atomic parity violation and direct low-mass searches, driven largely by one carbon transition excess.
arxiv-2602-11463:
Radar through walls is distorted by the wall itself. Kainat Yasmeen and Shobha Sundar Ram propose deep neural networks that value wall thickness, dielectric, and conductivity profiles from broadband scattered fields measured on the transmitter side. Knowing the wall lets its effects be deconvolved from target spread.

Single deep and convolutional networks, plus dual networks with generative adversarial components, all handle the highly curved inverse spread regression. Training uses simulation data from full-wave solvers, validated on simulated and real walls at about ninety-five percent scores. The work turns wall profile from a tuning headache into a learnable regression task.
arxiv-2602-11563:
Atoms excited to Rydberg states can make light beams interact with each other, a trick at the heart of quantum optics, yet its role in microwave and radio sensing is still murky. Xinghan Wang and three co-authors shine light through cold atoms under electromagnetically induced transparency and watch how photon-photon interaction reshapes the spectrum. In a three-level setup, stronger interaction widens the lines and shifts their centers.

A four-level setup dressed with microwaves shows strong widening with no detectable shift, a surprise the authors capture with a simple dephasing model while the three-level data fit a conditional superatom picture. Comparing three models clarifies when many-body effects matter in these spectra. The work also maps when microwave fields can be measured in the nonlinear regime without biasing the result.
arxiv-2602-11663:
People who survive near-death events often share their stories to process trauma and articulate belief. Most research studies solo accounts, not how such stories travel together online. Yifan Zhao and three co-authors analyze 200 randomly sampled TikTok videos tagged for near-death experiences. They also study the comment sections. Spiritual and religious themes appear in the majority of posts. They serve as a way to explore personal meaning and make sense of faith.

Videos with spiritual themes draw more engagement than others. They also foster deeper conversations about faith and meaning. The pattern suggests the platform supports community-level engagement with spirituality, not just isolated confession. The findings point to design lessons for online spaces that host shared expression in specialized communities. There, belief is worked out in public, in dialogue, rather than declared once and left alone.
arxiv-2602-12263:
Building operator lists for non-relativistic effective theories by hand is error-prone, with spin repeats and repeated fields tripping up counts. Yong-Kang Li led this work with two co-authors, giving a systematic frame that joins three-dimensional Euclidean symmetry to internal symmetries. A double cover of rotations extends Hilbert series to non-relativistic systems and removes spin-induced repeats.

A generalised Young tensor method, built on SU(2) semi-standard tableaux, then builds operator bases with repeated fields at any mass dimension. Cross-checked against Hilbert series, the methods yield complete bases for three cases. These are heavy-particle and heavy-quark theories to dimension 9, pion-less theories with nucleon contacts and three-body terms, and spin-half dark matter-nucleon operators to fourth order in velocity.
arxiv-2602-12363:
Mathematicians use many notions of sameness, from group actions to pullbacks, and a single frame that unifies them would clarify their links. Nizar El Idrissi works alone here, introducing a general equivalence relation on the global class of morphisms of a category. The definition is broad enough to subsume several older notions, rather than treating each as a separate invention.

Group-action relations, pullback relations, and coarse operator-based relations on continuous Bessel families all emerge as special cases of this one link. The paper also gives frame-theoretic examples, showing how the abstract definition lands in concrete settings. Readers get a unifying lens: familiar notions of sameness become instances of one general construction, with their shared structure made explicit.
arxiv-2602-12963:
Does behaving optimally require an internal model of the world? Alfred Harwood and two co-authors quantify the question information-theoretically. For a controlled Markov process with n states and m actions, assume a uniform prior over transition dynamics. They prove that observing a deterministic policy optimal for any non-constant reward reveals exactly n log m bits about the environment.

That mutual information bound holds across finite, discounted infinite, and time-averaged objectives, giving a precise lower bound on the implicit world model optimality demands. The result is clean and general: optimal behaviour cannot be information-free, and the price in bits grows with states and actions. For AI theory, it formalises how much world knowledge success must encode, even when no explicit model is built.
arxiv-2602-13063:
The EMML recipe reconstructs images under Poisson noise and belongs to the expectation-maximisation family, but its deeper structure has been unclear. Antonin Clerc and three co-authors reinterpret EMML as mirror descent applied to a reparametrised objective. That viewpoint lets convex constraints enter through Bregman projections while preserving the multiplicative update structure that keeps EMML lean.

The authors then prove the limited recipe converges to a answer of the limited maximum-odds task. Number tests on hyperspectral unmixing show the limited version converging in fewer iterations than standard EMML. For image reconstruction, the reinterpretation is both conceptual and practical: an old recipe gains constraints and a convergence story through a modern tuning lens.
arxiv-2602-13363:
Coding agents that write software on their own raise a sharp misuse question: can they also build the tools of a scam? This study tests that risk directly for spear-phishing sites, comparing different language models on both ability and willingness to produce website code bases that attackers could misuse. The comparison matters because agents act alone, at speed, doing work that once needed skilled programmers.

The effort produced a data set of 200 website code bases plus logs from 40 coding agents, and analysis shows which model traits track with phishing-site performance and which do not. Researchers and defenders concerned with agent misuse can use the data set to build better guards. Tailia Malloy leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13463:
A planet-forming disc's mass sets its whole budget for making planets, yet measuring it is indirect: molecular hydrogen cannot be seen directly, and carbon monoxide ratios are poorly pinned down. The standard route converts dust continuum flux to total mass by assuming a dust-to-gas mass ratio, epsilon, which is itself poorly constrained. This paper asks how epsilon shapes what we see, running planet-bearing hydrodynamical simulations of dusty discs while varying the ratio.

If a planet mass can be estimated independently, the authors suggest, disc morphology could then constrain epsilon in observed systems relative to one another, sharpening total mass estimates across discs. The link between shape and ratio turns a modeling choice into a measurable feature. Matthew Murray leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13563:
Signal boosters for faint quantum signals face a snag: Kerr effects distort squeezing and degrade gain and quantum efficiency under strong drive. This paper proposes a flux-pumped superconducting booster built from evenly threaded SQUIDs that reaches a Kerr-free operating point under suitable drive conditions.
