Henry Méndez, Georg Heimel, Stefanie Winkler, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2015. They challenge the standard story of molecular electrical doping in organic semiconductors. The usual view says a dopant molecule hands a whole charge to the host material, freeing a mobile charge carrier.

The authors show that a fundamentally different process can take over, depending on the host type. In small-molecule materials, dopant and host can lock together into charge-transfer crystallites, tiny ordered crystals with shared charge. These crystallites themselves act as the electrical dopants. The result matters for organic lights, solar cells, and transistors, where controlled doping makes devices work and design rules had assumed one mechanism only.
openalex-w2321443763:
Hazem Kalaji, Anjana Jajoo, Abdallah Oukarroum, and colleagues published this review in Acta Physiologiae Plantarum in 2016. They survey chlorophyll fluorescence as a way to watch plant health without harming the plant. Leaves re-emit a flicker of light during photosynthesis, and that signal betrays stress long before wilting shows.

Fluorescence readings report on photosystem II, the water-splitting engine of photosynthesis. They reveal the state of its reaction centers, light-harvesting antennae, and both electron entry and exit sides. The review gathers fast-fluorescence studies across drought, heat, salt, and other stresses. Portable meters now take the method outdoors. The authors see wide use ahead in crop breeding trials and field monitoring of stressed stands.
openalex-w2512047063:
Gabriella Morais Duarte Miranda, Antônio da Cruz Gouveia Mendes, and Ana Lúcia Andrade da Silva wrote this 2016 article on population aging in Brazil. It appeared in the Revista Brasileira de Geriatria e Gerontologia. The authors ask whether public policy is ready for a much older country. Their case study mixes national data systems with interviews from health and social policy actors.

In 2010 Brazil had thirty-nine older people for every hundred young people. By 2040 the estimate jumps to one hundred fifty-three per hundred. Interviewees said the country is not prepared, pointing to strains on pensions and health care. Older patients bring more disease, disability, and lasting effects, needing steady, team-based care. The authors urge the state to plan specific policies that protect quality of life in old age.
openalex-w2547739063:
Muhammad Awais Khan, Dorcus C. Gemenet, and Arthur Q. Villordon wrote this 2016 review in Frontiers in Plant Science. It surveys root system architecture in root and tuber crops such as cassava, potato, sweetpotato, and yam. Root shape decides how well a plant takes up water and nutrients and anchors itself. It also shapes how crops cope with drought and other stresses.

The authors note that root research on these crops lags far behind work on cereals. Most studies examine only the harvested storage root, not the whole root system. They describe how the root systems of the four major crops are built. Storage roots, they explain, grow from shoot-born roots rather than from a seedling root. Pulling this scattered knowledge together should help breeders shape roots that tolerate harsh growing conditions.
openalex-w2982538063:
Manuel Ramos-Casals, Pilar Brito-Zerón, Stefano Bombardieri, and colleagues issued these recommendations in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases in 2019. They come from a task force of the European League Against Rheumatism, known as EULAR. The subject is Sjögren's syndrome, an autoimmune disease best known for dry eyes and dry mouth.

Treatment of this syndrome had barely changed in decades, with no target beyond easing symptoms. The task force set out to build the first EULAR guidance based on evidence and expert consensus. The recommendations cover both local treatments, such as drops and gels, and whole-body drug therapies. They give doctors a shared, current basis for choices that had long rested on habit and judgment alone.
openalex-w2984799663:
Karen de la Cruz-López, Leonardo Castro-Muñoz, Diego Reyes-Hernández, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Oncology. It examines lactate, a byproduct of sugar use, and its role in shaping the neighborhood around a tumor. That neighborhood, the tumor microenvironment, helps decide whether a cancer grows or stalls.

Tumor cells take in large amounts of glucose and release excess lactate even when oxygen is plentiful, a pattern first described by Otto Warburg in 1926. This metabolic shift is now counted among the hallmarks of cancer. Lactate does more than mark the shift: it regulates conditions around the tumor. The review covers that regulation and the treatment ideas that aim at lactate itself.
openalex-w3016898363:
M. Masiokas, A. Rabatel, A. Rivera, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Earth Science in 2020. It surveys the Andean cryosphere, the snow, ice, and frozen ground of South America's great mountain chain. Changes there can unleash hazards that threaten towns and works in the valleys below.

The authors describe current understanding of seasonal snow, glaciers, and mountain permafrost, with a focus on rock glaciers. They gather recent findings and set them against longer records to judge the direction of change. The picture matters far beyond high peaks, since Andean ice and snow feed rivers that millions depend on. The review closes by discussing open questions for the field.
openalex-w7204254663:
Ângela Maria Melo Sá Barros and co-authors at a public hospital in São Paulo's far south released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on digitalizing the medical protocol for postpartum hemorrhage. A leading cause of maternal death. When a mother bleeds heavily after delivery, results depend on the whole team using a managed protocol quickly and completely. The team ran a quasi-experimental before-and-after study with a approach at their public maternity hospital.

The study measures how moving care processes onto digital systems changed adherence to the hemorrhage protocol. Its design compares practice before and after digitalization in the same service. So managers can see whether the tools actually tightened protocol use at the bedside rather than assuming digitization helps by default.
openalex-w7204994563:
Maria Dailiana Andrade de Queiroz Saif and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on the teacher in contemporary times: mediation, digital transformation. Building student self-rule in a schooling system in transition. Social, cultural, and technological change is redefining the teaching role and identity. The study follows three axes: the shift from transmission to teaching mediation in digital culture, the problems of integrating tools into schooling. The relational, formative, and structural problems of teaching work.

Today's teacher guides learning, manages conflict dialogically, and promotes student self-rule, they find, needing knowledge well beyond curricular content. Consolidating teaching mediation, the authors conclude, depends on joining reflective training, infrastructural support, and ongoing public policies that valorize the teaching profession.
openalex-w7206168763:
Paulo Eduardo Macedo de Moraes Filho and four colleagues review a blood marker that may flag Alzheimer's disease years before symptoms show. Alzheimer's involves a buildup of amyloid protein in the brain and changes to tau protein that damage connections between nerve cells, and those changes can begin long before memory fails. The team reviewed recent studies, published between 2024 and 2026, on a tau fragment measured in blood.

The studies link blood levels of this marker to amyloid buildup and tau disease in the brain. It also helped spot preclinical changes, sort patients, and follow them over time. The authors see real promise for earlier and simpler diagnosis, while warning that labs still need shared standards and agreed cutoff values before routine clinical use is safe.
openalex-w7212032363:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho leads a team on the gap between the right to inclusion and its life in real schools. A seat in a common class, they argue, is only the start. Staying, taking part, learning, and belonging count just as much. Their study reads a set of key works on inclusive schooling in Brazil. It asks what teacher growth and joint work can change.

Enrollment alone, the studies show, does not make a school day inclusive. Schools must spot the blocks that keep students out and act on them. Ongoing teacher learning and shared planning open the way. So does work that gives each student real access to the full curriculum. The authors sort their reading into three strands: rights and blocks, teacher growth, and joint planning for access.
openalex-w7213261263:
Ronald Rojas Concepcion leads a team that sums up the risks of pulling stuck back teeth. Such pulls are among the most done cuts in the tooth trade. Harm can come from the tooth's stay, or from the cut itself. The team read past work in Portuguese from 2017 to 2026, in a wide sweep of stores. Eight studies made the final cut of their sweep.

The harms they sort span dead feel in the lip and tongue, dry holes where the tooth sat, and germs in the wound. Fresh ways to cut draw their share of the read. Sound-wave tools slice bone with less shock. One plan keeps the crown but leaves deep roots in place when nerves run close. The team's map of risks and new ways helps the tooth surgeon pick, case by case, the path of least harm.
openalex-w7213316563:
Vera Lucia de Oliveira Jordao writes on the school head team's part in the school of all. A school of all takes each child as he or she comes, lame, slow, deaf, or bright. The head team's calls shape that school: its plan, its staff's growth, its doors and ramps, and its ties with homes. Jordao read laws and past work to weigh the team's weight.

The head's work, she finds, is not mere forms and stamps. It is a craft of teach and rule at once. Where heads lead with aim, the school of all takes root. Where they lag, it stays a line in the law. The blocks she logs span thin funds, thin training, and old views of what a child can be. Her close: heads trained for the task, and a school air where each child's place is not in doubt.
openalex-w7213428163:
Luana Hillebrand Braga and co-authors count cases of airsacculitis in broiler chickens at a federally inspected plant. Their 2026 observational study uses official records from a cooperative in western Paraná, covering January to December 2025. Airsacculitis is a respiratory problem linked to carcass condemnation after slaughter.

Cases occurred throughout the year, the records show. Partial condemnations predominated over total ones, and cases clustered in winter months. That pattern suggests a seasonal influence on the disease. Management, housing conditions, and flock health likely shape occurrence as well. The authors stress steady health monitoring and preventive measures on farms to cut losses in the production chain.
openalex-w7213466863:
Andréa Queila de Barros e Silva and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva examine ongoing teacher training in Brazil. Their 2026 qualitative article uses library research and content analysis. It asks how teaching practice, understood as praxis, connects with teachers' permanent formation.

Praxis is built where theory meets practice, the authors find. Critical reflection lets teachers question and reshape their own work. Ongoing training rebuilds teachers' knowledge and supports shared learning inside the school. Teaching thus develops through reflection, experience, knowledge, and institutional conditions together. Training that is joined up and committed to real school life matters most, they conclude, rather than isolated courses taken away from practice.
openalex-w7213901863:
Nathália Neves Gonçalves and co-authors review the heel prick test and newborn health in Brazil. Their 2026 narrative review, in English, traces the national newborn screening programme. The test detects metabolic, genetic, and hormone diseases early, allowing action before lasting harm occurs.

The programme first covered six diseases. A 2021 law expanded it toward fifty diseases in fourteen groups. Even so, structural, logistical, and training problems persist, the authors find. Information about the test is also spread unevenly, they argue. Better publicity and more reliable performance of screening are proposed so that a vital early intervention reaches every newborn properly.
openalex-w7213942463:
Giovanna Azevedo Rodrigues and co-workers propose a model for machine-themed delusions. Some patients mix a fragile sense of self, literal thinking, swinging moods, and bizarre ideas of being hunted. Their 2026 review, in English, says standard labels capture such cases only in part.

Four axes sort the proposed model. They cover ego fragility, weak cause-and-effect thinking in relationships, limbic and mood dysregulation, and developmental potentiation. Phenomenological psychopathology grounds the model. It is offered as a starting point for testing, not as settled fact. Its aim is an account of how machine-like delusional beliefs form in schizotypal cases.
openalex-w7213974163:
Maria Eduarda Carvalho Lobo leads a review of tirzepatide's cardiovascular effects in type two diabetes. Their 2026 review searches PubMed and a health library for the last five years. Randomized trials, reviews, and meta-analyses on adult patients were included.

Tirzepatide, a dual gut hormone receptor drug, cut glycated haemoglobin more than basal insulin and other diabetes agents, the review finds. Low blood sugar episodes were fewer. Weight loss was expressively large, often passing a substantial share of body weight, with relevant gains in cardiometabolic risk. Cardiovascular disease is the main killer in this population, the authors note, which makes those combined effects clinically important.
openalex-w7214090363: Victor Ferrarezi Nagel leads a case report on surgical treatment of complex facial fractures, from a university in western Paraná, Brazil. The sample opens by noting that the frontal bone forms the upper third of the face and houses the frontal sinus, whose front wall is thick and resistant. The case's clinical details do not appear in the sample provided, so this record is flagged as thin evidence.
openalex-w7214145263:
Gleidson Agra da Silva and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva survey studies on student participation in Brazilian high school management. Their 2026 review searched three sources in early 2025. Ten papers from 2020 to 2025 were selected and read by content analysis.

Four recurring themes sort the field. The student union serves as a space for student voice. Youth protagonism builds leadership, while challenges and resistance limit student voice. Formative effects and political learning complete the picture. Conceptual advances and successful cases exist, they find. Institutional, cultural, and training barriers still block real participation. Democratic management needs public policy, ongoing training, and genuine openness to dialogue with the young.
openalex-w7214147263:
Cristina Morais Cuquigia Maindo and co-workers teach geographic coordinates through the Cartesian plane in Uíge, Angola. Their 2026 case study works with secondary school pupils. Observation sheets, diagnostic questionnaires, hands-on tasks, a field diary, and pupil work supplied the data.

Using the Cartesian plane as a teaching strategy raised grasp of latitude, longitude, parallels, and meridians, they find. Pupils linked math knowledge to maps and to locating points on Earth's surface. Joining mathematics and geography is judged a sound approach for this topic. Learning became deeper and better set in context, the authors conclude, than coordinates taught as stand-alone definitions.
openalex-w7214682963:
Socorro Moreira Silva led a 2026 study of the administrative team behind health care for federal civil servants at a university in northern Brazil. These technical staff run the integrated subsystem that looks after employee health, yet their work is often invisible. The qualitative study reads laws, institutional manuals, administrative reports, and scientific publications to map what the team does and what blocks it.

Administrators, the authors find, organize appointments, manage documents, follow expert examination processes, operate the federal health information system, and connect teams and sectors across the institution. Their obstacles include overloaded work, too few staff and too little technology, constant need for training, and weak institutional recognition. Strengthening this back-office work, the authors argue, through qualification, better conditions, and integrated processes, directly improves how well employee health services function.
openalex-w7214797263: Teruhiko Ishikawa led a large Japanese team in a 2026 study in The Journal of Antibiotics. It searched for inhibitors of histidine kinases, enzymes bacteria use to sense their surroundings, possible targets for new antibacterial drugs. Their approach used amino acid mapping to guide the choice of chemical scaffolds. They then searched a virtual library of over twelve million compounds for candidate hits. The sample for this entry holds only the title page and author list, without an abstract or results, so no compounds or findings are described here.
openalex-w7215049763: Camila Santos led a seven-author 2026 veterinary case report on an intestinal leiomyoma in a dog treated with enterectomy. That surgery removes a section of intestine and joins the healthy ends. Leiomyoma is a benign tumor from the gut's muscle tissue, and surgery is a main treatment option when it affects the gastrointestinal tract. The report set out to describe the case, its diagnosis, and its treatment. The sample for this entry ends mid-abstract, before the case details and outcome, so those specifics are not described here.
openalex-w7215970763:
Júlia Alves Perucci led a 2026 field study of an outreach project called Educating to Prevent, on child and adolescent health, at a college in southern Brazil. Twenty-seven health students from different courses, who ran health education for school pupils between 2022 and 2025, filled in a structured questionnaire about their academic formation and interprofessional skills. Learning to work across professions is a stated goal of health training, often hard to fit in.

Scores were very high on items about general formation and nearly as high on interprofessional practice, with no real difference between the two blocks. Students stressed the growth of collaborative competencies and valuing their bond with the school community. Even without a curriculum designed for it, the authors conclude, health education with children and teens served as a true space of learning across professions, steadily building both formation and teamwork skills.
openalex-w7218770163:
Ademir Henrique Manfré and Eduardo Henrique Batoqui Munhoz reported, in 2026, a qualitative master's study of how neurotypical children perceive autistic peers in the early years of primary school. Framed by neurodiversity and the United Nations goal of inclusive school environments, they interviewed eleven neurotypical students aged seven to ten. The interviews took place at a municipal public school in the interior of São Paulo state, asking how the children see and rethink their peers' schooling.

Three themes grouped the children's views: mediation and welcoming, valuing what the autistic classmate cares about, and critical awareness of prejudice against inclusion as a structural barrier. The views were strong and positive, yet gaps in the process stayed visible. Such inclusion, the authors conclude, demands systematic teaching interventions and awareness drives across the whole school context, not goodwill alone.
openalex-w7220706163:
Plinyo Paccioly Rodrigues Santos wrote a 2026 article setting the cangaço, the banditry of Brazil's backlands, beside today's criminal factions and their pull on young people in the Northeast. The comparison claims no continuity. The cangaço grew from land held by few owners, local boss rule, private violence, weak institutions, and honor codes. Factions run illicit markets, prisons, urban and digital networks, and territorial control at far larger scale.

The contact point is what armed organizations offer where the state feels absent, discontinuous, or repressive: prestige, protection, identity, income, and recognition. Youth adhesion, he argues, has no single cause and is not simple poverty. Inequality, school rupture, precarious work, daily violence, belonging, guns, illegal markets, incarceration, and policy deficits interact. His answer joins qualified repression of economic structures with territorial social prevention, full-time schooling, mental health, income policy, and reintegration, under Brazil's constitutional duty of integral protection.
openalex-w7220743863:
Francisco Alexandre do Nascimento Neto led a 2026 functionalist linguistics study of new words in Brazilian Portuguese as actually used in digital environments. Word creation widens the lexicon, the team notes. So they combined a literature review on neology, borrowing, and related concepts with real usage data from a large Brazilian corpus project and from posts on a major social network.

Four words from the corpus showed distinct processes: one displayed grammaticalization and formal neologism, while the others showed widened or shifted meanings in use. A politically charged coinage drawn from the social network posts completed the set. Digital environments are relevant spaces for the lexicon's manifestation, circulation, and renewal, the authors conclude: communicative needs and interaction contexts favor the creation and transformation of words. The study grounds claims about language change in attested examples rather than invented ones.
openalex-w7221021963:
Lucas da Silva de Castro, Paulo de Oliveira Fonseca Filho, and Luciano da Silva Lima evaluated wearable devices for catching atrial fibrillation, a common heart rhythm disorder that raises stroke risk. Their 2026 integrative review compared smartwatches and portable monitors against traditional tests such as the Holter monitor.

Fifteen studies survived their screening. Most devices showed good sensitivity and accuracy, and continuous monitoring beat intermittent checks, with some devices catching nearly all episodes. Performance still varied by device and study design, and false alarms worried several authors. The reviewers see wearables as a promising tool for watching at-risk patients at home, while calling for standard testing and further study.
plos-pbio-0020163:
Mazahir T. Hasan, Rainer W. Friedrich, Thomas Euler, and co-workers built a glowing sensor mouse in PLOS Biology in 2004. Their mice make fluorescent proteins that light up when calcium rises inside cells. Calcium spikes are a basic signal in nerve and muscle cells, so the glow reports cell activity.

A drug switch called TET control lets researchers turn the sensor on only when and where they want. That keeps the sensor from disturbing growth when it is not needed. With it, activity in living brain tissue can be watched under a microscope. The tool opened a path to watching whole circuits at work, a goal that later calcium imaging methods built on.
plos-pbio-0020363:
Bino John, Anton J. Enright, Alexei Aravin, and a large team predicted microRNA targets in humans in PLOS Biology in 2004. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that tune gene activity by binding to messenger RNAs. Each one may control hundreds of messages, but finding which ones was a fresh problem at the time.

The team wrote rules for spotting likely binding sites across human messages and tested them against known cases. Their target list gave the young field a map to work from. MicroRNAs are now known to shape development, immunity, and cancer. Early maps like this one set the terms for how targets are predicted and checked, and they remain a base that later methods refined.
plos-pone-0000063:
David G. Haskell, Jonathan P. Evans, and Neil W. Pelkey compared bird life across land uses in PLOS ONE in 2006. They surveyed birds in plantations, in forests, and in exurban areas, the low-density spread at a city's edge. Plantation land held far fewer bird kinds than the other two.

The authors call that bird life depauperate, thinned out. Forests held the richest mix, as expected, but exurban areas did better than plantations despite their houses and roads. The contrast warns that not all human land use is equal for wildlife. Tree plantations managed as single crops can be poorer habitat than lightly settled land. That ranking can guide land choices where birds are a concern.
plos-pone-0000163:
Frédéric Lemaire, Céline A. Mandon, Julien Reboud, and colleagues published this toxicology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It describes toxicity assays run in nanodrops, droplets so small that hundreds of tests fit in a tiny volume. The assays combine a living bioassay with morphometric endpoints, measurements of shape and form in the test organisms.

Small-scale tests use far less of a test chemical and far fewer animals. The authors show that nanodrop assays can still read out meaningful harm. The method points toward cheaper, higher-volume screening of chemicals and drugs, where testing capacity is often the bottleneck.
plos-pone-0000263:
Andreas Lamanda, Zeinab Cheaib, Melek Dilek Turgut, and colleagues published this biochemistry paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteins in saliva buffer acids, soaking up protons to protect teeth and the mouth. The authors study protein buffering in simple model systems and in whole human saliva, comparing the two.

Understanding saliva's buffering explains part of how the mouth resists acid attacks after eating. The authors measure how much of that protection comes from proteins rather than other components. The results have practical bearing on dental research and on designing artificial saliva for patients who make too little.
plos-pone-0000363:
Oren Kobiler, Assaf Rokney, and Amos B. Oppenheim wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study about lambda, a virus that infects bacteria. After entering a host cell, the virus faces a choice: multiply fast and burst the cell open, or stay quiet inside the host's DNA. Their work centers on one viral protein, CIII, that helps steer that choice.

CIII works by blocking a protease, an enzyme that cuts other proteins apart. By slowing that enzyme down, CIII helps tip the virus toward the quiet, dormant path. Working out how one small protein guides this switch helps explain how viruses balance attack and hiding, a basic question in virus biology.
plos-pone-0000463:
Gabriel del Rio and colleagues found a shared sequence pattern in a family of cell-death-related receptors, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dependence receptors are proteins that can trigger a cell to die when their partner molecule is absent. The team identified a novel motif, a recurring pattern of amino acids, in these receptors.

A shared motif is a clue to shared machinery: it marks the part of the receptor that likely does the common work. Motifs give biologists a handle for finding new family members in genome data and for guessing how the death signal is sent. Dependence receptors matter in development and in cancer, where their fail-safe killing can be lost.
plos-pone-0000563:
Eric Waltari and colleagues compared two ways of finding where species survived the ice ages, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Pleistocene refugia are the sheltered pockets where species waited out glacial cold. The team compared phylogeographic predictions, from DNA evidence, with ecological niche model predictions, from climate and habitat data, for locating those refugia.

Where the two methods agree, confidence is high; where they differ, each exposes the other's blind spots. Refugia matter now because they are often today's biodiversity hotspots and tomorrow's climate shelters. The study is a methods check with direct conservation use.
plos-pone-0000663:
Jack Merrin, Stanislas Leibler and John S. Chuang turned an inkjet printer into a tool for placing living bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many studies of interacting microbes need cells deposited in precisely defined patterns. Ordinary methods make that slow or costly. Their printer is piezoelectric, adapted from a design first built to print DNA microarrays.

The authors describe the device as inexpensive, and it can print patterns using multiple bacterial strains. Printing living cells like ink lets researchers set up microbial neighborhoods on purpose. Ecologists can then watch competition and cooperation unfold from known starting positions, a control that mixed cultures never offer.
plos-pone-0000763:
Michaela Frye, Amanda G. Fisher and Fiona M. Watt characterized skin stem cells by the chemical marks on their DNA packaging. Switching on the gene Myc pushes epidermal stem cells to leave their niche. They then turn into sebocytes and surface skin. The shift is tied to wide changes in gene transcription. Marks on histones, the packaging proteins, help set which genes can be read.

The team identified chromatin modifications characteristic of epidermal stem cells across the whole genome. Their title says these global marks define the stem cells, and that Myc-driven differentiation alters them. A signature of marks could let researchers recognize true stem cells without waiting for behavior.
plos-pone-0000863:
Murali Gururajan, Joshy Jacob and Bali Pulendran studied toll-like receptors in mouse B cells for PLOS ONE in 2007. Toll-like receptors are sensors that spot patterns found on germs and switch on the body's first line of defense. The team compared B cells from the spleen with B cells from mucosal tissue, the moist linings that meet the outside world.

For each cell group they asked which receptors are present and how strongly the cells respond when those receptors are triggered. The work maps immune sensing across two very different settings. It helps explain how B cells help start a broader immune response after they meet a threat.
plos-pone-0000963:
Ryan Nitta, Catherine Smith and Brian Kennedy tested how the retinoblastoma protein is broken down in cells missing certain lamins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lamins A and C are filaments that brace the cell nucleus. They are also needed to keep the retinoblastoma protein, a brake on cell growth, stable, though the route was unknown.

Two cancer linked proteins, gankyrin and MDM2, were natural suspects for the breakdown. The team report the loss runs through the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, but independently of both suspects. Ruling out the obvious routes is real progress. It tells the field where the true mechanism is not.
plos-pone-0001063:
Walter Weiss, Anita Kumar, George Jiang and colleagues tested a combined malaria vaccine in rhesus monkeys, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their earlier design used four antigens: DNA plasmids first, then a poxvirus boost. It protected a high percentage of monkeys against Plasmodium knowlesi malaria.

The vaccine covers several life stages of the parasite, including two blood stage antigens. This study asks how much protection depends on optimal DNA priming and on including those blood stage parts. Taking a working vaccine apart, piece by piece, shows which parts carry the protection. That knowledge is what lets a monkey success become a human candidate.
plos-pone-0001163:
Mucins are the main ingredients of mucus, and their genes contain long repetitive stretches that are hard to read. Yun Hee Jeong and colleagues examined one such gene, MUC2, in relation to stomach cancer, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The repetitive region, called a minisatellite, varies between people.

The authors report that rare versions of this repeat region influence susceptibility to gastric carcinoma. Mucin genes are well studied for how much protein they make, but their genomic variation is murkier because the repeats resist standard analysis. The study shows that even awkward repetitive DNA can carry disease risk.
plos-pone-0001263:
Keeping time, judging how long things last, depends on a network that includes the basal ganglia. Christian Beste and colleagues studied time processing in Huntington's disease, where the basal ganglia deteriorate, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Timing processes were already known to change in the disease.

This group-control study compared timing performance in Huntington's patients with healthy controls. Because the structures important for timing are also critical for the movement problems of Huntington's, the work links two features of one disease. Results like these can serve as sensitive measures of how the disease progresses.
plos-pone-0001363:
For HIV-positive mothers in low-resource settings, breastfeeding is often the only safe feeding option, yet it can transmit the virus. Louise Kuhn and colleagues followed mothers and infants in Zambia to study exclusive breastfeeding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Clear data on the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding for HIV prevention were needed to encourage breastfeeding support programs.

The authors report high uptake of exclusive breastfeeding and reduced early post-natal HIV transmission where replacement feeding is unsafe. Mixed feeding had been thought riskier than exclusive breastfeeding; their data support promoting the exclusive pattern. The findings influenced infant feeding guidance for HIV-infected women.
plos-pone-0001463:
Zhiping Wang, Shicui Zhang, and Guangfeng Wang wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how fish eggs fend off germs. Fish that lay eggs in open water leave them amid dense microbes. How the young live through those attacks was not known. The team tested the fluid inside fresh zebrafish eggs.

They show the egg fluid can kill germs on its own. The killing comes from defense parts passed from the mother. That maternal guard covers the days before the young fish can make its own defense. The finding adds a neat chapter to how animals protect their young at the most frail stage.
plos-pone-0001563:
Alassane Dicko and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot for children in Mali. The shot blends proteins from two strains of the blood stage parasite. A past phase 1 trial in adults in Mali had cleared the way. This trial moved the shot into young children, the group at most risk.

The team checked safety and immune replies in the children step by step. A shot that is safe in adults can act unlike in young children. Child data are thus the true gate for a malaria vaccine. This trial is a key rung on that climb.
plos-pone-0001663:
P. K. Vinod, Neelanjan Sengupta, P. J. Bhat, and their co-authors mapped how three signaling pathways jointly control a yeast gene in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, adapts to its surroundings to survive. When nitrogen runs low, it grows in chains of stretched cells called pseudohyphae, which help it forage. The switch is driven by a gene named FLO11.

The study integrates the cAMP-PKA, MAPK, and TOR pathways, three major signal routes that sense food and stress. The full text gives the model, the gene activity data, and how each pathway's push on FLO11 adds up. Yeast is a stand-in for cells in general, so rules found here guide work on how cells combine signals to make one decision.
plos-pone-0001763:
Heather Sadlish, Heike Rampelt, James Shorter, and their co-authors studied helper proteins that manage yeast prions in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Prions are proteins that fold into self-copying shapes. In yeast they create heritable traits. The cytosolic chaperone network, the cell's protein-folding crew, is closely tied to prion emergence and maintenance. The Hsp110 chaperone Sse1 exchanges nucleotides for Hsp70 chaperones.

The team reports that Hsp110 chaperones regulate prion formation and propagation through two discrete activities. The full text gives the yeast experiments and the activity separation. Yeast prions are a safe stand-in for the protein clumping behind human diseases like Alzheimer's, so their control crew is studied worldwide.
plos-pone-0001863:
Uri Yerushalmi and Mina Teicher used computer simulations of evolution to study timing in neural processing in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Recent studies suggested some neural mechanisms rest on the fine timing structure of spiking activity, the exact timing of nerve spikes. Less effort had gone into how such mechanisms evolve: could they arise, and must they?

Running such simulations, the authors argue temporal elements in neural processing are inevitable: selection produces them without being asked. The full text gives the simulation setup and the evolved networks. If timing codes arise inevitably, then brain labs should expect them in all brains, not as rare inventions of certain brains.
plos-pone-0001963:
Akira Kinjo and Haruki Nakamura analyzed what makes a protein family's signature, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Labs spot distant kinship between proteins by comparing them to a position-specific scoring matrix, a table that scores each spot in a sequence. Those tables seem to hold the essence of a family, but what that essence is made of was unclear.

The pair applied singular value analysis, a math tool that splits a table into ranked parts, to many such matrices. Their aim was to see which parts carry the family stamp. Knowing the anatomy of a signature can make homology searches sharper and faster.
plos-pone-0002063:
Isabelle Lombaert and co-authors rescued spit glands with stem cells after radiation, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Head and neck cancer is the fifth most common cancer, and survival is fairly high. Yet radiation often wrecks the salivary glands, leaving patients with dry mouths and a much poorer quality of life.

The team transplanted stem cells into irradiated glands in their model. As the title states, the transplant rescued gland function after the damage. A working rescue in animals is a first step toward giving cancer survivors back a basic comfort that radiation takes away.
plos-pone-0002163:
Crystal Jaing, Shea Gardner, Kevin McLoughlin, and co-authors built a gene chip for spotting the weapons of harmful bacteria, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. Known and unknown germs pose a steady threat to public health, and fast tools to detect and describe them are badly needed. Existing tests cannot cover the full range of what makes a microbe dangerous.

The team's functional gene array carries probes for bacterial virulence elements, the genes that let bacteria cause disease. A single test can scan a sample for many such genes at once. Tools like this help health teams name a threat early, before an outbreak grows legs.
plos-pone-0002263:
Farrel Buchinsky, Joseph Donfack, Craig Derkay, and co-authors studied children and adults with a rare airway disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis grows wart-like tumors in the airway, causing hoarseness and trouble breathing. It is caused by human papillomavirus types 6 or 11, and its course varies hugely, with patients needing repeated surgeries to keep the airway open.

The team compared cases by HPV type and by age at diagnosis. They report that the child's age, more than the virus type, tracks with how the disease behaves. That ordering helps doctors counsel families on what course to expect.
plos-pone-0002363:
Ted Cohen, Caroline Colijn, and Bryson Finklea asked whether surveys understate the burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. TB strains resistant to many first- and second-line antibiotics challenge a global strategy built on standard drug regimens. Highly resistant strains had already been blamed in outbreaks. Survey-based estimates guide the money and drugs sent to fight them.

The team used a simulation study to test how those estimates are built. Their modeling suggests survey methods can miss part of the true burden, for instance where resistant cases die or are treated outside the system. Getting the count right decides whether control programs are sized for the epidemic they actually face.
plos-pone-0002463:
Stjernman joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Martin Stjernman, Lars Råberg, Jan-Åke Nilsson, among others. Its subject is maximum Host Survival at Intermediate Parasite Infection Intensities. Although parasitism has been acknowledged as an important selective force in the evolution of host life histories.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002563:
Corcoran led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kelly E. Corcoran, Katarzyna A. Trzaska, Helen Fernandes, among others. Its subject is mesenchymal Stem Cells in Early Entry of Breast Cancer into Bone Marrow.

BCCs can achieve quiescence, without interfering with hematopoiesis. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002663:
A 2008 study by Rafael Sanjuán and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up a network model for the correlation between epistasis and genomic complexity. Authorship is credited in the record to Rafael Sanjuán and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The study of genetic interactions (epistasis) is central to the understanding of genome organization and evolution. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002763:
Lee Alan Dugatkin and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on cheating on the edge. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Lee Alan Dugatkin, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. We present the results of an individual agent-based model of antibiotic resistance in bacteria. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002863:
Bilada Bilican and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was induction of olig2 + precursors by FGF involves BMP signalling blockade at the smad level. The catalog record names Bilada Bilican first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. During normal development oligodendrocyte precursors (OPCs) are generated in the ventral spinal cord in response to Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signalling. It goes on to note a further point. There is also a second, late wave of oligodendrogenesis in the dorsal spinal cord independent of Shh activity. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002963:
Christopher Love, Shuguang Zhang and Andreas Mershin chased the source of a steady voltage in a potted fig tree in 2008. It has long been known that many plants hold an electrical potential between their xylem, the water-carrying tissue, and the soil. What creates that voltage stayed controversial for years.

After ruling out stray capacitive and inductive effects from the setup, the team probed the sustained difference in a Ficus benjamina tree. Published in PLOS ONE, the quirky study treats a textbook curiosity with care. Its results bear on claims that trees might serve as living power sources.
plos-pone-0003063:
Amit Bharadwaj, Sadhu Leelavathi, Sudeshna Mazumdar-Leighton and co-authors studied a heat- and alkali-tough enzyme in 2008. Understanding protein stability under several extreme conditions at once remains a major challenge. The xylanase from Bacillus sp. NG-27, called BSX, works best at high temperature and alkaline pH and resists denaturants.

A partly exposed valine at the protein's start plays a critical role in stabilizing it, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, one residue with an outsized effect is a neat lesson for enzyme engineering, where industrial users prize exactly this toughness. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003163:
Alma Fulurija, Thomas A. Lutz, Katja Sladko and colleagues test vaccination against the hormone GIP as an obesity treatment in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The World Health Organization counted more than one billion people worldwide as overweight and at risk of chronic illness, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and stroke. Current therapies showed limited efficacy and often had unpleasant side effects.

The authors explore blocking GIP by vaccination as a fresh route to weight control. Readers get a bold idea tested at an early stage. Even readers who doubt the approach will find the reasoning useful for judging obesity research claims.
plos-pone-0003263:
Lauren McDaniel, Mya Breitbart, Jennifer Mobberley and colleagues sequence viruses from Tampa Bay in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Phage integrase genes often play a role in establishing lysogeny in temperate phage, by catalyzing integration of the phage into one of the host's replicons. To investigate temperate phage gene expression, an induced viral metagenome from Tampa Bay was sequenced by 454 methods.

Readers get a metagenomic analysis of lysogeny, the state where a virus hides in its host, and implications for prophage gene expression. Coastal virus communities affect marine bacteria and carbon flow, so their hidden state matters to ocean ecology.
plos-pone-0003363:
Søren Søgaard Lund, Lise Tarnow, Anne Sofie Astrup and colleagues trial metformin in type 1 diabetes in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite intensive insulin treatment, many patients with type 1 diabetes have longstanding inadequate glycaemic control. Metformin is an oral hypoglycaemic agent that improves insulin action in patients with type 2 diabetes. The team investigated effect of a one-year treatment in type 1 patients.

Their randomized study tests adjunct metformin treatment in patients with persistent inadequate control. Readers get trial evidence on borrowing a type 2 drug for type 1 care. Even a modest insulin-sparing effect matters over a lifetime of injections.
plos-pone-0003463:
Heekyung Chung and co-authors measured mutation rates in repair-defective cells in this 2008 study. Some cells cannot fix mismatched DNA letters properly. In such cells, repeated short DNA stretches in genes mutate often. Two tumor suppressor genes, TGFBR2 and ACVR2, carry such fragile stretches.

Breaks in those genes cut off signals that restrain colon tumors. The team clocked how fast the coding repeats in each gene mutate. Direct rates help explain how colon cancers form in these patients. The numbers sharpen models of microsatellite-unstable cancer growth. Colon tumors with broken repair are a large and well studied cancer group.
plos-pone-0003563:
Xiao-Ning Zhang and co-authors studied early blue light responses in a plant in this 2008 paper. Cryptochromes are blue light sensors found across many life forms. They steer development and help set daily clocks. In Arabidopsis, cryptochrome 1 drives an early response to blue light.

A protein named HFR1 proved crucial for that first response. It helps regulate the whole set of genes reacting to the light. Without it, the early transcriptome response falters. The finding maps a relay between light sensing and gene control. Light is the main timing cue for plant growth in fields and forests.
plos-pone-0003663:
Rivka Inzelberg, Edna Schechtman, and Shraga Hocherman published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Visuo-motor coordination means turning what the eyes see into planned, guided movement. That chain needs thinking skills and motor skills, both of which Parkinson's disease impairs.

The team measured these coordination deficits in patients and set them beside their motor impairments. The results show where the chain between seeing and doing breaks in this disease. Such detail can guide therapy and tests that track how the illness advances beyond tremor and stiffness alone. Tests like these can also help track change over time.
plos-pone-0003763:
Kristoffer S. Larsen, Jing Xu, Silvia Cermelli, and colleagues published this cell transport study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cells move their inner cargo along microtubule tracks using motor proteins such as dynein. How that motor's activity is regulated was not well understood. The protein BicaudalD helps dynein do its job.

The team studied BicaudalD during the transport of lipid droplets, the cell's fat stores. They found it actively regulates the motor's activity rather than just linking cargo to track. The work shows how cells steer fat cargo with precision inside the cell.
plos-pone-0003863:
Rui Wang-Sattler, Yao Yu, Kirstin Mittelstrass, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Smoking exposes the body to nicotine and causes a multitude of metabolic changes that are poorly understood. The KORA study is a large health cohort in the Augsburg region of Germany.

The team quantified 198 metabolites in 283 serum samples from the cohort. Comparing smokers and non-smokers revealed distinct variations tied to nicotine consumption. These first results show how deeply tobacco use marks the chemistry of human blood. Such profiles could one day flag harm from smoke sooner.
plos-pone-0003963:
Wenyan Zhang, Gongying Chen, Anna Maria Niewiadomska, and co-authors studied how HIV disarms cell defenses in 2008. Human APOBEC3 proteins can block many retroviruses, including HIV-1. To spread, HIV must suppress several of these defender proteins. Its Vif protein carries out that suppression.

Their PLOS ONE article maps which parts of Vif and APOBEC3 must meet. Distinct contact points are needed against different defender proteins. That detail shows how one viral protein handles a whole family of foes. Blocking those contacts could let natural defenses stop HIV again. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004063:
Akira Mamiya, Jennifer Beshel, Chunsu Xu, and co-authors recorded airflow sensing in fly brains in 2008. The mushroom body is a higher center in the Drosophila brain. It is best known for handling smell information. How its neurons respond to non-smell senses was not known.

Their PLOS ONE article characterizes mushroom body responses to airflow. Airflow is a key cue for a flying insect's orientation. Responses there suggest the center merges several senses, not smell alone. That merging may help flies link wind with odor plumes. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004163:
Jessica Stolze-Rybczynski and colleagues published this fungal study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most of the 30,000 known species in the group Basidiomycota shoot off their spores with a fluid droplet. The droplet, called Buller's drop, races across the spore surface and powers the launch. In yeasts, rusts, and smuts of the same group, spores are instead discharged straight into the air.

The team compared these discharge mechanisms and how they were adapted across the group. Tracing the changes shows how a single spore-launching trick was reshaped for different lifestyles. The study adds a mechanical chapter to the evolution of fungi.
plos-pone-0004263:
Hans Gross and colleagues published this bee cognition study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Numerical abilities have been studied in many vertebrates, but convincing accounts of number sense in invertebrates are few. Honeybees, with their many impressive cognitive feats, are prime candidates for such a test.

The team tested whether bees can generalise a visual task by number, applying a learned count to new images. Their study asks whether a bee's brain tracks how many items it sees, not just what they look like. A positive answer would show that number sense does not require a big brain.
plos-pone-0004363:
Pawan Gupta and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. TR2 is an orphan nuclear receptor expressed specifically in early embryos. It is a transcription factor that controls key stem cell genes, including Oct4, a master stem cell gene. TR2 can act as both activator and repressor in gene control.

The team describe HDAC3 as a molecular chaperone that shuttles phosphorylated TR2 to PML bodies, storage sites in the nucleus. They call this a novel, deacetylase activity-independent function of HDAC3, which usually edits gene activity chemically. A familiar enzyme moonlighting as an escort changes how TR2's targets get controlled.
plos-pone-0004463:
Two sulfur-bearing spots on a virus shell protein are vital for infection, show Samuel Campos and Michelle Ozbun in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is L2, a minor part of the shell of human papillomavirus type 16, a virus that can cause cancer. L2 does a job that is essential for infection, but that job was not well understood.

The two spots are cysteine residues, building blocks that can link to each other. The team showed they form a bond inside the L2 molecule, and that breaking them cripples the virus in human skin cells. A known target for antibodies sits near the same region. Together, the details sketch how L2 helps the virus enter cells, and where vaccines or drugs might block it.
plos-pone-0004563:
Melanoma cells answer a gene-awakening drug in varied ways that may predict who benefits, report Ruth Halaban, Michael Krauthammer, Mattia Pelizzola, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug is decitabine. It reactivates genes silenced by DNA methylation, a chemical mark that can shut genes off in cancer.

Decitabine helps some cancer patients but not others, especially those with solid tumors. The team carried out an integrative analysis of how melanoma cells respond at the epigenetic level, the level of marks rather than the DNA code itself. Patterns in that response carry clinical implications: they may separate likely responders from patients who would only suffer side effects. Such sorting is the heart of personalized cancer care.
plos-pone-0004663:
A growth factor shields salivary glands from radiation damage, show Kirsten Limesand, Sherif Said, and Steven Anderson in PLOS ONE in 2009. Radiation is a primary or secondary treatment for head and neck cancer. A common side effect of irradiation to the head and neck is xerostomia, severe dry mouth, caused by salivary gland dysfunction. Tens of thousands of new cases result from radiation treatment each year.

The factor is IGF-1, insulin-like growth factor 1. The team reports that it suppresses radiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction in their experiments. Preserving saliva is not a small comfort: it protects teeth, speech, taste, and eating. A protectant that can be given around radiation sessions would improve life for many cancer survivors.
plos-pone-0004763:
Caterina Longo and colleagues built core shell gel particles that catch and keep fragile blood markers, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood holds a rich set of early disease markers waiting to be found. Three hurdles block that search, the authors note, starting with the tiny amounts of most markers in blood.

Large common proteins swamp the signal, and markers break down fast after drawing. The new particles harvest rare markers, concentrate them, and protect them from decay. Better capture could make early disease tests far more sensitive. It may open marker hunts that now fail. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004863:
Hans Herfarth and colleagues studied frequency and nature of incidental extra enteric lesions on MR enterography in bowel disease, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The aim was to determine occurrence of extra enteric findings in a large cohort undergoing magnetic resonance enterography and classify clinical significance. The team retrospectively analyzed over a thousand examinations in about a thousand patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

Incidental findings are common and mostly benign. Some require urgent follow up care. Radiologists need clear reporting pathways. Patients benefit when scans check beyond the bowel. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004963:
For sperm to fertilize an egg, it must fire its acrosome. The acrosome is a cap of enzymes that helps sperm penetrate the egg's coat. Luis Federico Bátiz and colleagues studied a mouse defect in this step. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The mice carry the hyh mutation. It changes one building block in the protein alpha-SNAP.

Sperm from these mice have a defect in the acrosome reaction. The study traces that failure to the single mutation. A tiny genetic typo breaks the final step of fertilization. The work shows how sensitive the sperm's firing machinery is. It also gives researchers a precise model of one cause of male infertility.
plos-pone-0005063:
Gut germs influence diabetes risk in animal models. The mechanism behind that influence was murky. Paul Bollyky and colleagues named a relay in PLOS ONE in 2009. The relay is Myd88, an adaptor in the toll-like receptor pathway. That pathway senses microbes. The team tested Myd88's role in pancreatic beta cells.

Myd88 contributes to beta-cell homeostasis after injury. Without it, the insulin-making cells recover poorly. The finding ties gut microbes to the pancreas through an immune relay. It also reframes beta-cell health as partly an immune story. Diabetes research often treats these cells in isolation. This work shows their microbial environment matters. The relay could become a treatment target.
plos-pone-0005163:
Stare at a moving pattern and a still dot can vanish. The illusion is called motion-induced blindness. Po-Jang Hsieh and Peter Tse tracked the eyes during it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They measured microsaccades, tiny involuntary eye movements. They also measured eyeblink rates. Volunteers reported when the dot was visible or gone.

Microsaccade rate varied with subjective visibility. The eyes move differently when the dot is seen versus unseen. This was the first psychophysical data on the link. The eyes betray the mind's seeing. Such links help scientists study visual awareness itself. Awareness is hard to measure directly. Eye behavior offers an objective window into it.
plos-pone-0005263:
In Crohn's disease, the gut is inflamed, and certain chemokines, signals that call in immune cells, run high. One of them, CXCL10, tracks with disease activity. Grip and Janciauskiene tested in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether a statin drug could lower it.

Statins are cholesterol drugs that also calm chemokine production in heart patients. Patients with Crohn's disease who took atorvastatin showed reduced plasma levels of CXCL10, as the title states. The result hints that a familiar heart drug might also help soothe gut inflammation. A cheap pill used for years in heart care would be easy to test in gut clinics, since its side effects and safe dose are already well known.
plos-pone-0005363:
When E. coli DNA is damaged, the bacterium sounds an alarm called the SOS response. Two genes, recA and lexA, regulate each other in a feedback loop at its heart. Shimoni and colleagues analyzed the randomness of that circuit in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Gene circuits do not run like clockwork; molecule counts are small and noisy. A stochastic analysis treats that noise directly instead of averaging it away. The results show how a bacterium can mount a reliable alarm from unreliable parts, a core lesson in systems biology. Noise is not a flaw in the cell's alarm. it may let a few cells act fast while the rest wait, a spread of bets that helps a whole colony live through a hard hit.
plos-pone-0005463:
Konstantin Kadzhaev and colleagues hunted genes that make a germ dangerous, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Francisella tularensis is a germ that can cause severe and sometimes fatal illness in people. Its most harmful strains belong to one branch of the species.

Using mice infected through the skin, the team tested which germ genes are needed to cause disease. Each gene that proved vital is a clue to how the germ attacks the body. Such clues can guide the search for drugs or vaccines against a germ that is also feared as a possible weapon.
plos-pone-0005563:
Wenrui Duan and co-authors studied a mutant cancer gene in transgenic mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Changes in the gene p53 are among the most common faults in human lung cancer. One hotspot for those changes sits in the part of the protein that grips DNA.

The team built mice carrying that mutant gene in their lungs. They watched how lung tumours arose across the animals' lives and how the pattern changed with age. The model helps show how one famous gene fault drives lung cancer over time. Age shifts in tumour patterns matter because lung cancer is mainly a disease of older people.
plos-pone-0005663:
Moritz Wildgruber and co-authors used magnetic nano-sensors to track immune cells in artery disease in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Monocytes are blood cells that enter tissues and become defenders or healers. In people they come in at least two groups whose shares shift with heart disease, sepsis, and viral infection.

The sensors let the team profile those groups over the course of atherosclerosis in animals. Watching the groups rise and fall could one day guide treatment of artery disease. The method also promises faster blood tests from tiny samples. Heart artery disease remains a top killer, and blood cell groups that track it could guide care earlier.
plos-pone-0005763:
Abhay Sharma and Priyanka Singh tested a bold claim in fruit flies in 2009: that a father's gained traits can pass to offspring through sperm. Most known cases of such inherited effects involve exposures before birth or during sperm formation. Adult experience reshaping the germline was less established.

Using a Drosophila model, the team looked for gene-activity patterns from the father's brain turning up in the next generation via sperm. Any solid case would stretch the rules of inheritance. Their systems approach lays out the evidence and its limits, a useful base for a debated topic.
plos-pone-0005863:
Alexander Wittenberg and co-authors showed in 2009 that sex reshuffles the genome of a wheat pathogen to an extraordinary degree. Mycosphaerella graminicola is a haploid fungus that briefly turns diploid to produce spores. In that brief phase, matching chromosomes can swap parts.

Some chromosomes proved surprisingly dispensable or unstable through meiosis. That plasticity helps the fungus adapt fast to resistant wheat varieties and fungicides. It is bad news for breeders, but knowing the mechanism guides more durable resistance strategies. The paper is a striking case of genome flexibility in a plant enemy.
plos-pone-0005963:
Turning down one cell signal can stretch life in yeast, and perhaps in mammals too. Linda Enns, John Morton, Piper Treuting and colleagues tested that hope in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper disrupts protein kinase A, a signal enzyme, by removing one of its control parts, a change known to leave mice lean and sensitive to insulin.

The title gives the verdict: the mice aged in a healthier way. Healthy aging, as opposed to mere long life, is the prize most aging research now seeks. The work ties a single signal pathway to that prize in a mammal, and it gives drug and diet studies a target that has already passed a real test in mice.
plos-pone-0006063:
You cannot study appetite if you cannot measure a meal. Richard Wong, Matthew Piper, Bregje Wertheim and colleagues solved that basic problem for the fruit fly in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents a reliable way to measure how much food Drosophila eats while left alone, in steady conditions, in normal culture.

Earlier measures were unreliable or disturbed the flies they watched. A sound intake measure serves studies of behavior, nutrition and drug dosing, all of which lean on knowing the dose a fly truly ate. The method is a modest tool on its face, and a foundation for a large share of fly research.
plos-pone-0006163:
Prolactin was thought to be a mammal hormone until fish told a longer story. Xigui Huang, Michelle Hui, Yun Liu and colleagues discovered a novel prolactin in non-mammalian vertebrates in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper places the find in the hormone family that includes growth hormone and somatolactin, kin proteins with similar gene structure, and traces its role in the fish retina.

The new hormone takes part in teleost retina development, the title reports. A hormone family that predates mammals changes how its whole evolution is told. The fish eye also gains a growth signal to study, in an organ where prolactin's presence was itself a surprise.
plos-pone-0006263:
A harmless bacterium used in some immune therapies needed its identity settled. Vikram Saini and colleagues studied Mycobacterium indicus pranii in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their polyphasic taxonomic analysis combined many kinds of evidence. By growth and metabolism, the germ had been grouped with fast-growing relatives.

Multiple lines of evidence establish it as a distinct species, the authors conclude. Correct naming matters for medicine, since this organism is given to patients. It also matters for comparing research across labs. The study closes a classification debate with a broad evidence base.
plos-pone-0006363:
The tips of chromosomes hold repeat blocks whose names and counts shift from tip to tip. Xuefeng Zhu and Claes Gustafsson mapped the packing of DNA at two such blocks in baker's yeast for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. All yeast tips share the same kind of end repeats, but the blocks next to them vary in place and count.

The two block types, called X and Y prime, proved to have sharply unlike packing. Packing decides which genes near the tip are on or off. Genome wide maps let the team see the split at every tip at once. The work shows that like DNA can be packed in unlike ways, with real effects on the cell.
plos-pone-0006463:
Derek Alsop, Jennifer Ings, and Mathilakath Vijayan studied stress and breeding in zebrafish for PLOS ONE in 2009. Stress is known to harm reproductive performance, but the pathways are not fully mapped. Hormones of the stress system act on the brain-pituitary-gonad axis, the chain that controls reproduction. One key stress hormone in that chain is ACTH.

Their title reports that ACTH suppresses estradiol release from zebrafish ovarian follicles when gonadotropins stimulate them. Estradiol is a key egg-related hormone. A direct brake at the ovary helps explain how stress cuts fertility. The fish model gives a clean way to trace those effects.
plos-pone-0006563:
Stephanie Wai, Scott Gerber, and Rong Li studied repeated marking of a yeast polarity factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell polarization is essential for processes such as cell migration and asymmetric cell division. A common regulator of polarization in most eukaryotic cells is the conserved Cdc42 protein. In yeast, its exchange factor is Cdc24.

The team examined multisite phosphorylation of Cdc24 during yeast cell polarization. Many phosphate tags, rather than one switch, tune the factor's behavior. Multisite control allows graded, robust responses. Yeast polarization is a model for how all cells pick a front and back.
plos-pone-0006663:
Alice van Gemert and co-authors watched RNA move inside living fly muscle cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. In skeletal muscle, each muscle cell, commonly called a myofiber, is actually a large syncytium containing numerous nuclei. Experiments in fixed myofibers show mRNAs remain near their nucleus of origin. The team monitored mRNA movement in vivo in Drosophila body wall muscle cells.

Their title reports the presence of myofiber domains: each nucleus governs its local territory. Local control lets a giant cell vary protein production by region. Watching it live confirms what fixed tissue suggested. The finding shapes models of muscle disease, where domains break down.
plos-pone-0006763:
Ben Adams and Durrell D. Kapan modeled how human travel spreads mosquito-borne disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. City people travel often and widely. Much of that travel follows structured commuting patterns. Mosquitoes bite locally, but people carry infections between neighborhoods. The authors asked how commuting shapes disease dynamics. Dengue is their motivating example of a vector-borne pathogen.

Their analysis used a metapopulation model of connected patches. Movement data linked the patches as commuters do daily. The model shows human movement can dominate spread patterns. Mosquito control alone may miss the human half of transmission. The work gives city health planners a more realistic spread picture.
plos-pone-0006863:
Ignacio J. Gomez Portillo and Pablo M. Gleiser modeled brain networks that rewire themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Brain functional networks map regions as nodes and coordination as links. These networks show a robust small-world structure. They also contain highly integrated modules. A static model cannot capture how connections adapt.

Their adaptive complex network model lets links change with activity. Adaptation rules generate the small-world, modular pattern naturally. Such models help explain how brain organization emerges and stays flexible. They also provide test beds for ideas about learning. The work bridges network theory and neuroscience in a compact model.
plos-pone-0006963:
Grégory Lacraz, Marie-Hélène Giroix, Nadim Kassis, and colleagues tested a diabetes treatment in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. In type 2 diabetes, the insulin-making islets of the pancreas become inflamed and scarred. That inflammation may start in the islets' own blood vessel lining. The team studied islets from GK rats, a diabetic strain.

They measured genes tied to vessel activation and oxidative stress. Then they gave a treatment called IL-1Ra and measured again. Gene expression for activation and stress went down with treatment. The result supports calming islet inflammation as a way to protect insulin output.
plos-pone-0007063:
Bédis Dridi, Mireille Henry, Amel El Khéchine, and colleagues improved gut microbe detection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two methane-making archaea live in the human gut. Methanobrevibacter smithii and Methanosphaera stadtmanae help drive digestion. Yet tests found their DNA in stool at low and variable rates. The team blamed weak detection methods for the mismatch.

With an improved DNA protocol, they found both microbes at high prevalence. The earlier scarcity was a measurement problem, not a biological one. Reliable detection matters because these archaea affect gut gas, digestion, and possibly disease.
plos-pone-0007163: Myong-Hee Sung, Luigi Salvatore, Rossana De Lorenzi, and colleagues studied sustained oscillations of NF-κB in PLOS ONE in 2009. NF-κB is a transcription factor that rises and falls in waves inside cells. Their work showed that these sustained waves produce distinct patterns of genome scanning and gene expression. In other words, the rhythm itself carries information. The timing of the signal, not just its strength, helps decide which genes a cell switches on.
plos-pone-0007263:
Eric Fimbel, Stéphane Lauzon, and Constant Rainville compared humans with computer algorithms on a planning test in 2009. The Tower of London test assesses executive functions such as planning. It was inspired by artificial intelligence tasks originally built to test problem-solving algorithms in machines.

The authors compare human performance with exploration algorithms on the same test. They focus on search patterns rather than absolute execution times. Their PLOS ONE comparison shows where human planning matches machine search and where it differs. Psychologists can use the benchmark to judge both patients and algorithms more fairly.
plos-pone-0007363:
Pontus Nordenfelt, Susanne Bauer, Per Lönnbro, and colleagues reassessed a cell model for studying bacterial killing in 2009. HL-60 cells treated with retinoic acid become neutrophil-like. Neutrophils are white blood cells that engulf and kill bacteria, and HL-60 cells carry the same azurophilic granules that store killing compounds.

New approaches to the neutrophil phagosome prompted a fresh look at this model. The authors study phagocytosis of Streptococcus pyogenes by the differentiated cells. They examine roles of azurophilic granules and the enzyme NADPH oxidase. Their work tests how faithfully the model mimics real neutrophils.
plos-pone-0007463:
Soledad Sacristán and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on powdery mildew fungi, parasites that infect nearly ten thousand plant groups. These fungi live entirely on their hosts and constantly overcome plant defenses. How they adapt so fast at the molecular level was poorly understood. The team studied a family of their virulence effectors, the proteins used to attack hosts.

They found these effectors evolve in step with LINE-1 retrotransposons, mobile pieces of DNA often called jumping genes. That coevolution suggests the jumping genes help shuffle or spread the attack proteins. A parasite that can reinvent its weapons quickly is hard for plants to resist. The finding offers a mechanism behind the mildew's speed. It may also guide efforts to breed more durable crop resistance.
plos-pone-0007563:
Tamim Salehzada and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how muscle cells choose their fate. Building and repairing skeletal muscle takes several coordinated steps. Stem cells wake, multiply, then mature into muscle fibers. Hundreds of genes switch on and off along the way. The team studied an enzyme called RNase L, which cuts RNA, and its influence on that choice.

RNase L regulates the myogenic and adipogenic potential of the cells. In plain terms, it helps decide whether they become muscle or fat. An RNA-cutting enzyme in that role shows how much control sits after genes are read. The balance between muscle and fat matters in aging and disease. The study adds a new switch to the known controls of muscle maintenance and repair.
plos-pone-0007663:
Jinte Middeldorp and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a variant protein in the brain's support cells. Astrocytes make GFAP, a structural protein with several splice variants. Two variants produce a form with a shifted tail, detectable by an antibody called GFAP+1. That form had been reported in astrocytes and in degenerating neurons in Alzheimer's disease. The team used an affinity-purified version of the antibody to test the claims cleanly.

The purified antibody revealed a specific astrocyte subtype carrying the variant. Unpurified serum, by contrast, cross-reacted with a neuronal protein in Alzheimer samples. That cross-reaction could mislead anyone reading such stains. The paper is both a discovery and a caution. A cleaner tool finds a real subtype, while the dirty tool invents a false one. Dementia research, which leans on GFAP stains, needs exactly that distinction.
plos-pone-0007763:
Kunihiro Kishida and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests whether a DNA variant in mitochondria relates to temperament. Mitochondria are the cell's energy centers, with their own small genome. One variant, A10398G, had been linked to mental disorders such as bipolar disorder.

The team studied healthy young adults in Japan. Healthy volunteers let researchers see gene effects without illness in the way. They measured temperament traits and compared them across variant groups. If such links hold, small energy-gene differences might nudge personality. The study treats that idea with proper caution.
plos-pone-0007863:
Cyndi Chen and Chih-Pin Liu published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a new kind of regulatory T cell in mice. Regulatory T cells keep the immune system from attacking the body. Most known types carry the marker Foxp3, but this population does not.

The cells are specific to a mouse autoantigen, a self molecule. Their regulatory function depends on three things. They need the signal IFN-gamma, the gas nitric oxide, and direct contact with target cells. Antigen-specific regulators are more potent than general ones. This new group may offer a precise tool against autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0007963:
Kareem Elsayad and Katrin Heinze set the working rules for a metal film lens in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thin metal films can bend light in ways that beat the usual limit on fine detail. That trick, called a superlens, could image glowing molecules with rare sharpness.

The pair worked out when the lens truly works for such imaging and when it fails. Clear rules matter because near-field lenses are touchy; small shifts in setup can spoil the gain. Their bounds help builders design setups that gain real sharpness rather than chasing a mirage.
plos-pone-0008063:
Andrew Shepherd and colleagues found a new control on the Notch signal in fly embryos for PLOS ONE in 2009. Notch steers the fate of cells in nearly every tissue as an animal grows. Most known controls act on the Notch protein after it is built.

This control acts earlier, on the cutting and finishing of the Notch message RNA. Holding the message back lowers how much protein the cell can make. An early brake like this adds fine timing to a signal whose doses must be exact for organs to form rightly.
plos-pone-0008163:
Nicole Nasby-Lucas and colleagues followed white sharks into their open ocean months in PLOS ONE in 2009. White sharks are well watched near coasts, but in the eastern Pacific they vanish offshore for up to five months. Tags that record depth, light, and place let the team follow that hidden season.

The sharks shared a broad offshore feeding ground and used its waters in set ways, diving and cruising in patterns tied to its conditions. The first full portrait of that season fills a blank in the species' life. It also tells protectors which waters matter most.
plos-pone-0008263:
Katja Linher, Paul Dyce, and Julang Li grew germ-like cells in the lab in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Stem cells from fetal pig skin had earlier formed oocyte-like cells in culture. Oocytes are the egg cells of reproduction. Before eggs can form, primordial germ cells must be specified. Those are the early cells set aside to become sperm or eggs.

The team showed skin-derived stem cells could produce primordial germ cell-like cells in vitro. That step bridges skin stem cells and later egg-like cells. The work matters for fertility research and animal breeding. It also probes how cell identity can be redirected.
plos-pone-0008363:
Caren I. Lanting and colleagues studied pregnant smokers in the Netherlands in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Smoking is a major cause of illness and death, including during pregnancy.
