A keyword mechanism, sharpened by contrastive learning, helps the model separate charges that look confusingly alike. On two real legal datasets, the system beat five comparison methods across the subtasks. Their code is released openly, as decision support research showing how structure inside legal tasks can be exploited rather than flattened.
plos-pone-0357763:
Susanne Vogeler, Matthew Parker, Samuel Robson, and Alex Ford wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on small aquatic animals called amphipods. These shrimp-like creatures are widely used in laboratory ecotoxicology, tests of how pollutants affect living things. The authors record their baseline locomotion behavior, how they normally move.

A baseline matters because a chemical's effect can only be judged against what untreated animals do. If normal movement is not well described first, later changes may be missed or misread. Ecotoxicology labs gain a reference for designing cleaner experiments, and the work supports using animal behavior as an early warning of water pollution.
plos-pone-0357963:
Lijun Zhang led a team of five authors building a deep learning tool for lung nodules, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. A nodule on a lung scan poses a dreaded question: harmless, or cancer? Their model views the nodule from several angles and uses attention to weigh what each view shows, classifying nodules as benign or malignant.

Zhang's multi-view approach helps radiologists sort worrisome nodules from benign ones with greater confidence. Fewer missed cancers and fewer needless biopsies are both wins. Attention maps can also show which views drove the decision, aiding trust. Tools like this are judged by whether they help in real reading rooms, and multi-view designs match how radiologists actually inspect a nodule.
plos-pone-0358063: Mesquita and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tracking disease outbreaks with digital data. Drawing lessons from past pandemics, the team picked key signals and grouped them with clustering methods. Their aim was nowcasting, a fast estimate of current outbreak levels before official counts land. Strong digital signals can give health officials a head start when a new threat spreads.
plos-pone-0358263:
Esther Su led a team of eight authors reviewing research practice for older adults living with HIV, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their topic was co-design: involving the people a study serves in shaping the study itself. Older adults with HIV are often left out of that planning, even though the research is about them.

Su's group gathered what has been tried and judged how genuine the involvement was. Their review shows that real partnership improves both the quality of studies and the chance that findings get used. For research teams, the message is plain: bring older patients in early as co-creators, not as subjects asked for opinions at the end.
plos-pone-0358363:
Xiaofang Xiong studied young firms and data in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. New ventures now collect large amounts of data but often lack the skill to turn it into advantage. Xiong tested how data capability and fresh business model design work together to shape how well a new venture performs.

The study's core lesson is that data alone does not pay. Returns appear when a firm also reshapes how it creates and captures value, so insight can change offers, prices, or service. Founders reading this gain a warning against buying tools before fixing strategy. Investors, too, can ask sharper questions: not how much data a startup holds, but what its model does with that data.
plos-pone-0358463:
Thomas N Slavens and Hamid Shabgard looked beyond air temperature in building design, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. What bodies actually feel is operative temperature, a blend of air heat and radiant heat from surfaces. The authors explored that fuller measure as a space for finding design ideas borrowed from nature.

Slavens and Shabgard argued that designing for felt temperature can reveal features that air-only targets miss. Nature offers models, from termite mounds to animal coats, for staying comfortable with little energy. Buildings use a huge share of world energy for heating and cooling, so better comfort per unit of energy matters at global scale. The paper reframes an old design variable as a source of fresh ideas.
plos-pone-0358763:
Shih-Han Kao and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on traumatic brain injury. It is a pilot study of blood taken after moderate-to-severe injury. The authors profile methylation of cell-free DNA in blood, chemical marks on DNA fragments that float free in the bloodstream.

Their signatures are enriched for brain cell types, meaning the marks can hint at which brain cells were harmed. A blood test reflecting brain injury could help when scanning is hard or repeated checks are needed. Brain injury specialists and biomarker researchers are the audience for this early test of the idea.
plos-pone-0358863:
Michele Conconi, Raphael Dumas, and Nicola Sancisi rebuild the joints of a leading digital human body model, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The TLEM 2.0 model simulates muscles and bones for movement science, but its knee and ankle were simplified to hinge like connections that let bones drift and overlap unrealistically. The authors reconstructed the true three dimensional motion of four joints, knee, kneecap, and two ankle joints, by maximizing how well the bone surfaces fit together through movement.

From those motions they identified the ligament fibers that stretch least, set the contact points between bones, and defined the model's neutral posture. In the rebuilt chain, bones neither separate nor interpenetrate during motion, and ligaments lengthen in a lifelike pattern. The upgrade sharpens everything the model is used for, from estimating joint forces to designing rehabilitation robots, by making the skeleton move the way skeletons actually do.
plos-pone-0359663:
Nanthida Phattraprayoon, Nut Koonrungsesomboon, and Mingkwan Na Takuathung wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a systematic review, with a meta-analysis, of nebulized salbutamol for the fast breathing of newborns whose lung fluid clears slowly, called transient tachypnea. Salbutamol is a standard asthma drug, given here as a mist.

The review weighs efficacy, whether the mist actually shortens the breathing trouble, across the trials done so far. Newborn units need that pooled answer before adopting a drug borrowed from asthma care. Neonatologists deciding treatment for fast-breathing newborns are the readers for this synthesis.
plos-pone-0359863:
Amaraporn Rerkasem and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in upper Northern Thailand, it gathers what providers from several professions think about preparing dialysis access in good time. That access, usually a vein and artery joined in the arm, must mature before dialysis can use it.

The study is exploratory and mixed-methods, mixing surveys with interviews across professions. Late access creation forces patients onto temporary catheters, which carry infection risk. Kidney teams in Thailand and similar systems can use providers' own accounts to find where the preparation pathway stalls.
plos-pone-0359963: Jo and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on trauma patients who need very large blood transfusions. The team searched for signs, known right when a patient reaches the emergency room, that predict death. They left out patients with severe brain injury so the signs would reflect bleeding risk alone. The data came from one hospital's past records. Early warning signs help trauma teams act fast.
plos-pone-0360063:
Kapina Mwampembwa and colleagues characterized in 2026 how neutrophils behave in patients with multiple myeloma, a cancer of the plasma cells in bone marrow. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells and the first responders of the immune system. In myeloma, the cancer and its treatments reshape the immune environment, and neutrophils are part of that story.

Functional characterization means testing what the cells actually do, not only counting them: how they attack microbes, release their contents, and respond to signals. Knowing whether a patient's neutrophils are weakened or overactive could help explain infections and complications that myeloma patients suffer. The study adds cell level evidence from a setting where such detailed immune work is rarely reported.
plos-pone-0360163:
Fang Wang, Jianqiong Li, and Yingjie Shen wrote this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a qualitative evidence synthesis about dementia care supported by artificial intelligence. The people whose views matter here are family and informal caregivers, the unpaid relatives and friends who carry most dementia care.

The synthesis will gather caregivers' acceptance of AI tools, their concerns about them, and what they expect. Planning the review in advance keeps its methods open and checkable. Designers of dementia technology need this caregiver view, since tools that families distrust will sit unused no matter how clever they are.
pmc-13142163:
Ingrid Ya I Sun leads a 2026 guide and study on spotting early communication signs of autism in toddlers. Autism spectrum disorder is diagnosed clinically, and social communication deficit is a core criterion, yet the practical use of language, called pragmatics, is checked less often than formal language. The presented script observes social and early communication skills before speech.

The script was applied to twenty-two children aged eighteen to thirty-six months, half with confirmed autism and half whose suspected diagnosis was discarded. Children with confirmed autism scored higher on the script overall, which the authors read as showing more pragmatic difficulty. Early signs, they suggest, can be flagged cheaply before age three.
pmc-13194963:
Makiya Nakashima leads a 2026 study presenting CMR-CLIP, an artificial intelligence model linking heart scan images with written reports. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging shows heart anatomy, function, and tissue in one exam, but interpretation is slow and expert-dependent. Labeled training data are hard to gather at scale, so the model learns from image-report pairs instead.

Trained on over eleven thousand studies from one institution, treating each scan as a video, the model was tested internally and on an external set. It classified several heart muscle diseases with high accuracy, including amyloidosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy above ninety-five percent. Such models, the authors suggest, could make heart disease diagnosis more consistent.
pmc-13197463:
Thomas K van der Made and colleagues describe a 2026 shift to serum-free growth of human kidney cells. Proximal tubule cells line a key kidney segment that handles drug transport. Labs grow them in calf serum, which is not natural for human cells, so the team tested a serum-free recipe.

Adding human platelet extract, a blood-derived growth mix, kept cells growing over many rounds. A key drug transporter still worked, though uptake of a test dye ran lower without serum. Gene checks showed less inflammation signaling and more transport and cell-grip genes. Energy output rose in the tuned recipe. In tiny tube models, richer extract boosted survival and coverage.
pmc-13198663:
Chun-Hao Fan and colleagues studied walking force balance before knee ligament surgery in a 2026 cohort study. After anterior cruciate ligament repair, uneven leg loading can slow recovery. The team asked whether uneven downward force while walking before surgery predicts thigh strength balance a year later.

They tracked fifty-five patients before surgery and one year after. Motion capture, force plates, and muscle sensors measured gait and strength. Both loading groups eased pain and regained some force balance. The group that loaded the injured leg more before surgery improved thigh strength balance far more, nearing even. The group that loaded less kept extra muscle co-firing and gained little. Pre-surgery gait may flag who needs targeted rehab.
pmc-13200563:
Yusuf Bünyamin Ketenci and colleagues warn about muscle loss in time-restricted eating for fatty liver disease in a 2026 short communication. Time-restricted eating limits food to a daily window and aids liver fat loss. But muscle loss and weight regain could erase gains, a risk the authors say is underappreciated.

Muscle loss is common in this liver disease and worsens insulin resistance, inflammation, and scarring. Recent trials show notable muscle loss during time-restricted eating and calorie cutting. Up to sixty percent of patients regain weight after programs end, which refills liver fat and stresses metabolism. The authors urge adding resistance exercise and enough protein to any plan. Future trials should track muscle function and long-term weight keeping.
pmc-13202163:
Babies born with abdominal wall defects need intravenous feeding to survive, and a 2026 study by Naomi Wright tests a pragmatic version for hospitals that lack full neonatal nutrition services. The research article evaluates a simplified intravenous nutrition strategy for gastroschisis across seven pediatric surgery centers in sub-Saharan Africa.

Local protocols used glucose fluid as the base, adding amino acids and lipids where locally available, alongside early breast milk feeding. After implementation, two thirds of babies received the combined support, up from under one fifth before the change in practice. Median support lasted fourteen days among survivors, with no major complications observed, making the approach a feasible interim option.
pmc-13202863:
Pandemic disruption hit teenagers with HIV especially hard, and a 2026 cross-sectional study headed by Khanh Toan Tran measures that impact in Vietnam. The research article surveys 587 adolescents aged ten to fifteen who were receiving antiretroviral therapy at five central and provincial hospitals during 2020 and 2021.

About thirty-six percent reported a significant overall impact from the pandemic across life domains. Odds were far higher for adolescents in Ho Chi Minh City and for those in larger households or homes the family did not own. Twice-daily treatment schedules and caregivers needing social support added further risk, which argues for family-level support in future emergencies.
pmc-13207863:
Chemotherapy nausea control got much better in Sichuan over five years, and a 2026 comparison study headed by Weijie Xiong records the change against a 2018 baseline. The forward-looking multicenter study enrolled 1,985 patients receiving moderately or highly nausea-provoking chemotherapy across the province in 2023.

Overall nausea and vomiting fell from over four fifths of patients at baseline to well under three fifths in the new cohort. Delayed symptoms eased most, and complete control rates climbed for both chemotherapy intensity groups in every phase measured. Guideline-concordant preventive prescribing more than doubled, led by wider use of one drug class for the strongest chemotherapy.
pmc-13207963:
A cholesterol drug may also rewire inflammation after stroke, and a 2026 pilot study led by Huijie Dong reads those changes in blood gene activity. The research article compares twenty-four patients with brain-heart syndrome and prior coronary disease, half adding evolocumab to rosuvastatin and half on the statin alone.

Sequencing and machine learning singled out four candidate biomarker genes that differed between the treatment groups. Three rose and one fell with the added drug, and they clustered in metabolism, signaling, and immune regulation pathways in the analysis. Immune cell mixes shifted only modestly, and outside data supported the markers' relevance, though the tiny sample demands caution.
pmc-13212163:
Weijun Peng and colleagues, in a 2026 retrospective study, trace how two drug-resistant bacteria spread through a pediatric intensive care unit. The organisms resist carbapenem antibiotics, a last-line drug class, so even small clusters in critically ill children demand urgent answers.

Five patients were involved in clusters seen in early 2024, and the team applied root cause analysis to find where control had failed. Sampling of 145 environmental specimens found one organism on hands, sinks, and devices, while the other appeared on bronchoscopes and hands. After targeted changes, no further clusters appeared during 2024, supporting structured outbreak review as a practical control tool.
pmc-13212263:
Mohammad Hossein Harirchian and colleagues describe, in 2026, a woman with multiple sclerosis whose new symptoms turned out to be a brain lymphoma rather than a relapse. She had received rituximab for years, a drug that removes B cells from the blood, yet the cancer still grew inside the nervous system.

The patient, aged 58, developed headache, vomiting, imbalance, and thinking problems over about a month. Scans looked unlike her earlier multiple sclerosis lesions, and tissue testing confirmed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The case warns clinicians to watch for warning signs of a second disease, even when a familiar diagnosis seems to explain new decline.
pmc-13212563:
Nahid-Al Mahmud and colleagues introduce in 2026 a compact neural network for recognising underwater sounds, such as ships picked up by sonar. Noise, fading signals, and shifting water conditions make the task hard, while many accurate models are too heavy for real-time use.

Their design mixes efficient local feature extraction with attention modules that track longer patterns, joining the two through an adaptive fusion step. Tested on two public ship-sound collections, the system scored above 98 percent accuracy on both. It did so with only about half a million parameters and very low delay. That balance could suit monitoring equipment with limited computing power.
pmc-13212863:
Charlene Andraos and colleagues review in 2026 a laboratory system that watches living cancer cells continuously instead of checking them once at an experiment's end. The device tracks electrical impedance as cells grow, move, invade, or die, producing a moving picture rather than a snapshot.

The review surveys uses since 2020 across drug testing, gene silencing, immunotherapy, nanomedicine, and three-dimensional tumour models. Real-time traces can reveal brief or adaptive responses that single time-point assays miss entirely. The authors compare the approach with conventional tests, discuss its measures, and note limits. They see a growing role in early drug development and personalised oncology research.
pmc-13214063:
Amanda L. Gustafsson and colleagues investigate in 2026 why grip strength fades in rheumatoid arthritis, testing whether the brain matters alongside sore joints. Weak hands are usually blamed on joint damage alone, yet motor areas of the brain could also shrink into the picture.

Fifty-nine women with established disease had grip measured, joints assessed, brains scanned, and immune cells profiled. Weaker grip tracked greater disability and, independently, smaller volume in premotor and supplementary motor brain regions. Blood cell patterns suggested muted immune responsiveness in weaker patients. A six-month hand exercise pilot in twelve women raised grip at three months, though the gain softened later, and brain volumes shifted in region-specific ways over time.
pmc-13214363:
Garen J. Wintemute leads a team reporting in 2026 the fourth wave of a yearly American survey on political violence, tracking change from mid-2024 to mid-2025. More than eight thousand panellists answered, with a completion rate near ninety percent.

The share calling violence usually or always justified for at least one of twenty political goals rose modestly, from about a third to just over a third. Willingness to commit violence barely moved, and expectations of firearm use did not change. Party gaps stayed wide: supporters of the MAGA movement far more often justified violence than strong Democrats. One small bloc, MAGA supporters outside the Republican Party, scored highest on many measures.
pmc-13215163:
Judit Kende and co-authors write in 2026 about a fresh look at 100 past studies of which immigrants people want to let in. Most past polls asked about immigrants as one big group. That hides the fine choices people make when they weigh one person at a time.

The pooled work covers more than 140,000 people in 36 lands. Each study showed fake immigrant profiles that mixed traits such as job, faith, and legal path. Traits tied to work, culture, aid needs, and legal steps swayed picks in most lands, though party lines split views. On the whole, people said yes to most profiles more often than harsh talk would suggest. The authors ask how laws and speeches build the split between favoured and shunned newcomers.
pmc-13216163:
Noppol Arunrat and co-authors present a 2026 field study of heavy metals moving from soil into rice near an abandoned zinc mine in western Thailand. The legacy of mining can reach dinner tables through the rice crop, and the team traced each step of that path.

Soil, roots, stems, and grain from twenty paddy fields were tested for nine metals. Bulk soil levels sat within national limits, yet pollution indices flagged extremely severe cadmium and mercury contamination everywhere. Roots held arsenic and mercury strongly, while copper, zinc, and manganese travelled readily into the grain. In the grain, four metals breached food safety standards, and estimated health risks for adults and children exceeded safe thresholds by wide margins.
pmc-13216763:
Yiğit Can Güldiken and co-authors present a 2026 case-based review pairing two autoimmune diseases that almost never meet. One is acute motor axonal neuropathy, a Guillain-Barré variant that paralyses; the other is ankylosing spondylitis, the spinal arthritis. Earlier overlaps were usually blamed on anti-TNF drugs; this patient took none.

The 35-year-old painter developed weakness in all four limbs over months, with severe muscle wasting, yet reflexes stayed normal. Nerve tests fit the axonal neuropathy, spinal fluid protein was raised, and further testing found HLA-B27 positivity with inflamed sacroiliac joints on MRI, confirming the spondylitis. Plasma exchange improved his bulbar function. With no infection or drug trigger found, the authors suggest a shared, unexplained autoimmune root worth remembering in similar presentations.
pmc-13217663:
Camille Wittesaele and co-authors present a 2026 mixed-methods study of clinic attendance for babies of teenage mothers in South Africa's Eastern Cape. Scheduled well-care visits carry vaccinations, growth checks, and HIV services, yet attendance by this high-risk group was largely unmeasured.

Records for 415 children showed attendance starting strong at 85.1 percent for the six-week visit, then sliding to 49.7 percent by eighteen months, with peaks where visits matched vaccination dates. Interviews with sixteen mothers, read through a behaviour framework, found determination rather than indifference: mothers organized, persisted through harsh staff attitudes, and valued the knowledge gained. Money, distance, weather, and missing childcare help were the brakes. The authors argue that kinder nurse interactions and practical support could lift attendance.
pmc-13218063:
Qianshuai Li and colleagues built a 2026 prediction model for hypothalamic obesity, the severe weight gain that can follow surgery for craniopharyngioma, a tumor near the brain's appetite control center. Damage to the hypothalamus during treatment can leave patients unable to regulate hunger. Knowing who faces the highest risk could guide closer monitoring after surgery.

The team reviewed records of 136 patients treated at a Zhengzhou hospital between 2018 and 2024 and split them into training and validation groups. Patients who developed hypothalamic obesity tended to start with a higher body mass index and lose more blood during surgery, and those two factors stood out as independent risks. Older age at onset and smaller tumors were protective. The resulting model discriminated well in both groups, with accuracy scores near 0.86, which the authors offer as a tool for early, targeted follow-up.
pmc-13221163:
Raju Vaishya and colleagues chart fifty years of research on bone and joint infections in children, in a 2026 bibliometric analysis covering 1976 to 2025. These infections remain a major cause of illness in childhood. The team mapped 1,556 publications, examining output, citations, and collaboration networks with mapping software.

Journal articles dominated, though reviews carried the strongest citation impact. Most work came from a few high-income countries, led by the United States and the United Kingdom. Nearly one paper in five had never been cited. Keyword clusters centered on bone infection, joint infection, key bacteria, diagnosis, and treatment. The authors call for broader collaboration to even out a concentrated field.
pmc-13222463:
Rangesh Modi and co-authors report a transplant patient whose anti-rejection drug levels spiked after heavy green tea drinking, in a 2026 case report. A 44-year-old woman with a liver transplant and Crohn's disease arrived with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and bloating on a stable tacrolimus dose. Her blood level measured well above the safe range.

Infection, liver trouble, and a bowel flare were ruled out, and gut examinations were unchanged. Holding the drug and stopping the non-commercial green tea with orange extract normalized levels within a day, and symptoms cleared fully. She later resumed her old dose safely. Herbal products, the authors warn, can quietly disturb narrow-margin drugs.
pmc-13223863:
Hind Qajia and co-authors document widespread bleeding brain emboli from heart valve infection, in a 2026 radiology case report. A 40-year-old intensive care patient with infective endocarditis lost consciousness during admission. Infected fragments breaking off the heart valves had showered the brain, a complication seen in up to forty percent of such patients.

MRI showed many small lesions above and below the tentorium with bleeding inside them, plus bleeding over the brain surface and a thin blood layer under the skull lining. One frontal lesion measured nearly three centimeters. The case demonstrates how multiparametric MRI sorts out these mixed injuries, which strongly influence prognosis and surgical timing in endocarditis care.
pmc-13224663:
Xulong Liao and colleagues report a 2026 eye-surgery study on scarring of the lens capsule after combined cataract and retinal operations performed without fitting a replacement lens. The capsule can turn fibrotic, which complicates later lens placement. Charts covered seventy such operations, fifty with thorough polishing of the front capsule and twenty without.

Scarring severity scored far lower in the polished group on a thirty-six-point scale. Diabetes, silicone oil left inside the eye, and skipping the polishing each raised the risk of heavy scarring. Polished eyes also had much better odds of receiving a later lens inside the capsular bag, the preferred position, supporting polishing as a simple preventive step.
pmc-13224763:
Selin Gümüşderelioğlu, G W Gant Luxton, and Daniel A Starr review a 2026 synthesis of how cell nuclei travel to their correct positions during development. A protein bridge called the LINC complex ties each nucleus to the cell's internal scaffolding and motors. Faults in that bridge cause muscle and nerve diseases, yet the control logic of nuclear movement is still being mapped.

Three worm development models anchor the review, covering nuclei crossing a huge egg cell, sliding within skin precursors, and squeezing through narrow gaps. Different tissues deploy different bridge part combinations, and splicing variants of one part can favour opposite motors. One migration route even runs four parallel pathways at once, offering principles relevant to immunity and cancer spread.
pmc-13225663:
Weijia Zhang and co-authors compare a 2026 methods study of place cells, the hippocampal neurons that fire only when an animal sits in a particular spot. Rodent laboratories usually detect them with a spatial-information measure plus stability checks, while human studies favour a different statistical test. Whether the two styles find the same cells matters for translating decades of rat work to people.

Applying several detection pipelines to rat and human recordings, backed by simulations, the team found the methods respond to different features. One reflects how sharply peak firing stands out, the other how consistent firing stays across trials. Rat samples included a strongly tuned population that human samples lacked, with human cells clustering at the weaker end.
pmc-13230263:
Carmine Porcaro and colleagues present in 2026 a way to simulate blood flow with red cells at a much larger scale. Detailed models that track each flexible cell are accurate but too slow for big vessels or devices. Treating blood as a simple fluid is fast, yet it misses effects that come from the cells themselves.

The team first ran detailed cell simulations to record how cells deform and what drag and lift they feel. Those records trained simpler rules for a faster solver that treats cells without drawing each membrane. The faster solver can handle hundreds of thousands of cells at far lower cost. Tests covered plasma separation devices and narrowed channels that mimic blocked veins.
pmc-13231063:
S Gorji and colleagues describe in 2026 an unusual salvage for a forearm flap that could not drain blood well enough. A circular saw injury left a large palm-side forearm defect with a broken wrist bone and cut artery, tendons, and nerve. A big combined thigh flap was moved to cover the defect, with vessels joined to arm vessels.

No suitable vein remained at the far end, so the team drained extra blood through a wrist bone using a small coupler into the bone interior. Congestion cleared, blood flow held, and no further revision was needed. Later liposuction thinned the flap, and by one year the patient managed daily life and work. Bone drainage may rescue flaps when normal veins run out.
pmc-13231163:
X Charlene Liao and colleagues describe in 2026 a woman with a rare developmental syndrome whose weight and behavior improved on tirzepatide. Smith-Magenis syndrome brings learning disability, strong food seeking, obesity, and hard-to-manage aggression. The thirty-one-year-old had carried obesity since childhood and had not responded well to standard behavior care.

Weekly tirzepatide, raised to a modest dose, led to a loss of close to a tenth of her body weight over ten months. Fasting glucose improved as well, and caregivers saw less food seeking and impulsivity at home. Measured aggression scores fell in a clear way during treatment. One well tolerated case cannot prove benefit for the syndrome, yet it invites careful study in similar patients.
pmc-13232563:
Sung-Doo Baek and colleagues solve in 2026 the streaky film problem that blocks large perovskite light panels. Perovskite inks dry unevenly at scale, leaving rings and patchy crystals that waste light. Their recipe blends three solvents and pairs open-air blade coating with vacuum drying to steer how the film forms.

Flow inside the wet film spreads material evenly, while the solvent mix controls when crystals start and grow. Finished films showed smoother coverage, fewer defects, and stronger light output. Near-infrared panels kept high efficiency as area grew from small test cells to a device large enough for vein imaging. A working vein viewer built from the big panel shows the method in action.
pmc-13232863:
Guoqiang Sun and colleagues present in 2026 a forecasting network built to predict power generation and demand more sharply than standard sequence models. Grid operators lean on such forecasts to schedule plants and keep supply matched to use. The design stacks gated memory layers and inserts self-attention at several levels to spotlight the most telling time steps.

Trials ran on three real energy datasets from regional grids and solar records. Against ten rival models the new network won consistently, cutting average error by more than three quarters versus basic recurrent baselines. It also matched heavyweight attention models on accuracy while training faster and leaner. Removal tests confirmed each design piece earns its place, which supports real dispatch use.
pmc-13233663:
Maximilian Krause and Matti Schneider wrote a 2026 paper on a new way to measure how much a material sample's stiffness wobbles. Engineers test materials on tiny blocks of microstructure. A small block's stiffness lands near the true value but jitters around it. For heat flow, a known tensor captures that jitter.

The pair extend the idea to elasticity, where the matching object is an eighth-order tensor, the elastic fluctuation tensor. They show it takes on the symmetry of the material group, so a randomly spun microstructure yields a round, even pattern. Group theory then packs the huge tensor into small forms for each symmetry class and trims math errors. Tests on fiber-filled polypropylene and copper crystals matched the predicted rates. The biggest wobbles hid in stiffness parts most studies skip.
pmc-13234063:
Mohammad Hossein Karami and Omid Moini Jazani published a 2026 review of MXene quantum dot polymer composites for medicine. MXenes are two-dimensional materials with strong electrical conductivity, flexibility, and a friendly profile toward living tissue. Blended with quantum dots inside polymers, they form smart materials that can carry drugs, respond to triggers, and release cargo on target, especially against cancer.

The review describes microrobots and delivery platforms built from these composites, including systems that carry several drugs at once for combined effect. The same blends serve tissue engineering, flexible electronics, and energy storage. Persistent problems include making the materials at scale, keeping them stable, and satisfying regulators. The authors see the composites as a platform technology whose biomedical promise now needs manufacturing and safety work to catch up.
pmc-13234163:
Milit S Patel and colleagues published a 2026 debate article on treating stage III lung cancer that cannot be removed surgically. For years the standard has been chemotherapy and radiation together, followed by a year of the immunotherapy drug durvalumab, a sequence set by the PACIFIC trial. The authors argue that this one-size-fits-all recipe no longer fits the evidence.

Tumors with particular molecular fingerprints may answer better to targeted drugs or different drug combinations, and the order of treatments could matter as much as the ingredients. The article weighs biomarker-guided refinement, novel immunotherapy pairings, and alternative sequencing for specific patient groups. It reads as a companion piece to debates over surgery in the same disease stage, mapping how non-surgical care is fragmenting into molecularly defined lanes.
pmc-13237263:
Abdalrhman Alras and a large clinical team reported in 2026 the case of a boy of about eleven whose hearing disorder had been mistaken for autism for eight years. Enlarged vestibular aqueduct syndrome is a birth defect of the inner ear. It causes hearing loss that grows worse with time and can look like social withdrawal and speech delay. High-resolution imaging finally set the diagnosis right.

The team warns about diagnostic overshadowing, where one label hides the true condition. Children suspected of autism deserve a full hearing check, since lost sound input in early years reshapes how speech and social skills develop. Finding the defect matters in practice, because timely steps such as cochlear implants can still change the child's path. The case adds weight to routine hearing tests in developmental work-ups.
pmc-13237863: Mice engineered to model ALS and frontotemporal dementia are the subject of a correction notice. The original study built knock-in mice carrying the C9orf72 poly-glycine-alanine change, and reported mild movement test changes and protein shifts matching the human diseases. The correction states that the funding section listed a wrong grant number. Funding numbers tie a paper to the grants that paid for it, and funders audit them, so the journal corrects the record.
pmc-13238263:
Targino and colleagues review the living ecosystem of the mouth and its role in gum disease. Periodontal disease destroys the tissue and bone holding teeth, and remains a leading cause of tooth loss worldwide. Two puzzles persist: many patients struggle to follow treatment routines, and the disease's inner workings are still only partly understood.

The review sets out how bacterial communities on teeth shift from balance to harm, and how the body's response drives much of the damage. That ecological view suggests therapies beyond scraping and antibiotics, such as rebalancing the community itself. For dentists, it reframes gum disease as a disorder of a whole ecosystem, not a single germ.
pmc-13240063:
Wanyanhan Jiang and team link short bursts of dirty air to hospital stays for diabetes in a 2026 Sichuan study. People with type 2 diabetes often carry heart disease, hypertension, or vessel damage as well. The team asked whether dirty air days push such patients into hospital, and at what cost.

More than ninety-two thousand stays were studied with a design that matched each patient's stay day with near control days. Nitrogen dioxide and particle pollution showed the clearest effects about a week after exposure. Women and older patients were hit hardest. Costs of stays tied to pollution ran into millions of yuan for each illness group.
pmc-13240163:
Chenbing Chu and colleagues study how three top predators sharing one Chinese forest influence each other's habitat choices in a 2026 paper. Amur tigers, Amur leopards, and Asiatic black bears all hunt or forage around Hunchun, and earlier work often ignored competition between such heavyweights when explaining where they live.

Six years of infrared camera records from 2014 to 2019 showed tiger and leopard densities rising while bear numbers held steady. Statistical models found each species' choices shaped by its own density, by rivals, by environment, and by prey. Bear habitat selection shifted with tiger and leopard density. The authors advise managing competition and space, not just restoring prey.
pmc-13240263:
Shogo Hamaura and colleagues measure how fat around the heart affects electrical readings during ablation in a 2026 study. Generator impedance, the resistance the ablation machine sees, guides treatment of irregular heart rhythms, and tissue inside the heart itself contributes to that reading in ways that were poorly understood.

In 104 patients, fat volume measured on pre-procedure scans strongly predicted the intracardiac impedance recorded with a special catheter. Blood sodium and haemoglobin also played roles, while body mass index alone did not. The inside-heart reading in turn predicted generator impedance during burning. Patients with the most heart fat relative to their size showed the highest values, suggesting personalised energy settings.
pmc-13240363:
Ali Talib Hashim writes a 2026 reply to a reader's letter about his systematic review of tongue transplantation. The reader had asked why commentary and review pieces sat inside a review that also pooled numbers. The reply sets out the two layers of the work.

Only studies with patient numbers and outcomes that could be pulled out fed the pooled maths, Hashim states. Pieces such as a commentary and a review stayed in the descriptive part, where they trace how the field grew. The forest plot marks them as not estimable, so they carry no weight in the pooled results. He accepts the split should have been stated more plainly and pledges clearer wording on methods.
pmc-13240463:
Andrea Calderone and colleagues review whether acceptance and commitment therapy builds self-compassion in adults with mental health problems in a 2026 systematic review. The therapy trains psychological flexibility, learning to accept difficult thoughts while acting on chosen values, and kinder self-relating is one hoped-for result.

Ten studies met the criteria, half of them randomised trials, after searches of four databases to August 2024. Improvements within treatment groups were common, yet comparisons against control groups swung from negligible to large, and one waitlist trial showed a striking gap. Self-criticism barely moved in the single trial reporting it. Bias concerns touched most trials, so the authors call the promise real but unsettled.
pmc-13240963:
Julie Buisson and co-authors offer a 2026 review of how chromatin, the packaged form of DNA, may generate force inside the cell nucleus. Forces usually travel inward from the cell surface to the nucleus. The reverse direction, from nuclear changes outward, is far less understood.

The review explains how loose and compact chromatin states store and release mechanical energy. Unpacking chromatin may push on the nuclear membrane and, through it, on the cell skeleton and attachment points. The authors treat chromatin as a tension-bearing structure that can form droplet-like condensates. Understanding this reverse pathway could clarify how cells choose their fate and how diseases linked to abnormal nuclei develop.
pmc-13241563:
Zyada and colleagues at Cairo University review the long non-coding RNA XIST and its tangled role in breast cancer. XIST normally silences one X chromosome in female cells. The review traces how it interacts with microRNAs, transcription factors, and signaling pathways inside tumors. Its effects reach drug resistance, the tumor surroundings, and cancer stem cells.

Crucially, XIST does not behave the same in every breast cancer subtype. It often promotes tumors, yet in some luminal and triple-negative settings its role looks more restraining. That split personality complicates any single reading of its levels. The authors still see promise in XIST as a diagnostic marker, a prognostic sign, and a drug target.
pmc-13241763:
Homero V. Rios-Figueroa and Candy O. Sosa-Jiménez describe a 2026 dataset of three-dimensional hand shapes for the Mexican Sign Language alphabet. Research on automatic recognition of this language is scarce, and shared datasets are rare. Their collection covers the static letters of the alphabet.

Fifteen people each performed twenty-one letters once, using the right hand. A depth sensor captured the three-dimensional points of each hand shape. One clear image per performance was chosen and exported as coordinate text files. The strategy favors variety between people over repetition by the same person. The dataset is openly licensed through a public repository, giving recognition researchers a starting resource for this language.
pmc-13241963:
Chiara Cazzorla and co-authors present a 2026 observational study of life quality after diet freedom in phenylketonuria, a genetic disorder that forces a strict low-protein diet. The drug pegvaliase can bring blood phenylalanine down enough to liberalize eating. The team followed Italian patients who reached that point.

Seven participants who had historically struggled with the diet were tracked for up to a year after liberalization. Their blood phenylalanine fell by a large share on average. Quality of life scores improved steadily, most clearly on measures of the disorder emotional, practical, and social weight. Patients reported better energy, sleep, mood, and social functioning. Injection-site discomfort and early anxiety were the main downsides noted.
pmc-13242763:
Qiqi Zhu and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study linking alcohol, gut bacteria, and worsening prostate inflammation. Alcohol aggravated an autoimmune prostatitis model, raising pelvic pain and inflammatory signals. The team traced the effect through the gut community.

Transplanting gut material from alcohol-fed sick mice copied the worsened state in recipients, proving the microbes carried the effect. Alcohol reduced one Lactobacillus species sharply. Feeding that bacterium, or injecting its released vesicles, eased pain and inflammation. The vesicles entered immune cells and blocked a pathway that drives harsh immune attack. Adding back the blocked signal reversed the benefit. The authors propose microbe-based therapy for alcohol-aggravated prostate pain.
pmc-13243163:
Elyor Berdimurodov and colleagues reviewed five years of progress in turning plant waste into glowing sensor particles. Their review appeared in Bioresources and Bioprocessing in 2026. Carbon quantum dots cooked from fruit peels, leaves, and farm waste fluoresce brightly and cost little to make. Between 2021 and 2025, researchers refined recipes using heated water, microwaves, and pyrolysis, sometimes finishing in ten minutes.

The dots come out a few nanometers wide, partly graphitic, and their glow can be tuned by what they are made from and what they are doped with. Sensors built on them detect iron at extremely low levels, spot antibiotics through glow changes, and catch farm and household chemicals such as glyphosate, ammonia, and formaldehyde. Selectivity and sensitivity rival conventional quantum dots without the toxic metals. The authors call biomass dots a sustainable platform ready for wider sensing use. Remaining work centers on standardization and real-world samples.
pmc-13244563:
Ngoc Hai Tran and colleagues present a five-step surgical technique, named DARIP, for the deadliest form of placenta accreta in mid-pregnancy. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2026. A thirty-five-year-old woman at nearly twenty-two weeks arrived with vaginal bleeding, and ultrasound showed placenta percreta, where the placenta grows through the uterine wall. In low-resource settings, removing the uterus is not the safest answer.

The procedure works through five moves. It clears the bladder-uterus plane of new vessels, drains amniotic fluid, and places a rectangle of blood-stopping stitches. Only then does it cut the uterus, through the blocked-off zone, and sew the placental bed. The authors call DARIP promising for second-trimester disease and share a video of the operation. They insist it belongs in expert centers and needs testing in larger series before adoption.
pmc-13244963:
Laura Kim and colleagues tested pressurized oxygen for ME/CFS, an exhausting illness with no approved therapy. Their study appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2026. Thirty patients, mostly women in their early forties, completed forty hyperbaric oxygen sessions. The team tracked functioning, fatigue, pain, exercise capacity, grip strength, thinking speed, and standing tolerance. Brains were scanned before and after, against thirty healthy controls.

Physical functioning, the main outcome, improved meaningfully during treatment, and pain and fatigue scores fell by clinically important margins. Patients also exercised longer, gripped harder, and processed information faster after the sessions. Brain scans showed the thalamus's connection pattern shifting toward the healthy profile, and that shift tracked who responded. Treatment was well tolerated. The authors link the benefit to correcting disturbed thalamus function. Without a placebo arm the proof stays early, but the signal spans symptoms, performance, and brain measures alike.
pmc-13245563:
Priscilla Mpasi, Tiffany Chalk, and Leah A Jones mark twenty years of a Delaware consortium for mothers and babies in 2026. The group held its annual summit in April 2026 with more than 400 partners and advocates. Babies helped in its first years are now nearing parenthood themselves.

Over two decades the consortium raised the share of healthy births and built a continuum of care for mothers and infants. Goals now include cutting infant deaths further and reaching deeper into at-risk neighborhoods. Fairness across race, ethnicity, and place stands out as the hardest current challenge. The anniversary piece looks back at hard lessons and ahead to the next twenty years.
pmc-13245763:
Zhang, Sun, Chen, and co-authors optimized the water passages of a large drainage pumping station in this 2026 PLOS One engineering study. Vertical mixed-flow pumps move floodwater at scale, and badly shaped intake and discharge passages waste energy and destabilize flow. Traditional tuning changes one factor at a time; instead, the team combined orthogonal experimental design, which tests factor combinations efficiently, with computational fluid dynamics simulations.

Their scoring system weighed hydraulic loss, flow uniformity, and inflow angle together. The winning intake design kept losses tiny and delivered nearly perfectly uniform, near-vertical inflow, while the discharge design flowed smoothly without separation and fit the station's layout. A physical model test confirmed the predictions, reaching strong efficiency at the design point with simulation and experiment agreeing closely.
pmc-13247263:
Guo and colleagues tested a two-drug combination against advanced head and neck cancer in this 2026 phase 1b/2 trial in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Patients received toripalimab, an immune checkpoint drug, plus cetuximab, an antibody blocking a growth receptor. One group had already failed platinum chemotherapy; another, selected for a positive PD-L1 marker, was previously untreated. Eighty-eight patients enrolled across several centers.

Tumors shrank in sixty percent of the platinum-resistant group and about forty-four percent of the untreated group, with median survival around fourteen and eighteen months respectively. Patients whose tumors scored positive for PD-L1 benefited more. Severe side effects affected roughly half of patients, but no new safety problems appeared. The authors call the pairing promising for a cancer with few good options.
pmc-13248263:
Lai and colleagues followed two hundred children wearing overnight corneal reshaping lenses, in a 2026 BMC Ophthalmology study. These lenses slow worsening eyesight in myopia, and the team compared a smaller optical zone design against a larger one. Children aged seven to twelve were grouped by both lens type and starting prescription strength.

After one year, eyes grew least in the group pairing moderate myopia with the smaller zone. That group also had the highest share of children whose myopia did not progress. The authors conclude the smaller design controls myopia better, especially for children who start with milder prescriptions.
pmc-13248463:
Guo and colleagues grew sheep womb-lining organoids in the lab, reported in Veterinary Research in 2026. The luminal epithelium is the surface where an embryo first meets the mother, and flat cell cultures fail to copy its structure. The team built three-dimensional organoids from that surface layer using a tuned growth medium.

The organoids showed the right markers, secreted mucin, and answered hormones much like real tissue. Turned inside out, they matched the womb's natural orientation, and embryos placed with them grew and spread better. Gene readings confirmed a close match to native lining. The authors offer the system for studying pregnancy recognition and fertility treatments in livestock.
pmc-13248963:
Maswanganyi and colleagues tested a rapid blood infection panel in Limpopo, South Africa, reported in 2026. Bloodstream infections kill many patients, and remote labs often wait long for conventional identification. The team ran two hundred forty-seven positive blood cultures through both the BioFire BCID2 panel and the standard VITEK2 system at a routine laboratory.

The rapid panel matched the standard closely, with sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy all above ninety-five percent. About a quarter of samples held more than one microbe, and the panel also flagged drug resistance genes, most often one linked to broad antibiotic resistance. The authors recommend the panel where fast answers can change treatment.
pmc-13249963: Scientific Reports retracted this 2025 article in 2026, and this note records the withdrawal. Chandra and colleagues had used machine learning to predict the compressive strength of polymer-infused bricks, with SHAP analysis to explain the model. Editors later found the paper overlapped substantially with an earlier submitted, then withdrawn, manuscript that shared only two authors. The authors could not adequately explain the authorship change, given the stated contributions. The editors therefore lost confidence in the article's integrity and retracted it.
pmc-13250463:
Aynaz Esmailzadeh and colleagues review artificial intelligence for metabolic syndrome in this 2026 paper. The syndrome is a cluster of belly fat, blood sugar, and blood pressure problems that raises heart disease and diabetes risk, affecting roughly three in ten adults worldwide.

Following standard review methods, the team searched four databases in 2025 and kept 12 studies that fit. Most used learning algorithms on body measures and simple tests to spot or predict the syndrome, scoring well on accuracy tests. Only three studies touched prevention or long-term care, and none reported uncertainty ranges or explained their models. The authors want stronger outside testing before clinic use.
pmc-13250863:
Han, Wu, and Wu compare two antibiotic-loaded materials for treating long-standing bone infections. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study covers two hundred forty-four patients with chronic osteomyelitis treated between 2017 and 2024. One group received vancomycin in bone cement alone, and the other an added calcium sulfate carrier holding the same drug.

The combined material controlled infection in about seven of eight patients, versus roughly three of four with cement alone. Reoperations and overall complications both fell sharply in the combined group. Blood inflammation markers also dropped further, and quality-of-life scores for physical health and energy ran higher. The authors judge the combination a promising upgrade for this stubborn infection, worth wider clinical use.
pmc-13251763:
Tsotetsi, Nkoana, and Khan review a structured dry eye diagnosis system and its scarce use in African clinics. Their 2026 Clinical Optometry paper covers the JENVIS Pro Dry Eye Report, a software report paired with a corneal imaging device. Dry eye disease troubles the eye surface with unstable tears, discomfort, and blurred vision.

Seventy sources fed the review of disease patterns, risk factors, and diagnostic methods. The JENVIS system combines objective tear measures with symptom scores and proved reliable and reproducible in the literature. African studies still lean on older tests such as the Schirmer strip and dye break-up timing. The authors advocate wider JENVIS adoption in Africa to standardize diagnosis, teach patients, and guide evidence-based care.
pmc-13251863:
Yuwen Wang and a large team steer stem cells with twisted nanoparticles in this 2026 study. Bone repair needs stem cells that reliably turn into bone, and the handedness of tiny particles, whether they twist left or right, can change how cells respond.

Three particle versions were compared: left-twisted, right-twisted, and untwisted. The left-twisted ones entered cells most readily and switched on the strongest bone-building and blood-vessel signals, with more mineral laid down. Printed into 3D scaffolds and placed in rats with large skull-bone gaps, the left-twisted version healed bone fastest. The authors name particle twist as a design dial for regenerative materials.
pmc-13252763:
Katy Chalmers and co-authors study how feedback shapes expert surveys in this 2026 methods paper. Core data sets, the agreed minimum every registry should collect, are built by Delphi surveys, where stakeholders score items over rounds and re-score after seeing group feedback.

Inside a real core set project, round-two participants were split by chance into standard feedback or an enhanced version adding the top five items from round one. Both groups prioritised more items in round two, and agreement between them rose. The extra top-five summary barely changed what got prioritised, though. The authors say feedback design still needs work, including talking with stakeholders about how they read it.
pmc-13253063:
Nobuto Hirai and colleagues report two tricky stent cases in this 2026 paper. Both women had a narrowed innominate artery, the first branch off the aorta toward the right arm and brain, and the usual route through the leg arteries was unsafe for each.

The first patient, aged 74, had a swollen aorta making leg access risky, so the team worked through the arm, holding a balloon downstream to shield the brain. The second, aged 80, had blocked leg arteries on both sides; a filter guarded her brain artery while the stent went in from the arm. Neither woman suffered a new stroke. Protection plans must be tailored case by case, the authors conclude.
pmc-13253363:
Ari Hoffman, Thais Vasconcelos, and Eric Hagen survey plant blindness in this 2026 study from Michigan. People tend to overlook the plants around them, a bias called plant awareness disparity, and that neglect starves plant conservation of public support.

The team surveyed 318 people in the southeast of the state, testing attention, attitude, knowledge, and interest in plants across sex, schooling, and age. Non-males showed more interest and attention, and the youngest adults knew the most. When asked to build an ecosystem from parts, bees were the single most chosen living feature across all groups. The authors propose bees as ambassadors to carry plant campaigns.
pmc-13253763:
Brian Overbeek and co-authors tackle volunteer training for emergency care in a 2026 study. Community first responder systems send nearby trained volunteers to medical emergencies, often in rural areas where ambulances arrive late. Training lets volunteers handle more kinds of emergencies, but budgets are limited.

The team built a math model that weighs where volunteers live and when they are free. Tested on a real system in Lincolnshire, United Kingdom, the model beat simple greedy training plans by a wide margin. Success was measured as the chance that at least one volunteer reaches an incident before the ambulance. Limits on volunteer workload also changed the best plan.
pmc-13254163:
Ayano Ikeda and colleagues report a layered blistering skin case in a 2026 case report. A 60-year-old woman developed redness and blisters on her back and upper arms. Tests confirmed IgG/IgA pemphigus, a rare blistering disease where the immune system attacks skin cell links, with antibodies to desmoglein 1.

During her course, she later developed bullous pemphigoid, a second blistering disease. She had taken two diabetes drugs, linagliptin for six years and tofogliflozin for five months. A drug stimulation test was positive for tofogliflozin and negative for linagliptin, so the authors consider possible drug involvement in the second disease.
pmc-13254363:
Samar Abdelbaset and co-authors test a coated nanoparticle to protect rat testes in a 2026 study. Cisplatin, a key cancer drug, harms male fertility through oxidative stress. Forty-five male Wistar rats were split into nine groups, comparing plain selenium nanoparticles with versions coated in gum arabic, a plant gum.

The coated particles worked best after cisplatin. They restored antioxidant enzyme activity, lowered a fat damage marker, and cut inflammatory signals. DNA damage fell, cell death signals were suppressed, and testis tissue structure looked restored. The authors credit better uptake and shared antioxidant action from the coating.
pmc-13255063:
Zhao, Chen, and Wang present a lab protocol for detecting protein S-glutathionylation in the model plant Arabidopsis during stress. This reversible change helps govern protein stability and signaling, but its fragile disulfide bonds break easily and samples oxidize after harvest, so direct checks in living tissue have been shaky. The method uses no transgenic plants.

Instead, a chemical toolkit tags proteins through propargyl glycine feeding and click chemistry. The protocol covers whole-proteome counting, pulling out tagged targets for western blotting or tandem mass spectrometry, and imaging the change in place. Step-by-step steps make the workflow easy for other plant labs to adopt.
pmc-13255463:
Lisa Eiring and colleagues test peer-run mock oral exams for medical students in a 2026 study. Students often enter oral exams underprepared and stressed. About 190 third-semester students at a German university practiced in groups of five, swapping teacher and learner roles across two simulated exams three months apart, with trained senior-student tutors giving structured feedback.

After training, students reported more confidence and less exam stress, and more rated their own performance highly. Tutors saw better-structured, deeper answers in the second round. Later real exam results also trended favorably. The authors call the format a low-cost complement to the standard curriculum.
pmc-13255763:
Danilo de Souza Sanches and a large team present a 2026 meta-analysis of phytase, an enzyme added to pig feed, judged on both technical and economic grounds. Much of the phosphorus in plant feed is locked in phytate, which pigs cannot digest without the enzyme. The analysis pooled studies comparing standard diets, phosphorus-reduced diets, and reduced diets plus phytase.

Cutting phosphorus without the enzyme hurt growth, lowering weight gain and final body weight. Adding phytase to reduced diets restored performance and sometimes improved it beyond standard diets. Profitability rose with enzyme use even when its price fluctuated. The authors conclude that phytase lets producers cut phosphorus, and the pollution that follows it, while keeping pigs growing and margins healthy.
pmc-13255863:
Ramaditya Srinivasmurthy and a large team present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of checkpoint immunotherapy in locally advanced head and neck cancer. These drugs transformed care for recurrent and metastatic disease, yet trials in earlier, curable-stage disease disagreed. The team pooled randomized trials and split results by tumor biomarkers and patient features.

Across everyone, adding checkpoint inhibitors did not improve outcomes. Patients whose tumors expressed PD-L1, the drug target's partner protein, did benefit, while those without expression fared worse when immunotherapy was added. The same split appeared among patients fit for cisplatin chemotherapy. HPV status did not show the same clear pattern. The authors conclude that PD-L1 testing should guide who receives these drugs in locally advanced disease, rather than offering them broadly.
pmc-13256063:
Zahra Khazaei and co-authors review a 2026 challenge in prostate cancer: telling harmless tumors from dangerous ones. The review surveys prognostic biomarkers across imaging, blood and tissue tests, and genetic data, and how combining them sharpens prediction. The goal is treatment matched to each man's actual risk.

Magnetic resonance imaging and PET scans with prostate-specific tracers lead the imaging side, offering detailed pictures of tumor extent and aggressiveness. Ultrasound still guides biopsies but predicts outcomes weakly on its own. Molecular tests add information that pictures cannot give. The authors also look at artificial intelligence and advanced image analysis as emerging helpers. Their overall message is that integrated, multi-source assessment beats any single test for deciding who needs treatment now and who can safely watch and wait.
pmc-13256363:
Daniel R. Alfonso and co-authors report a 2026 study loading the chemotherapy drug mitoxantrone into NU-1000, a zirconium-based metal-organic framework full of ordered pores. Such sponges can carry large drug quantities and release them at the tumor. The particles kept their crystal structure and shape after loading, and uptake reached roughly forty percent drug by weight, mostly within three hours.

A polyethylene glycol coating steadied the loaded particles in body-like fluid. The coated carrier alone barely harmed cultured cervical cancer cells, showing good compatibility. Loaded particles, though, killed cancer cells more effectively than free drug at short exposure times. The authors present NU-1000 as a promising delivery platform that combines high capacity with stability, an early step toward gentler chemotherapy dosing.
pmc-13257063:
Ting Luo leads a 2026 review that brings chickpea nutrition, health effects, and stress tolerance into one account. Chickpea is a major legume that supplies digestible protein and helpful plant compounds. Drought, heat, cold, and salty soils still limit harvests in many regions.

Nutrient and metabolite evidence is summarized first, covering proteins, minerals, and isoflavones linked to chronic disease prevention. Physiology sections then explain how the plant rewires metabolism under water and temperature stress. Precision breeding routes for hardier, higher-quality varieties are outlined. Uses for processing by-products receive attention as a way to cut waste. Breeders and food scientists share the intended audience. Future work, in the authors' view, should join resilient cultivars with new functional foods built from the crop.
pmc-13257363:
Qiao Peng and colleagues link a mitochondrial splitting protein to stress-driven depression-like behavior in mice in a 2026 study. Chronic social defeat is a standard model for stress effects on mood. Brain tissue from the hippocampus, a memory and emotion region, was examined after defeat.

Defeated mice showed more Drp1, the protein that pinches mitochondria apart, driving excess splitting. Energy production faltered, oxidative stress rose, cleanup of worn mitochondria stalled, and excitatory signaling weakened. Injecting a Drp1 blocker into the hippocampus reversed those cell problems. Social avoidance, loss of pleasure, and despair-like behavior all eased with treatment. Neuroscientists gain a concrete chain from stress to organelle shape to behavior. Drp1 control is proposed as a treatment strategy, with the usual distance between mouse results and human depression kept in view.
pmc-13258063:
Alice Rueda leads a 2026 prospective cohort trial of a digital suite for stress in frontline nurses. The suite combines a virtual reality stress session, short teaching on coping, phone check-ins during daily life, and wearable sensors. Ninety-nine nurses, with a mean age of 33.7 years and eighty-seven percent women, enrolled in 2023. They had at least two weeks of baseline monitoring, one virtual reality session, and twelve weeks of follow-up.

Virtual reality raised stress during both runs, though less the second time, and ninety-two percent of nurses felt stressed in the session. Most returned to their emotional baseline afterwards, while twelve percent had lingering distress. Anxiety and stress scores fell two weeks later but were not sustained at twelve weeks. Data completion passed ninety percent, which the authors call a sign of feasibility.
pmc-13258163:
Bárbara Salinas Orellana and co-authors optimize phenolic extraction from a local Argentine cannabis strain's leaves in a 2026 study. Leaves are a by-product beside the prized flowers, and ultrasound extraction was tuned by response surface methods for solvent strength, ratio, power, and time. Energy use and carbon cost were measured alongside yield.

The tuned process reached high phenolic and flavonoid levels with strong antioxidant activity. Yield plateaued after a few minutes of sonication, longer than the model first suggested. Brine shrimp safety testing showed no significant toxicity at tested levels. Each batch used modest electricity, giving a low carbon cost per unit of antioxidant recovered. Cosmetic and food developers gain a circular use for farm residue. Scaling economics remain to be proven outside the bench.
pmc-13259263:
Ramya Shekhar and a large Indian team hunt the best tomato lines for greenhouse growing. Indeterminate types, which keep climbing and fruiting, suit off-season protected production. Their 2026 trial grew fifty-seven genotypes for two years and scored sixteen yield and quality traits.

Every trait varied significantly across the lines. Fruit weight and fruits per cluster looked directly selectable, being highly heritable with strong expected gains. Grouping split the lines into seven clusters, each championing earliness, nutrition, or fruit size. A multi-trait index crowned three elite genotypes, named PIDGT-39, PIDGT-42, and PIDGT-29. Breeders now have parent stock shortcuts from this work.
pmc-13259363:
Juan María Nogales and coauthors build a small battery test tool with a fixed math method in a 2026 paper. Wave based tests show battery health, yet cheap gear warps the read. Their math treats the shunt part as wave based and wipes out board fault effects.

A two block build makes test waves and reads the reply under chip control. Sims with two battery models proved the fix brings back true reads. Bench tests on a plain circuit hit small size error at the top test rate. Phase reads need an input tweak for the low wave range. Cheap health checks gain truth with no costly parts.
pmc-13260063:
Jingjing Liu and Peng Liu reviewed in 2026 whether treatments designed for degenerative brain diseases might also help people with tinnitus. The condition is the sense of sound when no outside sound is present, and it has no reliable cure. The reviewers note that tinnitus shares several harmful processes with those diseases, including inflammation and damaged connections between nerve cells.

Candidate strategies they examine include calming inflammatory cascades, supporting growth factors for nerve cells, and limiting damage from excess glutamate, a key signaling chemical. Much of the support so far comes from animal and cell studies rather than patient trials. The authors map where the two fields overlap and where human testing still lags. They argue that this shared ground could speed the search for mechanism-based tinnitus therapies.
pmc-13260263:
Pere Bosch-Barceló leads a 2026 preliminary randomized trial in Parkinson's disease, combining treadmill training with a gamified virtual reality environment and brain stimulation. Walking problems in Parkinson's worsen when patients must think at the same time, and often persist despite medication. Twenty-three people with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's were assigned to treadmill only, treadmill plus virtual reality, or treadmill plus virtual reality plus stimulation. They completed twelve sessions over six weeks.

Attendance was high at ninety-two percent, and the program was safe and well tolerated. No statistically or clinically meaningful change in gait speed was observed. Balance improved across all groups by 1.48 points on a standard test. Interviews revealed greater walking confidence and new strategies for complex walking situations. The authors call for larger, sham-controlled trials before judging whether the combination truly works.
pmc-13260563:
Suhaib Tawil and co-authors told in 2026 the case of a toddler whose chest tumor was first read as the wrong cancer. The boy, nearly three years old, arrived with worsening breathing trouble and fever from a fast-growing mass filling one side of his chest. A small biopsy sample suggested embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and treatment began on that basis.

The tumor responded poorly, and repeated lung collapses forced urgent surgery at a specialist center. Removal of the mass, then a second operation for quick regrowth, gave enough tissue for a firm answer: pleuropulmonary blastoma, type three, the most solid form of this rare tumor. Gene testing found a harmful DICER1 variant, a change tied to a family cancer syndrome. The authors stress early gene testing, expert pathology review, and enough biopsy tissue in such cases.
pmc-13260963:
Younghoon Yang leads a 2026 imaging study of rotational subluxation patterns in knees lacking a working posterior cruciate ligament, a major knee stabilizer. In such knees the shin bone can slip backward and rotate under stress. The team reviewed 127 patients who had primary ligament reconstruction. Three-dimensional models from postoperative CT scans were registered onto preoperative stress X-rays to measure backward translation of each side of the knee joint and classify the rotation pattern.

Posteromedial subluxation, slipping toward the inner back, was far more common, in ninety-three cases or 73.2 percent, than posterolateral slipping, in thirty-four cases. Rotational laxity was greater in the posteromedial group. A positive dial test, a physical exam for corner injury, was associated with overall posterior laxity but not with rotational laxity. The authors warn against overtreatment based on rotation tests alone.
pmc-13261063:
Jonathan Barratt and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how doctors should judge whether treatments for IgA nephropathy truly work. This kidney disease, driven by immune deposits, often ends in kidney failure in adults and children. New disease-modifying drugs now slow function loss in late-stage trials, so fair yardsticks matter.

Protein in the urine is the longest-standing stand-in marker, since lasting proteinuria tracks closely with worsening kidney outcomes. Trials usually measure it over a full day, while clinics often rely on quicker spot samples that wobble with hydration and timing. Filtering rate, the direct measure of kidney function, anchors the other half of assessment, and even one-year slope changes predicted hard outcomes in past studies. The authors weigh both tools and their limits for building a full management strategy.
pmc-13261463:
Lokesh Murali and George Jacob examined in 2026 silver nanowire electrodes as cheaper back contacts for dye-sensitized solar cells. The standard contact uses fluorine-doped tin oxide, often topped with platinum, and its fabrication is costly and complex. Their study paired computer simulation with built devices to test how the contact's work function shapes performance.

Simulations pointed to energetics at the contact as the lever, and the bench results agreed. Cells with silver nanowire contacts converted sunlight at a rate close to the platinum-coated standard and far above bare oxide contacts. The authors credit the nanowires' higher effective work function for smoother charge collection. They argue the swap cuts both material and processing costs. The work supports nanowire contacts as a plausible base for scalable cells without the usual oxide layer.
pmc-13261963:
Faul and co-authors present a 2026 national study testing Germany's 2022 trauma team activation criteria, with a focus on older patients. The update added age-specific modifiers meant to catch severe injury risk in the elderly. The team tested whether response levels now line up with actual deaths.

They covered 66,273 trauma patients aged 60 and over from the TraumaRegister DGU between 2018 and 2023. Under the 2022 criteria, mortality showed a clean gradient: 20.2% for high risk, 9.0% for medium risk, and 4.2% for no call-out. The 2016 criteria produced uneven patterns. New modifiers strongly predicted death: multiple serious injuries carried 16.7 percent mortality against 6.7 percent without, and systolic blood pressure of 91–100 mmHg carried 13.1 percent against 7.3 percent without that sign. Blood-thinner use before injury raised mortality across all subgroups. The authors conclude the update improves triage accuracy for elderly patients.
pmc-13262263:
Larissa Ringelstetter and colleagues uncover a brake on the cell's low-oxygen alarm that works without its usual tools. RNF8 normally tags proteins for disposal, while HIF1α rallies genes when oxygen runs short. Their 2026 study shows RNF8 quietly opposing a rival protein that protects HIF1α in hypoxia.

Surprisingly, RNF8's tagging power was irrelevant to the effect. Instead, its forkhead-associated domain gripped the tail of HIF1α directly, shown by yeast two-hybrid tests. The grip held even when HIF1α could not be hydroxylated, the usual oxygen signal. This hidden association could matter for hypoxia-driven cancers like triple-negative breast cancer.
pmc-13262563:
Hao Tang and colleagues review the conversation between prostate cancer and the bone it invades. Prostate tumors in bone usually provoke extra bone building, orchestrated by resident bone cells. Their 2026 review weighs each cell type's contribution to that corrupt remodeling.

Bone-eating cells start the cycle but blocking them helps patients surprisingly little. Bone-building cells can either lull tumors to sleep or whip them into aggressive change, depending on signals. Osteocytes, bone's most numerous cells, release pro-invasion messengers when mechanical sensing shifts. Tumor exosomes reprogram the whole neighborhood in return. Breaking this self-reinforcing loop is the therapeutic prize.
pmc-13262863:
Solmaz Surano and co-authors run a randomized trial of online balance retraining after sudden vertigo in a 2026 journal article. Acute vestibular syndrome causes constant spinning dizziness, often from an inflamed inner-ear nerve. Retraining exercises help the brain adjust, but proof in acute cases is thin. Patients at nine Swedish hospitals got either online guided exercises or written instructions.

Of 184 people enrolled, 183 were analyzed, starting within a week of symptoms. After six weeks of training, both groups had improved, with no clear difference between them on a vertigo symptom scale. Gains in disability, balance, and walking speed also matched over 12 weeks. No serious harms were tied to either approach, and patients stuck with both well.
pmc-13263363:
Vivek Manyapu and Yo-Chia Chen report a 2026 journal article on raising lauric acid output from black soldier fly larvae. Lauric acid is a useful fat found in soaps, fuels, and antimicrobial products. The larvae were fed sweet potato and coconut mixes, some pre-fermented with bacteria, to see what drives production.

Sweet potato, not coconut, proved to be the main driver of lauric acid formation in the larvae. Pre-fermenting the feed boosted output further. Larvae on fermented sweet potato reached a remarkable lauric acid share of eighty-two percent of biomass fat. The authors explain that fermentation supplied building blocks such as oleic and linoleic acids and freed up sugars the larvae could convert.
pmc-13263563:
Kai-Uwe Lewandrowski and colleagues proposed in 2026 a shared plan for how spine care should be split among its many trades. Care today fragments among surgeons, pain doctors, therapists, and primary care, with fuzzy handoffs and drifting terms. Their plan grew from society statements, guidelines, and policy reviews.

Four parts anchor the design. First, clear role definitions assign who owns what: surgical care owns spine mechanics and rescue capacity, while non-surgical care runs goal-directed episodes with deadlines. Second, written triggers govern movement both ways, up to surgical review and back down when surgery is not the answer. Third, shared procedure language and follow-up rules standardize what teams promise and repeat. Fourth, borderline procedures with lasting effects on spine mechanics get joint oversight. The authors aim to cut low-value care and speed the right step-ups.
pmc-13264063:
Shyryn Almerekova and co-authors report the complete plastome, the DNA of the chloroplast, for a rare wild onion in a 2026 data paper.
