Allium microdictyon grows in the Kazakhstan Altay and is valued as food and medicine. Leaves from the Ivanovsky Range were sequenced with Illumina technology and assembled into a full circular genome for analysis.

The plastome measures about one hundred fifty-three thousand base pairs with the usual four-part structure. Annotation found one hundred thirty-seven genes, including protein-coding, transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA genes, plus hundreds of short repeat sequences. Family tree analyses placed it near close Allium relatives already in public databases. The sequence gives researchers a reference for evolution and population studies in wild onions.
pmc-13264363:
H. Chen and a very large team analyze triple therapy for lung cancer spread to the membranes around the brain in a 2026 multicenter retrospective study. Six hundred eighteen patients with a targetable EGFR mutation received regimens built on the drug furmonertinib across many centers. Triple therapy added vessel-blocking treatment and chemotherapy, including delivery into spinal fluid for some, and outcomes were compared with single or double combinations for survival and time until treatment failed.

Median survival for the whole group sat a little over a year from treatment start. Triple therapy patients lived notably longer on median than those on simpler regimens. Side effects were catalogued across groups. Retrospective design limits causal claims, yet the scale gives rare guidance for a complication with few proven options.
pmc-13264563:
Samuel C Marshall and colleagues wrote a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of femoral head fractures, breaks in the ball of the hip joint. Such breaks are rare, come from high-energy crashes, and often end badly. The team gathered work since 2009 to see how care and outcomes have changed.

The two main operations were fixing the bone in place and removing loose fragments. Bad outcomes such as extra bone growth, joint wear, and bone death ran from 9 to 37 percent. No clear link tied break type or treatment to good results.
pmc-13264763:
Quanfu Hu and colleagues use ultrasound texture analysis to separate two common benign salivary gland tumors in a 2026 study. Images from pathology-confirmed cases were segmented, texture traits extracted and the most telling subset chosen. Machine learning models were tested on a separate set, and explanation analysis linked top traits back to visible scan patterns.

Eight traits carried the discrimination. One tumor type showed smoother, more regular texture, while the other appeared more mixed and random. Test scores were strong across accuracy measures. Cutoff values for single traits are given. Texture scoring could support radiologists where biopsy is risky or unclear, pending checks at more centers.
pmc-13264863:
Shanquan Chen and colleagues check whether deworming reached children with disabilities fairly in an Indian trial in a 2026 secondary analysis. Over eighty thousand children aged five to seventeen in Tamil Nadu were included, with disability measured by a standard child functioning questionnaire. Treatment coverage across six rounds was compared by disability status with adjustment for social factors.

Children with disabilities, about one percent of the group, had higher unadjusted odds of missing treatment. School-only programs risk systematic exclusion, and this dataset quantifies that risk in a rigorous trial setting for program designers.
pmc-13265163:
Hanlu Zhang and colleagues map a chemical modification called lysine lactylation in oesophageal cancer, in a 2026 study. The modification attaches lactate-derived marks to proteins and may help cancer spread. Its role in spread to lymph nodes was poorly defined. The team compared tumours with and without such spread.

Protein profiling found many marked proteins, with overall marking higher when nodes were involved. Dozens of marked sites rose, while fewer fell. Many affected proteins sat outside the cell nucleus. pmc-13265263:
Haoyu Zhu and the team hunt for new germ-killing picks against Escherichia coli using machine learning, in a 2026 study. Early drug selection must balance killing power with safety and stability. A strategy scoring drug-likeness across many properties was built. Deep learning models scored about sixteen million shop compounds.

Fifteen picks were tested in the lab. Several showed clear germ-killing effect. One compound, called M2, had the most balanced profile, with the largest inhibition zone among picks. Docking and model runs backed binding to a bacterial target called PBP2. A rival-binding test added support that interaction, marking M2 for development.
pmc-13266363:

After full adjustment, rising aorta width and the ratio of junction to annulus stayed independently tied to severity, while raw junction width did not. pmc-13266663:

Timing and setting may explain varied breathing results across trials.
pmc-13266763:
Yuki Joyama, Stephanie Tuminello, and Emanuela Taioli discuss in 2026 what lung cancer research gains from databases that join many kinds of data. pmc-13266863:
Qing Shen and colleagues set out in 2026 the design of a trial testing a Chinese herbal granule for cough that lingers after an infection. Patients will receive a low dose, a high dose, or a placebo for fourteen days, with a short follow-up afterward. Outcomes include how many patients respond, how fast cough eases, quality-of-life scores, and traditional symptom measures. Safety checks cover side effects, vital signs, lab tests, and heart tracings. Results should show whether the herbal product deserves wider testing.
pmc-13267563:
Toni Franz and colleagues report a 2026 study of quality of life after focused ultrasound treatment for prostate cancer. Tiredness, pain, poor sleep, and weaker social life drove the dip. From three months on, scores recovered to starting levels or better. pmc-13268163:
Casado-Martínez P and colleagues report a 2026 study of a strength index guiding training in youth basketball. Each player trained three times a week beside normal basketball practice, with the focus set by their starting index band.

The high-index group gained the most push strength and squat strength, and their index fell as a result. The middle group also gained squat strength. Jump height and force did not change clearly in any group. No clear interactions between groups appeared. The authors present the outcomes as observations from real in-season work that can help coaches set training priorities.
pmc-13268363:
Júlia de Souza Lopes and colleagues present a 2026 case report on skin sporotrichosis caught from a pet cat. The authors stress that diagnosis joins the story, the lesion look, and lab proof, and that sick cats should be treated as infection sources.
pmc-13268463:
Luciana Volpon Soares Souza and colleagues present a 2026 image-based case report on lung injury from inhaling butane. CT scans showed widespread cloudy and solid patches through both lungs. After nine days in intensive care she recovered and went home. pmc-13268763:
Neal Masia and colleagues present a 2026 study of hospital finances under the US 340B drug discount program. Eligible hospitals also spent more on administrative salaries. The authors conclude 340B hospitals show consistently strong finances, outpacing ineligible peers. pmc-13269263:

pmc-13270663:

pmc-13270763:
Marwa M. Abokresha led a 2026 cross-sectional study, a one-time check, of diabetic gastroparesis in type 2 diabetes. Among 130 randomly chosen clinic patients, 13.1 percent showed delayed emptying on the scan. Those patients had higher body weight scores, longer diabetes, and poorer blood sugar control. Statistical analysis kept blood sugar control, body mass, and diabetes duration as independent predictors. Symptom scores agreed only weakly with the scan result, which the authors say helps explain missed cases.
pmc-13270863:
Sen Li is lead author of a 2026 journal article on Zexie decoction, a classic Chinese medicine prescription long used for hyperlipidemia, meaning high fat levels in the blood. The authors set out to find which of its compounds enter the blood and how they might lower lipids.

In mice fed a high-fat diet, the decoction showed clear lipid-lowering effects. Blood analysis found twelve absorbed parts, three original compounds and nine changed forms made by the body. Network analysis pointed mainly to a pathway called PPAR, a key lipid-control route, and computer docking showed major compounds bound strongly to two PPAR targets. A focused lipid scan found 36 changed fat markers.
pmc-13271063:
Jun Tan and colleagues describe in 2026 a catalyst-driven route to bridged bicyclic scaffolds that contain both nitrogen and oxygen. Computer calculations helped explain how the catalyst steers the outcome, giving chemists a reliable platform for new drug-like molecules.
pmc-13271363:
Albert Shieh and coauthors examine in 2026 whether a combined bone balance score can predict fractures around menopause. The score joins two blood markers, one for bone breakdown and one for bone building, into a single index. A higher score means building keeps ahead of breakdown.

The study followed 451 women in a long-running health cohort, with repeated measures across menopause stages. Over about fifteen years, 78 women broke a bone. Each standard rise in the balance score came with a lower fracture risk, near one fifth lower for any fracture site. The combined score may help flag women who need earlier bone protection.
pmc-13271463:
Andrada Pica is lead author of a 2026 journal article characterising the random positioning machine, a ground-based device that simulates microgravity for biology experiments by constantly reorienting samples. Such simulators let researchers study gravity effects in the laboratory, but hard numbers on this machine's performance were scarce.

The team recorded the machine's motion with sensors across its randomised, one-way, and single-axis modes, then modelled how gravity averaged out. All modes reached time-averaged gravity between one hundredth and one thousandth of Earth's, with spinning side forces under 0.08 g. pmc-13271563:
Swati Priyadarshini and coauthors report in 2026 the largest Indian case series on acute retinal necrosis, a fast-moving viral infection of the retina. Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster viruses appeared equally often in eye fluid tests. Despite antiviral treatment, many eyes later developed cataract or retinal detachment, and average vision worsened over two years.
pmc-13272063:
Bowei Yang and coauthors examine in 2026 how tea drinking and smoking combine in relation to accelerated biological aging among Chinese oilfield workers. Workers who both smoked and drank tea carried the highest odds compared with non-smoking non-tea drinkers. The combined pattern was stronger among non-shift workers. Sensitivity checks supported the main findings across analysis choices.
pmc-13272363:
Xinru Wu and coauthors chart in 2026 the growth of research linking gut microbes with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease using bibliometric mapping. One specialty journal served as the field's core outlet, and a Sydney-based research group ranked among the most productive. Keyword maps revealed the dominant themes and pointed to underexplored gaps for the next wave of studies.
pmc-13272563:

Most pregnancies in women happened naturally, and the median time from cell infusion to birth or loss was three years. No formal fertility guidance exists yet, the authors note.
pmc-13272963:
Anhar Abdel-Aziem leads a 2026 study making two coumarin-based compounds without solvents, by grinding, to add to primer paint for metal. Coumarins are natural ring compounds. The green method is faster, cheaper, and avoids hazardous solvents, and the products were checked with several spectroscopy tools.

Primers with the new compounds were stiffer, more heat resistant, and harder than the plain primer, with better adhesion and impact strength. One compound, which contains a pyrazole ring, performed best in salt spray tests for rust protection. Computer calculations supported its stronger grip on metal, linked to a smaller energy gap. The authors claim a dual gain in strength and corrosion protection.
pmc-13273463:
Raffi Tachdjian and co-authors studied long term preventive treatment patterns in hereditary angioedema in a 2026 claims study. Several non-androgen preventive therapies are approved in the United States, yet real world use, cost, and care patterns were little known. The team used a national insurance claims database.

They followed 328 commercially insured patients for a year after starting prevention. Most still claimed on-demand treatment during that year. Patients who refilled steadily cut their on-demand doses, while those with refill gaps or switches did not. Total yearly cost per patient rose sharply after starting prevention, driven by pharmacy cost, with only modest offsets in hospital care. Over half of patients had gaps, stopped, or switched within a year, which the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-13273563:
Gita S Prihanti, Anung P Illahika, and Noviana D Lestari screened plant compounds against two diabetes drug targets in a 2026 computational study. The blend of fenugreek, paitan, and turmeric is a traditional mix for blood sugar control. Its active compounds were identified by high resolution chemical analysis.

Two compounds bound moderately, one to each target. Long simulations then showed the SGLT2 pairing held together with favorable energy, while the DPP-4 pairing looked unstable and unfavorable. Motion analyses agreed. The authors call the results preliminary and ask for lab and animal tests before any diabetes use.
pmc-13273663:
Ekstrand and colleagues study how the brain follows a story, in a 2026 journal article. Volunteers watched a foreign film with subtitles. For some viewers the subtitles kept the plot intact. For others the subtitle order was scrambled.

Brain scans compared the two viewing conditions. Two networks changed how they connected during the intact version. One was the default mode network, active during inner thought. Key hubs were the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex. The other was the frontoparietal network, which supports control of attention. Scrambling the story weakened this pattern. The authors say coherent stories engage these networks in a shared way. Broken stories do not produce the same brain response.
pmc-13274163:
Chudan Xu, Matthew Snelson, and Francine Z Marques wrote a 2026 review article on poisons made by gut bacteria in a linked heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome. These illnesses often arrive together and feed each other. When kidneys fail, waste chemicals from gut microbes build up in the blood instead of leaving the body.

The review names key toxins, including TMAO and indoxyl sulfate, and traces how each harms vessels, kidneys, and metabolism. A leaky gut wall, chronic inflammation, and weak kidney filtering all raise toxin levels. Diets low in fiber and high in meat favor the microbes that make them. The authors close with gut-targeted strategies meant to cut toxin production.
pmc-13274863:
Karolina Pawłowska-Cyprysiak and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on what decides whether people with disabilities in Poland join digital skills training. Digital competence is now basic for work and daily life, yet training is often hard to access. The team surveyed 449 people with different disabilities and modeled their participation statistically.

One factor dominated: whether the training was seen as accessible. When people perceived training as inaccessible, their likelihood of taking part fell by more than seventy percent. Other personal factors mattered far less by comparison in the authors' analysis. They argue that making courses genuinely accessible, in format, tools, and setting, is the key lever for equal digital opportunity.
pmc-13274963:
Justin David and a large team report a 2026 journal article surveying work-related pain among Florida urologists. Surgeons commonly develop muscle and joint disorders from awkward operating postures, but urology-specific numbers for Florida were lacking. The state urologic society's ergonomics task force sent a questionnaire to its 504 members in 2023, and ninety-four replied.

Among those answering the key question, 45.3 percent reported work-related pain more than a quarter of the time. Major open surgery hurt most often, at forty percent of respondents, with endoscopic surgery close behind; robotic cases ranked lowest. About sixty-nine percent blamed uncomfortable operating positions, and thirty percent simply ignored their pain. Over seventy percent wanted formal ergonomics training.
pmc-13275763:
Wei-Hung Yang and co-authors ask a measurement question in a 2026 journal article: how many answer choices should a rating scale offer? Surveys and tests often use scales from a few points up to a smooth slider. Past studies disagreed on whether more choices make answers more reliable.

The authors treated all scales as points on one scale of fineness and tested them two ways. Computer simulations varied group sizes, test lengths, and formats from three points to fully smooth. A real test then gave a career interest survey to more than three thousand junior high students in ten formats. Reliability mostly rose as choices grew finer. Gains slowed at about seven to eight options, but the finest formats, including a slider, scored highest.
pmc-13275963:
Julie Rolling and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on helping young people haunted by traumatic nightmares. The patients had complex post-traumatic stress disorder after early, repeated trauma. Their nightmares keep the body on high alert and wreck sleep, yet treatments tested in youth are scarce.

Therapists gave thirty-nine patients aged fourteen to twenty-five four sessions of imagery rehearsal therapy. In this approach, patients rewrite a nightmare's story while awake and rehearse the new version. Weekly nightmares fell by about half, and distress dropped sharply too. Sleep quality scores improved, as did quality of life. Anxiety and depression scores stayed about the same. The authors call the brief therapy promising and easy to spread, including to low-resource settings.
pmc-13276163:
Gannah Samy and co-authors present a 2026 animal study on helping wrist joints fuse in rabbits. Arthrodesis, surgical fusion of a joint, treats severe joint damage but bone often fails to knit. The team tested a collagen and chitosan composite enriched with advanced platelet-rich fibrin, a blood-derived healing material.

Sixteen healthy male rabbits had the cartilage of a front wrist joint scraped away. Half received the composite and half did not. Over twelve weeks, treated joints showed thicker bone cortex and rising bone density on scans. The joint space narrowed steadily and the fusion ratio reached nearly seventy percent. The authors conclude the enriched composite improved bone growth and fusion in this model, and they flag its promise for wider surgical use.
pmc-13276463:
Songyi Wei and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on the hidden risks of disinfectants washing into rivers and lakes. Pandemic-era cleaning boosted public use of these chemicals. Many are water-repelling and linger, yet their ecological risks are barely assessed.

The team screened forty-two such disinfectants and antiseptics two ways. A ratio method comparing expected levels with harm thresholds flagged nineteen of twenty-seven scorable chemicals as high risk. Five, including chlorhexidine and triclosan, scored over a hundred times the concern level. A second method, borrowing drug-target mapping, linked ten chemicals to one hundred forty fish targets. Eight core targets touched behavior, hormones, nerves, digestion, heart, bones, and eyes in exposed zebrafish. The authors warn these common products deserve regulatory attention.
pmc-13276563:
Anusha Shetty and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on matching spinal screw size to each patient's bone anatomy. Pedicle screws anchor rods that stabilize broken spines, but a screw too wide can breach the bony tunnel it passes through. Direct links between tunnel dimensions and screw choice had not been established.

The team reviewed sixty adults treated for chest and lower back fractures, covering one hundred seventy-seven vertebrae. Most fractures were burst type at the junction of chest and lower back. Scans before and after surgery measured tunnels and screws. About twenty-three percent of screws breached their tunnel walls. Breach risk rose in narrow chest-level tunnels and when screws exceeded eighty percent of the tunnel width. The angle screws took did not follow the tunnel's natural angle. The authors advise routine scan measurement to guide each screw choice.
pmc-13276763:
Peerut Chienwichai and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on urine clues for catching intestinal schistosomiasis early. This worm infection burdens millions, but standard tests miss the first weeks before eggs appear. Chemical profiling of urine, called metabolomics, could expose the infection through the host's shifted chemistry.

The team infected mice with three intestinal Schistosoma species and sampled urine over time. Mass spectrometry detected more than twenty-three thousand chemical features. Layered statistics and machine learning narrowed these to seventy-one significant signals. Two candidate compounds stood out for separating infected from healthy mice early. One fell steadily from the first week and was clearly reduced by week two. The other rose and differed clearly by week four. The authors offer both as leads for a non-invasive early test.
pmc-13277063:
Shucheng Liang leads a 2026 systematic review of secondhand tobacco smoke and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises stroke risk. The review gathered observational studies, meaning studies that watch groups rather than assign treatment, from major databases through September 2025. The question was whether breathing others' smoke raises the risk.

Six studies with more than 420,000 people were included. Smoke exposure in the womb or childhood was steadily tied to higher risk in adult life. Evidence for adult exposure was mixed, though studies using body markers or dose patterns found clearer links. Some groups, including women and never-smokers, showed stronger ties. Cutting secondhand smoke may be an overlooked way to lower risk.
pmc-13277663:
Sarah A Laane and colleagues test online brain health training for adults with and without mental illness, in a 2026 study. Most mental health programmes target one diagnosis or group, which limits their reach. A universal programme built on reasoning strategies plus daily health education might serve everyone.

Three hundred seventy matched adults took six months of online training and were compared before and after. The group with mental illness began with more distress, lower resilience, and poorer life quality. Both groups improved on distress, resilience, quality of life, and meaningful activity after training. Clearer thinking rose only in the illness-free group completing the core course. Gains in clarity tracked gains in mental health across the sample.
pmc-13277763:
Malaz Elnagi Musa Elshiekh leads a 2026 case report of intestinal telescoping in a preterm newborn, a condition that can be mistaken for a more common gut emergency. The baby, born at about thirty-one weeks, went home on day twenty-two after care for breathing distress, infection, and jaundice. On day twenty-six the infant returned with mild belly swelling and rectal bleeding.

X-ray imaging was inconclusive, but repeated bleeding prompted an ultrasound, which showed one segment of bowel folded into another near the appendix area, with blood flow preserved. The fold reduced on its own under monitoring, and symptoms resolved without surgery. Ultrasound deserves an early place when newborn X-rays are unclear, the authors argue.
pmc-13278863:
Valeria Calcaterra and colleagues review dietary polyphenols in childhood obesity in a 2026 narrative overview. Polyphenols are plant compounds in fruit, vegetables, legumes, cocoa, and tea. Childhood obesity brings early insulin resistance, blood fat problems, and vessel damage, so food-based modulators attract interest.

The review covers how polyphenols may act on oxidative stress, inflammation, glucose and fat handling, blood vessels, and gut microbes. Observational work links Mediterranean-style eating, rich in these compounds, with healthier weight and metabolic profiles in young people. Trials in children, though, are few and inconsistent, blocking firm claims about benefit or long-term safety. The authors back whole dietary patterns over isolated supplements for now.
pmc-13279763:
Ljupcho Milosheski and colleagues present a 2026 dataset that pairs three dimensional room scans with Wi Fi signal reads. Indoor wireless must serve video, sensing and extended reality apps that need speed and low lag. Radio maps help plan access point places, yet real maps are hard to build from plain floor plans. New Wi Fi at high frequencies fades fast through walls, which sharpens the need.

The team scanned a multi room space with LiDAR, a laser measure tool, for high detail three dimensional point clouds. Wi Fi signal strength, called RSSI, was read in twenty setups. Two scenes were run: rooms empty and rooms with people in them. Both geometry and human presence shape signal spread. The open set can train and test models that forecast coverage from real room shape.
pmc-13279963:
Md Monirul Islam and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of how constant displacement shapes mental health among the Bede, river-nomadic communities of Bangladesh, in the first account of this experience. Flooding, riverbank erosion, and collapsing livelihoods keep these families moving several times a year along rivers such as the Jamuna. Unlike refugees displaced by a single event, the Bede live in near-constant motion. Their needs stay largely invisible to clinic-based systems.

Chronic movement acted as a long-running exposure rather than a crisis, building anxiety, physical exhaustion, and a disrupted sense of identity. Coping ran through group solidarity, faith practices, and careful handling of reputation. The authors recommend mental health support that is mobile, local, and grounded in their culture. Fixed facilities cannot reliably reach them. They press policymakers for livelihood security and services built around mobility, not fixed homes.
pmc-13280063:
Luigi Gargiulo and colleagues published a 2026 consensus paper defining moderate psoriasis, a severity band that guidelines describe inconsistently and that decides who qualifies for whole-body treatments such as biologics. Fifteen Italian dermatologists rated eighteen statements through a two-round Delphi process, a structured method for building expert agreement. Statements spanned skin severity, quality of life, symptoms, hard-to-treat body areas, and response to earlier therapy.

Twelve statements won consensus in the first round. The remaining six were rewritten for clarity, with sharper definitions of early and frequent relapse, quality-of-life thresholds, and mention of difficult or visible sites. All six then passed in round two, giving agreement on the final definition. The authors emphasize a view that goes beyond the standard area-and-severity scores. A shared definition, they argue, can open earlier access to systemic therapy and make decisions and research cohorts more consistent.
pmc-13280463:
Stacy B. Buchanan and team report a 2026 case of vaccine failure in a child with Down syndrome. Children with Down syndrome face repeat infections and may respond to vaccines in changed ways. Guide rules advise standard childhood vaccine schedules for them. Yet some show weak responses despite complete records. Their patient was a five year old with frequent respiratory infections, plus heart disease, laryngomalacia and reflux disease under care.

Despite full adherence to advised immunizations, infections kept coming. After an immunology consult, the child got the twenty three valent pneumococcal vaccine, a broader germ shot. The rate of respiratory infections then fell a lot. The case urges doctors to weigh vaccine response when repeat infections hit children with Down syndrome, even when records look complete. Widening the search past the usual comorbidities changed the path here.
pmc-13280663:
Farah Jaafar Mahdi and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a teen boy in Iraq with a rare swelling disorder. The disorder, called SAPHO, links joint pain with severe acne and bone swelling. His muscles had also weakened, which the team tied to the acne drug. He got better after the drug was stopped and swelling drugs were given. Care held even after steroid drugs ended.
pmc-13281263:

Blood was tested at the start and again about a year later. The team asked who fell ill, who got better, and why.

About one in five healthy teens developed anemia, while close to half of those with it recovered. School attendance and frequent fruit and vegetable intake guarded against new cases. Stunted growth raised the risk. The authors say teen anemia turns over fast, so one-time checks miss much.
pmc-13281763:
Suling Huang and colleagues built a nursing framework for liver patients with belly fluid in a 2026 study. In Chinese medicine, care is matched to a pattern of signs in each patient. The authors offer the frame for ward use and testing.
pmc-13281863:
Supawadee Intusup and colleagues judged a hospital asthma rulebook for children in a 2026 study. Asthma attacks are a top reason children land in hospital. Care still varies a lot from ward to ward. First breathing drugs came far faster by the last stage, in about seventy minutes. Use of inhaled steroids and high-flow nose oxygen rose. The authors weigh faster, better early care against higher resource use.
pmc-13282163:
Yannick Laurent Tchenadoyo Bayala and co-authors report a 2026 case of widespread bone pain in a man on long-term dialysis from Burkina Faso. Dialysis cleans the blood when kidneys fail. Over years, a protein called beta-2 microglobulin can build up and deposit in joints and bone. Magnetic scans showed a band-like pattern in his spine and nodules in his pelvis and thigh bones. No bone biopsy was available, so the diagnosis rested on history, labs, and imaging. A daily anti-inflammatory drug brought clear improvement within one month. The authors urge regional clinics to suspect this cause.
pmc-13282463:

The newer tool beat the others for TP53 but did not improve TERT calls. The authors conclude tool performance is gene-specific, reflecting the data each tool was trained on. pmc-13282863:
Dry age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss in older adults, anchors a 2026 investigation by Yujie Chen and teammates. The work focuses on the layer between retina and choroid, where immune change occurs. It examines how vessel cells and immune cells signal to each other.

Vessel cells appeared to drive these cells through a TNFSF10 signal and NF-kB activity. Blocking that signal path is proposed as a possible future treatment target.
pmc-13282963:

The model may help doctors judge outlook and drug choice.
pmc-13284263:
Catch-and-relay particle design brightens infrared glow nearly two thousand fold, describe Liyan Ming and Riccardo Marin in 2026. Lanthanide particles emit narrow, stable light bands prized for body imaging. Surface dyes gather light well, yet protective shells usually block that harvest.

pmc-13284463:
Sevda Boyanova and colleagues offer a 2026 primer on choosing and testing mouse models for Alzheimer disease research. Good phenotyping, they argue, means clear aims, sound controls, and honest limits, so that mouse findings have a fair chance to inform human trials and basic science.
pmc-13284563:
Sa Ra Kim and colleagues reported in 2026, in a Korean-language case report, a dangerous channel between the aorta and the oesophagus that masqueraded as a tumour. Needle biopsy at the reporting hospital triggered bleeding from the puncture site, which was clipped shut. Follow-up CT then revealed a thoracic aortic aneurysm with the fistula and a thickened oesophageal wall. The case warns that such fistulas can imitate tumours on scope views.
pmc-13284963:
Kadir Sinasi Bulut and co-authors compare two kinds of tonsil abscess that are easy to confuse, in a study published in 2026. One form sits beside the tonsil and is well known. pmc-13285363:
Hip drift in children who cannot walk is tied to how stiff their hip muscles are, a Danish cohort study by Muhammed Bakhtiyar and co-authors reports in 2026. The study drew on a national follow-up program and covered 422 children at the two lowest movement levels, with 786 hips tracked by X-ray.

Stiffness in the muscles that pull the legs inward showed the steadiest link of the three muscle groups tested. The authors back routine stiffness checks to flag hips early.
pmc-13285563:
Extra slime helps a friendly bacterium survive the gut and settle in, Lohith Kunyeit and Reeta Rao report in a 2026 study. Health microbes often die off during making and gut travel. pmc-13286463:

pmc-13286863:

pmc-13286963:

pmc-13287063:

pmc-13287163:
Roberto Davoli and colleagues mapped gas movement through shallow soils at the Rotokawa geothermal field in New Zealand in a 2026 field study. They paired direct soil measurements and gas profiles at depth with drone heat surveys around collapsed ground features.

Collapsed features could focus, trap, or redirect escaping gas. The authors suggest that gradual sealing near the surface may help explain falling diffuse emissions reported at the field, alongside deeper and environmental causes.
pmc-13287563:
Su Min Park and Jung-Ju Lee report in 2026 a case of immune brain inflammation linked to antibodies against a protein called LGI1. Such illness usually arrives fast, with confusion and seizures over days or weeks. Their patient instead declined slowly over a long period before seizures began.

They hope wider awareness will shorten delays and improve chances of recovery for patients whose illness unfolds over months rather than days.
pmc-13288163:
Sangita Bhattarai and co-authors surveyed 228 school students in 2026 in three government schools in Tansen, Nepal. Ages ran from ten to nineteen. pmc-13288763:

Several trials reported short-term gains in pain or disability. Results conflicted across studies, and differences in design blocked any pooled analysis. pmc-13288863:

pmc-13288963:

pmc-13289163:
Filipa Godoy-Vitorino and co-authors chart vaginal fungi in Hispanic women in Puerto Rico in a 2026 study. Fungi form a small but active part of the vaginal ecosystem, yet they are rarely mapped. Bacterial community types were recorded alongside.

pmc-13289363:
Guoxin Cai and colleagues report a 2026 phase II biomarker study on camrelizumab plus chemotherapy before surgery for lung cancer. Three cycles of the immune drug plus chemotherapy came first, then surgery to remove the tumor.

pmc-13289763: Editors and the publisher of OncoTargets and Therapy issued a 2026 retraction notice for a 2018 article on MFAP2 and gastric cancer by Wang and coauthors. The notice documents those overlaps in detail but adds no new findings, keeping its scope narrow.
pmc-13290063:
Christine M. Lovly and coauthors present a 2026 real-world study on HER2-mutant advanced lung cancer in the United States. pmc-13290763:

pmc-13291063:
Personal growth after the shock of illness is modeled in a 2026 survey study led by Zheyuan Xia, focused on patients with autoimmune diseases in Anhui Province, China. pmc-13291163: Rutvi Mistry and co-authors published a short correction in 2026 to a study on doped ceria sensors for acetone. The evidence here is just that brief correction notice. It states that an older version of three figures was printed by mistake. The note reprints those figures and their captions. No new findings are given, so the sensor results cannot be judged from this note alone.
pmc-13291263:
Building a research career inside a steel firm is the theme of a 2026 interview on additive manufacturing. The speaker works in process and product work at ArcelorMittal. She has watched its 3D printing activity grow for ten years. Her own path grew with that program.

pmc-13291563:
Off-label weight loss use of diabetes drugs carries hidden danger. Andrej Belančić and Bojan Jelaković warn of this trend in a 2026 commentary. GLP-1 drugs transformed diabetes and obesity care. Social fame now drives cosmetic use beyond labels.

The authors call this off-label zone a new danger area. Prescribers should stick to approved uses, they argue. Agent-specific safety watch must grow sharper. pmc-13291663:

Deep block proof still rests on sparse reports. Head-to-head trials are the next need.
pmc-13291863:
Barun Kumar and colleagues score whole-body inflammation against dental implant failure in a 2026 cohort study. Failures were split into early, within a year, and delayed.

High burden scores clustered in both failure groups far more than in successes. Each extra point on the score raised overall failure odds by about eighteen percent. pmc-13291963:
Xinyi Huang and colleagues untangle how an excited oxygen atom reacts with ethylene, in a 2026 kinetics study. The reaction matters in air chemistry, plasma combustion, and space ice models. Textbooks assumed the oxygen inserts straight into the molecule. Experiments plus theory here point to a subtler opening move. Weak van der Waals attraction between the partners forms a shallow dip before any bond breaks.

That dip creates a submerged peak on the energy path, slowing the reaction and bending its temperature behavior. It also demotes one attack route, on the carbon-hydrogen bond, to a minor channel. Addition to the carbon-carbon double bond dominates instead. Computed rates matched laboratory measurements closely across conditions. Hydrogen atom yields were measured and explained within the same picture. The authors argue that even feeble attractions can steer reaction pathways. Modelers of complex-forming reactions should not skip them.
pmc-13292263:
Samuel Friese and a large team test a 2026 feasibility idea: screening for arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy by listening to the heart's magnetic field. This inherited condition disturbs both heart mechanics and electrics, and diagnosis is tricky. Patient signals looked shrunken, with smaller loop dimensions than controls, most clearly a reduced area during the T wave and lower peak amplitude during the QRS complex. Age did not explain the gap in controls, and the ST segment showed no difference. pmc-13292563:
Godwin Pius Ohemu and co-authors address a 2026 message to Africa as Nigeria prepares to host the fifth Global High-Level Ministerial Conference on antimicrobial resistance in Abuja. The piece lays out seven priority areas for governments, communities, and health systems. Its charge: convert a diplomatic first into durable change at home.
pmc-13292663:
Fusun Ozer's team tests a 2026 dental adhesive tweak: mixing PVM/MA copolymer into three bonding systems to see whether dentin bonds last longer. Half of each group was sheared immediately; the rest endured 20,000 hot-cold cycles first.

pmc-13292763:

All piglets in the group died within 48 hours after birth, with no outward injury or major organ defects. Checks after death found bleeding inside the wall of the left ventricle in every piglet examined, without rupture of the heart. The authors suggest weak vessel walls from cloning and gene load may have failed under the blood flow shift at birth. The report flags a hidden cause of early death in such pigs.
pmc-13293563:
John Broughan leads a 2026 pilot study on taking vital signs just before primary care visits, rather than during them. Basic measures like pulse and blood pressure guide care, yet taking them eats into short appointment time.

Most patients called the step positive and helpful. The doctor rated it helpful in every visit checked and said it improved engagement and use of time. Staff themes echoed time saving and smoother visits.
pmc-13293763:
Wujing Cao and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a smart nanoparticle pill to carry a brain-protecting drug for ischemic stroke. Swallowed care is ideal for long use, yet gut walls, the blood-brain barrier, and poor brain retention block most drugs.

Uptake into blood reached 86.1% with no clear toxicity, a value the authors report. In rats with blocked brain arteries, the pill shrank damaged areas and calmed inflammation better than free drug.
pmc-13294063:
Melania Prete leads a 2026 systematic review on fibromyalgia among cancer patients. Widespread pain, fatigue, and poor sleep overlap heavily between the two conditions, and cancer drugs can trigger or worsen fibromyalgia-like symptoms. Searches of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus covered 2014 to 2024, with bias checked by standard tools and reporting by PRISMA rules.

Fibromyalgia did not seem to raise cancer risk, yet it amplified pain, raised symptom burden, lowered quality of life, and hurt treatment adherence. pmc-13294263:
Tuo Ji and coauthors screen a traditional herb for Alzheimer protection in a 2026 combined computer and cell study. pmc-13294363: Huijuan Dong and coauthors issued a 2026 author correction for their article on market share and material limits in power system change. Two figures and linked source data were faulty. Copper had not been split from other special materials in one chart. Traces in one panel of a second chart wrongly copied a twin panel. New figures and data now sit in the online texts, with the old ones kept as extra files. The notice covers figures and source data only.
pmc-13294463:
Kaili Fan leads a 2026 survey on why young nurses plan to quit. The lens is ward climate and work drive. A path model tested drive as the bridge from climate to quit plans.

All three scores linked with each other. Drive partly carried the climate effect. It explained 34.78% of spread in the reported model. A warm, humane climate thus keeps young nurses in part by keeping them keen at work. Bosses gain a lever beyond pay: daily culture that feeds energy and pride.
pmc-13294763:

Hospital patients with schizophrenia received accelerated high-frequency repetitive stimulation at one of the two times of day. Records came from the Third People's Hospital of Fuyang for late 2023 to mid 2025.

Both groups slept better and showed fewer symptoms at discharge than on admission. Morning treatment was linked with lower sleep-quality scores and longer night-time sleep than afternoon treatment, even after matched checks. Symptom and thinking scores did not differ by timing, while side effects were somewhat more common with morning sessions.
pmc-13294963:
Tugba Sardohan Koseoglu, Aykut Yalabik, and Hasan Koseoglu turn an ordinary pencil lead into a drug sensor, in a 2026 analytical study. pmc-13295063:
Asena Serap Karatutlu and colleagues compare a scarring-related protein in blood and saliva in kidney disease in a 2026 study. Blood decorin rose slightly with advancing stage, though not clearly enough to count as a firm pattern. Saliva levels were clearly lower in patients than in healthy volunteers and drifted down across stages, making saliva a candidate worth larger, longer studies.
pmc-13295563:
Abuzar Khan and colleagues build a deep learning system that turns workplace survey answers into a calibrated mental health risk score, in a 2026 study. pmc-13296063:
Jingyuan Zhang and co-authors test three paths from screen time to well-being among Chinese youth, in a 2026 study. Most programs aim at feelings and habits in the single user. pmc-13296163:
Laura Martínez-Martínez and co-authors profile, in 2026, the Murciana chicken, an endangered native breed from southeastern Spain now being recovered. They describe its population trend, body features and laying and growth performance for low-input farming.

Numbers have risen in recent years, suggesting recovery efforts are working. The birds show moderate growth, size and egg output suited to extensive systems rather than intensive sheds. The authors present the breed as a useful local genetic resource worth conserving. Its hardiness and fit with sustainable farming add to the case for continued protection.
pmc-13296463:
Takahisa Yamaguchi and co-authors ask whether simple scan measurements can predict chemotherapy success in oesophageal cancer, in a 2026 study. pmc-13296863:
Hoejin Jung and colleagues review thermal designs borrowed from marine invertebrates in a 2026 article. Shells, porous skeletons, and adaptive surfaces of sea creatures manage heat in varied ways. The review gathered studies that tied such features to measured thermal performance.

Long-term survival under pressure, salt, and temperature swings also needs proof.
pmc-13297163:

pmc-13297363:
Tom Trapphoff and colleagues review whether freezing early embryos can alter the chemical marks that steer gene use, in a 2026 article. pmc-13297463:
LinShu Liu and colleagues test how PFOA, a long-lived industrial chemical, reshapes gut microbes and, through them, the gut lining, in a 2026 study. pmc-13298063:
Maryam N. ALNasser and Wayne G. Carter review plant compounds that may block NMDA receptors, in a 2026 systematic review. pmc-13298263:

pmc-13299263:
Dimitri Trubetskoy and colleagues test whether skin can serve as an entry point for the coronavirus behind COVID-19, in a 2026 laboratory study. The authors call skin a possible but likely limited interface.
pmc-13299663:

pmc-13300463:

pmc-13300563:

pmc-13300763:

pmc-13300963:
Jenny Lue Solomon and co-authors review B cells and their depletion across autoimmunity and atherosclerosis in a 2026 article. pmc-13301563:

The morning block from eight to noon ran best, at under half a percent. The early block stayed the only independently risky window after regression adjustment. pmc-13301663:

pmc-13301763:

About a third died during roughly four and a half years of follow-up, and those with high scores fared notably worse. The score stayed predictive after adjustment, while rival inflammation indexes did not. Clinicians could use this cheap blood-based score to flag patients needing closer follow-up.
pmc-13302063:

Products were coded across several dimensions, and the AI group sat for structured interviews.

They also named their own limits more often and ran longer as extended analogies. Interviews showed trainees used the tools chiefly for ideas, images, and creative wandering rather than facts, a pattern the author reads as support for representational thinking.
pmc-13302363:
Míriam Mayal Etreros and colleagues present, in a 2026 case report, a clot forming on a mechanical heart valve during pregnancy. Her clot appeared after switching from warfarin to injected heparin, a common but risky change in pregnancy.

Scans showed partial improvement and the pregnancy went on without her condition worsening. Delivery used a planned caesarean designed to limit strain on the heart, producing a stable early baby. After birth she recovered well and later had the mechanical valve replaced, by choice, with a tissue valve.
pmc-13303563:

pmc-13304063:
