pmc-13305663:
George Gyader and co-authors examined retirement readiness among council staff in Ghana's Upper West Region in a 2026 qualitative case study. They asked younger and mid-career workers how they thought about, planned for, and felt prepared for life after service.

Interviews covered 33 employees aged 25 to 45 across five departments and all 11 local assemblies. Awareness was high yet planning was often delayed, with hopes centred on money security, owning a home, health care and family time. Land buying beat bank products because trust in banks had faded, and secrecy about savings reflected local social pressures.
pmc-13306163:
Jiabao Cui and colleagues test patchouli oil against acne-linked germs and inflammation in a 2026 lab study. Lab analysis found alpha-guaiene, patchouli alcohol, and alpha-bulnesene as leading parts of the oil. Germs tested were Cutibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus epidermidis, plus two inflamed cell models.

The oil stopped germ growth at a modest dose and damaged germ membranes, causing cell contents to leak. In both cell models, it cut release of inflammatory signals such as tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-6. Treated skin cells were also shielded from damage and from excess growth. The authors conclude the oil attacks acne through two routes at once, germ-killing and calming. They propose it as a natural option for acne products.
pmc-13307163:
Xingchuan Huang found a phosphatase that props up a plant immune receptor in a 2026 Arabidopsis study. Protein Phosphatase 5 is widespread in animals, yet its plant role was unknown before this work on the receptor SUMM2.

Plants lacking PP5 lost the self-attack symptoms caused when a kinase chain guarding SUMM2 breaks down. Lab binding tests showed SUMM2 touching both PP5 and the chaperone HSP90, and receptor levels fell without PP5 in reported checks. The authors argue PP5 helps the chaperone complex keep SUMM2 stocked for defence. The find adds a new part to the known guard chain for this key immune switch.
pmc-13307563:
Waresi Tuersong and co-authors survey in 2026 drug resistance in Haemonchus contortus, a gut worm that harms sheep, in two pastoral counties of Yili, Xinjiang. They checked 150 adult male worms for three gene changes tied to benzimidazole resistance in the beta tubulin gene.

One change, F167Y, never appeared in any worm they tested during the survey. A second change, E198A, dominated both sites, with resistant gene shares of 64.7 percent and 52.7 percent at the two places. A third change varied by place and often came paired with E198A in Teksi county. The authors warn that benzimidazole drugs no longer work well there.
pmc-13307663:
Basílio Felizardo Lima Neto and co-authors study in 2026 blood donors in the dry inland region of Brazil for Toxoplasma gondii infection, and what it means for transfusion safety. They tested 646 donors in Ceará and Paraíba with antibody checks, gene based tests, and surveys on daily habits.

Past infection was common, as 281 of the 646 donors carried IgG antibodies in their blood samples. Fresh infection signs were rare, and no donor tested positive on the gene based check used here. Older age raised the odds of past infection, while careful salad washing lowered them in the final model. Low fresh infection points to low risk for people who receive blood there.
pmc-13308863:
Mihail Basa and co-authors review in 2026 hospital cases of pertussis, or whooping cough, in children in Serbia from 2015 to 2025, hunting signs of severe disease. Their set held 107 children with lab confirmed illness at a top tier centre, and models weighed who needed intensive care, breathing machines, or died.

Thirteen children needed intensive care, and five died, all of them unvaccinated babies under two months old in this set. Born early status strongly foresaw intensive care and machine need, and high white cell signs also tracked with severity. Virus co infection, found in 22.4 percent, tracked with worse ends. Mother shots in pregnancy could shield the youngest.
pmc-13308963:
Yuka Oda and colleagues describe in 2026 a thirty-nine-year-old woman whose heart attack came from a spontaneous tear inside a coronary artery, followed by artery spasm attacks. Emergency imaging showed a dissection blocking the main front artery of the heart. A stent restored flow at the worst point.

New chest pain with shifting heart tracing changes followed, and imaging showed diffuse narrowing in the right artery that relaxed on its own, marking spasm. Seventeen days later, the original dissection had worsened toward the artery's origin, and a fresh dissection appeared in the second artery. Another stent procedure stabilised her course. The authors suspect repeated spasm drove the progression and recurrence. Checking for spasm alongside dissection, they argue, belongs in managing such patients.
pmc-13309563: Ze Wang is first named on a 2026 correction notice in Scientific Reports for a study of hormone therapy in advanced prostate cancer. Corrected here is Figure 3, whose risk analysis, prediction chart, and survival curves were misrepresented during revision. The notice supplies the corrected figure and captions, which link deep testosterone reduction in the first treatment year to later cancer progression risk. No new patients or experiments are added; the item exists solely to replace the faulty figure so the study record reads correctly.
pmc-13310663:
Bo Wei and co-authors mine layered data for drug targets in chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps in a 2026 study. The disease is common, stubborn, and driven by tangled inflammation. Single data layers miss much of that tangle, so gene, cell, and genetics layers were fused.

Public cell and tissue data sets yielded 4,460 changed genes and 732 hub genes, while genetic causal screening added 1,673 disease-linked genes in the pipeline. Crossing those lists with druggable genes left 43 candidates. Learning models settled on three key genes: IL4R and IMPA2 raised in disease, PRR4 lowered. Immune cell mixes shifted as well, and 26 candidate drugs were predicted, with docking checks supporting several. Dish tests backed the gene findings.
pmc-13310963:
Natan Gottari and colleagues study tail loss in two wall lizards across Italian cities in a 2026 field study. Lizards shed tails to escape predators, so tail loss rates may mirror attack pressure. How urban land cover shapes that pressure, and at what scale, was unclear.

Field teams checked 386 lizards at 33 sites in four metro areas along a city gradient. Two thirds showed past tail loss, with higher rates in one species and in larger animals. Forest cover within 50 m of each capture site best foretold loss, with less forest tied to more loss. Wider scales, predator counts, and cat colony distance added little.
pmc-13311163:
Rena I Kosti, Ioanna Panagiota Kalafati, and Matina Kouvari reframe in 2026 the traditional Mediterranean lifestyle as more than a menu, grounding their essay in the study of food culture. UNESCO listed the Mediterranean diet as cultural heritage about fifteen years ago, covering a whole way of living. The authors name three pillars holding that way of life together.

Cheerful frugality comes first: modest eating aligned with natural rhythms, felt as contentment rather than want. Belongingness follows, the social closeness built around shared food and the group. Purpose in life, fed partly by faith life, rounds out the triad. Working as one, the pillars grow dispositional mindfulness, which the authors cast as the means steering people toward moderation. Greek ideals of self-supply and self-control structure their roadmap to moderation. Health campaigns, they argue, should copy the lifestyle's mind, not only its foods.
pmc-13311363:
Arjun Chakraborty and co-authors report their 2026 modeling study on finding surgical site infections in records without hand review. Chart checks by staff are slow and costly, yet these infections harm many patients each year.

The data held about 30,000 surgical cases from two Seattle-area hospitals. Each case joined procedure details, lab values, drug records, and notes from a week before to 90 days after surgery. Many machine learning methods, including newer language and deep learning tools, were trained to flag infections. The study weighs whether such a system beats older approaches and could make infection watching far cheaper.
pmc-13311663:
Bachera Aktar and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, who actually governs public health services inside the informal settlements of Dhaka. Formal state structures are largely absent there. Services instead emerge from shifting cooperation among officials, elected representatives, local leaders, private providers, and residents. The team drew on multi-method fieldwork using methods that involve residents as partners, carried out between 2021 and 2023 in two settlements.

From that material the authors build a framework they call multi-layered hybrid governance, describing arrangements that are fragile yet resilient at once. Hybrid governance can keep services running where the state cannot, and in that sense it works as a form of local resilience. Yet it can also deepen unfairness, favoring residents with political connections or strong social networks. The paper urges policymakers to treat these informal arrangements as real governance worth engaging with, not as gaps to ignore.
pmc-13311963:
Mathilde Mussmann von Arenstorff and co-authors report a 2025 case series on trabeculotomy surgery for children whose eye pressure rose from steroid treatment. When maximal drops fail, surgery must protect sight.

The series covered 13 eyes of eight patients aged 7 to 17 treated in Copenhagen from 2018 to 2022, followed for two years. Mean pressure fell from 29.7 mm Hg before surgery to 15.1 mm Hg at 24 months, staying under 16 at every check in this series. All eyes came off pressure drops, and no complications occurred. Pressure stayed controlled even though steroids continued for the underlying illnesses.
pmc-13312363:
Isabel Galriça Neto writes a 2026 theoretical and reflective article on what gives palliative care its distinct identity as a field. Rather than a specialty of disease-directed treatment, palliative care is presented as a shift of medicine's center. The shift runs from disease to person, from cure to care, and from length of life to its quality and meaning.

The article builds on Cicely Saunders's concept of total pain and on international consensus documents. Those documents consolidated the field's pillars: holistic interdisciplinary care, relief of suffering in all its dimensions, an ethical frame of dignity and proportionality, and support for families through bereavement. Neto examines how everyday patterns of interaction among patients, families, and professionals express that identity in practice. She treats those relational patterns as markers by which the field can recognize and teach itself.
pmc-13312463:
Jun Liu and co-authors describe, in a 2026 paper, a pollen-shell drug carrier designed to release its cargo precisely in the inflamed colon. Ulcerative colitis treatment suffers when drugs release too early, leave too fast, or enter cells poorly. Their carrier uses chrysanthemum sporopollenin microcapsules, whose walls contract in acid and expand in alkali, coated with a chitosan-butyrate layer that behaves the opposite way, gelling in acid and shrinking in alkali.

Together the layers form a gate that stays shut in stomach fluid and opens in intestinal fluid. The spiny shell sticks to the gut lining, butyrate both targets and calms inflamed tissue, and the drug mesalazine rides inside fat bubbles that improve its uptake. Tests showed the expected pH-triggered release, stronger gut adhesion, and combined anti-inflammatory action. The authors offer the dual-gating idea as a general design for oral carriers bound for the colon.
pmc-13313263:
Juan Yang and colleagues map gene changes in pig placenta cells hit by Japanese encephalitis virus in a 2026 study. The mosquito-borne virus uses pigs as its main host for growth. It can linger in the placenta of pregnant sows and cause major breeding losses, yet the cell response there was poorly known.

Working with porcine trophectoderm cells, the team first refined the list of pig microRNAs by small RNA sequencing, adding hundreds of new ones. They confirmed the virus infects these cells well and harms them badly. Paired gene and microRNA reads then showed more than 1000 changes during infection, counted in the report, with microRNAs at the center of control over immune genes. The work lays out targets that might limit virus harm in pig breeding.
pmc-13314263:
Marwa Saleem Hajeel and Monyer Abdulamier Abd Alfatlawi characterize, in a 2026 molecular study, the hydatid cyst parasite Echinococcus granulosus in cattle slaughtered in Al-Diwaniyah, Iraq. The zoonotic tapeworm cycles between dogs and livestock and burdens animal production and human health. Inspecting 150 cattle at an abattoir between January and June 2024, the team found fertile cysts in thirty animals. They sequenced four genetic markers in ten isolates and built family trees against references.

Thirty cattle, 20.0 percent of those inspected, carried cysts. All four markers amplified in every isolate tested. Sequences matched worldwide references closely, with the housekeeping marker matching least tightly at a mean of 96.95 percent. The trees placed the Iraqi isolates inside the sheep-strain complex, genotypes G1 to G3, with traces of local variation. The authors say the pattern fits dog-driven transmission with regional lineages, and offer the data as a baseline for One Health control in Iraq.
pmc-13314863:
Muhinat B. Bello and colleagues audit reform programs in Nigerian prisons in a 2026 study. They checked whether medium-security facilities in Kwara State have schooling and trade training that work in practice, not just on paper.

Using a checklist across three custodial centers, the team logged what rehabilitation resources and activities could be seen on site. The study leans on social learning theory from Bandura in 1977, as cited, which holds that inmates learn by watching prosocial models. Where such models are thin, old habits persist and reoffending follows. A share of 67 percent of the centers lacked a working education program by the figures given, and all centers shared deep gaps, as the authors report. The audit names fixes for crowded, underfunded prisons.
pmc-13315063:
Pradeep Venkatesh reviews tyrosine kinase blockers as a future path for retinal disease, in their 2026 paper. Shots against VEGF have saved sight in wet macular degeneration and diabetic macular edema over two decades, yet they cost much, carry risk, and must repeat forever to hold gains.

Dual-path drugs and slow-release implants ease the load but fall short of ideal, the author argues. Kinase blockers could cut the shot burden by shutting several growth signals at their root. The review walks through what protein kinases are, how their receptors fire, and what signals follow, then weighs the role of blockade in eye care. The goal is lasting control of blinding disease with fewer needle visits.
pmc-13315763:
Elena Ammendola and colleagues test, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, whether a simple sweat-response test can stand in for skin biopsy in fibromyalgia. Fibromyalgia involves small-fibre pathology and autonomic dysfunction, and the sympathetic skin response is easily obtained in clinic as an autonomic marker. The team studied 393 patients who underwent thigh and ankle skin biopsy, palm and sole skin-response testing, and clinical evaluation.

The response was similarly absent at hand and foot whether biopsy results were normal or abnormal. Hand amplitude was reduced with denervation, and foot latency was prolonged with abnormal biopsy, but overall the response predicted biopsy results poorly, with an r-squared of 0.04. Foot latency and nerve fibre density tracked with associated-symptom scores, and foot amplitude tracked inversely with anxiety, depression, and fatigue. The authors conclude the two tests capture different aspects of the disease and complement rather than replace each other.
pmc-13315963:
Armess Prince Gynth Sossou and Masato Yayota tracked in 2026 how molasses changes rumen fermentation of a Guinea grass and cowpea silage mix. Tropical grasses hold little soluble sugar, which hampers silage making, so molasses is added as a fermentable boost, and the team followed metabolites over time in lab fermentation.

Molasses lowered effective protein breakdown from 53.7 percent to 47.6 percent. Most rumen metabolites built up within the first four hours, while indole-3-acetate fell sharply under molasses. Fat breakdown was moderated, and carbohydrate and antioxidant linked responses were promoted, reshaping the fermentation profile.
pmc-13316163:
Shiyao Bai and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2026 why macrophages in asthma fail to clear material properly, merging human, animal, and cell evidence. Macrophages normally engulf germs and debris, and faults in that job may drive airway disease, but the mechanisms were scattered across study types.

Following PRISMA rules, searches to March 2026 gathered 37 studies from 1982 to 2025. Fault patterns depended on asthma type, what the cells had to swallow, and the local environment. Mechanisms sorted into eight groups, forming a layered framework that links molecular faults to cell behavior and disease features.
pmc-13316663:
Simona Abou Tayeh and Nakhle Ayoub report, in 2026, sustained remission in a seven-year-old girl with a blistering skin disease called epidermolysis bullosa simplex. Her skin blistered from infancy after minor friction, mainly on the soles and in the nappy area, and walking became difficult in warm weather. No cure exists for the condition.

Whole exome sequencing found a harmful change in the KRT14 gene, which helps hold skin cells together, confirming the diagnosis. At age seven she began low-dose oral isotretinoin taken every five days. Blistering then fell markedly, with 120 days free of new blisters at first report and about 225 days by revision. The timing suggests benefit beyond the natural course, the authors argue.
pmc-13316763:
Shangyong Zuo and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, oral nanozymes built to treat inflammatory bowel disease while also lighting it up on scans. These enzyme-like particles can mop up harmful oxygen radicals in the gut wall, where inflammation, oxidation, and barrier damage feed each other.

The review sorts designs into single-signal approaches, guided by CT or by light and sound imaging, and combined approaches that merge structure and function on one platform. Swallowed particles must survive the gut, prove their enzyme action, and stay safe long term, all open problems the authors flag. Their design principles aim at particles that both heal and report, sharpening early testing in animals.
pmc-13317763:
Dengxiong Li and his team outline, in 2026, a vision of surgery reshaped by four technology families working together. Operations have moved from open cuts to keyhole and robotic techniques, with better outcomes. The authors argue that anatomy knowledge and manual skill alone now limit further progress, while cost, training, safety and global gaps persist.

Smart software can guide planning and steering. Gene tools support treatment matched to each patient's biology. Bioengineering offers engineered tissues and regrowth options, and planned rehabilitation rounds out recovery. Together, these tools let surgeons handle complex cases with more precision and tailor care to each person. The review surveys evidence for each strand and considers how joining them might reshape daily surgical practice.
pmc-13318363:
Eren and colleagues measure the strain on family caregivers of dying patients with pressure injuries in this 2026 study. Pressure injuries are painful wounds from lying in one position, common in palliative care. Unpaid relatives provide much of the daily care. The team surveyed caregivers at a state hospital using a burden interview and a social support scale.

The study covered 138 caregivers, who reported a high level of burden overall. Burden ran higher for caregivers with lower income, those who found care tasks difficult, and those whose family and social life suffered. Feeling well supported by others went with lower burden, suggesting support protects caregivers. Eren argues that services for these patients should treat caregiver support as essential, not optional.
pmc-13318663:
Jiongrui Cao and co-authors offer a 2026 pharmacovigilance analysis of two cancer immunotherapy drugs. They compare ipilimumab plus nivolumab against nivolumab alone in lung cancer. The focus is severe kidney and pancreas side effects. Reports came from the United States FDA adverse event database.

The dataset covered reports from early 2004 to mid 2025, totalling 2,292 reports. Combination therapy showed strong signals for glomerular kidney injury. Nephrotic syndrome carried a reporting odds ratio of 37.25 in their analysis. Pancreatic harm also signalled strongly for the combination. Median onset was 73 days for kidney events and 84 days for pancreas events in that group. The authors urge closer organ monitoring than standard checks provide.
pmc-13318863:
Karthikeyan Thirugnanam and co-authors report a 2026 study of a blood protein as an early warning marker for postpartum haemorrhage. Heavy bleeding after birth is a leading cause of maternal harm and death. Prediction today rests on clinical judgement, which can be late. The team reasoned that proteins from vessel-lining cilia might signal risk.

Four candidate proteins were measured by blotting and immunoassay. One, PDGF-BB, differed consistently across both methods. Higher levels linked independently to lower bleeding risk. The adjusted odds ratio was 0.62 in their model, suggesting protection. A threshold of 11.5 pg/mL separated risk groups with strong discrimination in their analysis. The authors call for prospective studies to confirm timing, cause, and diagnostic value.
pmc-13318963:
Akua A. Obeng and colleagues offer a 2026 evolutionary genomics perspective on preterm birth and pregnancy. Birth timing varies widely across species, shaped by long change over time. Preterm birth can follow infection, anatomy, injury, age, or multiple pregnancy. Each cause touches partly separate gene networks.

Starting from about 1,500 pregnancy-related genes, the authors hunted for recent shifts. Many relevant genes show lineage- or group-specific shifts. They include progesterone signalling, innate immunity, and placenta regulation genes. DNA sites are flagged where CRISPR disruption would likely alter labour or birth. Examples sit in hormone receptors and placenta-only genes such as LGALS13. The framework separates conserved, risky targets from flexible ones for safer future studies.
pmc-13319863:
Anjana Giri and co-authors study a common plastic softener chemical in medaka fish in a 2026 article on male fertility across generations. The chemical can disrupt hormone signals, and the male hormone receiver gene helps sperm form and work. Whether chemical harm marks that gene in sperm and passes the mark to later young was the core question.

Fish exposed to the chemical showed lower fertility in the first group and again two generations later, with changed testis shape in both. Chemical marks on the gene rose in sperm of the first group and stayed high in later groups, while gene voice fell in body cells. The marks track with lasting harm, a warning for hormone disrupting chemicals at large.
pmc-13320463:
Yuqing Zhang and co-workers report in 2026 on a new mouth rinse built for people who wear braces or other fixed dental gear. Braces make teeth hard to clean, so gum disease, decay, and loss of minerals from enamel are common risks. The rinse mixes a strong germ-killing compound called DMAHDM with an extract from honeysuckle flowers.

Lab tests showed the mix lowered signals that drive swelling, cut bone loss near teeth, and helped keep mouth germs in better balance. It also slowed mineral loss, kept calcium and hardness in enamel, and did not harm brace parts after long contact. Safety checks over 60 days supported further study as a daily aid for brace wearers.
pmc-13320563:
Chalida Sri-in and colleagues survey, in 2026, mosquitoes and their viruses across Khao Yai National Park in Thailand, a World Heritage site of forested mountains. Collections ran monthly for two years at eight sites spanning a wide altitude range. Identifying which species live where helps judge disease risk for visitors and nearby communities.

Just over a thousand mosquitoes were gathered, representing thirty-six species in five genera, with Culex the most varied group. Virus testing found Japanese encephalitis virus and Tembusu virus in one Culex species, and dengue virus in Aedes aegypti. Higher sites held simpler mosquito communities, though the altitude pattern was not perfectly steady. Temperature, humidity and rainfall varied alongside mosquito numbers. The authors offer the dataset as a baseline for surveillance.
pmc-13322863:
Nicola Sariye Pollmann leads a case report in 2026 on a severe clotting disorder arising after liver transplant. The patient, who had autoimmune hepatitis, developed complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy, with anaemia, small-vessel clots and organ strain in the period after surgery.

Care began with total plasma exchange, followed soon after by ravulizumab, a drug that blocks complement factor C5. Kidney function then improved enough for dialysis to stop, and liver function also got better, with benefit still present six months after treatment began. Gene tests found variants in CFHR5 and in complement component C6, the latter classed as of uncertain meaning. The authors stress the mixed causes behind such cases.
pmc-13322963:
April Chiu and a Mayo Clinic team introduce, in 2026, an AI pipeline that speeds detection of leftover leukaemia cells after treatment. Flow cytometry can find measurable residual disease in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, but expert manual analysis is slow and scarce. Missing rare abnormal cells risks false comfort.

Their system cleans raw cytometry files on its own, clusters cells, squeezes dimensions, flags anomalies against healthy controls and downsamples while preserving rare events. A neural network trained on expert-defined normal patterns then does the gating itself. Files from positive and negative cases processed in the cloud matched expert review almost exactly. File size and cell counts fell sharply, and analysis time dropped from nine minutes to under one minute per case. An aberrancy score split leukaemia from background cells with excellent accuracy.
pmc-13323363:
Barbara Buchberger and co-authors trace how infection hygiene became institutionalised in Germany, in a 2026 historical article written in German. Structured infection prevention feels settled today, yet dedicated bodies, evidence-based rules and cross-sector teamwork emerged only through long development and repeated health crises.

Industrial growth and crowded cities in the late 1800s strained water and sewage systems and sparked severe outbreaks. Air and soil pollution pressed after the 1920s, and hospital-acquired infections took focus after 1950. A royal testing institute for water supply and sewage in 1901 marked a key step. Today the Robert Koch Institute and its KRINKO commission carry the legal mandate under the national infection protection act.
pmc-13323563:
Masahiro Hada and colleagues studied patients whose chest pain comes from coronary arteries that look open on angiography, a condition known as angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries. Their 2026 report draws on a prospective, multicenter Japanese registry, the J-CMD, in which patients took invasive tests with acetylcholine provocation and flow reserve measurement. The goal was to sort these patients into endotypes, meaning the distinct vessel faults behind their symptoms.

Epicardial vasospasm, a cramp of a large heart artery, proved most common at 44.2%, followed by microvascular spasm at 16.5%, combined disease at 8.7%, and isolated microvascular dysfunction at 5.0%. Overlap was frequent, and combined disease appeared more often in women than in men. The authors argue that full invasive testing matters because the fault pattern differs by sex and age, and treatment should follow the precise diagnosis rather than a single label.
pmc-13324663:
Takumi Kodama and colleagues build CT-based models that estimate when lung cancer will return after focused radiation, in a 2026 study. Standard radiomics predicts whether relapse happens but ignores the gap between scan traits and each patient timing.

The cohort held 143 patients with stage I to II non-small cell lung cancer treated with stereotactic ablative radiotherapy. For patients whose follow-up ended early, the team estimated virtual return times with a Bayesian method. Regression models then linked scan features to those times. Best models scored area under the curve values of 0.926 and 0.763 for one-year relapse in internal and external tests. Direct timing estimates may sharpen early risk calls before treatment starts.
pmc-13325163:
Jinxiao Yang and colleagues measure how high-rank coal soaks up carbon dioxide in a 2026 storage study. Burying CO2 in coal seams could serve climate goals, but capacity must be predicted before injection.

Anthracite from the south Qinshui basin was tested across pressure, temperature, and water levels. Pressure raised uptake until near the supercritical point, while heat and water both cut it. A micropore filling model, the D-A model, fit the data best and anchored a capacity forecast. Most stored gas sits adsorbed in the coal, though the free share grows with burial depth. Dissolved share falls with depth instead. The forecast splits storage by state and depth.
pmc-13325463:
Carmen Díaz-López and co-authors build a health-first framework for indoor air in child care and schools in a 2026 review. Children aged 0 to 12 spend long, busy hours in crowded rooms where air risks differ from adult workplaces.

Following PRISMA rules, searches across three databases from 2018 to 2025 yielded 26 studies for synthesis. Carbon dioxide breaches were common where ventilation relied on people opening windows. Five drivers shaped exposure, from crowding and cleaning to season and outdoor pollution. The authors convert the evidence into a three-level checkable pathway aligned with European and United States standards, using in-use measures such as peak levels and time out of range.
pmc-13326263:
Tesfatsiyon Ergando and colleagues report the first cases combining focal pulsed field ablation with Watchman FLX Pro left atrial appendage occlusion. Their 2026 paper describes two patients who underwent concomitant ablation with the Sphere-9 catheter and appendage occlusion, a pairing increasingly considered for patients at high risk of both clots and bleeding. Emerging data suggest pulsed field ablation raises peridevice leak rates, making device sizing after ablation a live question.

Post-ablation appendage changes were managed with tailored upsizing in one case and standard sizing in the other. At six months, both patients held sinus rhythm on antiplatelet therapy with no clot or bleeding events, and cardiac CT confirmed well-seated devices with peridevice leak of 2 mm or less. The authors present the cases as proof that the combination can work with careful sizing, while noting that two cases cannot settle the optimal strategy and larger experience must follow.
pmc-13327863:
Shuna Shi and co-authors compare nerve disease patients with and without connective tissue antibodies in a 2026 cohort study. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord, and many patients also carry antibodies tied to connective tissue disease. The study followed 205 patients whose disease was confirmed by aquaporin-4 antibodies.

Just over half, 108 patients or 52.7 percent, carried the extra antibodies, and that group showed higher lymphocyte counts, higher spinal fluid white cell counts, and more signs of antibody making inside the spinal fluid at first attack. Lesion sites and lengths looked alike at onset, and patients were followed for 18 months for relapse timing and disability. The extra antibodies may mark a more inflamed form of the disease.
pmc-13328263:
Nathan Eisenstadt and colleagues ask what keeps men attending a voluntary domestic abuse program in a 2026 study. Such programs can cut repeat abuse, but dropout blunts both their effect and its measurement, and most prior work covers court-ordered groups. The team analyzed attendance at REPROVIDE, a voluntary 23-week program for men in relationships with women.

More pre-group assessment sessions, older age, self-referral, employment, and higher income all went with attending more sessions, as did greater depression severity and stronger reflective functioning on their measures. Refusing to state income, court or social care involvement, and referral by services went with fewer sessions. Front-loading assessment contact may be a simple lever for holding participants.
pmc-13328363:
Natalie Mlcuchova and co-authors review gene variants that steer metformin handling in Europeans in a 2026 narrative review. Response to the diabetes drug varies between people, partly by genes for the transporters that move it through gut, liver, and kidney. Searches of a pharmacogenomics database and the literature framed the summary.

Seven transporter genes carrying twelve common variants were identified. They span the OCT and MATE families plus the glucose carrier GLUT2. In total, 63 studies fed the discussion of benefit and side effects per variant. Study designs and reporting varied so widely that the authors propose a shared framework for future work. Testing the full variant set together could one day tune metformin use to each patient.
pmc-13328463:
Xinlan Zhao and co-authors review gut microbes as a treatment target in sepsis organ failure in a 2026 article. Sepsis still kills many patients, and its variety defeats single treatments. Gut bacteria escaping the bowel wall feed the fire: runaway inflammation and the antibiotics themselves loosen the barrier, letting microbes and their products reach organs.

Shifted metabolite output and immune confusion follow, driving further organ damage in a loop the authors map from the literature. Interrupting that traffic, by guarding the barrier, reshaping the microbe mix, or blocking harmful products, offers fresh targets beside standard antibiotics and support care. The gut may be sepsis care's most underused lever, they argue.
pmc-13329863:
Nikita Shiliaev and colleagues present a new way to watch protein turnover inside living neurons in a 2026 study. The method, called ARGO, uses a built-in colour ratio signal to show and count protein replacement with fine detail. It is low cost, flexible, and suited to animals whose genes can be edited with ease.

The team tracked a synaptic vesicle protein, SNG-1, in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Turnover speed was steady within one neuron but differed between neuron types. Each contact point held two separate protein pools that did not mix. In a mutant with a faulty ubiquitin enzyme, turnover slowed even though total protein stayed normal. The tool may clarify how synapses keep their protein supply in balance.
pmc-13333163:
Paige Gurizzian and colleagues map 2026 gut immune-cell findings in a case series plus literature review. Gut histiocytosis is an uncommon, varied finding that may reflect reactive, infectious, medication-related, or tumor processes. Because lesions are often found by chance on biopsy, their true frequency, cause spectrum, and best diagnostic approach remain poorly defined. The team studied adult patients at the Cleveland Clinic Foundation with immune-cell involvement of the gut found on tissue specimens from 2007 through 2022.

A literature review of adult cases published on PubMed from 2002 through 2022 placed the clinic cohort alongside published cases. Extracted data covered patient mix, presenting symptoms, scope indications, anatomic spread, scope findings, linked conditions, and staining and gene results. The series helps pathologists and gastroenterologists sort incidental histiocytic findings by likely cause. It also maps when further workup is warranted and when watchful follow-up suffices.
pmc-13333363:
Sajid Kadir and colleagues propose a bedside ultrasound routine in 2026 for watching the right side of the heart struggle after lung transplantation. Right ventricular failure is a frequent early problem, worsened when the new lungs resist blood flow. Yet chest ultrasound views are poor after the wide chest incision, and pressure catheters come out within days.

Their protocol adds Doppler checks of the common femoral vein in the groin. There, a backed-up right heart sends abnormal pulsing flow that any clinician trained in vein access can record. They illustrate it with a 77-year-old recipient who had right heart weakness and graft trouble bad enough to need ECMO support. His vein waveforms were markedly abnormal in step with invasive signs of congestion, then normalized as his pressures recovered, ECMO was removed, and he improved. The authors suggest the groin vein check as a practical add-on for tracking.
pmc-13333463:
Huan Zhang and colleagues compare the kidney risks of three last-resort antibiotics in a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis. Polymyxin B, colistin sulfate, and colistimethate sodium anchor treatment of drug-resistant Gram-negative infections, yet each can injure the kidneys, and head-to-head evidence has been thin.

Searching six databases through April 2026, the team combined direct and indirect evidence across observational cohorts. Against colistin sulfate, colistimethate sodium carried higher odds of kidney toxicity, tripled in the network estimate at an odds ratio of 3.65, while polymyxin B showed no clear difference from colistin sulfate in the network but fared worse in direct comparisons. Unexpectedly, colistimethate sodium patients showed lower 28-day death estimates than the other two groups, with no differences in bacterial clearance or hospital stay. Because every included study was observational, the authors label the renal ranking provisional and call for prospective trials before practice shifts.
pmc-13335463:
Chunbo Xie and co-authors traced how sperm build their tails in a 2026 genetics study centered on the kinesin KIF6. Late in sperm development, gene transcription shuts down, so how flagellar parts arrive on schedule was a puzzle.

Screening kinesin genes in men with immotile sperm found two harmful homozygous KIF6 variants in unrelated patients, and mice carrying matching mutations reproduced the infertility. In mutant testes, most messenger RNAs stayed normal while proteins for the axoneme and energy metabolism dropped. The team showed KIF6 partners with the RNA-binding proteins FMRP and FXR1 to form transport complexes that ferry the needed transcripts, including those for DNALI1 and HK1. Broken transport strands the building instructions, leaving sperm unable to swim.
pmc-13336063:
Xinlong Li and colleagues present 2026 reaching high-density and stress-tough maize breeding via seed-stock new ideas. As a global crop, maize is central to meeting this demand. Raising planting density has long been seen as a good way to lift maize output in most growing regions.

In this view, the authors propose to raise planting density by tuning plant shape and weighing group-level and single-plant advantage. They also raise single-plant output by tuning yield parts, ideal ear shape, and boosting light-capture power. Gene stacking has been proposed to boost stress toughness, together with strengthening lodging toughness, and moving flower opening earlier in the day to escape heat stress. Also, raising nutrient use power can reduce fertilizer need, while increased light-heat tolerance can broaden eco range.
pmc-13336363:
Sibin Wang and co-authors looked at perovskite-based X-ray detectors on the road from lab materials to hospital imaging in a 2026 article. Metal halide perovskites absorb X-rays strongly, shrug off defects, and process at low temperature, making them attractive and cheap detector candidates.

The authors insist hospital readiness takes more than sensitivity records. A working medical detector must also deliver on spatial resolution, noise spectra, detective quantum efficiency, dynamic range, pixel uniformity, lag and ghosting, radiation hardness, readout compatibility, and safety. The review first uses standard detector materials to set those hospital requirements, then audits perovskite progress against them. The gap analysis tells materials researchers exactly which building problems stand between promising crystals and hospital scanners.
pmc-13336463:
Jiaxin Hao and co-authors charted how dengue fever enters China through its southwestern border in a 2026 epidemiological study. Yunnan Province is the country's main gateway for imported dengue, and knowing the routes sharpens prevention.

From 2012 to 2023 the region reported 6,205 imported cases, about 20.2 percent of its dengue burden in the study's accounting. Myanmar supplied 86.6 percent, then Laos and Cambodia. A counterfactual model estimated what COVID-era border closures prevented: predicted cases ran roughly 16 to 315 times the observed counts during 2020 to 2022, then 2023 overshot predictions by 45.0 percent as travel rebounded. Social network analysis mapped three transmission groupings. The patterns show border health policy rides on cross-border mobility itself.
pmc-13336563:
Huanpeng Chen and colleagues present a 2026 cancer study on making CAR-T cell therapy work against solid tumors. Engineered T cells often fail to enter such tumors, fade quickly, or miss changed targets. The team paired CCL3, a signal that draws immune cells in, with IL-7, a factor that helps T cells survive.

Together the two signals beat either one alone, improving tumor entry and lasting killing power without clear side effects. The mix raised RUNX3 and favored resident memory T cells that stay in tissue. Tumors also gained more helpful macrophages and dendritic cells. The approach could make cell therapy stronger and harder for solid tumors to escape.
pmc-13337063:
Qinglong Wang and co-authors herd magnetic nanorobots into swarms to superheat tumors in a 2026 study. Light-heat therapy is gentle and controllable, but loose particles convert light poorly, lose heat fast, and need risky high doses. Magnetic fields gather their building blocks into a reconfigurable microswarm that packs heat sources tightly together.

Packed swarms ran 23 °C hotter than scattered particles under near-infrared light in the reported comparisons, with steadier heating across scales. Magnetic reshaping also tuned the heated area, trading coverage against intensity. Cancer cell killing improved 7-fold versus scattered systems in the study tests. Swarming turns a dosage problem into a geometry problem, a promising shift for precise heat therapy.
pmc-13337463:
Yi Ruan and co-authors build a model to predict how neck lymph nodes respond to radioactive iodine in thyroid cancer in a 2026 study. Patients with differentiated thyroid cancer often receive iodine-131 after node surgery, yet responses vary. The team split patients into excellent and non-excellent responders using blood, imaging, and follow-up criteria.

Guided first by an inflammation gene dataset, they pulled imaging features from pre-treatment CT scans that might reflect inflammation. Selection methods narrowed the features. A combined clinical-radiomics model separated the groups well in training and validation, with sound accuracy checks and clinical benefit across useful thresholds. A nomogram version aids bedside use, though outside validation is still needed.
pmc-13337763:
Solomon B. Makgoeng and colleagues test trial entry rules with real health records in a 2026 methods study. Strict eligibility rules can protect trial validity, yet they also slow enrollment and limit how far results apply. The team emulated dupilumab trials for asthma and COPD.

Health records yielded large new-user groups, with 388,051 people for COPD and 915,154 for asthma in the reported counts. Only part of each trial's rule set could be copied from records. Robust weighting estimated yearly flare-up rate ratios, and sensitivity values gauged hidden bias. The approach shows how data-driven rules might widen who trials represent without losing rigor.
pmc-13337863:
Tessa van Amerongen and colleagues reflected in 2026 on the lasting impact of diagnostic experience in gastrointestinal stromal tumours, a rare cancer with vague symptoms. Efforts to speed diagnosis assume earlier is always better, yet pathways for rare tumours are complex and poorly mapped. In a nationwide study, nearly half of patients waited at least a month for diagnosis and one in five waited at least three months.

Longer waits alone did not predict worse quality of life, but patients who felt their diagnostic journey harmed their well being reported worse outcomes years later, on average 5.9 years after diagnosis. Uncertainty, frustration, fear, and lasting physical limits shaped that experience. Care should therefore address the diagnostic journey itself, not only its length.
pmc-13338663:
Puig-Esteve and Morrison mapped the literature in 2026 on occupational resilience, the idea that taking part in meaningful daily activities helps people adapt and recover through hardship. The term is used in occupational therapy and science, but its definitions and uses were scattered. Their scoping review searched databases and hand sources for work from 2000 to 2025 linking the concept to activity under adversity.

Thirty-seven studies qualified, and they used the term in unlike ways: as a fixed trait, a personal capacity, a shifting process, or an outcome of adaptation. Meaningful activities seemed to soften suffering, steady emotions, and rebuild purpose, roles, routines, and identity after hardship. Most work focused on single people in job settings and skipped structural forces and fairness. The authors propose a process-based definition joining personal, setting, and activity strands, and call for theory and therapy built around the activity effects of trauma.
pmc-13338863:
Artem Bobkov and a large team study digital tools and outpatient care access across Russia in a 2026 panel study. Telemedicine counts are treated carefully, as registered activity rather than proof of wider access. Regional data covered 85 territories from 2018 to 2024.

Doctor visits per 1,000 people stood in for contact intensity, and clinic capacity per 10,000 stood in for structure. A total of 595 region-year records came from official statistics as reported. National telemedicine totals were read separately as a signal shaped by reporting rules. The design warns against reading remote visit counts as direct proof that care became easier to reach.
pmc-13340563:
David Thomas and William P Whitehouse audited emergency seizure care in 2026 for children later sent to intensive care with prolonged convulsive seizures. Care before intensive care was weighed against national rules in a look back at children sent to one child intensive care unit over 2004 to 2005. Of 739 admissions, 36 were for seizures.

Among 32 children past the newborn stage, 26 had notes for audit, and prolonged fever seizures were the top cause at 9 of 26. Of 19 children moved by ambulance, just six got treatment before hospital, and just one of those six got rule based treatment. The audit exposes early treatment gaps that cost time in a time critical emergency.
pmc-13340663:
A blocked bowel in a young child turned out to be lymphoma, in a 2026 case report from South Sudan by Lohide Daniel Lopura and Chol Makur. The 5-year-old boy arrived with severe belly pain, swelling, vomiting, and fever, and imaging pointed to intestinal obstruction.

Surgery revealed a large mass in the cecum with swollen nearby lymph nodes, and tissue study identified primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Childhood lymphoma of the colon is rare and seldom found before an emergency operation. The authors note surgery often serves both to relieve symptoms and to secure a diagnosis, while the best timing for chemotherapy remains unsettled.
pmc-13341363:
Caroline Bickelmann and colleagues tested inflammation signals in 2026 on pancreatic alpha cells and glucagon control in type 2 diabetes. Insulin resistance and obesity linked inflammation drive the disease. Inflammation signals are known to harm beta cells, yet their effect on alpha cells and glucagon control was poorly mapped. The team exposed alpha cell line alphaTC1 and isolated islets to three signals: interleukin 1 beta, tumour necrosis factor alpha, and interferon gamma.

Cell survival and hormone function were read by WST-1 and LDH tests, gene and protein tests, and ELISA, with glucagon promoter activity by reporter tests. If inflammation raises glucagon, it worsens high blood sugar from the other side of the islet. The work maps a neglected inflammation route in diabetes biology.
pmc-13341563:
A nicotine receptor gene variant ties into lung inflammation in a 2026 study by Himani Adhikari and colleagues. The project enrolled 412 COPD patients and 390 controls aged 41 to 80 in West Bengal, India, genotyping the CHRNA5 variant rs16969968 by PCR-based methods.

The AA genotype clustered among patients and came with worse lung function in smokers. Carriers showed lower CHRNA5 expression but higher MMP-9, a tissue-cutting protease, in gene, protein, and lung fluid measures. Computer modeling suggested the amino acid swap subtly alters the receptor. The work links a dependence-associated variant to inflammatory signaling inside the lung itself.
pmc-13341663:
A citrus peel flavonoid shields liver and gut from fatty diets, in a 2026 mouse study by Zhuoqun Meng and colleagues. Sinensetin was given to mice on a high-fat diet that otherwise produces liver fat, inflammation, and scarring alongside a leaky intestinal barrier.

Treated mice showed less liver steatosis and inflammation and a restored gut lining. Gut microbe sequencing and short-chain fatty acid measures suggested a chain: remodeled microbes raised fatty acids, which switched on mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria, quieting the TLR4/MAPK inflammatory route in both organs. The authors frame it as a microbiota-to-mitophagy defense network worth testing further.
pmc-13342163:
Rebuilding the throat with a loop of intestine is evaluated by Alissa De Baets and research partners in a 2026 cohort analysis. Twenty-two patients with hypopharyngeal cancer underwent total laryngopharyngectomy with free jejunal transfer, most (63.6%) as salvage after failed earlier treatment.

Mean age was 65.6 years and follow-up averaged 3.9 years. The transferred jejunum succeeded in 95.5% of patients. The commonest complication was a pharyngocutaneous fistula in 6 patients (27.3%), half managed without reoperation. All primary-treatment tumors were stage IV, underlining that this formidable surgery serves the most advanced disease, where swallowing and survival outcomes both matter.
pmc-13343663:
Songbo Zhang and colleagues tested ylang ylang oil in 2026 as a green tick killer against Haemaphysalis doenitzi, a livestock pest. Growing resistance to man made tick killers plus safety worries for nature and people drive the hunt for swaps. The team tested fumigant and contact killing of Cananga odorata oil plus three plant compounds, lilial, cinene, and alpha amylcinnamaldehyde, in lab tests.

Fumigation and dip tests plus biochemistry tests probed kill power and routes. Plant based tick killers could cut chemical residues in livestock systems if field kill holds. The study names candidates for greener tick control in animal farming.
pmc-13344363:
Lu Zhang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the rise, success, and limits of targeted drugs for melanoma carrying a BRAF gene change. More than half of melanomas carry this change, which switches on a growth pathway and drives rapid cell division, making it a natural drug target.

The review traces BRAF blockers and MEK blockers, which act further down the same pathway, from discovery through approval and clinical use. Both drug classes first shrink tumours, yet nearly all patients later develop resistance and relapse, at the original site and elsewhere. By mapping how tumours escape these drugs, the authors point to where new combinations and strategies must focus if lasting control is to replace short-lived gains.
pmc-13345963:
Anna E Spiro and colleagues introduced in 2026 a scalable framework, called SAGE-net, for training sequence-to-function models on personal genomes. Such models predict how a DNA sequence shapes gene regulation, yet they struggle to capture differences in gene expression between individuals.

Training on personal genomes improved prediction for unseen people, but the gains came mainly from finding predictive variants rather than learning a regulatory grammar that transfers across gene regions. The framework is built to scale to many genomes, which matters as personal data grow. The authors argue that scalable software, not only bigger models, will decide whether personal genomics can move from cohort averages to individual prediction.
pmc-13347163:
Shasha Han and colleagues chart twenty years of kidney biopsy results in older Chinese patients, in a cohort study from 2026. The set held 594 patients aged 60 years or more biopsied at Beijing Hospital from 2005 to 2024, grouped into four five-year spans. Older patients formed a growing share of all native biopsies over time.

Nephrotic syndrome stayed the top reason for biopsy though its share fell, while biopsies for long-term kidney disease rose sharply across the spans in the reported trend. Primary glomerular disease made up 54 percent of cases, led by membranous disease, while diabetic kidney disease led the secondary group. The mix is shifting as the biopsied population ages.
pmc-13348063:
Agnieszka K. Szczepankowska, Bożena Cukrowska, and Tamara Aleksandrzak-Piekarczyk report the complete genome of a probiotic cheese bacterium, in an announcement from 2026. Streptococcus thermophilus ST250 comes from the NORDBIOTIC collection and stands out for breaking down reactive gliadin fragments, a trait not seen before in its species. Combined short and long reads closed its genome.

The single circular chromosome spans 1,829,878 base pairs in the reported assembly, giving a full parts list for a strain also held in a German public collection. A closed genome supports safety checks, trait hunting, and fair comparison with dairy strains that lack the gliadin trait.
pmc-13348663:
Dawid Buczyński and colleagues report a puzzling case of severe high cholesterol that looks inherited yet tests negative, in a case report from 2026. A 75-year-old woman carried widespread artery disease and a native LDL cholesterol of 6.7 mmol per litre, scoring 9 points on a Dutch clinic scale that labels her case definite familial disease on clinical grounds alone.

Gene tests found no faults in the three classic genes, though a variant of unclear weight appeared in a fourth gene, CELSR2, in the reported scan. A separate lipoprotein(a) level of 407.5 nmol per litre added its own risk, showing why clear clinical cases can still hide their genetic cause.
pmc-13349763:
Qi Xia, Qinghai Li, Chao Ding, and Jun Wang pool accuracy data for scans hunting small-bowel tumours, in a meta-analysis from 2026. Small-bowel tumours are rare and vague in symptoms, so four databases to August 2025 were searched, bias was graded. One arm per study group was kept for the main pool to avoid double counting, leaving 21 studies for combined scoring.

Pooled sensitivity reached 0.91 and specificity reached 0.88 in the reported fit, with a summary curve value of 0.95 that marks strong overall sorting. Spread among studies was large, and dedicated gut-filling scan types split out in side analyses, so modality choice still matters for a hard-to-find tumour group.
pmc-13349963:
Yicong Zeng and colleagues questioned in 2026 whether a new angiographic index, NH-IMRangio, adds diagnostic value beyond routine clinical and cardiac MRI measures in survivors of sudden cardiac death. The original study by Sedoud and colleagues reported higher index values in myocardial disease than in electrical heart disease, with moderate discrimination.

The letter notes a mean of about 46.5 in myocardial disease versus 34.1 in electrical disease, an area under the curve near 0.75, with a best cutoff near 41.5, yet asks whether the index improves on information already available from history, examination, and MRI. Without incremental value analysis, a novel marker may impress without changing decisions. The critique calls for head-to-head comparisons before NH-IMRangio enters routine use.
pmc-13350363:
Fan Xie and colleagues tested the DeepSeek-R1 language model in 2026 for turning free-text rectal cancer MRI reports into structured data and helping stage tumours. Structured reports aid treatment planning, but radiologists vary in whether they like writing them.

The study used 465 reports, with 60 spent tuning the task and screening several model families and sizes. The best performer was then judged on staging the tumour's depth and node status, scored for accuracy and speed. pmc-13350463:
Hyewon Park and co-authors weighed in 2026 early effects of Korea's Serious Accidents Punishment Act on work health, using a nationwide difference-in-differences design from 2017 to 2023. Injury, disease, and fatality rates were tracked pre- and post-enforcement. The study tests whether accountability law swiftly shifts safety outcomes, or whether effects take longer to show in national stats.
pmc-13351063:
Menglu Yang and co-authors showed in 2026 that noninvasive electric stimulation restores corneal nerve density and feeling in diabetic nerve harm through a potassium channel route. Recordings showed a rapid charge shift on stimulation plus higher in-cell calcium. Blocking intermediate and small potassium channels wiped out the gain, pinning the KCNN channels. The therapy gives a noninvasive route to regrow corneal nerves in diabetes.
pmc-13351963:
Olaf Suess and co-authors weighed in 2026 clinical outcomes 24 months after cervical disc surgery with a new gliding and springy disc prosthesis, made to keep motion while absorbing compressive loads. The gliding surface allows physiological motion with progressively rising resistance across six degrees of freedom, while the springy core absorbs axial loads. Early results back safety and efficacy, informing surgeons weighing motion-preserving cervical surgery.
pmc-13352163:
Odile Léa Zobo and co-authors charted in 2026 challenges in rolling out open-source digital lab work in sub-Saharan Africa. The team systematically logged technical, logistical, and teaching snags in setting up QuPath. It is an open-source platform for stain-based biomarker scoring at a referral centre. Infrastructure, training, quality control, and workflow fit each posed distinct hurdles. These differed from high-income settings. The lessons give a workable blueprint for other African centres seeking affordable digital lab work.
pmc-13354563:
Deniz Demirci and co-authors surveyed 302 physiotherapy students in Istanbul, Turkey, in a 2026 study of exercise habits. Students answered forms on how much they moved, what kept them from exercise, what they knew about exercise rules, and how much they used social media. Most were women, and their mean age was about 21 years.

Nearly half were classed as highly active, yet very few knew the right weekly amounts for moderate or hard exercise. Students sat for long parts of the day, and heavier social media use linked weakly to seeing more blocks to exercise. The results suggest that even health students need clearer teaching on exercise rules.
pmc-13355463:
Shohei Tobu and co-authors tested a new collagen thread in 2026 as a suture for urethral wounds in rats. Suture material can shape swelling and scarring as tissue heals, and excess scarring harms repair. Wounds sewn with the collagen thread showed less lining thickening and fewer cells tied to swelling and scar signals than the standard suture. A muscle marker tied to scarring was also less marked. The authors say the thread alters early healing responses, a step toward gentler surgical materials.
pmc-13356563:
Mozamil Mohamed and colleagues weighed surgery against watchful non-operative care for stab and gunshot wounds where bowel or omentum pushes out, in a 2026 review that pools prior studies. From 292 records, 20 studies entered synthesis and 13 entered pooling. Watchful care cut needless open surgery with a pooled odds ratio of 0.61, without raising death or harm. It looked safest when only omentum pushed out, where failure stayed under 15 percent. The authors judge the approach safe and preferable in selected stable patients, at moderate proof certainty.
pmc-13358563:
Ada Breitenbucher and co-authors tell a cautionary case in a 2026 report. A 55-year-old man grew weak in both legs over three weeks, with numbness and trouble passing urine. Scans showed a long inflamed stretch in his spinal cord, and a blood test pointed to an immune disease that attacks the cord's insulation.

He improved at first on immune treatment, then worsened after going home, which raised doubts about the diagnosis. A biopsy of the cord lesion gave a different answer: a primary glioblastoma, a fast-growing brain-type tumor. The case shows how a tumor can mimic inflammation, and why doctors must rethink when a patient stops following the expected path.
pmc-13359863:
Yuheng Xue and co-authors read fitness in horse sweat in a 2026 study. As young Yili horses train, their sweat changes form: thick and muddy at first, then foamy, then thin and clear. The team collected sweat and blood from six horses at each stage and profiled the small molecules in both.

Horses at the muddy stage carried higher blood levels of branched-chain amino acids, muscle fuels, and lower levels of glycine than horses at later stages. Their blood chemistry also kept shifting after exercise, unlike the others. The team traced shared pathways between sweat and blood, a step toward using sweat as a window on training state.
pmc-13360163:
Beiqi Yang and co-authors published a 2026 study of how the red swamp crayfish copes with heat and cold. The team compared a bred line of crayfish with normal farmed stock. They read gene activity in the belly nerve cord, a control center for the body. Body traits were checked alongside the gene data.

The bred line turned out to handle cold well, not just heat. Under cold stress, the active genes mostly ran body chemistry, while under heat stress they mostly handled protein folding. The bred line also switched on immune genes under stress more than normal stock did. The authors say some heat-linked genes could guide breeding of crayfish that stand up better to hot water.
pmc-13361963:
Ahmet Genç and co-authors tested a hormone as a death-risk marker in weak hearts in a 2026 study. Parathyroid hormone, best known for calcium control, also reflects strain across the heart, kidney, and mineral systems. The team asked whether it predicts death in heart failure with reduced pumping strength, and whether it adds warning power beyond the standard marker NT-proBNP. They analyzed 1,594 patients whose hearts pumped at 40 percent strength or less.

Patients were grouped by hormone level, and survival was charted for each group. Layered models tested whether the hormone improved prediction once the standard marker was already in. A cheap blood test that sharpens risk sorting could help doctors decide who needs tighter follow-up or stronger therapy in this high-risk group.
pmc-13362363:
Maciej Skrzypek and co-authors report a 2026 case-control study on genes that help the body break down foreign chemicals. They tested four gene variants, in CYP1A1, CYP2D6, NAT1, and NAT2, for links to cancer of the womb lining. They also compared gene activity in tumor tissue and in healthy tissue from controls.

Tumor tissue also showed more CYP1A1 and CYP2D6 activity than healthy tissue. The authors call the work early and say larger studies must check the results, but the findings point to genes worth a closer look in cancer risk.
pmc-13362763:
Anda Sipola and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study on fat-like carrier molecules designed to ferry DNA into cells. The ring-linked carriers folded into bubbles that wrapped up more than 80 percent of the test DNA at the best mixing ratios, far better than the plain versions. Particle sizes varied widely, yet the pattern was clear: the ring link strongly shaped both assembly and DNA grip. The results give gene delivery designers a fresh building block to test in cells next.
pmc-13363363:
Battamir Ulambayar and colleagues present a 2026 study of diet and mental well-being among Hungarian adults at high heart and metabolic risk. Using a 2019 European health survey, they studied 2,785 adults with obesity, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol, scoring well-being on a standard five-question index. About a quarter of the group fell into the poor well-being band.

Low intake of fruit, vegetables, fish, and even fruit juice each tracked with higher odds of poor well-being, as did drinking too little water. The links held after accounting for income, schooling, activity, and self-rated health. Since the data are a snapshot, cause cannot be proven, yet the authors argue diet support belongs inside care plans for this group.
pmc-13363463:
Yirui Chen and colleagues offer a 2026 review on how ultra-processed foods may age the brain through the liver. Candidate routes include broken food structure, fast eating, additives, a leaky gut, and liver fat stress that fans body-wide swelling and vessel harm. Cause is not proven, and many routes overlap with plain metabolic disease. The authors argue the processing itself deserves study as the upstream exposure, not just the nutrients inside.
pmc-13363663:
Natalia Alaniz-Salinas, Rachel Engler-Stringer, and Hassan Vatanparast report a 2026 study of what Saskatchewan elementary students actually eat at lunch. Using photos of trays before and after eating to weigh waste, they assessed 379 children aged 5 to 13. They compared home-packed, school-provided, and mixed lunches for energy, nutrient content, and a nutrient-density score.

School-provided lunches carried less energy, sugar, and fat at similar protein, and earned the highest density scores. Even so, lunches of every kind supplied under a quarter of daily needs for fiber, vitamin D, calcium, and potassium, and older children got a smaller share of their larger needs. The authors offer the numbers as a baseline for judging school food policy.
pmc-13365363:
Yafei Wu and co-authors follow older Chinese adults for twenty years to test whether the ratio of fat mass to lean mass predicts death better than weight alone. Over a median follow-up of just over eighteen years, 2,446 participants died. Men in the lowest third of most ratios faced significantly higher risk than the middle third, and the relationships were L-shaped rather than straight lines. No ratio predicted cardiovascular death in either sex. The authors present regional body composition as a refinement over body mass index for judging risk in older adults.
pmc-13365863:
Ryoji Tokiya and co-workers tell in 2026 of beam care after breast cut surgery in a woman past 60 who has Poland syndrome, a rare birth flaw that thins one chest wall. She had left breast cancer and a thin chest on that side. Care took the breast off and rebuilt it with a belly flesh flap.

Beam care then ran on the rebuilt breast with safe lung and heart dose. She had no lung harm from the beams and no local return of the ill at five and a half years. The case shows beam care can work safe in this rare frame.
pmc-13367963:
Yan and colleagues use single-cell sequencing to study fetal testes in Klinefelter syndrome, where males carry an extra X chromosome, in 2026 developmental biology research. Their role was little known compared with sperm-producing cells.
