pmc-13370263:
Daiyu Yang and co-workers sum up in 2026 how yogurt, the sour milk food, shapes gut germs and health past the gut. Proof grows that the food shifts germ mix, gut wall strength, and immune acts. The team sorts yogurt types, from plain to pro and mixed forms.

Their frame splits direct gifts of the food, like live germs and sour make goods, from next step goods made by home germs and host acts. Form mix, strain picks, and folk gaps blur proof. Long lot trials and multi mark reads must firm the claims, they hold.
pmc-13371463:
Yavuz Özden and Ferhat Omurca built a computer tool to spot a common stomach germ in a 2026 study. The germ, called H. pylori, is now found with tissue tests that slow care. Their tool learned from plain white-light scope photos taken in one clinic, with no special dyes or lights.

The study used 172 patients and 1,000 photos in all. The tool scored well in tests, with scores near nine out of ten for sorting sick from well. A fresh check on 52 later patients gave much the same result. The work hints that plain scope photos may one day guide care on the spot.
pmc-13372363:
Zhang and colleagues evaluate continuous Z-plasty for repairing facial scars, in a 2026 plastic surgery study from Ningbo, China. Z-plasty rearranges skin flaps in Z shapes to reorient a scar and spread tension; the continuous version strings several along one long scar. The series covers 21 patients between January 2020 and December 2022, 9 men and 12 women with a mean age of 36.7 years, scored before and after surgery with the Vancouver Scar Scale and followed for recurrence.

Scar scores improved from a median of 8 before surgery to a median of 3 afterward on the standardized scale. Scar width narrowed from 4.5 millimeters to 1.5 millimeters across the group. At a median follow-up of 18 months, no patient had recurrence or complications, and satisfaction surveys matched the photographic improvement. The forehead was the commonest site treated. Zhang concludes the technique is effective and safe for facial scars, while calling for comparison trials against revision methods.
pmc-13375963:
Martina Kadláčková and colleagues build a rapid blood-spot test for atypical myopathy in horses in a 2026 study. The disease, caused by maple toxins hypoglycin A and methylenecyclopropylglycine, kills over 70 percent of affected horses within 72 hours. Early diagnosis needs fast detection of toxins and metabolites, yet existing assays require derivatisation and serum or urine samples.

The new flow injection tandem mass spectrometry method needs only 50 microlitres of whole blood on a dried spot, with minimal preparation and results within one minute. Nine analytes, including the toxins and seven acylcarnitines, were measured with low detection limits and excellent linearity. Analytes stayed stable in dried spots at room temperature short term and at minus 20 degrees longer term. The test could bring life-saving speed to equine clinics.
pmc-13377763:
Mengqi Gao and co-authors traced a burst chain in a grave gut gland ill in a 2026 study. The ill can turn to a body-wide fire that kills. Cells of the gland spill their power-part code, which lights that fire. What drives the spill was the ask.

One-cell reads and gene grip tests found a switch that turns on a freight gene. That pair breaks power parts and packs their bits in sacs for spill. Mice bred with the switch off in the gland fared in a next way. The chain gives drug hunts a clear first link to cut in this fast, grave ill.
pmc-13378263:
Yi Liang and co-authors introduce a 2026 model for how ferroelectric materials switch under real, changing voltages. These materials store charge in a way that can flip, which makes them useful for memory devices. Older models assumed a steady electric field, which real devices rarely provide.

Their new model follows how tiny switched regions form and grow when the field keeps changing. It can fit switching data from several materials and reveal how fast region walls move over time. Linked to circuit simulation software, the model connects material behaviour to device design. That link may help engineers design memory and other circuits together with the materials they use.
pmc-13379763:
Aishwarya Saini and co-authors present a 2026 case report on rebuilding the teeth of a patient with ectodermal dysplasia, an inherited condition affecting teeth, hair, nails, and sweat glands. The patient had many missing teeth, small teeth, and poorly developed jaw ridges, which make dentures hard to fit. The bite height had also dropped.

Care combined approaches for the two jaws. The upper jaw received a denture supported by the remaining teeth, while the lower jaw received one held by implants placed with digital planning and a printed surgical guide. The final teeth restored appearance, chewing, and comfort. The patient reported clear satisfaction with the result.
pmc-13379963:
Jianlei Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 trial in Tibet on giving oxygen during stomach camera examinations in older patients. At high altitude the air is thin, and sedation adds risk that blood oxygen will fall. The trial took place in Shigatse, about 3,800 metres above sea level.

Patients aged sixty or over were assigned by chance to high-flow oxygen through the nose or to a standard nasal tube. Low blood oxygen during the procedure was far less common with high-flow oxygen. The result supports using high-flow oxygen for sedated examinations in elderly patients at altitude, where even brief drops in oxygen can be dangerous.
pmc-13380663:
Wardah Ikram published a 2026 cross-sectional study linking thyroid hormone imbalance with heart and vessel health. The thyroid gland helps set heart rhythm, blood pressure, and vessel function, so too much or too little of its hormone can strain the heart. The study involved outpatients and people attending community screening.

It was run at a medical college in Lahore during 2019 and included 424 adults. Based on blood tests, people were grouped as having normal, low, or high thyroid function. Each person had blood pressure measured and a resting heart tracing recorded. The analysis looked for links with high blood pressure, abnormal tracings, rhythm problems, and unhealthy blood fats.
pmc-13382763:
Kaide Xia, Bingpeng Gao, and Junwen Wang map heart, kidney, and metabolic involvement in heart disease deaths across the United States in 2026 work. Using national death records from 2014 to 2023, they tracked how rates changed over time and place. They also asked whether gaps linked to social vulnerability grew wider.

Crude death rates rose over the decade, and the gap between the most and least vulnerable areas widened as well. County results ranged widely, and 356 counties counted as both high risk and getting worse. The authors single out 85 top-priority counties where focused prevention and care could cut the most deaths.
pmc-13386963:
Wei and colleagues report mediastinal B-cell lymphoma arising during pregnancy, in a 2026 hematology case report with review. The lymphoma grows as a bulky mass that can squeeze the airways and heart. A 29-year-old woman, pregnant for the fourth time with no deliveries, developed a cough at 15 weeks that antibiotics failed to clear. By the 28th week she could not lie flat, with worsening breathlessness and swallowing difficulty, and scans revealed a mediastinal mass compressing her chest structures.

An emergency caesarean section delivered the baby, whose Apgar scores were 6, 7, and 7 at 1, 5, and later minutes after birth, freeing the mother for lymphoma treatment. Wei reviews published cases to map how care shifts by pregnancy stage: chemotherapy timing, birth decisions, and protection of the fetus pull. The authors stress diagnosis, since respiratory symptoms in pregnancy are dismissed as minor illness, and tailored plans balancing patients whose risks change week by week.
pmc-13388763:
Moffitt and colleagues raise antibodies against known pieces of MUC16, the protein behind the CA125 cancer test, in 2026 cancer biomarker research. The current test's antibodies recognize undefined targets on the protein, one reason the test throws false positives and negatives and cannot screen the general public. The team immunized rabbits with three peptides from the protein's repeating region, sequences known letter by letter. They purified the polyclonal antibodies and profiled them with binding assays.

All three peptides worked as antigens, yielding antibodies that bound expressed pieces of the repeat region. Antibodies against peptide 2 were the stars: they bound tandem repeats tested and detected MUC16 from ovarian cancer cells in a resonance assay. They stained MUC16-positive cancer cells in flow cytometry. Because their targets are defined, antibodies could anchor next-generation assays with behavior. Moffitt presents peptide 2's antibody as the candidate for rebuilding the CA125 test on ground.
pmc-13389763:
Sruthi Sivabhaskar and co-authors test, in 2026, a shortcut for outlining organs at risk during internal radiation therapy for gynaecological cancers. High-dose-rate brachytherapy needs fresh outlines of the bladder, rectum, bowel, and sigmoid for every treatment session, a slow task that varies between staff.

The team studied 50 treatment sessions from 25 past patients and built patient-specific rings based on margins from the target volume to two dose levels. Organs were drawn only inside those rings, and dose results were checked against standard practice. Radiation planners gain a method that could cut outlining time while keeping dose accuracy and patient safety, an important gain for busy treatment centres.
pmc-13390163:
Dang Thanh Hong, Nguyen Thi Hong Duy, and To Thi Kim Quyen build, in 2026, a new questionnaire that aims to predict test anxiety in medical students rather than merely measure it. Existing tools mostly score how severe anxiety is, which does little to guide prevention.

Their Test Anxiety Predictors Inventory was developed and first validated at Can Tho University of Medicine and Pharmacy. A census survey ran there from December 2024 to March 2025. It gathered nearly four hundred valid responses. A thirty-item draft pool had earlier been piloted in a smaller student group. Medical educators, especially in settings with limited support staff, gain a tool meant to flag at-risk students early and point to specific, changeable causes.
pmc-13390363:
Feng Xu's team examined how blood lead levels relate to body makeup in 1,522 American women aged forty to fifty-nine from national survey data spanning 2011 to 2018. Lead harms bone, but its links to muscle and fat across menopause were unclear.

Postmenopausal women carried higher blood lead plus lower bone density and lean mass. Higher log-transformed lead tracked inversely with lumbar bone density, lean mass index, and fat mass index, with the bone link significant before menopause and the muscle and fat links stronger after it. The findings add body-makeup risk to lead's known skeletal toll.
pmc-13390463:
Christen L. Grettenberger's team studied 240 genomes and mixed-genome-built genomes from Ferrovaceae, iron-rusting germs found in acid mine drainage worldwide, to gauge their cleanup potential. Mine waters pollute downstream wild places, and germ iron rusting could help clean them.

The group's family-tree and body diversity proved greater than known. All taxa likely rust iron through a cyc-2-like protein, and some possibly use an Mto-like route, plus likely no-oxygen light-eating in some members. Diverse side-by-side groups may split slots along resource slopes, backing tougher, faster iron rusting for treatment systems.
pmc-13390963:
David Shengelia and colleagues report, in 2026, emergency coil treatment of a burst aneurysm on the gastroduodenal artery. Aneurysms of this artery are among the rarest of visceral artery aneurysms, but rupture carries a high risk of death and demands immediate action.

The patient arrived with worsening diffuse abdominal pain and one episode of black vomit, suggesting internal bleeding. Contrast-enhanced scanning confirmed rupture of the aneurysm, and the team chose coil repair through a thin tube over open surgery. The coil sealed the vessel from inside. Scan-guided doctors gain a worked emergency case. It supports inside-the-vessel repair as a gentler rescue when a rare deep aneurysm bursts. Speed was key from the first scan, since a burst here can drain blood fast.
pmc-13391763:
Golaleh Karbasi and colleagues validate, in 2026, a Persian questionnaire measuring whether older Iranian adults would adopt mobile health tools for osteoporosis care. Bone thinning is rising among older adults, and phone-based support could aid self-management if patients will use it.

The survey is for adults aged fifty and more, with or without the disease. It was built from known models of tech uptake and health beliefs. It adds faith in one's own skill, digital skill, and fear of new tech. Digital health teams gain a tested tool made for Iran. Uptake studies there can gauge real barriers. They need not fear quirks from a survey built in the West and moved as-is.
pmc-13392663:
Mohannad Abuajamieh and co-authors fed laying hens a yeast-derived fibre called beta-glucan. They then hit the birds with short daily heat waves to test whether the feed additive could protect laying and gut health. One hundred sixty young hens ate four dose levels for a month before facing four days of heat reaching well above comfort for several hours daily. Output, egg quality, blood measures, and gut lining were all recorded.

Heat slashed feed intake, laying rate, and egg quality while wearing down the gut lining. Hens on the highest dose kept laying at a notably higher rate. They also produced heavier daily egg mass, converted feed more efficiently, and kept taller gut villi than unsupplemented hens under the same heat. Blood measures showed no harm from the additive. The authors recommend the higher dose as a practical shield during hot spells.
pmc-13393063:
Yi Yang and five colleagues mapped the published evidence on pairing the Mediterranean diet with physical activity to protect thinking in older adults. Drugs for cognitive decline remain limited, so lifestyle routes draw strong interest. Their scoping review searched five databases and organised studies under a standard framework, concentrating on how the two habits might reinforce each other rather than on either alone.

The diet brings plant compounds and healthy fats that calm oxidative stress and inflammation while feeding brain support systems. Activity raises cerebral blood flow, delivers antioxidants better, and triggers growth factors that keep brain circuits plastic. Together the pair seem to steady energy handling and lower inflammation more than either alone. The authors describe a virtuous cycle in which food supplies the building blocks that exercise-driven repair requires.
pmc-13393263:
Qingjian Xie and twelve colleagues identify platelet factor 4, a protein released by blood platelets, as a circulating protector in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis linked to faulty SOD1. The hunt began in a United Kingdom Biobank cohort of over half a million people, where platelet measures tracked disease risk, and blood tests showed the factor running low in patients. Giving the protein to mice carrying the human disease gene changed their course strikingly.

Treated mice lived longer, kept motor function, showed calmer nerve inflammation, and retained more connections between nerves and muscles. The benefit was selective, appearing in SOD1 models but not in models driven by two other ALS genes. Tracing the mechanism, the factor docks onto a cell receptor and switches on a cleanup pathway that clears SOD1 clumps and damaged mitochondria without the usual recycling route. The authors propose a platelet-to-neuron axis as new therapeutic ground.
pmc-13393463:
Alaa O Oteir and colleagues examine how emergency medical workers in Jordan view point-of-care ultrasound before hospital arrival in a 2026 survey study. Portable ultrasound at the scene could aid fast decisions, but its uptake depends on training, equipment, and provider confidence.

A multicenter questionnaire reached 621 emergency providers, most of them men with about ten years of service, while fewer than a quarter reported prior ultrasound training. Attitudes, perceived benefits, and barriers were scored and compared across groups. The paper gives managers concrete evidence on what helps or blocks wider use of bedside ultrasound in ambulances.
pmc-13393763:
Brendan Coutu and colleagues assess consolidative radiation after stem cell transplant for relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma in a 2026 single-institution study. Between 5 and 30 percent of Hodgkin patients fail first treatment or relapse, and high-dose chemotherapy with autologous transplant is standard salvage care, yet the value of added radiation remains disputed.

The team reviewed 179 consecutive patients treated from 2000 to 2019, of whom 72 received post-transplant radiation at a median dose of 36 gray, mostly to involved sites. Median follow-up reached nearly five years. The paper helps oncologists judge whether extra radiation after transplant improves control without undue harm.
pmc-13394263:
Sara Hogmark and four colleagues report one-year secondary outcomes from a trial of coil placement timing after second-trimester medical abortion. One group had the coil placed at once. The other waited two to four weeks. One hundred seventy-nine women took part, and about seven in ten in each arm completed the year. The hope for immediate placement was higher long-term use through convenience.

The result ran the other way. Fewer immediate-placement women still used a coil at twelve months. Expulsions were far commoner in that group, over a third against a tiny fraction with delayed fitting. Almost all came in the first six months. Later pregnancies ran somewhat higher after immediate placement, and abortion numbers did not differ. Satisfaction among continuing users was high in both arms, though immediate-placement women were less keen to recommend the timing.
pmc-13394463:
Junyan Che and co-authors report, in 2026, a light-based computer that reuses small cores over time to do big jobs. Demand for artificial intelligence grows far faster than chip power, so light offers a fast path. Their indium tin oxide parts shift light phase in a very short length. The parts can be reset billions of times with little wear.

A small two-by-two array sorted fashion images with scores matching full software runs. It also beat a five-bit rival and ran at well over a thousand frames each second. Settings could be tuned across nine bits of range at fast rates. The team frames the design as a route to leaner AI hardware.
pmc-13395363:
Amani A. Niazy leads a 2026 lab study of a cancer drug, 5-fluorouracil, turned against a stubborn hospital germ. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, swims, swarms, and builds biofilms that aid its spread. Cultures were dosed with rising amounts of the drug. The team measured three kinds of movement, loose DNA output, and gene activity.

All movement types fell as dose rose. Genes for the tail motor and hair-like grippers switched down, as did genes for a slime helper. Loose DNA dropped at one day but climbed by two days at high doses, with repair genes waking up. The authors call the drug a multi-sided brake on germ traits. Dose and timing shape the effect.
pmc-13396163:
Kim and co-authors present, in 2026, a geometric framework for metasurfaces, flat patterned materials that steer light and other waves. Many designs encode a momentum profile across the surface, which breaks the regular pattern that makes analysis tractable. The team shows such surfaces can be read as Moiré lattices, formed by laying a 1D periodic layer over a 2D Bravais lattice, the standard grid types of crystallography.

From that picture they derive conditions, rules for when the combined pattern repeats, exposing hidden order in seemingly random structures. Each surface can then be redrawn as a compact superlattice, which sorts its radiation into defined diffraction orders. The framework matched 2D sampling theory for local metasurfaces and pinned down rules for spin-dependent designs. Experiments on fabricated photonic crystal slabs confirmed the predicted valley addressability, a way of routing waves by valley index.
pmc-13396463:
Wenbo Wang and co-authors shrank a carbon dioxide sensor onto a single silicon chip, and report it in 2026. The design uses the non-dispersive infrared method, where gas absorbs a chosen band of infrared light, but builds the light source and the heat-based detector together on one substrate using microsystem fabrication.

Portable uses, from wearables that track breathing to handheld air monitors, need sensors that are tiny and quick, while bench instruments rely on separate bulky chambers. The team co-designed the optical chamber and layout from the physics of light transfer and heat coupling, aiming to catch more of the infrared signal and cut thermal cross-talk. The result targets fast, stable readings in a far smaller package.
pmc-13396663:
Jenna Turocy and others probe chromosome wreck after DNA snaps in human embryos in a 2026 paper. DNA mend in human embryos is dimly known, and snaps can shed chromosomes with grave growth costs.

With CRISPR guides aimed at heart zones of chromosomes 16 and X, the team found snap-born wrong-count sets at mixed spots, with lopsided loss and second-wave wreck of other chromosomes. The work shows how one aimed snap can snowball into wide gene mess. Embryo labs gain a stark warn for gene edits in early life.
pmc-13396763:
Molly L. Shen and others score protein team-ups in cell sacs in a 2026 study. Cell sacs ferry mixed protein loads that tune tissue calm and cell talk, and birth paths should sort proteins in teams or apart, yet old load reads miss those teams.

The team scored pair team-ups for up to 240 protein pairs with antibody dot grids, proving the score by tweaking known sac birth paths and tracking team shifts between states. The score bares which proteins ride as one in sacs and how stress reshuffles the ride. Sac labs gain a sharp gauge for load teams.
pmc-13397663:
Menghan Liu, Dan Lin and Ronghua Zhou pool trial evidence on blood filtering during heart surgery to protect the kidneys. Their 2026 review updates earlier work with trial sequential analysis, a check on whether enough data exist. Kidney injury after bypass surgery stays common and hard to treat, while filters that soak up inflammation signals are used more and more.

Randomised trials were gathered from five databases through 8 February 2025, following PRISMA reporting rules. Only adult heart-surgery patients counted, with filtering during surgery compared against standard care. Pooling used random-effects models, spread between trials was measured, and subgroup and sensitivity checks probed how firm the verdict on kidney injury and other outcomes really is.
pmc-13397763:
Houchun Liu and colleagues map how a pig virus rewires host genes to copy itself. Their 2026 study pairs two genome-wide scans (one for open DNA regions, one for active genes) in cells infected with porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus. The virus spreads fast among herds, and whether it bends host DNA packaging to aid itself was unknown.

Against uninfected controls, infected cells showed 8,664 DNA regions with changed openness and 4,037 genes with changed activity. Motif hunting in the open regions flagged control sites where gene switches bind. Crossing both lists left 1,352 shared genes, a shortlist of host players the virus may depend on and that drug or breeding work could target.
pmc-13397863:
Supanji Supanji and colleagues report a case series on a gentler buckle operation for detached retinas. Their 2026 study covers seven patients (seven eyes) whose retinas had lifted after a tear, letting fluid slip underneath. The classic wrap-around buckle supports the whole eye wall but takes long and can starve the front of the eye of blood; a segmental buckle braces only the torn zone.

All seven patients had the segmental operation as their first repair and were followed for six months. Every buckle sat at good position and height, and each detachment settled within 24 hours of surgery. The authors present the targeted approach as a sound primary fix in skilled hands, with the drainage of trapped fluid part of the routine.
pmc-13397963:
Settawit Chatsuntiprapa and team split apart two body traits to see which one predicts death after liver cancer embolization. Their 2026 work covers 415 people with liver cancer that could not be cut out, treated by chemoembolization, a method that sends chemo drugs straight into liver tumor blood vessels. A combined label for low muscle plus belly fat had given mixed results, so the team tested each trait on its own.

Using base CT scans, they measured muscle size and belly fat area and tracked people for a median of 21.4 months. Low muscle predicted death in men, cutting median life from 25.4 months to 14.4 months, but showed no clear link in women. Belly fat alone predicted life span in neither sex, and the combined label added no value. The work urges sex-specific care for muscle loss in liver cancer.
pmc-13400163:
Enrique Grande and colleagues report DUTRENEO, a randomized phase 2 trial testing whether an 18-gene tumor inflammation signature could select bladder cancer patients for immunotherapy before surgery, in this 2026 study. It could not. Patients were stratified by the bulk-tissue score and randomized around neoadjuvant checkpoint inhibitor treatment. The trial missed its primary endpoint, showing the bulk score does not enrich for responders when used in real time.

Rather than stopping at the negative result, the team asked why, profiling tumors with single-cell spatial transcriptomics: 377 genes measured across roughly 5.4 million cells. Response turned out to depend on geography that bulk assays average away: how close CD8 T cells sit to cancer cells, and whether checkpoint molecules are co-expressed inside cancer-rich neighborhoods. In non-responders, fibroblast-rich communities walled the immune cells out. The study is a cautionary landmark for biomarker-guided trial design.
pmc-13400463:
Michelle Misselwitz, Nicholas J Herkert, P Lee Ferguson and Heather M Stapleton present, in 2026, a method to measure chemical exposures in the placenta. The placenta feeds a fetus through pregnancy and touches it for months. What reaches the womb can shape later health. Trace levels and the placentas mixed makeup make testing hard.

Their method pairs a tuned extraction step with high-resolution mass spectrometry and labeled standards for 119 compounds. Spiked samples and a standard reference sample checked its accuracy. Applied to 50 samples from a North Carolina cohort, the method found 72 compounds in at least one case. Hits included flame retardants, pesticides, plastic-linked chemicals and factory pollutants.
pmc-13400663:
Taisuke Nozu leads a Japanese multicenter study, published in 2026, of bone loss around the arm implant after reverse shoulder replacement. Bone can thin where the implant shields it from load, and shorter stems were designed to reduce that effect. Data in Asian patients were limited.

After matching, 35 shoulders with standard stems were compared with 35 with short stems. At two years, severe bone resorption appeared in about two thirds of the standard group but only about a third of the short stem group. One outer zone of the upper arm bone was hit most often. Statistical modeling searched for factors tied to severe loss, including stem fill and alignment.
pmc-13401163:
Muhammadtaher Abdulrazaq Abdulrasol, Wafaa A Abd El-Ghany, and Harith Abdulla Najem report a 2026 field investigation of pigeon paramyxovirus-1 in domestic pigeons across seven Egyptian governorates. The virus, a pigeon variant of avian paramyxovirus type 1, causes nerve, gut, and breathing problems in pigeons.

Between April and September 2025 the team collected 39 pigeons aged 3 to 14 months from live bird markets and private lofts. More than 60 percent showed nerve signs such as twisted necks, head tremors, and circling, plus greenish diarrhea and eye inflammation. Postmortem findings included brain hemorrhages and swollen kidneys. The birds' tissues were tested by virus isolation in embryonated chicken eggs and by RT-PCR to confirm the virus.
pmc-13401763:
Zakaria Toufga and co-authors report a 2026 fatal case of spinal infection that ate through into the aorta. Their patient was a 60-year-old woman with three weeks of severe, worsening low back pain, high fever, and chills.

Blood tests showed striking inflammation, and cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine found infectious spondylodiscitis at the T12-L1 level, with a destructive inflammatory tract pushing forward. It formed a direct fistula into the abdominal aorta, with a large infected pseudoaneurysm, a contained bulge of the artery wall. Emergency aortic repair was planned, but she deteriorated within hours into septic shock that resisted treatment and died the same day. The authors stress the catastrophic potential of vertebral bone infection with vascular complications, and the diagnostic value of contrast-enhanced MRI when back pain and fever collide.
pmc-13402063:
Yusuke Kitani and colleagues reviewed six pregnant patients who had keyhole appendix removal at one center between April 2020 and April 2025. The women were 28 to 37 years old and 15 to 33 weeks pregnant. Surgeons used a three-port method in every case, kept belly pressure at 10 to 12 mmHg, and chose lying position by stage of pregnancy.

Operations took a median of 84 minutes, blood loss was nil in five cases, and hospital stays ran a median of five days. Tissue results ranged from mild inflammation to one gangrenous appendix. No case switched to open surgery and no pregnancy complications followed. Kitani and the team credit position and port changes matched to gestational age for making keyhole surgery workable in later pregnancy.
pmc-13402263:
Aminath Shiwaza Moosa leads a Singapore team that built a new itch questionnaire for multi-ethnic Asian patients, arguing older tools each cover only a slice of the problem. Draft questions came from past literature, expert talks, and interviews with 13 patients and 10 primary care doctors. The draft then went to 250 people, with and without itch, who answered it three times over about a week alongside two established scales.

The final tool holds 10 questions in three parts: how bad the itch is, how it dents quality of life, and how it is managed. Scores tracked the 5-D pruritus scale and the Dermatology Life Quality Index closely, with correlations of 0.67 and 0.77 in the reported tests. Repeat answers proved steady, with an intraclass correlation of 0.93 and internal consistency of 0.94, supporting clinic use for tracking itch over time.
pmc-13402663:
Jiawei Da and a large team tie the spread of C4 grasses across East Asia to shifts in rainfall timing driven by the subtropical westerly jet stream. C4 grasslands expanded worldwide in the Neogene and reshaped mammal evolution, yet each continent moved on its own clock, hiding the driver. Working on the Chinese Loess Plateau, the team read oxygen isotopes in rainfall traces and clumped isotope soil temperatures across 7 to 2.5 million years ago.

Warm times, with the jet pushed poleward, brought more spring rain; cool times concentrated rain in summer instead. Carbon isotope records show the richest C4 ecosystems tracked that summer rain band as it slid, finally covering the southern plateau margin during late Pleistocene cooling. The authors say their model sharpens the East Asian paleomonsoon picture and explains why high-latitude C4 belts marched toward the equator.
pmc-13403163:
Yue YANG and colleagues run a randomized trial of autonomous bladder training for neurogenic bladder, the emptying failure that follows spinal cord injury and other nerve disease. In a single center, 168 adults were split evenly between four weeks of structured training plus routine rehabilitation and routine care alone. Training mixed induced voiding, sensory awareness, pelvic floor work, bladder-sphincter coordination, and desensitization.

Leftover urine after voiding, the main outcome, improved far more with training: an adjusted extra reduction of 55.8 milliliters against routine care in the reported figures. Flow rate, bladder pressure, and symptom scores also favored training, and antibiotic-treated urinary infections occurred in 9.5 percent against 27.4 percent, though urine cultures were not always confirmed. A twelve-week look suggested partial holding of gains. The authors ask for longer multicenter trials before firm adoption.
pmc-13403363:
Bert Lenaert led a 2026 study that tracked Dutch firefighters for two years to see what predicts mental resilience. At the start, 528 firefighters from 11 regions took part. The team measured sleep quality, sense of coherence, meaning in life, and support from workmates.

Follow-up surveys drew 237 people at one year and 203 people at two years. A strong sense of coherence at the start predicted resilience after one year. Meaning in life also predicted resilience by the two-year mark. Sleep quality and workmate support showed no such link, so belief and meaning look like useful targets for support programs.
pmc-13403463:
Mimi Wai Man Chan, Janet Wing Hung Sit, and Suzanne Hoi Shan Lo looked again in 2026 at interview records on life after stroke. The wider set held 26 transcripts from people living at home after a stroke. Material on loneliness was drawn from 20 of those talks and sorted into themes.

Three threads ran through the accounts. People felt cut off from group life and set apart from others. Close ties faded as friends and family grasped less of their daily world. Many also lost hope, drive, and a sense of purpose. The authors say loneliness care should sit at the heart of stroke recovery plans and rules.
pmc-13403763:
Mohammed Kanan and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a quick electric scan of body makeup can forecast trouble in liver scarring. Body shape and muscle mass shape how cirrhosis unfolds. Their group followed 566 clinic patients who had the scan at entry.

Higher body fat tied strongly to metabolic fatty liver as the cause of scarring. More lean mass in the trunk and left arm tied to lower odds of severe fluid and confusion events at entry. One mid-range belly fat measure tied to fewer new severe events later. No scan measure tied to liver cancer. The cheap scan may aid risk sorting in clinics.
pmc-13404363:
Abdul Momin Rizwan Ahmad and co-authors gave an updated review in 2026 of iron deficiency anemia, the world's most common anemia. The condition drives about two-thirds of all anemia cases and touches near 1.2 billion people. Signs range from tiredness and pale skin to spoon-shaped nails and pounding heart.

Causes span poor intake, weak absorption, higher needs, steady blood loss, and two infections. The review walks through how doctors confirm the fault, with marrow checks as the top standard. Four broad fixes anchor prevention: wider diets, iron pills, crop breeding for iron, and food fortifying. Cheap plans fitted to each place are the pressing need.
pmc-13405063:
Mushuai Hao and colleagues test how the lowering speed of squats affects strength gains, in 2026 work with sports students. Thirty university participants trained with loaded squats twice a week for eight weeks. Groups differed only in eccentric tempo, the time taken to lower the weight.

One group lowered over four seconds, another over two, and a third chose its own pace. All groups improved their maximum squat significantly, with no clear difference between groups in the statistical tests. Effect sizes favoured the two-second group most in the reported ranking. Two groups also jumped higher after training, measured by countermovement and squat jumps, while sprint times over 30 metres completed the test battery.
pmc-13406163:

Children lacking the hormone now face daily injections that poorly mimic natural release. Their candidate, VTRC-01, packages hormone instructions in fat particles for injection into muscle.

The mRNA version drove lengthwise growth comparably to the standard drug in the reported results. Treated animals also showed a clear anabolic response above normal growth in healthy controls. The authors present the work as early evidence that the body can be reprogrammed to make its own hormone supply.
pmc-13407163:
Zheyuan Zhang and colleagues, in 2026, tested whether hidden instructions planted in surgical videos can mislead the artificial intelligence models proposed as operating-room assistants. Such prompt injection attacks slip deceptive text or images into material a vision-language model is asked to read, and surgery is a high-stakes place to test the risk.

The strongest baseline performer reached 0.80 mean accuracy, yet every model dropped sharply under attack, and one fell to 0.24 when misleading visuals persisted across frames. A bleeding-detection case study showed attacks working from either direction, and reasoning traces revealed corrupted perception mid-chain rather than a flipped final answer. Guardrails, the authors conclude, must come before live deployment.
pmc-13407563:

Nearly every attempt ended in festering wounds; many fractures still mended, while other patients lost limbs or died. pmc-13407663:

pmc-13408463:
Lea Aylin Schmitz and co-authors measure in 2026 how strongly the first bacteria of dental plaque stick to five commercial filling materials. The other two, Streptococcus mitis and Streptococcus sanguinis, attached in significantly greater amounts to one particular composite than to its rivals. pmc-13410463:
Ming-Ju Hsieh and co-workers study in 2026 whether a gene variant shapes how mouth cancer behaves. The gene, NAP1L1, helps pack DNA and has been linked to growth in several cancers. The team focused on one variant, rs11180813, in people with oral squamous cell carcinoma.

pmc-13411563:
Kendra Maass leads the INFORM program team reporting in 2026 that blood tests can find tumor DNA in children with high-risk solid cancers. Childhood tumors offer few molecular handles, samples are tiny, and patient numbers are small. Liquid biopsies collected prospectively from 130 young patients were put through optimized cell-free DNA methods.

Shallow whole-genome reading of blood DNA reliably spotted tumor signal. A scoring trick combining fragment length and chromosome changes lifted accuracy to about 95 percent, detecting tumors in 93 percent of patients. Deeper sequencing then found drug-target changes, though usefulness varied strongly by tumor type. Serial samples also traced how tumors evolve, which may sharpen how children get sorted into treatments.
pmc-13413563:
Bin Zuo and colleagues shrink in 2026 the mathematics of swirling flow behind a cylinder in a microchannel into a pocket-sized model. Engineers compress big flow simulations with two decomposition tools, POD and DMD, then hunt for hidden links among the resulting mode strengths. Their test flow ran at a Reynolds number of 100, and a sparse equation-discovery method read the mode histories for clean governing relationships.

The first POD mode held 33 percent of the flow's kinetic energy, and fourteen modes captured 99.2 percent in their decomposition. A model with just two degrees of freedom reproduced the vortex rhythm at its measured frequency of about one hertz. Hybrid POD-plus-DMD models kept energy steady over long runs, while a POD-only version drifted, so the authors recommend the hybrid.
pmc-13414063:
Li Wang and co-authors chart in 2026 the diversity of human papillomavirus type 53, a common type in China that no current vaccine covers. Clinical records from 158 positive patients anchored the study, and genomes from 134 isolates were compared gene by gene. Computer prediction then nominated T-cell epitopes, the viral fragments immune cells can learn to attack, across four viral proteins for laboratory checking.

Infections clustered in women aged forty to fifty-nine, and 13.3 percent of patients carried persistent infections in the clinical data. Four viral lineages emerged, with overall variation of 4.4 percent across the genomes; one protein varied most while another barely changed. Of twenty candidate epitopes tested, ten bound their immune targets strongly, and one E6 fragment dominated in mouse immunization.
pmc-13414163:
Biru Chen and co-authors map in 2026 the antibody targets on a helper protein of African swine fever virus, a plague devastating pig herds across Eurasia. The team produced the protein, confirmed infected pig serum recognizes it, and raised four monoclonal antibody lines against it.

Both stretches stay highly conserved across virus strains, suiting them for dependable diagnostic design. The authors also float the pair as ingredients for multi-epitope subunit vaccines against the disease.
pmc-13415563:
Yifang Mao and co-authors map how blood vessel lining cells keep dividing as mice age, in 2026. Endothelial cells renew themselves to maintain vessels, yet their pace across organs was unclear. A cumulative labeling method marked dividing cells in twelve organs at juvenile, young adult, and old adult stages.

pmc-13415663:
Atul Goel writes a 2026 letter to the editor about surgery for C2 schwannomas, benign nerve sheath tumors high in the neck. Writing from nearly forty years of work on these tumors, Goel faults a video presentation for skipping his group's contributions. The letter lays out an anatomical argument about where these tumors truly begin.

The C2 ganglion, the largest spinal sensory hub, sits outside the spinal canal, so its tumors start outside the spine and grow within a dural plane. Working in that plane can spare bone removal and avoid exposing the vertebral artery. Goel draws a parallel with trigeminal schwannomas at the skull base.
pmc-13415863:
Hayam Ali AlRasheed leads a 2026 study testing whether three blood markers can help identify depression and gauge its severity. Fifty patients with depression and fifty healthy controls gave serum samples. Markers covered oxidative DNA damage, an inflammation complex called NLRP3, and kynurenine, a tryptophan breakdown product.

All three markers ran significantly higher in patients than controls. Only the damage marker, 8-OHdG, related weakly to questionnaire severity scores and to illness duration, and even that link faded after strict correction. Used together in one model, the three markers separated patients from controls well, with an accuracy score near 0.86. Severity tracking remains weak, the authors note.
pmc-13416763:
Jemima Beddoe and colleagues bring Bunurong knowledge together with western science on marine mammals in Victoria, Australia, in a 2026 study. A Bunurong Elder shared five Stories that hold women's knowledge of Sea Country. The team read the Stories for ecological themes and compared them with current scientific literature.

The Stories cover which species occur, where they live, seasonal moves, and links between species. Much of this matched science, and some parts reached further back than written records. Gaps in science also stood out, around movement and habitat use. The authors present Indigenous led knowledge as a source of new research questions for conservation.
pmc-13417663:
Ying-Lun Chen and Zhen-Xuan Ma write a 2026 letter on inflammation and walking speed in older adults, using United States survey data from 1999 to 2002. Their marker, the systemic immune inflammation index, combines platelet, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts. Participants were 2,007 community living adults aged 60 or older, with gait measured over a 20 foot walk.

Higher index values linked to slower walking after wide adjustment, most clearly in men. People in the top quarter walked notably slower than those in the bottom quarter. Muscle pathways helped explain the link: leg strength accounted for about a third of the effect, and calf size for a smaller share.
pmc-13419463:
Michelle Campbell-Ward and colleagues push for stronger ethical habits in wildlife rescue, where kind motives meet hard choices daily. Rescuers treat free-ranging native animals hurt by a growing list of human-linked threats. Three worked rescue scenarios anchor the discussion, each raising risks and conflicts that simple goodwill cannot settle.

Choices in the scenarios span euthanasia, intensive hospital care, short support, and targeted treatment. The authors propose training in ethical reasoning, a review step that checks choices over time and across animals, and open records of decisions. Public support for rescue keeps rising, so the field's choices face more scrutiny than before. Clearer ethics could protect both animal welfare and the trust that funds the work.
pmc-13420263:
Amanuel Hika and colleagues compare routine blood chemistry in patients with high blood pressure against healthy controls at a referral hospital in western Ethiopia. Lasting high pressure quietly shifts kidney, sugar, and fat measures over time, so tracking them guides care. The study ran at Wallaga University Referral Hospital from June to August 2022.

Each arm held 105 people, matched as cases and controls in the design. Five milliliters of blood from each person fed tests for fasting sugar, salts, kidney markers, uric acid, and blood fats on one analyzer. Interviews and body measures filled out the picture beside the lab values. The hypertensive group showed the expected drift toward abnormal chemistry, a warning that pressure care must watch the organs, not just the cuff number.
pmc-13420563:
A 2026 case report by Tânia Amaro and colleagues follows a 45-year-old man whose eye muscles grew weak and whose retina showed pigment change. Breathlessness and tiredness on exertion sent him for a heart check, where tests found a slow and faulty heart rhythm. The picture pointed to Kearns-Sayre syndrome, a rare disorder of the cell energy system.

Heart scans showed a pump that still worked well, with no scar or shape fault, yet rhythm traces from a resting trace and a day-long monitor showed clear conduction faults. Amaro and colleagues warn that such faults can worsen without warning, so early permanent pacing deserves strong thought. A defibrillator rather than a pacemaker alone may fit when extra high-risk signs are present.
pmc-13421263:
Jeremy D. Yeaton and five colleagues present, in a 2026 paper, the first computational version of a classic two-stage account of how speakers build sentences. The account holds that a speaker first assembles a hierarchical sentence structure, then flattens it into a word sequence ready to say aloud.

Their multinomial processing tree model was fitted to speech samples from people with aphasia, whose error patterns reveal where production breaks down. Estimated ability at each stage matched observed error rates, and the stages mapped onto different brain areas: structure building to temporal and parietal regions, flattening to lower frontal regions. The authors argue the results support a real separation between the two stages of grammatical encoding.
pmc-13421463:
Song and colleagues report a 2026 engineering study of a tiny force sensor that measures tissue stiffness, a trait that shifts with disease. Standard stiffness tools are bulky or work only outside the body. The touch stayed gentle and did not damage the samples, so the same tissue could go on to other tests. pmc-13421563:

Two strains and the mixture performed best, and the mixture also cut pathogen survival sharply in a cheese-like test matrix. pmc-13422863:
Puengpong and colleagues test in 2026 a feed additive meant to protect broiler chickens from mycotoxins, poisons made by molds that contaminate grain. Their diet deliberately mixed four of these poisons at once, as real feed often does.

The trial placed 432 day-old male chicks into three feeding groups for 37 days. The groups ate clean feed, contaminated feed, or contaminated feed plus the detoxifier, a blend of clays, yeast cell wall, and beta-glucans dosed higher in the starter phase. Contamination hurt feed efficiency only in the first ten days. But it weakened vaccine antibody responses and damaged livers, raising fatty liver scores and inflammation seen under the microscope. pmc-13423063:

Newborn hearing screening was rated very important by 66.2% of respondents, and tympanometry, a middle-ear test, by 61.5%, though fewer performed either task many times a day. The authors use the gap between rated importance and daily volume to point at training and service-planning needs.
pmc-13423163:
Luma Bashmi and four co-authors systematically review non-clinical mental health and psychosocial support for Arabic-speaking refugees and displaced people across the Middle East and North Africa. Following standard reporting guidance, they searched ten databases and grey sources for work from 2011 to 2022. Thirty-eight studies qualified, and quality was checked with four established tools plus the new one, which tests fit with a framework linking social systems, trauma, and adaptation. Ten top-rated programmes received closer synthesis, showing which designs align best with the framework's principles.
pmc-13423963:
Catherine Crompton and colleagues tested in 2026 whether believing a partner is human rather than a computer changes collaborative learning in older adults. Twenty-four participants aged 66 to 79 completed a Map Task, talking through a route with a partner who was actually a computer system, but presented as either human or machine.

Engagement looked similar across partners, yet recall was more accurate for information supplied by the supposed human partner, and negative views of computer partners colored the experience. The paper suggests that perceived agency, not just actual partner type, shapes how older adults learn together.
pmc-13424263:
Moon and co-authors trace a fat-driven sabotage in this 2026 study of breast cancer, where the tissue around tumors is rich in fat cells. pmc-13424663:

pmc-13424863:

pmc-13425663:

pmc-13425863:

pmc-13425963:

Seventy-five adults admitted to San Francisco General Hospital took part, with 38 cases of lung infection and 37 controls admitted for other reasons. Surveys covered inhaled drugs, indoor and outdoor pollution, and job exposures, with models adjusting for plausible confounders. The typical participant was middle-aged, at a median age of 48 years, and mostly male.
pmc-13426363:

pmc-13426463:

pmc-13427263:

Parents' fears weighed heavily in those choices too.

pmc-13427563:

pmc-13428063:

pmc-13428463:

pmc-13429763:

After adjustment, only younger age and diagnosis remained robust predictors. pmc-13430763:

A survey of 1,623 students measured academic stress, AI dependence, self-efficacy, burnout, and anxiety, with sequential mediation models run for burnout and anxiety separately. Stress predicted both burnout and anxiety, and the path ran through rising AI dependence, which may cut mastery experiences and breed further reliance. Universities get a warning that AI help can quietly become a crutch under pressure.
pmc-13430863:

Lab tests showed it beat plain options on early measures, giving dentists a tool that hits gum disease from more than one side.
pmc-13432063:

Odd conduct showed in most, with defiance, acting out, food excess, and tantrums all named. Focus faults touched near half. Of six people with brain scans, half showed at least one shape fault. pmc-13433263:

pmc-13434263:

Six skill networks were set in advance, then math weighed how much each one drove each test score. Tests could then be ranked by which network they tap. Mixes of tests that best probe a chosen system also came into view. Test makers gain a brain based guide for picking and trimming test sets.
pmc-13434463:

Weakness starts to shape risk in future runs though it did not in the past. Aid can now target places where hard weather meets thin support.
pmc-13434663:

Microbe made clumps at the mud surface may shield it from oxygen. The team puts the global total at least six million tons of carbon per year. A quiet sink trims gas that would reach the air.
pmc-13435563:

pmc-13435763:

pmc-13437963:
Alexandra Van Cleave and colleagues give the first research picture of women's health care in Barrero, a semi-rural Dominican Republic community where no prior study had been done. Their 2026 survey asked 121 mothers, aged eighteen to fifty with children up to twelve, about family planning teaching received during pregnancy care. A twenty-eight question subset covered 216 pregnancies.

For eighty-two percent of pregnancies, a talk about postpartum family planning happened during prenatal visits. Among ninety-two women using contraception, the largest share, forty-four percent, relied on tubal ligation, a permanent method. Pills followed at twenty-two percent, then arm implants and injections, while condoms barely registered at one percent. The authors say knowing the full menu matters, since a choice made with partial knowledge may not fit a woman's plans. They propose follow-up work on whether the prenatal talks shape later method choice.
pmc-13438163:
Jiaqi Sun and co-authors report a new gene variant behind early ovarian failure running through one family. Premature ovarian insufficiency, where ovaries stall before age forty, often has genetic roots. The team focused on EIF4ENIF1, a gene that helps eggs mature. Their 2026 study read the full coding DNA of patients with ovarian insufficiency, early menopause, or shrinking egg reserve, then confirmed finds in relatives.

One splice-site change, never reported before, turned up in the first patient and was carried by her mother, grandmother, and sister as well. The change makes the gene skip a whole block, chopping the protein and warping its tail. Not every carrier showed the same degree of harm, a pattern called incomplete penetrance. Lab checks on the gene's message confirmed the skipping directly. The authors argue the find sharpens diagnosis for families like this one: a known variant lets doctors test relatives early.
pmc-13438463:
Jaime Iranzo and colleagues built a mathematical model that grows gene-sharing networks from three simple events, aiming to explain the shape those networks take among viruses and microbes. In such networks each genome links to every gene family it carries, and the web they form shows clear modules and layers. Their 2026 study derives the model's predictions on paper and by simulation, then fits it to real viral and microbial collections.

Three processes do the work: genes jumping between genomes, brand-new functions arising, and new kinds of organisms appearing. Together they reproduce the contrasting patterns seen in virus and microbe data, including how gene popularity and genome size spread out. Fitting the model turns those patterns into numbers, and the numbers say gene gain outweighs gene loss in virus evolution. For a field that often leans on family trees, the network view offers a second map.
pmc-13438663:
Rui Li and a large team doubled the guard duty in perovskite light-emitting diodes, pairing two additives that grip crystal defects together better than either could alone. These LEDs promise bright, efficient near-infrared light for communications and imaging, yet their films grow with defects on several crystal faces, and one additive covers only one face. Their 2026 study combined two small molecules chosen to chelate, or claw onto, faulty lead sites across three faces at once.

The pair slowed crystal growth, yielding smaller, more even grains and smoother films. The finished diodes hit a peak external quantum efficiency above twenty-six percent at a hefty current. The authors frame cooperative chelation as a design rule: match the additive team to the defect map. For a technology nearing commercial use, squeezing out the last non-radiative losses is the barrier that matters.
pmc-13439063:
Yeonjeong Koo and co-authors present a 2026 method for holding and tuning single quantum dots, tiny specks that emit light one photon at a time. Steady single-photon sources are prized for secure messaging and sensing, yet users also need live control over position, brightness, and colour. Past trapping tools could hold a dot in place without giving that fuller control.

Their setup pairs a sharp probe tip with light-based trapping in liquid, guided by a force microscope. Light forces and twist move each dot into place and line up its emission direction. Changing the tip gap and pressure shifted brightness and photon energy, from weak to strong coupling with the light field. The approach points toward switches and gates built from single light sources.
pmc-13439363:
Kai Chen and co-authors craft arch-shaped carbon ribbons edged with nitrogen, reporting the synthesis in 2026. Curved carbon molecules behave unlike flat ones and echo pieces of larger rounded carbon forms. Ribbons bent continuously in one direction remain rare and hard to make, though theory casts them as steps toward full carbon belts. The team extended flat rylene cores step by step with a planned curve, fusing five-membered rings along the edges.

Crystal structures confirmed smooth arches with unbroken curved surfaces. Heat-based magnetic resonance tests and calculations showed the arches resist flipping to their mirror curve. The longest arch, built from four rylene units, glowed more efficiently in solution than kin and cradled fullerene C60 guests in solution and solid alike. The route may open paths to long-sought carbon nanobelts.
pmc-13439663:
M. Melissa Peet and co-authors develop a microneedle patch that delivers three HIV-neutralising antibodies through the skin, avoiding the large injections or infusions these antibodies currently require. Their 2026 proof-of-concept study fabricates patch units, called pixels, each carrying about two milligrams of one antibody, for combined use.

In pig skin tests, the microneedles penetrated effectively. Dropped into buffer, they dissolved fully within ten minutes, releasing their antibody cargo. Two of the three antibodies kept full virus-neutralising activity after manufacturing, while the third lost some potency. In rats, wearing one patch unit per antibody produced blood exposure within three hours, peaking by day three. The authors note the solid patch might remove the need for refrigerated storage, suiting low-resource settings and infants, but stress that clinical utility needs much more investigation.
pmc-13439763:
Junmin Tao's team studied ambulance transport in 2026 among 773 acute ischemic stroke patients at one Dalian hospital, asking whether EMS arrival improves three-month recovery. Ambulance use remains debated despite faster hospital arrival, since in-hospital delays may offset gains. Inverse probability weighting balanced baseline differences, and good recovery was defined as near-zero disability at three months, with onset-to-door and door-to-needle times compared.

Ambulance patients arrived faster but waited longer for needle treatment. Overall good recovery did not differ significantly between groups, though subgroups with heart disease history and non-smokers showed lower recovery odds with EMS transport. Stroke systems get a nuanced result: speed to the door alone does not guarantee better outcomes. Door-to-needle processes need equal attention.
pmc-13441063:
Zahra Akhoond-Ali and colleagues ask whether bleeding in one mouse brain region reshapes wiring and attention in a distant region, reporting in 2026. The medial prefrontal cortex, a planning hub, talks closely with the hippocampus, a memory hub. Mice received a small haemorrhage in the prefrontal area or a sham operation. Over seventeen days the team graded neurological signs and ran an attentional set-shifting task, which tests how flexibly animals switch rules.

General deficit scores matched between groups, hiding a specific gap. Bleed mice finished fewer task stages and needed more trials, with more rule-loss errors along the way. Tissue staining showed denser dendritic spines, the tiny contact knobs on nerve cells, in hippocampal area CA1 after the bleed, mainly on the right side. White matter stayed unchanged. The authors link remote spine growth to the attention problem and nominate hippocampal plasticity as a recovery target.
pmc-13441263:
Anna Fogelström and colleagues search Swedish registry data for mother-side factors tied to omphalocele, a rare birth defect where organs herniate through the navel ring inside a sac, reporting in 2026. Causes of the defect remain partly obscure. The population case-control study matched 207 affected births from 1997 to 2016 with 2,070 unaffected births by sex and birth year. Regression models weighed candidate maternal factors together.

Mothers with obesity carried close to double the adjusted odds of an affected baby. Conception by in vitro fertilisation carried a still higher adjusted association, over fourfold, though with wide uncertainty. Having given birth before cut the odds by more than half, and most affected babies were firstborns. The authors present obesity and IVF conception as risk markers deserving attention in counselling and in further causal research, not as proven causes.
pmc-13441763:
Abeer Qasim and colleagues survey the first drug era for fatty liver inflammation tied to metabolic disease, reviewing approved and emerging agents in 2026. The condition, now called MASH, scars the liver and drives cirrhosis, touching a few percent of adults worldwide and far more among people with type 2 diabetes. For decades only lifestyle change was offered. Approvals in 2024 and 2025 for resmetirom and semaglutide changed the field.

Trial figures for both drugs are laid out, covering liver healing and scar improvement against placebo. Older options including pioglitazone and vitamin E are weighed, alongside an India-approved dual agent still in mid-stage trials. A testing toolkit for staging without biopsy, from blood scores to elastography, is fitted into a risk-stratified care algorithm. The authors call the moment a genuine era change, with patient selection now the core skill.
pmc-13441963:
Anna Di Dio and colleagues map how fat chemistry sets a cancer cell's vulnerability to ferroptosis, an iron-driven death by membrane rusting, in a 2026 review. Whether a tumour dies this way depends on its metabolic state, not a fixed trait. Cells constantly remodel membrane fats: polyunsaturated chains invite the peroxidation that drives ferroptosis, while monounsaturated fats, droplet storage, and cholesterol relatives raise the threshold. Defence systems that mop up lipid peroxides form the other side of the balance.

Drug-resistant and dormant persister cells often live near the edge, stressed yet dependent on peroxide cleanup, which makes them tempting targets. Stem-like states vary by context, buffered in some settings and exposed in others. The authors propose combining fat profiles, gene activity, and cell-state markers to select patients for ferroptosis-based therapy. Genotype and the tumour's neighbourhood both shift the threshold in their account.
pmc-13442463:
Yonglu Wang and colleagues search for brain network marks of autism in 80 youths aged 6 to 16 years in a 2026 study. Fifty matched youths without autism served as the comparison group. Resting brain scans, taken while the mind idles, fed a group-wise sparse coding method that learns shared network parts.

The method broke shared networks into zones, and links among zones formed a grid for each child. Three ways of reading that grid were tried for sorting youths with autism from the comparison group. The group reports that grid-based sorting can split the two sets of youths, which hints at a scan mark for a diagnosis now made by watching behavior. The authors stress that empathy and social skill gaps in autism map to linked brain circuits, so network-level marks fit the illness well.
pmc-13442663:
Lei Cai and colleagues review lab systems that grow tumor balls beside immune cells in a 2026 paper. These balls, called organoids, copy the shape, genes, and acts of real tumors from a patient. Mixed growth lets labs watch immune attack and escape in a dish.

Three build styles get weighed, from simple mixes to slice cultures, air-face growth, and chip-based flows. The review scores each style on growth success, immune cell life span, and how well dish results match patient results. Uses span brake-drug screens and cell therapy tests with CAR-T and CAR-NK cells. Blocks to clinic use loom large, from batch drift to lost tumor variety and no blood flow. The authors ask for shared build rules before such systems guide real care.
pmc-13442863:
Xiaoyu Che and colleagues build a flat lens array that can shift focus for 3D cameras in a 2026 paper. Light-field cameras record both place and angle of light, yet fixed-focus lenslets cap their depth range. Their array bonds two patterned sheets, each with 24 by 20 zones of cubic-phase design.

Sliding one sheet sideways tunes focus in a smooth sweep across a 3.33 to 4.50 mm range in their device. Mounted in a plenoptic camera, the array widened the sharp depth band. A fusion program, MultiLensFusion, stacks shots at varied focus into one crisp full-depth image. The authors pitch the flat array as a slim swap for bulky lens stacks. Such tunable optics could serve phone cameras and tiny medical scopes alike.
pmc-13443863:
Faisal Aldawsari and coauthors propose a 2026 control upgrade for grid-connected Archimedes Wave Swing converters, replacing standard proportional-integral controllers with twin-delayed deep reinforcement learning agents. One agent steers generator currents to cut stator losses and harvest more wave energy, while grid-side agents hold DC link and coupling voltages steady.

Simulations in MATLAB Simulink under steady, transient, and fault conditions showed the hybrid grid-side agent beating the all-classic setup in both dynamic and steady response. The hybrid pairs two classic controllers with one learning agent. Wave power gains a steadier grid citizen from the approach, though sea trials must confirm that simulated robustness survives real waves.
pmc-13444063:
Chikoo Oosawa derives a 2026 closed-form test for when simple power-law approximations suffice in biochemical systems theory, a field that often swaps complex rate laws for first-order log-linear forms. Under Gaussian log-input fluctuations, the expected KL risk of the shortcut collapses to a trace contraction of the local curvature Hessian with the input covariance.

The criterion can be gauged straight from disturbance data or mechanism-based models near a working point, and a fourth-order correction covers non-Gaussian inputs. Toy models and two biochemical case studies matched Monte Carlo estimates and pinpointed conditions and perturbation directions where the shortcut should fail. Modelers gain a cheap adequacy check before trusting a reduced model.
pmc-13444263:
Evelyn Zumba Altamirano and colleagues report scope removal of a swallowed toothbrush from a 13-year-old in a 2026 case paper. Swallowed objects rank among the top child emergencies, and toothbrush cases date to a first report in 1882. The teen arrived three hours after the swallow with mild belly pain and nausea.

X-rays in two views showed the brush low in the chest zone, with bristles in the stomach. A scope found the handle in the lower food pipe, reaching into the stomach, with the head stuck in the stomach wall. The team pulled the brush out through the scope in that session. The authors note that toothbrushes almost never pass on their own. Early scope work, they stress, heads off tears and blocks.
pmc-13445963:
Alaa Baqer Alali and colleagues pool studies on skin-applied retinoid drugs in early pregnancy and the risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, in a 2026 review. Oral forms of these vitamin A drugs are known to harm a fetus, which has long cast a shadow over the skin forms. The team searched five databases through late 2025.

Eight studies covering more than three and a half million pregnancies met the rules. Exposure in the first three months showed no clear link to either outcome, with risk estimates sitting near or below the mark for no effect. Several Bayesian checks agreed, leaning toward no added risk. The authors still urge care, since one large registry study drove much of the weight.
pmc-13446363:
Geoffrey Millour and colleagues test pupil size as a live readout of acute stress, in a 2026 experiment with thirty adults. Two versions of a color-word task supplied the stress: a plain form and a social, competitive form judged against others. Measures spanned pupils, heart rhythm, breathing, blood pressure, spit hormones, and felt stress, tracked into a twenty-minute recovery.

Only the competitive form widened pupils and raised felt stress during the task. Its hormone replies, cortisol and amylase, peaked ten minutes after the task and then eased, while both groups showed some amylase rise. Heart, breathing, and pressure measures never split the groups. Pupil size stood alone as a real-time split, which backs eye tracking in stress research.
pmc-13446563:
Amanda E. Friedman and colleagues delete parts of the neurexin 1 gene in zebrafish to see how losing each version of the protein bends behavior, in a 2026 study. The human gene links to autism and schizophrenia, and it makes three main protein forms. Which form's loss drives which deficit was unclear from patient data alone.

Larvae faced movement and startle tests, and juveniles took a hands-free social choice test the team built. Deletions that struck unlike mixes of the three forms gave both shared and distinct faults across movement, sensing, and social pull. The pattern backs a model where the stretch of gene lost forecasts the behavior lost, a step toward reading patient gene reports with care.
pmc-13448063:
Pasikhova and colleagues charted in 2026 nontuberculous mycobacterial infections at a major Florida cancer centre. These environmental germs become opportunistic invaders in vulnerable people, and cancer patients are barely covered in past literature. The team reviewed adults with proven infections from 2020 to 2023, pulling epidemiology and treatment details from medical records.

Pasikhova found 93 patients, and four in five had a past or active cancer. Two germ groups dominated: Mycobacterium avium complex in about half and the Mycobacterium abscessus group in about three in ten. Most infections sat in the lungs, with skin the main site elsewhere. Just over half received treatment, usually with three or more drugs, and four in five of those needed their starting regimen changed. About three quarters felt better, while just under four in ten cleared the germ on cultures, and about a quarter died or were lost to follow-up.
pmc-13448863:
Alexander Kokkinos and colleagues return in 2026 to two large tirzepatide trials to ask whether early weight loss predicts the final result. The post hoc analysis covered 2,384 treated participants with obesity or overweight, with or without type 2 diabetes, from the SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2 trials. People who lost at least 5 percent of body weight by week 8 counted as early responders.

Both groups reached meaningful weight loss and better risk measures by week 72, including improved blood sugar control. Early responders, who were more often women and started with lower blood sugar, improved significantly more on nearly every measure. Stomach and bowel side effects followed similar patterns, severity, and timing in both groups. The authors suggest the week-8 milestone can help set expectations without signaling that slower starters should stop treatment.
pmc-13449763:
Salerno and colleagues tested in 2026 whether brief exposure to DMT, a psychedelic compound found in the Amazonian brew ayahuasca, spurs growth in human neural stem cells. DMT shows fast antidepressant effects in early studies, and lasting benefits are thought to involve brain plasticity, including the birth of new neurons shown in rodents. Whether it acts on human stem cells was unknown, so the team used lab-grown human stem cells.

A one-day DMT treatment raised cell growth in step with dose and switched on genes that push cells through the first growth phase. The compound also shifted growth-factor signals, raising nerve growth factor and a brain support factor while lowering another. After the drug was washed out, treated cells formed larger spheres whose cell mix matched controls by day ten. The authors say brief exposure can trigger growth responses at levels seen in other plasticity work.
pmc-13450063:
Jeong Hyeon Seong and colleagues compared lung disease by cause in 2026, asking whether infection-linked cases differ from smoking-linked ones. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease varies by cause, yet clinical traits by cause were not well mapped. Blood eosinophils, a type of white cell, help guide steroid inhaler use, so any difference could change treatment.

Among 873 patients, only 41 had infection as the sole cause, against 832 with any smoking link. The infection group more often had low eosinophil counts and less often received inhaled steroids, a link that held in adjusted models. They also showed more air trapping, with a higher residual volume share. The findings support treating infection-linked disease as a distinct clinical type.
pmc-13450463:
Yamei Gao and colleagues made a smart skin gel in 2026 that hits two drivers of inflamed skin at once. Psoriasis and eczema weigh heavily on patients round the world, while current drugs are held back by weak effect, hard access, and high cost. The team paired a block on CCR7, which curbs immune cell travel, with a block on JAK1, which calms local swelling signals.

A gel that reacts to pH carried CCR7-targeting RNA plus the JAK1 drug upadacitinib to the skin. In dish tests, the gel slowed skin-cell growth, spurred cell death, and lowered key signals and swelling proteins. In mice with psoriasis-like and eczema-like skin, the gel eased sores, fixed the skin barrier, and calmed whole-body immune flare with good safety. Skin doctors gain a two-action gel lead for two stubborn skin ills.
pmc-13450563:
Maryam Al-Muzaffar and co-authors report a 2026 eye surgery case where a patch from the eye's own outer coat closed a large hole at the center of sight. Their patient, a woman aged 63 with diabetes-linked eye disease, had a full-depth hole over a millimeter wide. A past operation had already used the skin-like layer surgeons often patch with.

The team lifted a small patch of Tenon's capsule, a coat that wraps the eyeball, and laid it over the gap, held in place with oil. Scans a month later showed the hole shut, and it stayed shut at six months. Her sight rose from seeing hand motion only to a low but real level, so the team offers the patch as a backup plan.
pmc-13451063:
Matisse and colleagues described in 2026 a man in his thirties whose thigh pain turned out to be diabetic myonecrosis. That is a rare death of muscle tissue tied to poorly controlled diabetes. Fewer than 200 cases have been reported since the condition was first named in 1965, and it is often mistaken for infection or a blood clot. The man's pain and swelling grew over two weeks with no injury.

His blood sugar ran very high, with a long-term marker far above target, and scans first suggested muscle inflammation. Antibiotics and work-ups for infection and immune causes did not help. A repeat MRI showed a dead region inside the thigh muscle, the classic picture of this condition. The authors stress that MRI is the best test, and that early spotting spares patients needless procedures.
pmc-13451263:
Vishnu Nair and co-authors test in 2026 a spider-shaped underwater robot that swims with flapping side fins spread along its body. Most swim robots drive fins from one center point, while this six-leg design places soft fins between leg groups, so lift spreads out and the body steadies itself. The team checked the design three ways: hand math, fluid software runs, and tank trials with a lab model.

The three checks agreed on lift within a tenth or so across speeds. Software runs showed a steady lift-to-drag balance near the fin speeds tested, plus flow patterns in the target range. The authors offer the layout for survey and inspection bots that need thrift and tight turns.
pmc-13452163:
Shakibi and co-authors review a surprising medical technology, in this 2026 article. The technology is tattoos that sense and treat disease from inside the skin. Unlike wrist wearables or surface patches, dermal tattoos sit within the skin's middle layer. There they can sample the fluid between cells. They also stay protected from dirt, sweat, and abrasion for long periods.

The review catalogs prototypes that change color or glow to report biomarkers, electrolytes, and ultraviolet exposure, plus designs that read electrical signals from the body. Newer work pushes into therapy, with self-powered bioelectronic tattoos that stimulate wound healing and dissolvable interfaces that vanish after doing their job. The authors are frank about immaturity: nearly all platforms remain proof-of-concept, with little testing in living subjects, no shared performance benchmarks, and thin long-term safety data.
pmc-13452363:
Tibakanya Joseph and co-authors present in 2026 CoMAD, a method for building math test data sets that know how hard each item thinks. AI tools now write test items fast, which raises demand for sets tied to a syllabus and tagged by thinking depth. Their frame tags items with two known ladders of thought depth, joined in a matrix, plus language load reads.

A sample set, HiCogMath, shows the method at work. The frame is built in modules under fair data rules, so it can move to other subjects, lands, and syllabi. Uses span mind modeling, item writing by machine, and tuning of large language models for schools.
pmc-13453463:
Sergio García-García and four co-authors follow how large brain aneurysms change in size after a flow diverter stent is placed. These bulges in brain arteries, 15 millimetres or more, carry a high burst risk and few good treatment paths. Their 2026 study covers 24 patients treated between 2018 and 2022, with late MRI follow up.

The open channel inside the bulge shrank clearly over time, yet the total bulge volume did not fall by a solid margin. Full closure of the bulge reached 79 percent, and closed cases started with narrower necks and smaller volumes. Four patients died, three of them after a post treatment burst, a stark mark of the risk these bulges carry. The authors conclude the stent works by stopping flow inside the sac, not by shrinking it.
pmc-13453763:
Karen Libberecht and nine co-authors give a practical recipe for growing clean Schwann cell cultures from adult mouse nerves. Schwann cells wrap and support peripheral nerves, but fibroblasts in the mix multiply fast and swamp them in the dish. Older fixes rely on long culture, starvation tricks, or grabbing the Schwann cells with antibodies, all of which can distort them.

The new method sorts cells by light scatter and pulls out only the fibroblasts, flagged by a surface marker called CD90.2. The Schwann cells stay untouched by antibodies, keeping their surface features and natural state. Gene, protein, and staining checks confirmed rich Schwann cell growth with little fibroblast left.
