The team offers the protocol as a fast route to true to life cells for nerve studies.
pmc-13454063:
Gopal Singh Jamnal builds a forecasting framework for company earnings growth that tries to stay accurate, explainable, and causally honest at once. Classic models lean on stiff linear rules, while black box models hide their reasons. His 2026 framework, called TRuE-XAI, trains tree based classifiers on SEC filings from United States listed firms across 2014 to 2024.

The best setup, a TomekLinks cleaned XGBoost model, reached an F1 score of 0.467 with accuracy of 0.849. Short if then rules explain single calls, while importance checks name steady drivers across models. Causal tools then test which drivers truly move the odds: profit margin change, sales growth, and asset turnover helped, while inventory load and one cash ratio hurt. Placebo checks backed the causal reads. Jamnal offers the stack as decision support for investors and regulators.
pmc-13454263:
Lin Jing and seven co-authors stack two patterned surfaces to block radiative heat flow across a broad band, without any metal. Metal reflectors fail where electric conduction or material clashes rule them out, and classic non metal designs hit a bandwidth wall. Their 2026 design pairs two aperiodic layered reflectors whose pass bands are deliberately offset.

A computer search tuned the pair for thermal decoupling in a thin, cheap stack. Tests showed an 82 percent cut in radiative exchange by angle resolved measures and a 62.5 percent cut by direct power readings, against plain fused silica. The pair held up across build errors and a working range of 320 to 500 kelvin. The authors offer the all dielectric design for insulation and heat control in tight spaces.
pmc-13454663:
Tomohiro Matsuo leads a twelve-author study, from 2026, of what helps heart patients regain daily living skills in community rehabilitation wards. Patients move to such wards after acute care to continue cardiac rehabilitation, and most improve. Which traits predict the biggest gains was unclear, so the team drew on a multicenter Japanese registry.

This interim look covered 198 patients averaging about 78 years old. Gain was scored with a standard independence measure. Patients who arrived with better leg strength and balance, sharper thinking, and a longer ward stay gained the most. Those who arrived already highly independent gained least, since they had little room to rise. The authors suggest that simple admission tests plus adequate stay length can flag who will benefit most from post-acute rehabilitation.
pmc-13455463:
Tingting Yang and colleagues introduce a deep learning tool for predicting traits from DNA in a 2026 study. Genomic selection ranks breeding candidates from genome-wide markers. Deep learning has begun to beat older statistical models, though complex gene patterns remain hard to capture. The new framework, Gsformer, offers two designs: one pairing convolutional networks with self-attention, one using sparse attention to save time. It was tested on pig, cattle, chicken, mouse, wheat and maize.

Gsformer generally ranked among the top two models against five rivals. Its full design led for cattle fat percentage. Its sparse design led for chicken egg weight, pig growth age and mouse anxiety. Sparse attention at a 20 percent setting matched the full design on most traits. Gene explanations pointed to growth and body size pathways in pigs. Breeders gain a flexible, cheaper predictor, with the sparse version recommended when a small accuracy trade is acceptable.
pmc-13456963:
Kadelka and Coberly present BoolForge, a Python toolbox for building and probing Boolean networks, the on off switch models used to mimic gene regulation and cell decisions. Real biological networks show canalization, a layered logic where some inputs can force the output and mute the rest, which steadies cell behavior. Existing software rarely lets users dial that property in. Their 2026 paper describes a generator and analyzer built around that gap.

Users can mint random Boolean rules with a set canalizing depth and layer structure. They assemble networks with tuned wiring and logic. They then measure canalization, robustness to flips, modularity, and attractor states, the end patterns a network settles into. Controlled generation lets researchers build fair null models, the baseline worlds a real network must beat, and test theory on ensembles rather than single cases. The package installs with one pip command, and a tutorial set ships with it.
pmc-13457463:
Fei Lu, Jinsu Wang, and Xinglong Zhai ask whether merging culture and tourism policy makes cities ecologically tougher. Using panel data from 284 prefecture-level Chinese cities between 2010 and 2023, their 2026 study treats the staggered rollout of culture-tourism integration policies as a natural experiment. A multi-period difference-in-differences design compares cities before and after adoption against cities yet to adopt, measuring urban ecological resilience.

The policies lifted resilience significantly, and the finding survived propensity matching, placebo tests, instrumental variables, and double machine learning. Three channels carried the effect: industrial structure moved upmarket, green technology innovation rose, and public environmental awareness grew. Every region gained, though central and western cities gained most, and effects ran stronger in larger administrative centers and cities without official historic-cultural status. The authors present the strategy as proof that development and ecological protection can advance together, with possible public-health bonuses.
pmc-13458363:
Fernando Valdivieso-Rivera and colleagues find a molecular bodyguard that keeps brown fat mitochondria whole when obesity tries to shatter them. Brown fat burns energy and supports glucose control, yet obesity fragments its mitochondria and dulls their output. Their 2026 study pins the protection on E4BP4, a transcriptional repressor that partners with the fat regulator PRDM16.

Working through a DNA enhancer 65 kilobases upstream of the Cers6 gene, the pair switches that gene down. That cuts production of C16:0 ceramide, a fatty molecule that builds up and breaks mitochondrial networks apart. Boosting E4BP4 in brown fat kept mitochondrial networks intact and oxidative capacity high, and the animals' whole-body glucose handling improved without any weight loss, keeping the metabolic gain apart from mere slimming. The authors cast ceramide control as a lever for defending brown fat in obesity, with possible bearing on diabetes therapies that bypass the scale.
pmc-13458663:
Qianxin Zhou and colleagues report a salvage pairing for lung cancers that have escaped their targeted pills. When EGFR- or ALK-driven tumors resist the matching kinase inhibitor, many lean on MET overexpression as an escape route. Their 2026 single-center retrospective study follows 23 heavily pretreated patients with proven MET overexpression who received a MET inhibitor layered onto their original EGFR or ALK drug.

The combination shrank tumors in 69.6 percent of patients, with 16 partial responses and six more holding stable disease. Median time before progression ran 6.9 months. Tumors staining strongest for MET, scored IHC 3+, responded more often than the IHC 2+ group, hinting the biomarker's intensity grades the benefit. Side effects stayed mostly low-grade and manageable. In a population with few options left, the authors call dual blockade a viable resistance-breaking strategy and a real-world complement to trial data built on MET gene amplification rather than protein overexpression.
pmc-13458763:
Fina Amreta Laksmi and colleagues improve a low-calorie sweetener enzyme with a single amino acid switch in a 2026 study. D-allulose, a fructose epimer with anti-obesity and anti-diabetic promise, is made by d-allulose 3-epimerase, yet natural enzymes lack the efficiency and heat tolerance for cheap large-scale production. A single E35H change in Arthrobacter psychrolactophilus epimerase was modelled by AlphaFold and molecular dynamics, then tested by spectroscopy and thermal unfolding.

The change raised catalytic efficiency 1.4-fold, through a 1.3-fold fall in Km and a 1.1-fold rise in kcat, while loosening the active site as hydrogen bonds at residue 35 fell from six to five and local flexibility rose at residues 35 and 6. Overall fluctuations fell, and melting temperature rose slightly from 92.6 to 94.3 degrees Celsius. Food engineers gain a hotspot rule for balancing flexibility and rigidity in epimerase design.
pmc-13458863:
Teresia Mutavi and colleagues test whether lay helpers in Nairobi can learn a brief therapy for anxious and depressed teenagers, and whether supervision is where the learning actually happens. Their 2026 evaluation trains 17 non-specialist providers in PRO-ACT, a four-to-six session cognitive-behavioral program, rating their skills with standardized role plays before training, after training, and after clinical supervision. Eighteen adolescents then received the intervention and completed symptom scales.

Training alone moved nothing measurable. Supervision changed the picture: potentially harmful behaviors dropped significantly, and basic or advanced competencies rose by about two items. The teenagers' anxiety and depression scores on the RCADS fell, by roughly three points each, although the PHQ-9 depression scale did not budge, a discrepancy the authors leave visible. With no control group, the study claims only preliminary promise, yet it argues task-sharing programs should budget for sustained supervision, not just workshops.
pmc-13459163:
Junyan An and co-authors built a bedside prediction tool for a painful problem: a first attack of pancreatitis caused by very high blood triglycerides often comes back. Their 2026 study reviewed 278 patients admitted with a first episode between 2019 and 2023 and followed their records for three years. The team combined admission blood tests, lifestyle history, and muscle density measured on CT scans to find which factors forecast recurrence, then turned them into a scoring chart called a nomogram.

Within three years, 82 patients, 29.5 percent of the cohort, suffered a recurrence. A combined sugar-and-fat index and a smoking history raised the risk, while denser skeletal muscle and higher blood albumin, a nutrition-related protein, lowered it. The finished nomogram distinguished future recurrence well, with an accuracy score of 0.896 on the standard curve measure, and it held up under internal re-testing. The authors suggest using it to target follow-up.
pmc-13459363:
Luzheng Zhang and co-authors review how hydrogen sulfide, a gas the body makes in small amounts, fine-tunes the cardiovascular system by chemically tagging proteins. The tag, called S-persulfidation, converts a sulfur site on proteins into a more reactive form that shields it from permanent oxidative damage, reversibly. Their 2026 review synthesizes how detection methods evolved, from early biotin-switch assays to modern reactivity profiling, and how the tag acts across heart and blood vessel biology.

The modification adjusts blood vessel tone by changing how ion channels open, including potassium and calcium channels. Inside cells it steers kinase signaling chains, the Keap1/Nrf2 antioxidant sensor system, and enzymes that keep mitochondria producing energy. It also touches gene-control proteins and protects the cell's protein quality-control machinery. The authors assess delivery systems for sulfur-based drugs as a translational frontier.
pmc-13459463:
Peiqian Wu and co-authors tested whether creativity is best predicted not by single traits but by the general factor of personality. That factor is one broad dimension summarizing how socially effective someone's overall trait profile is. Their 2026 study measured the Big Five traits and several kinds of creativity in the same participants. It used both questionnaires and performance tasks to reduce self report bias, then asked whether the general factor tracked creative traits, creative skill, or both.

The general factor correlated consistently with every indicator, with correlations exceeding 0.60 across the questionnaire based measures used in the study. Latent estimates for performance based skill were lower, ranging from 0.31 to 0.40 across the analyses the team reported. Creative traits aligned far more strongly with the general factor, with a correlation of 0.75 for traits and only 0.36 for tested skill. Broad personality shapes self described creative character far more than tested skill.
pmc-13460163:
Cheng Zhang and colleagues surveyed in 2026 United Kingdom medical trainees about on-call schedules, sleep knowledge, and sleep quality. One hundred seven trainees answered an online questionnaire between February and April 2025, most of them resident physicians. The survey covered daily routines, sleep habits during on-call and off-call periods, daytime sleepiness, and insomnia severity, alongside basic questions testing what trainees know about sleep.

On-call days ran a median of thirteen working hours against nine on ordinary days, and sleep shrank from about seven hours to about six. That squeeze matters for trainee health and for patient safety, yet solid data on ideal shift length and frequency remain scarce. The pilot maps the problem locally and sets up larger work on scheduling and sleep education.
pmc-13461463:
Ritchie Edward Brown, Dalva L. R. Poyares, Stephen Sheldon, and Radhika Basheer introduce in 2026 a collection of eight review articles surveying sleep science in 2024. The set ranges across pediatric sleep, non-drug treatments for better sleep, and fresh brain mechanisms by which physical and social stress reshape sleep and waking. Three of the eight reviews concern the youngest sleepers, a group the editors say gets too little attention given the clinical stakes.

One review maps how infant sleep matures across the first six months using the two standard measurement traditions, movement trackers and parent diaries. Another tackles fragmented sleep in critically ill children, linking disruption to altered brain development and proposing gentler light and sound in intensive care. A third covers childhood narcolepsy, often missed until the late teens.
pmc-13462063:
Eric Stahlberg and co-editors introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a collection on digital twins for cancer care. A digital twin is a computer copy of a real thing, kept in sync with data to guide decisions. NASA first used the idea for spacecraft. Oncology, the editors argue, is a hard test ground: cancers are complex, vary a lot, and data are often scarce.

The collection gathers work where twin methods meet artificial intelligence in cancer care. Papers range from comparing smart-city twins with tumor twins to building data warehouses for urinary cancers and weighing what patient advocates need. Shared success factors recur: patients taking part, doctors trusting the twin's insights, and long data records from many people. Lessons from one patient's twin could seed twins for the next. The editors present the field as early yet promising for lighter cancer burden and better outcomes.
pmc-13462763:
A-Ram Jeong and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, the family tree of Fusarium fungi causing wilt in watermelon and melon across Korea. The genus holds over 400 species grouped into complexes, many living in soil and hard to tell apart. Two specialist forms were long blamed for these wilts, yet work hinted that more species join in. The team gathered thirty-three isolates from growing regions.

Gene sequencing at loci sorted the isolates into five species complexes, only one the classic oxysporum group. Shape and microscope traits backed the assignments. Infection tests proved a representative from each complex could cause wilt in both watermelon and melon. The result widens the suspect list beyond the two traditional forms. The authors argue that diagnosis and disease control for these crops must use family-tree-aware tests, since look-alike fungi from other complexes can produce the same disaster.
pmc-13463863:
Aurora García-Camacha Gutiérrez leads a survey of nurses in Spain on care fitted to each older patient. Care that fits the person is a mark of quality, yet heavy workloads since COVID-19 have strained it. The team asked ninety-six nurses to rate such care and the ethical tone of their workplace.

Nurses rated personal-fit care well overall, with top marks for heeding each patient's clinical state. Fitting in patient choices and keeping hygiene routines personal scored lowest. A fairer, more supportive workplace tone tracked with stronger personal-fit care. Hospital nurses rated care higher than nursing home nurses, a gap the authors say needs targeted training and team support.
pmc-13464263:
Theodora C. Esomonye and seven co-authors trial a burst-learning course that teaches residents to read electrocardiograms. Internal medicine residents face rhythm problems daily, yet formal ECG training stays thin and accuracy runs low. Their course ran fourteen weeks with twelve short case sessions on twenty high-risk rhythms.

Twenty-six residents took the opening quiz, and fifteen finished the closing one. Confidence in reading traces and handling rhythm problems rose clearly after the course. Knowledge scores, though, barely moved between the two rounds. The school kept the course on its regular schedule for its low cost. Deeper skill gains, the authors say, will need a longer dose and paired testing.
pmc-13464563:
Sebastian Zapp and three co-authors audit the proof behind permanently listed digital health apps in Germany. Since 2019, app makers can win insurance coverage by showing benefit in comparative studies. The team combed four databases for studies from 2020 to 2024 that judged those app trials.

Of more than four thousand six hundred papers screened, sixteen fit the audit. Weakness showed up most in validity, openness, and fairness of the trials behind the apps. Small patient groups, self-reported outcomes, and passive comparison groups were common flaws. Dropout ran high, and blinding was rare. Stronger methods and fuller reporting, the authors argue, must pair with real-world data before the apps earn lasting trust.
pmc-13465963:
Spencer Collins, Tyler Williams, Edgar Sanchez, and Devendra Agrawal review what drives mast cell activation syndrome, a disorder that produces scattered symptoms across many body systems, in a 2026 article. Because its signs are vague and varied, doctors often miss or delay the diagnosis. The review maps the pathways that push mast cells into overdrive.

Both allergy-linked and non-allergy routes can trigger the cells, and inner signaling chains then amplify the response. Once activated, mast cells release histamine, tryptase, and a crowd of other mediators that spread the disturbance further. The authors close by pointing to targeted blockers of these pathways as promising treatment directions for a condition with few good options today.
pmc-13466263:
Takayasu Ohtake and Shuzo Kobayashi introduce a journal special issue on chronic kidney disease by surveying what biomarkers can do for it. Kidney disease is rising worldwide, and blood and urine markers promise earlier warning than standard kidney function tests alone.

One highlighted marker, ADMA, tracked both heart artery hardening and kidney decline in patients not yet on dialysis. A urine protein called L-FABP predicted kidney decline in diabetic and hypertensive patients whose standard scores still looked preserved. Another study built a heatmap estimating lifetime kidney-failure risk from a single kidney score plus age. Ohtake stresses markers are not yet full diagnostic tools, but they already guide risk sorting and treatment choice.
pmc-13466663:
Hongying Ma, Weiwei Zhang, Hong Liu, and Lei Liang report a large abdominal tumor found during pregnancy that was first mistaken for a uterine fibroid, in a 2026 case report. The patient, thirty-two and fourteen weeks pregnant, also had a low-lying placenta. Scans showed a huge quiet mass above the womb threaded with connecting vessels.

A multidisciplinary team judged the growth a desmoid-type fibromatosis, a tumor that invades locally without spreading, arising here from the ileocecal region where small and large bowel meet, an extremely rare origin. At the patient's request the pregnancy was ended and the mass removed in open surgery. Such tumors appear in only a few people per million each year.
pmc-13466763:
Alex Novikov and colleagues engineer immune cells guided by a natural growth factor fragment to attack cancers driven by the HER receptor family, in a 2026 study. Standard engineered T cell therapy aimed at HER2 alone struggles with safety problems and tumors that shed the target. Their reporter system reads which receptor pairs a tumor actually displays.

The beta form of neuregulin-1 grips this receptor family flexibly, so cells built around it kept working even in models that had lost HER2. In three-dimensional tissue models the approach killed tumors strongly while releasing a calmer mix of inflammatory signals than current clinical designs. Natural killer cell versions were built alongside the T cell ones.
pmc-13466863:
Yun Xiao, Zhourui Liu, and Sha Li report a cancer growing inside the pulmonary artery of a young man. The tumor is so rare that it is often mistaken for something else before surgery, as their 2026 case report shows. The thirty-five-year-old had chest pain on exertion for a month, steady vital signs, and no heart murmur. A heart strain marker in his blood ran high.

Ultrasound showed an irregular solid mass, roughly four by two centimeters, sitting at the pulmonary valve with a wide base and fuzzy edges. Advanced scans showed mild tracer uptake and unclear borders, which raised suspicion of malignancy rather than a clot. Surgeons removed the growth, and the authors use the case to sharpen recognition of primary pulmonary artery synovial sarcoma.
pmc-13466963:
Hao Chen and colleagues report a robot-assisted removal of a lung lobe after drug treatment shrank a locally advanced cancer, in a 2026 case report. The patient, a fifty-one-year-old man, had stage IIIA squamous lung cancer in the left lower lobe with nodal spread. Chemotherapy combined with the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab brought a partial response before surgery.

Treatment like this leaves scarred, sticky tissue, so the team chose a modular robotic system from a Shanghai maker for the operation and lymph node clearance. Blood loss came to only twenty milliliters, and docking the robot took five minutes. The case argues that modular platforms can handle the harder resections that follow modern pre-surgery drug therapy.
pmc-13467163:
Woźnicki and co-workers in Poland dosed in 2026 two lines of glioblastoma cells with ophiobolin A. The fungus made compound can cross into the brain, home of this most grave tumor. The team read the first hours of the cells' answer: which death and stress genes switched. Death marks came from a flow count. A smart learning pass then sought the gene marks that best split dosed cells from clean ones.

Dosed cells leaned toward the self kill path: two death genes rose, and one guard gene slid. Rust defense genes woke too, as if the cells fought back. The count of cells in early death grew. In one line, the gene set told dosed from clean with strong skill. The authors flag the work as a first hint, from one run.
pmc-13467663:
Berlinches de Gea and colleagues test whether tiny soil predators help plants grow better than fertilizer does in this 2026 experiment. Protists and nematodes are microscopic animals that eat soil bacteria, reshaping the microbial community and cycling nitrogen. The team grew Cannabis sativa plants with different mixes of these predators, with and without added nitrogen, and measured growth and soil changes.

Adding predators raised plant biomass by up to 53 percent at any diversity level. Where predator diversity was highest, the rise reached 60 percent. The growth boost tracked shifts in the bacterial community and richer carbon and nitrogen cycling functions. Added nitrogen, by contrast, mainly changed nutrient levels in plant and soil rather than biomass, suggesting predator diversity could help cut fertilizer use.
pmc-13467863:
Weijie Wang, Wei Zheng, Yuanyuan Cai, and Fenfen Shen present a meta-analysis, published in 2026. It asks whether the triglyceride-glucose index predicts early death in sepsis. Sepsis is the dangerous body-wide response to infection. The index is built from blood fat and sugar readings. It estimates insulin resistance. Earlier studies disagreed about its value in sepsis care.

The authors pooled eight studies with 14,772 patients. A higher index was associated with clearly higher odds of dying. Deaths counted were in hospital or within thirty days. The pattern held across age and sex mix. It also held across diabetes status. The simple index carries prognostic information, they conclude. The underlying studies were all observational, though.
pmc-13468163:
Li and colleagues report in 2026 that a maize gene called ZmWRKY83 works against the plant's own tolerance of waterlogging, the soil flooding that starves roots of oxygen. The gene's activity dropped in roots under waterlogging, which hinted it acts as a brake. The team raised its activity in test plants to see the effect.

Plants with boosted ZmWRKY83 grew normally in good conditions but suffered more after flooding, with lower shoot and root weights. They formed fewer adventitious roots, the emergency roots that help flooded plants breathe, and showed more membrane damage with weaker antioxidant defenses. Gene activity scans pointed to hormone pathways, and the team confirmed the gene directly switches off an auxin-related gene, weakening the growth hormone response that aids survival.
pmc-13468763:
Kouris, Vrochidou, and Papakostas surveyed a 2026 systematic review of computer vision and sensor methods for inspecting power transmission lines. Checking overhead lines by hand is costly and slow, while drones, advanced cameras, and deep learning have reshaped the work. Their search began with 1,493 Scopus records on the topic.

After staged screening and quality scoring under PRISMA guidelines, 148 studies from 2018 to 2026 were retained by Kouris. The synthesis covered flying platforms and sensors, vision methods by task, datasets and metrics, and industrial adoption in the field. Models from the YOLO family dominated real time deployment on small devices, while Transformer architectures gained ground steadily. Persistent gaps included scarce public datasets, weak transfer to new domains, and limited field validation.
pmc-13469263:
Monika Filipkowska and four colleagues published this 2026 analysis of drug-resistant bacterial infections caught in intensive care units across Poland from 2019 to 2023. Using national surveillance data from every Polish ICU, they worked out standard infection ratios. These compare counted cases against the 2019 level, for MRSA, vancomycin-resistant enterococci, and Klebsiella strains making enzymes that defeat modern antibiotics, including the New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase.

Risk varied sharply by region. MRSA ratios ran high in the Lublin, Subcarpathian and Silesian regions, while Lodz stayed low. Vancomycin-resistant E. faecalis cases rose several-fold in Lublin. E. faecium was centred in the Holy Cross region. The steepest growth came from Klebsiella pneumoniae carrying the New Delhi enzyme. Its ratios in Lower Silesian and Silesian units reached several dozen times the 2019 level. The authors urge stronger surveillance and infection control, while noting their data cannot prove the pattern came from the pandemic.
pmc-13470263:
Liu and colleagues review evidence for traditional Chinese medicine treatments of allergic eye disease, covering allergic conjunctivitis and its severe springtime relative, vernal keratoconjunctivitis, in a 2026 planned review. Both are immune-driven inflammation of the eye surface, causing itching, redness, tearing, and mucus. The authors searched five sources for studies published between January 2010 and May 2026, then weighed clinical results alongside safety evidence and how the therapies act for herbal and related therapies.

Clinical evidence clustered on common allergic eye disease and vernal disease, and the reviewers found no eligible studies for two related conditions, atopic and giant papillary eye disease. Oral herbal mixtures and combined Chinese plus standard therapy supplied most of the clinical evidence. Herbal eye remedies, above all Houttuynia eye drops, gave a smaller but more eye-specific signal. Liu stresses these approaches remain adjuncts with uneven evidence quality, never stand-ins for established eye care.
pmc-13470863: Gorash and colleagues published this 2026 correction to their study on genomic prediction of wheat resistance to Fusarium head blight, a fungal disease that damages grain. The notice fixes a capitalization error in the original title and corrects several reported numbers. Among the changes, the accuracy gain for one prediction model becomes 0.08 rather than the value first printed, and results text on marker sets is updated so the published record matches the underlying analysis.
pmc-13471663:
Özgün Elmas and Mustafa Cemali compare in 2026 how the balance of daily occupations relates to activity, fitness, and body makeup in older adults. Occupational balance means feeling that daily activities sit in the right mix, a concept occupational therapists track. One hundred fifty adults aged sixty five to seventy five were sorted by a standard activity questionnaire into inactive, minimally active, and active groups.

Balance was scored with an eleven item questionnaire, fitness by a stand and walk test plus grip strength, and body makeup by a commercial analyzer. Every measure differed across the three activity groups. More active elders reported better occupational balance, stronger grips, and more skeletal muscle. The authors also charted how balance correlates with the other measures across everyone, arguing daily routine shape deserves a place beside exercise in healthy aging advice.
pmc-13471963:
Alberto Rosmaninho and three colleagues set out in 2026 a simple way to carry a patient's natural head position into digital dental planning. The problem is a level reference: without one, a smile design can be tilted, and the usual guide, a line through the pupils, can mislead when faces are uneven. Their alternative draws the horizontal line directly behind the patient in the first front-facing photograph, so the photo itself holds the reference.

The method was tried in the aesthetic rehabilitation of one male patient, whose planning was run under both the new approach and the pupil-based approach, with mock-ups made for comparison. Differences between the two plans showed how a shifted reference changes treatment choices. Because the technique needs only routine photographs and no extra gear, it offers clinics a cheap check on alignment, with the clear limit that the report rests on a single case.
pmc-13472563:
Ke Chen and fifteen colleagues published this 2026 randomised controlled trial of a precision synbiotic, a paired prebiotic and probiotic, in 390 healthy toddlers aged one to three. One arm received the human milk sugar 2′-fucosyllactose plus two infant-derived Bifidobacterium strains. One received the bacteria alone, and one received a maltodextrin placebo, for twelve weeks with twelve more weeks of follow-up across multiple centres. The main outcome was upper respiratory tract infections over the full period.

The synbiotic clearly outperformed placebo. Respiratory infections struck 55.4 percent of synbiotic children against 85.4 percent on placebo, an absolute cut of thirty points. Pneumonia, diarrhoea and eczema all fell too, with eczema dropping from 13.1 to 1.5 percent in the synbiotic arm. The probiotic alone reduced only eczema. Stool testing showed the synbiotic reshaped gut microbes and enriched two Bifidobacterium species carrying milk-sugar use pathways, while a gut inflammation marker fell by week 24.
pmc-13472963:
Shabir A Madhi and eighteen colleagues published this 2026 report of a randomised phase 1/2 trial of GBS6, an experimental vaccine against group B Streptococcus. The bacterium causes illness in newborns. No licensed vaccine exists despite decades of work. The trial tested the six-strain conjugate vaccine in healthy women in South Africa. Pregnant participants in South Africa, the United States and the United Kingdom were also enrolled, and their infants were followed after birth.

In the pregnant stage, 216 women received GBS6 or placebo, and 209 infants were born into the study. Reactions were mostly mild or moderate. Adverse events, serious ones included, matched closely between vaccine and placebo groups in mothers and infants. Most babies were born at term. Two newborn sepsis deaths occurred, one in each group, and neither was judged vaccine-related. The vaccine produced strong antibody responses. They conclude GBS6 was well tolerated in this trial.
pmc-13473063:
Nigliato and co-authors studied PTPA, the activator of the tumor-suppressing phosphatase PP2A, in malignant pleural mesothelioma, the asbestos-linked cancer of the lung lining. Their 2026 analysis combined cancer genome data with lab tests putting PTPA back in low-expressing mesothelioma cells.

Losing one copy of the PTPA gene was common, occurring in 26% of the 87 patients in the genome cohort, and it tracked with much shorter survival. Putting PTPA back cut colony formation and growth without anchorage, and it raised the phosphatase's activity in the treated cells. Treated cells also aged into senescence more readily under oncogene stress and responded better to carboplatin. Mesothelioma of the pleura accounts for 90% of mesothelioma cases, the authors note.
pmc-13473863:
Jhaveri and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a tissue stain can stand in for gene sequencing to find PTEN-deficient breast tumors in the phase III CAPItello-291 trial. Loss of PTEN, a brake on a growth pathway, helps select patients for the AKT blocker capivasertib plus fulvestrant, but sequencing is the usual route. The team ran the stain, called immunohistochemistry, on 367 tumor samples and compared it with sequencing results.

About one in five samples stained as PTEN deficient. Against sequencing, the stain agreed in 87 percent of cases overall, catching about seven in ten sequencing-positive tumors and clearing nearly nine in ten negative ones. Among stain-positive patients, those on the drug pair lived a median of just over nine months without progression against under four months on the control pairing. The authors say staining may widen access to the treatment by flagging extra patients who could benefit.
pmc-13474163:
Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 an extract of the plant Parnassia palustris against brain glioma in mice, while tracking gut microbes. Glioma-bearing mice received the extract by stomach tube every other day, or a control solution. Tumour growth was followed by fluorescence imaging, and brain and gut samples were analysed after treatment.

The extract significantly suppressed tumour growth on imaging and by final tumour weight. Treated tumours showed lower cell density and fewer abnormal nuclei. A key growth pathway, PI3K/Akt, was inhibited, with proliferation marker KI67 down and tumour suppressor p53 up. Gut microbe diversity itself did not change, but composition shifts accompanied the antitumour effect. The authors are careful to report correlation, not causation, between microbe changes and tumour response. They present the plant extract as a candidate worth further study.
pmc-13474563:
Zhang and Plumeré reviewed photosystem-based electrodes in 2026, devices that wire nature's light-harvesting proteins to solid surfaces to make electricity or fuels from sunlight. Photosystems, the protein machines of photosynthesis, split charge with superb efficiency and use only common elements. Their weak points are fragility and the hard task of linking them well to an electrode.

The review covers the three main families, photosystem II, photosystem I, and bacterial reaction centers, and the ways teams anchor them to electrodes as light-driven anodes or cathodes. It traces electron paths between protein and surface, including short-circuit routes that waste charge, and compares full cells that run with or without added voltage. The authors stress shared test tools and performance measures so groups can spot bottlenecks and compare designs fairly, a step they see as key to making these bio-devices practical.
pmc-13474763:
Lin and co-authors describe anesthetizing a 63-year-old woman whose cervical cancer had spread into her heart, planting a mobile tumor in the right ventricle and main pulmonary artery. Their 2026 case report details surgery on a heart-lung bypass machine to remove a metastasis so rare that autopsy studies put cardiac spread from cervical cancer near 1.2% of cases.

The anesthetic plan revolved around not shaking the tumor loose: a slow, titrated induction, continuous ultrasound imaging of the heart from the esophagus. Cerebral oxygen monitoring read 56 to 59% at baseline, with her heart's pumping fraction preserved at 61% before surgery. Resection succeeded without major problems, pathology confirmed metastatic squamous cell carcinoma, and at eight months she remained alive on adjuvant chemotherapy. The team distills lessons on induction, monitoring, and bypass planning for tumors inside the heart.
pmc-13474963:
Biton and co-authors compared in 2026 two surgical routes for women with a ruptured hemorrhagic ovarian cyst bleeding into the abdomen. One route, vNOTES, operates through the vagina with an endoscope, leaving no abdominal scars, while the conventional route uses several small abdominal ports. The multicenter retrospective study covered hemodynamically stable women treated at two referral centers between January 2020 and December 2025.

Forty-two women were included, thirteen treated with vNOTES and twenty-nine with conventional laparoscopy. Operative time, blood loss, transfusion rates, and complications were similar between the groups, with no conversions to open surgery. Pain twelve hours after surgery was significantly lower after vNOTES, at 1.9 versus 3.2 points on the pain scale reported in the study, and genital self-image scores at six months also favored vNOTES. Sexual function scores were comparable. The authors note the approach choice was not randomized.
pmc-13477063:
Keisuke Shibagaki and co-authors weigh valve replacement timing in 2026 for patients born with a single working heart chamber. All had prior repair of their shared inlet valve, called plasty. Thirty kept the repaired valve, while nineteen later got a replacement once leak was controlled. Survival and progress to the final Fontan stage were compared.

About a third needed replacement within ten years of first repair. Early first repair and severe leak at first repair each raised that risk. Ten-year survival matched between groups at roughly three quarters. Replacement after repair gave results on par with repair alone in this small set.
pmc-13478063:
Afsaneh Amouzegar and colleagues sequenced in 2026 germline cancer genes in 346 mucosal melanoma patients treated at MD Anderson, comparing variant rates with population controls. Mucosal melanoma is rare and aggressive, and the role of inherited variants was poorly understood.

Inherited pathogenic variants appeared in 10.7 percent of patients, most often in CHEK2, ATM, and MITF. Two variants, MITF p.E318K and CHEK2 c.1100delC, were significantly enriched, with odds about six and seven times control rates. Variant carriers more often had two or more affected first-degree relatives. The findings support genetic testing in this population.
pmc-13478863:
Avila and colleagues release CASCADE, an open source pipeline that reads recordings from five brands of electrode array. Multi-electrode arrays are grids of contacts that listen to neurons. Each brand ships closed software locked to its file format, so labs cannot compare results across devices. CASCADE is a Python tool. It ingests recordings from 3Brain, Axion, Cortical Labs, MaxWell, and Multi-Channel Systems hardware. It computes the network measures in one pass.

Beyond firing rates and bursts, CASCADE scores avalanches, cascades of firing that ripple through a network. It scores criticality, a balance point between order and chaos some theories link to brain function. Benchmarked on six recordings from all makers, the pipeline returned criticality values because each file passed through the same math. The tool is free on GitHub and PyPI. Shared plumbing, the authors argue, lets results from different benches be compared head to head.
pmc-13479563:
Lifang Ye published a 2026 quasi-experimental study, as sole author, of a growth mindset program for Chinese university students required to study English. Students outside English majors often lose motivation in these compulsory courses. One hundred twenty first-year students in whole classes were assigned to the program or to regular teaching, sixty per group.

The twelve-week program wove mindset lessons into normal English classes. Measures tracked students' second-language motivational self system, meaning the English speaker they hope to become, fear becoming, and feel expected to become, plus their academic engagement. The analysis tests whether the motivational self explains any engagement gains from the mindset work. The framing draws on possible selves and self-discrepancy theory to unify two research traditions.
pmc-13479863:
Mayank Tripathi and coauthors published a 2026 surgical report of a custom 3D-printed titanium breastbone and rib implant after near-total breastbone removal. The patient, a 28-year-old man, had a giant cell tumor of the sternum. Large removals endanger the chest wall's rigidity and leave the heart exposed, while standard reconstructions sacrifice anatomical fit.

The workflow ran from CT scans through virtual resection planning, computer design with rib-coupling flanges and soft tissue eyelets, a plastic rehearsal model, and metal printing. The implant was fixed to a sliver of remaining upper sternum, the lower remnant, and rib stumps in one operation. Double-layer mesh and preserved chest muscle closed the wound without a skin flap. The authors document the full blueprint alongside the intermediate outcome.
pmc-13479963:
Jinhan Wang, Bing Niu, and Lingling Zhang published a 2026 survey study of how frailty shaped older adults' communication choices during the COVID-19 pandemic. Lockdowns forced social contact onto phones and screens, and frail elders may have been least able to adapt. The sample held 5,115 community-dwelling adults in Sakai City, Japan, averaging about seventy-five years of age, assessed in November 2020.

Participants were classed as frail, pre-frail, or robust from muscle function, nutrition, and related traits. Statistical models compared use of video calls, telephone calls, and face-to-face contact across the three groups. The question matters for emergency planning: if frailty predicts digital exclusion, outreach during the next crisis must supply devices, training, or safe in-person alternatives for the frailest residents.
pmc-13480263:
Crivelaro and Saadi wrote in 2026 on a case that pairs two fixes for a torn aorta. One is a stent graft that seals the tear. The other is nerve burns at the kidneys that tame blood squeeze. The tear, a type B aortic dissection, splits the wall of the body's main vessel. The stent can seal it, yet wild squeeze keeps strain on the wall. The case under read, by Chen and co-workers, did both fixes in one stop for a man whose squeeze would not yield.

His right kidney vessel drew blood from both the true and false paths of the tear, a hard map for safe work. Scan plans set the route, and both nerve burns were done with no harm. The authors frame the pair as a dual strike, on form and on force at once.
pmc-13481563:
Claudio Santiago Dias and co-authors present a 2026 study of faith and breast screening among older women in Brazil. Data came from a national ageing study baseline in 2015 and 2016, covering 3,120 women aged fifty to sixty-nine who identified as White or Black, including Brown. Screening history split into never screened, screened on time, and overdue.

Evangelical women were more likely than Catholic women to have never had a mammogram and to be overdue. Frequent service attendance cut the risk of never screening. Among Black Evangelical women the never-screened risk rose, yet high attendance erased much of it, while White Evangelical women mainly risked drifting overdue. Faith can thus block or boost screening depending on practice and belief, and outreach through congregations may reach women that clinics miss.
pmc-13481763:
Jing Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 toolkit for dialling gene activity up or down in a stubborn hospital germ. Acinetobacter baumannii resists many drugs, yet labs lacked graded switches to study its genes. The team mined gene activity data for always-on control regions, then tested 25 candidates with a glowing reporter gene.

Nineteen switches worked, spanning a wide range of strengths, and protein checks confirmed the glow matched real output. Each switch also kept its own rhythm across growth phases, which adds a timing choice. As a proof run, driving a native resistance gene cluster harder made the germ shrug off streptomycin more strongly. The graded set lets researchers tune one gene at a time instead of blasting it, a finer tool for hunting drug targets.
pmc-13481963:
Anisa S Y Noordzij and co-authors present a 2026 validation of a Dutch version of a short vertigo symptom questionnaire. Beyond plain translation, the team asked whether Dutch and British patients read the items the same way. Data came from trial patients aged fifty and above with long-standing balance symptoms, 322 Dutch and 296 British.

The Dutch form read clearly and measured one main symptom dimension, much like the original. Reliability scores rated excellent in both versions. Small cultural twists appeared: Dutch patients reported nausea less readily yet unsteadiness more readily at the same overall severity. Those twists barely moved total scores, so cross-country comparisons stay fair. The study shows how fine-grained checks can certify a translated scale for shared research.
pmc-13482163:
Presotto and an international team ask in 2026 whether hunted animals change how they navigate, comparing two endangered mammal populations living with human hunting in Zimbabwe and Brazil. Their idea draws on the landscape of fear, the mental risk map prey animals carry, which can push them toward safer ground even when food there is worse. Using mapping software, movement records, and satellite data, they measured how faithfully each population reused its travel routes.

Both species leaned harder on habitual routes where hunting was present, retracing familiar paths instead of ranging freely across the landscape around them. Sticking to known routes may free attention for watching out for people and other signs of danger, trading efficient navigation for vigilance in risky places. The authors raise a wider worry, that simplifying travel this way could dull the richer navigation skills animals pass to their young in hunted landscapes.
pmc-13482363:
Ahmad and colleagues merge epidemic mathematics with neural networks in 2026 to check whether an outbreak model with education campaigns settles down or keeps spreading. Their SEIR model sorts people into susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered groups, then splits the infectious group by whether people received health education. A physics-informed neural network learns the model's behavior while a Lyapunov function, a mathematical energy-like score, is built into training to enforce stability.

The team derived the model's basic reproduction number, the average count of new infections from one case, to locate the tipping points between a fading outbreak and a settled endemic state. The network both traced infection curves over time and verified that those states are globally stable. Outbreaks return to them from any starting point tested. They present the hybrid as a data-light way to confirm stability results that pure analysis struggles to prove for complex models.
pmc-13482563:
Lu Han and five colleagues showed in 2026 that the gut bacterium Eubacterium rectale eases bowel inflammation in mice. IBD involves a disturbed gut microbiota, and whether this gut bacterium calms inflammation was unsettled.

In mice with induced colitis, the bacterium eased symptoms, restored gut barrier strength, and lowered inflammatory signals. It raised levels of the enzyme glutaminase 2, fixed glutamine use in gut lining cells, and dampened the NF-κB pathway; without glutaminase 2 the benefit vanished. The findings point to a live germ route for bowel disease built on the GLS2/NF-κB axis.
pmc-13483363:
Hannah A. D. King and co-authors describe a 2026 monkey study of a next-generation vaccine booster for HIV. Rhesus macaques got a poxvirus prime plus a protein boost wrapped in a military liposome formula, in two forms: one stuck to alum, one laced with a soapbark extract. The extract form is the candidate of interest.

The extract-laced boost raised antibody and T cell replies higher and kept them longer. Helper T cell peaks ran ten times above the alum form, and killer T cells topped one percent, a rare strength for protein boosts. Blood alarm signals rose in step with the stronger replies. Yet no form shielded monkeys from a rectal challenge with a hybrid virus, whose coat may hide from antibody side attacks. Stronger replies alone did not buy protection here.
pmc-13483563:
Yonghui Wang and colleagues study liver injury linked to the antibiotic tigecycline in very ill hospital patients. Published in 2026, the retrospective review covers 309 critically ill patients who received the drug intravenously at one Chinese hospital between 2020 and 2023. Liver injury was judged with standard biochemical criteria, and the team modeled which exposures predicted harm.

Injury developed in 71 patients, giving an overall rate near one in four treated cases. Longer courses and larger total doses each raised risk on their own, and risk first climbed then leveled off at the highest cumulative doses. Among affected patients the median onset was four days after starting treatment. The practical message is early and continued liver checks, with careful control of dose and duration.
pmc-13484463:
Botezatu and colleagues surveyed health staff about Romania's National Program for Women and Child Health in Bacău County, in 2026 health services research. The program funds preventive care and treatment services for mothers and children through public providers. The team questioned 54 staff from three public hospitals and ten family medicine practices during 2023 and 2024, asking about the program's relevance, funding, rules, and day-to-day running problems.

Physicians and nurses made up 75.9 percent of those surveyed, with economic experts and reporting staff forming the rest. Most rated the program highly important, citing the severity of the health problems targeted and its preventive benefits. They scored population impact and service coverage highly as well. Weaknesses clustered elsewhere: money was allocated and used unevenly, reporting practices varied between units, and monitoring systems were fragile. Botezatu urges tightening those everyday basics before expanding the program further.
pmc-13485663:
Shiran Zhang follows the eye's lens over eight years in highly short-sighted people to test whether it keeps fighting eye elongation in adulthood. Published in 2026, the prospective cohort draws 708 Chinese participants aged 7 to 50 from a specialist myopia program, each with at least two biennial visits. Lens thickness and calculated lens power are tracked against elongation speed.

Lenses thickened steadily with age in everyone. Lens power fell through childhood, then leveled for slow progressors while continuing to fall in fast progressors. In adults, power loss tied to eye elongation rather than to age itself, and mediation analysis gave elongation the direct role. The lens does keep compensating in grown adults whose eyes still stretch, which reframes high myopia as an active adult process.
pmc-13486663:
Yongbiao Zhai builds a frog-eye-inspired vision chip from ferroelectric transistors that sees motion as events instead of frames. Published in 2026, the system copies the amphibian retina's layered jobs, covering color sensing, spatial cleanup, and event-style encoding in hardware. The transistors respond across ultraviolet to visible wavelengths with responses in both directions.

Arrays reproduce center-surround processing, sharpening contrast while muting background noise in dim scenes. Steep switching lets the devices fire microsecond-scale spikes for moving features. Paired with an event-driven neural network, the demonstrator recognized dynamic facial expressions at 96.5 percent accuracy and predicted several moving agents' paths with under 5 percent error. Event cameras gain color and on-chip smarts that ordinary designs lack.
pmc-13487463:
Chen and a team in China built in 2026 a two in one vaccine for ducks against two viral diseases at once. One germ, duck enteritis virus, kills grown birds, while a newer goose parvovirus stunts young ducks and has cost farms dearly since 2015. No licensed vaccine exists for the newer germ. The team took a weakened enteritis virus strain they had built before. Into it they placed the VP2 gene of the parvovirus, its main shell protein.

The built virus made VP2 and packed it into virus like particles, empty shells that train the immune system. Given to ducklings, the shot proved safe with no ill effects seen. Treated birds cleared the parvovirus and stood up well to a strong dose of live enteritis virus later. The authors put the strain forth as a strong pick for joint control of both diseases in duck flocks.
pmc-13487563:
Gökçe Işıl Kurmuş introduces a 2026 case of rupioid psoriasis, a rare shell-crusted form of plaque psoriasis whose cone-shaped, dirt-dark lesions mimic oyster shells. The Greek root for filth gives the form its name, and bloody fluid trapped under thick crusts deepens the grim look. Look-alike conditions range from secondary syphilis to crusted scabies, so tissue and blood checks must separate them first.

Patients with this form often carry joint disease and nail involvement, and creams alone rarely control the stubborn plaques. The case features bimekizumab, an antibody that blocks two interleukin-17 family signals at once, with early and significant improvement promised in the report title. Rare-form evidence accumulates one case at a time, and rapid response to a dual blocker guides the next clinician facing identical crusts.
pmc-13490363:
Lella and team modeled diabetes that arises in pregnancy as a network problem, linking patients who resemble each other instead of scoring each woman in isolation. Gestational diabetes risk depends on tangled genetic, biochemical, and demographic factors that plain forecast models flatten. Their 2026 design builds a graph where patients are nodes, edges mark shared traits, and graph neural networks pass information along those edges, while a language model reads the unstructured clinical notes.

The combined model reached about 88 percent classification accuracy on the clinical dataset evaluated, beating the baseline learning methods compared. Three graph designs, covering neighborhood sampling, relation-aware messages, and time-aware attention, each contributed to the result. Privacy-preserving federated training and edge-dropping regularization guarded against overfitting and data exposure. Lella argues network context, the company a patient keeps in data, sharpens risk forecast.
pmc-13490563:
Milind Gayakwad and others launch a curated data set of grapevine leaf photographs for automated disease finding. In 2026, the collection, called GVLiD, contains 3,477 high-resolution images with expert-verified labels for black rot, esca, and leaf blight, plus metadata on location, lighting, weather, and camera. Unlike lab data sets, most images were taken in real vineyards.

Annotation reliability was very high, with agreement scores above 0.86. The data set aims to help computer vision and plant pathology team test models under variable field states, where changing light and natural backgrounds challenge rightness. Indian viticulture benefits directly, but the resource is designed for worldwide benchmarking of crop disease tracking.
pmc-13490763:
Feeley and six fellow ecologists reviewed in 2026 the idea of thermophilization, the slow shift of wild communities toward warm loving species as the climate heats up. When species move toward the poles or uphill to stay in their comfort zone, cold loving kinds shrink in number and warm loving kinds grow. The review sums up work from land, sea, and fresh water, and sets out how the shift is most often measured.

The main tool is the Community Temperature Index, one number that blends the heat needs of all species found at a site. Tracking that index over years gives a rate of change per year. The method can split the shift by cause, such as new arrivals versus deaths. The authors warn that labs use the tool in unlike ways, which blocks fair comparison across studies, and they call for shared rules.
pmc-13492363:
Guin and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study aimed at better drugs for cryptosporidiosis, an infection by the gut parasite Cryptosporidium. The disease causes life-threatening diarrhea in young children and lasting diarrhea in people with weak immune systems. An earlier boron-containing compound from the team worked when given by mouth, but infections returned a week after treatment stopped.

The team changed parts of that compound's benzoxaborole ring, a boron-based chemical structure, and tested each version. One version reached strong lab potency at a concentration of 0.025 micromolar while leaving human cells unharmed, and it cured infected mice with suppressed immune systems. Separating its two mirror-image forms showed one was twice as strong again. The other was about 400 times weaker. That gap pointed to a methyl group at one ring position as the key feature.
pmc-13493363:
Li and colleagues followed over two thousand Chinese adults with hearing difficulties for nine years to see how activity patterns relate to later thinking ability. Hearing loss is a leading dementia risk, and activity may protect the brain, but whether activity patterns over time matter was unclear. Participants were forty-five or older with normal cognition, and cognition was tested in 2020.

Li found an L-shaped relationship: activity protected against impairment up to a point, after which extra activity added little. Three patterns emerged, a large declining majority, a dropping group, and a rise-then-fall group making up about one in seven. That unstable group scored lower on cognition and mental status than the steady group. Its members were men, rural residents, drinkers, non-nappers, and people with depressive symptoms. The authors argue helping people with hearing loss sustain activity matters more than bursts.
pmc-13493463:
Joni Ilmanen and Salvatore Giordano analyze in 2026 whether tranexamic acid, a cheap drug that stabilizes blood clots, prevents the bleeding complications that send breast reduction patients back to the operating room. Their single-center review covered 656 consecutive patients operated between 2019 and 2024. Surgeons gave the drug into a vein, onto the wound, or both, by personal preference.

Bleeding requiring reoperation struck about two percent of treated patients against five percent of untreated ones, a better than twofold reduction. Curiously, treated patients had bigger resections, more measured blood loss, and longer operations, which makes the protective signal more striking. Overall complications and return-to-surgery rates matched between groups, and no drug side effects appeared. The authors back routine use while calling for a proper randomized trial.
pmc-13493863:
Zhai and colleagues redesign the control system of ultra-high-speed air-jet looms, the machines that weave cloth by shooting yarn across with air. Old loom drives waste energy, bolt separate controllers together awkwardly, and run unstably. Their 2026 design unifies three motors, for the main shaft, the warp supply, and the cloth take-up, under one controller. A companion vision system inspects cloth for defects automatically.

The inspection half, built on an improved YOLOv8n detection network, was trained on seven common defect types such as broken threads and stains. It scored near the top of the standard detection accuracy scale and ran at 156 frames per second, far faster than traditional checking. In factory tests it caught flaws as small as a fraction of a millimetre with a low false alarm rate. The fused drive also cut power use and monitored all three axes in real time.
pmc-13494063:
Xu and colleagues report in 2026 a case series on using an ultrapulse carbon dioxide laser to treat the lasting structural damage of acne conglobata. This severe acne's deep abscesses heal into sinus tracts, chronic cavities, and raised skin bridges on the face. Surgery for these scars means long recovery and frequent recurrence.

Thirteen patients treated between 2022 and 2026 underwent outpatient laser procedures under local anesthesia, vaporizing the roofs of tracts and cutting away skin bridges rather than excising down to fat. Between them they carried 301 skin bridges, 51 sinus tracts, and eight chronic abscesses, after a median seven years of disease. Pain during treatment was mild, wounds healed in a median of about twenty-two days, and no relevant complications such as bleeding occurred. Outcomes were tracked by recurrence, patient satisfaction ratings, and independent photographic grading.
pmc-13494163:
Tanvir M Huda and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial in Dhaka, Bangladesh, testing bovine lactoferrin against standard iron tablets for iron-deficiency anemia in women. Lactoferrin is a protein in milk that binds iron and fights germs, and smaller studies hinted it might raise hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying part of blood. Proof from low-resource settings was thin, so the team ran a head-to-head trial.

They assigned 555 nonpregnant women aged 18 to 49 to ferrous sulfate or to one of two daily lactoferrin doses, each with folic acid, for twelve weeks. Hemoglobin rose clearly on the iron tablets and barely moved on either lactoferrin dose, so lactoferrin failed the preset test for being no worse than iron. Side effects were alike across groups. The authors conclude lactoferrin should not replace iron tablets in settings like this one.
pmc-13495163:
Shadi Ghaemi and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study of Tehran adults, whether meal quality at dinner versus breakfast links to body shape. Timing of meals has drawn interest in weight research, and the quality of carbs, fats, and proteins may matter as much as their amount. The team studied 450 adults aged 20 to 59, using three food recalls and body measures.

Higher-quality carbs at dinner tied to body mass index in a curved pattern, rising then falling. Saturated fat tilted toward dinner tracked with higher index and with less muscle and lean mass. Plant protein tilted toward dinner linked with a lower index in a straight line, though with less lean mass. Animal protein tilted toward dinner slightly raised muscle. The authors read the pattern as favoring good carbs, unsaturated fats, and plant protein at dinner, while warning the design shows links, not cause.
pmc-13496163:
Diego Andres De León Rosas and co-authors report in 2026 a rare hernia through the upper lumbar triangle, a weak spot in the back wall of the abdomen. Their patient was a 71-year-old woman with a soft swelling on her left side that had grown over three months. Such hernias are easy to mistake for other lumps, so imaging played a central role.

Ultrasound showed a defect about four centimetres wide holding fatty tissue, and a scan confirmed the diagnosis without trapped bowel. Surgeons repaired the gap through an open cut, closing it with stitches and a plastic mesh fixed to nearby muscle and rib tissue. She recovered smoothly, with good pain control and no wound problems at one year.
pmc-13498863:
Nordheimer and Gofrit reviewed how drug treatments affect the local tumor in prostate, kidney, testicular, and bladder cancers, searching PubMed and Scopus through May 2026. The question matters because removing these organs is disfiguring surgery, and shrinking the tumor might reduce its extent.

Nordheimer found the evidence still short of replacing surgery. In prostate cancer, hormone treatment before surgery improved tumor margins and organ confinement but not biochemical survival, and chemotherapy or immunotherapy gave no local benefit. In kidney cancer, targeted and immune drugs shrank tumors by a seventh to a third, without improving recurrence-free survival. Testicular tumors after chemotherapy held viable cancer in up to a quarter of specimens. Bladder cancer fared best, with the tumor vanishing completely before surgery in about a third of patients on cisplatin chemotherapy, better still with added immunotherapy. The authors conclude attempts to skip local surgery belong inside clinical trials.
pmc-13499163:
Meng Li and Zhining Mo write in 2026 as kidney specialists responding to a proposed staging system for acute kidney injury based on a blood marker called cystatin C. The proposal reclassified many critically ill patients and predicted later death better than the usual marker. Writing to the journal editor, they welcome the aim of beating the older marker's limits while raising concerns that, in their view, block immediate bedside use.

One concern is that patients whose markers were falling were left out, which may inflate apparent risk and shrink how widely the system applies. Steroid drugs, common in intensive care for shock, raise cystatin C without true kidney decline and were not accounted for, which could mislabel patients. They also ask whether the new staging changes any real treatment choice, such as when to start dialysis, before it earns a place in practice.
pmc-13499363:
Guo and colleagues described their program to carry Duchenne muscular dystrophy therapies from rhesus monkeys toward patients, in a 2026 perspective. The disease, a progressive muscle wasting caused by loss of the protein dystrophin, involves thousands of variants and effects of age and disease stage. Mouse results alone cannot predict patient benefit. The team built monkey models by editing the dystrophin gene with CRISPR.

Guo recounts that their engineered monkeys carry a mutation in the common exon 45 to 55 hotspot and can be produced in under a year instead of six or seven. The monkeys develop degeneration, fibrosis, and motor impairment resembling early human disease, and revealed mechanisms including early immune activation and stem-cell dysfunction. On this platform the group tested circular RNA strategies that force exon skipping to restore the reading frame. One strategy is a single-cut DNA editing approach using a compact enzyme, bridging toward clinical application.
pmc-13499663:
Zhafira Fauziah and colleagues review in 2026 biosensors that use affibodies, small engineered binding proteins, to detect cancer markers in body samples. Late diagnosis is a core problem in cancer care, and standard tests carry limits that small, sturdy detectors might overcome. Their literature review covers what affibodies are, how they are made, and how they perform inside electrochemical and light-based sensor designs.

Across studies, affibody sensors detected markers such as HER2, a growth receptor overproduced in some breast cancers, with high sensitivity and specificity, meaning few missed cases and few false alarms. Reported strengths include very low detection limits, wide measurement ranges, and reliable results in real biological samples. Compared with antibodies and aptamers, two rival binding tools, affibodies offer easier synthesis, strong stability, and tight binding, marking them as promising diagnostic platforms.
pmc-13500463:
Thet Htar Swe, Ann Jirapongsuwan, and Mathuros Tipayamongkholgul survey in 2026 family planning use among women with HIV in Magway, Myanmar. These women hold the same rights to family life and contraceptive choice as anyone, yet services rarely tailor to their situation. Structured questionnaires based on a planned behaviour theory were completed by 349 women of reproductive age, and statistical models hunted for factors tied to current contraceptive practice.

Only about a quarter of the women were using family planning in the reported share, with condoms the commonest method. Fear of side effects was the leading reason women gave for stopping. Age, marital status, and number of living children all linked significantly to practice, alongside attitudes, perceived social norms, and perceived control over the decision. The authors recommend weaving family planning directly into HIV treatment services rather than running it separately.
pmc-13501763:
Wei Zhang and others track long-term sleep patterns and mental decline in Chinese adults aged fifty-five and older. In 2026, the long-term study clusters three waves of sleep data from 4,385 people by nighttime sleep and daytime napping trajectories. It then links patterns to mental change and impairment defined by aging-associated rules. One-time snapshots miss such trajectories.

Three patterns emerged: moderate-stable sleep with increasing napping, long-stable sleep with frequent napping, and progressively shorter sleep with infrequent napping. Both latter groups declined faster than the first, while only shortening sleep modestly raised impairment risk. The authors suggest tracking long-term sleep actions as an early public health target, pending mechanistic research.
pmc-13501863:
Andy Mprah, Melanie Haith-Cooper, and Fiona Meddings report a 2026 qualitative study of forced migrant fathers experiencing pregnancy and childbirth inside the British NHS. Research on migrant maternity care centres mothers, leaving fathers' views largely unrecorded. Using a hermeneutic phenomenological approach, the team held in-depth semi-structured interviews with fifteen fathers who had recently seen a child born while living in the asylum system. Framework analysis distilled their accounts into themes.

Three themes dominated: feeling sidelined, an alien NHS maternity journey, and life inside the asylum system itself. Fathers described being marginalized by cultural misunderstandings and language barriers at exactly the moments they wanted to support their partners. Resilience and improvised coping strategies ran through the stories alongside the frustration. The authors call for staff training, better communication, and resources shaped for these fathers, so maternity services involve them instead of overlooking them.
pmc-13503763:
Elaheh Amini and seven colleagues compare smart tools that map the five lobes of the lung on medical scans, in a 2026 study. Lobe maps guide surgery and radiation plans, yet good tools are scarce in clinics. The team weighed public models against one trained in-house and a paid product.

They built a set of 200 scans with expert lobe marks, graded from easy to hard. Forty test cases came from that set. No tool showed a steady bias, but public models grew shaky as cases got harder, most of all when a lobe was missing. The in-house model and the paid tool stayed sharp at all levels. A tweak that knows lung anatomy stopped false lobe calls in the local model.
pmc-13503863:
Rashmi Priya, Jürgen Horbach, and Smarajit Karmakar ask whether the brittle failure of glass can be softened from within, in a 2026 simulation study. Well-aged glasses tend to crack along one narrow shear band instead of yielding evenly. The team wondered if that fate is fixed by how the glass was made.

They seeded the glass with a few self-propelled particles that push through the material. At short push bursts, one wide band split into a web of bands, and the glass yielded more smoothly with higher yield stress. A neat trade-off emerged: more push from the particles offset slower outside shearing. Under steady load, stronger push delayed the point where the glass starts to flow. Long push bursts, though, cut the yield stress back down.
pmc-13504763:
Alonso-Moreno and colleagues test whether a small benchtop magnet can do a big hospital machine's job: reading metabolic fingerprints that reveal how sick a breathing patient is. Nuclear magnetic resonance profiling of blood captures hundreds of molecules at once, but full-size instruments are costly and scarce. Their 2026 study ran blood serum from patients with acute respiratory failure due to COVID-19 through both a high-resolution laboratory system and a compact benchtop unit. It graded patients from mild to very severe.

Both platforms found the same severity-linked patterns, and models separated hospitalised from non-hospitalised patients and moderate from very severe cases. Twenty-one molecules carried the signal, including glutamine, citrate, and lactate. Because benchtop instruments are cheap, need no cryogenic cooling, and take little expertise, the authors argue they could put metabolic triage into ordinary emergency departments during respiratory surges.
pmc-13505063:
Fehime Alkan Aygör leads a team grading five AI chatbots on tooth bleaching questions, in a 2026 study. Patients often ask chatbots about whitening, yet dental accuracy had barely been tested. Fifteen common questions were set by restorative dentistry specialists, at both student and specialist depth.

Each question went to all five chatbots in Turkish and English, three times a day for three days. Two experts scored the answers on a five-point scale. Chatbot choice drove accuracy strongly: ChatGPT-4 led, followed by Claude-Instant and GPT-3.5, with Gemini and Bing Chat well behind. Language and depth alone showed no clear effect, though both interacted with chatbot choice. Answers stayed steady across days. The authors warn that chatbots are not interchangeable health sources.
pmc-13506563:
Miklós Kopa and colleagues examine, in a 2026 review, whether the timing of surgery changes survival when cancer has spread to the spine. Their records cover 664 patients and 760 operations at Semmelweis University between 2008 and 2022. Pain affected most patients, and lung, kidney, breast, and blood cancers were the most common sources.

Median survival was 294 days, and about three in ten patients lived past two years. Surgery within set early windows gave no survival edge, while delays past one week linked to shorter survival. Pain eased in about nine in ten cases. The authors urge fast surgery for worsening weakness, with careful preparation for other patients.
pmc-13508463:
Zhenyu Li, Xiangfeng Duan, and Jinlong Yang introduce a special journal issue on the quantum foundations of precision chemistry, in a 2026 editorial. Precision chemistry means predicting and steering chemical change with hard numbers, and that rests on quantum mechanics. The editors survey progress on several fronts. Computer methods, some running on quantum hardware, now model molecule structure with growing accuracy. Simulations follow atoms through reactions, tunneling, and coupled energy surfaces in fine detail. Makers can also build quantum materials to exact designs.

Measurement tools round out the picture, from cold-matrix spectroscopy to magnetic transport and electrochemistry, letting scientists watch quantum effects directly. The issue gathers ten contributions spanning algorithms, methods, materials, spectroscopy, and device work. The editors frame the collection as a progress report on a fast-moving field. For chemists, it offers a single doorway into how quantum thinking is sharpening prediction and control across the discipline.
pmc-13509463:
Masuruddin Shaik and Wei-Xi Huang review how shapes and surfaces copied from living things can cut drag for craft moving through air or water, in a 2026 survey. The review sorts designs into three families: fixed forms, water-repelling surfaces, and smart structures that change shape or behavior as flow shifts. Examples draw on wings, fins, skins, and other natural features refined by evolution.

Across lab tests and computer models, such features can steady swirling flow, delay the shift to rough turbulent flow, and calm the wake behind a body. Gains come with hard limits, since scaling up, joining parts, wear in harsh settings, and changing flow all remain problems. The authors close with a roadmap that favors designs serving several jobs at once and shared test standards for the field.
pmc-13512563:
Shahar and colleagues examined in 2026 how past terrorism exposure relates to later local violence exposure among 362 Israeli teenagers, using survey waves from 2008 and 2010. They asked whether aggression and having committed severe violence changed the link between rocket and terror exposure and later seeing or suffering violence.

The pattern fit dual-vulnerability ideas better than simple stress models. Past terror exposure predicted more later witnessing mainly among teens with low aggression or low severe violence. At higher levels of those behaviors, the link faded or even reversed. Witnessing and direct victimization also behaved differently. The authors suggest screening in chronically threatened communities should assess terror exposure and conduct together, and pair trauma care with school and community violence prevention.
pmc-13515763:
Maria Cristina Ferreira de Sousa and seven colleagues map what a promising anti-parasite drug actually touches inside cells, in a 2026 study. The drug, BKI-1708, attacks enzymes of Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite behind toxoplasmosis, and forces it into bloated multi-nucleus forms trapped inside host cells. Using affinity columns built from the drug plus mass spectrometry, the team fished out every protein that binds it, in both the parasite and human fibroblast host cells.

Beyond the expected enzymes, parasite proteins for cell division, skeleton, shipping, and gene control also bound the drug. Host cell binders centred on skeleton regulators and proteins that grip DNA and RNA, and infection reshuffled that host profile. Sousa's team reads the pattern as a many-target strike: the drug works by disturbing several processes at once, not by one clean hit.
pmc-13517363:
Victoria López-Lombó and five colleagues test a step-tracking app in teenagers in a 2026 randomised trial. Nearly four hundred adolescents, average age fourteen, took part for ten weeks. One group walked with the app at least three times weekly; the other kept usual habits. The team asked whether maturity and sex changed who benefited.

Maturity did not moderate the programme overall. Its fingerprints showed only in small, specific places: early-maturing boys in the app group trimmed fat mass and skinfold thickness versus controls.
