Boys' fitness gains in both groups owed mostly to puberty itself. Girls on the app, though, gained abdominal endurance and grip strength that controls did not. Effect sizes stayed small throughout. The authors keep the standard app as a fair school tool and treat sex-tailored designs as a hypothesis, not a verdict.
pmc-13517463:
García-Ramos and colleagues build a more sensitive test for tick- and flea-borne Rickettsia infections in pets. Their 2026 paper develops a droplet digital PCR assay. The method splits a blood sample into thousands of droplets to count tiny amounts of bacterial DNA. It addresses a diagnostic problem: these infections show vague signs and circulate at low levels.

The team validated the assay and applied it to blood from 170 Canary Islands dogs and cats suspected of rickettsial infection. Rickettsia DNA turned up in six dogs and no cats in this series. The authors are careful about readiness: more validation must come before routine use. They frame the method as a veterinary diagnostic candidate and a surveillance tool. It supports a One Health view. Animal and human infections of this group are linked through shared vectors and environments.
pmc-13518463:
Kathrin Hering and six colleagues update expert guidance on radiotherapy for invasive skin cancer in a 2026 opinion piece. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is the second commonest skin cancer, rising steadily in Germany, and surgery cures most cases. Radiation steps in when surgery is impossible, anatomically awkward around eyes, nose, or ears, or refused by the patient.

The authors walk through the toolbox: electron beams, surface X-rays, implanted sources, and megavoltage photons, matched by tumour thickness, site, and patient factors. Local control is excellent and cosmetic results kind, with quality of life often preserved or improved in early disease. Cautions remain for the young, who carry a small lifetime risk of a second cancer in the field, and for rare syndromes with heightened radiation sensitivity. New immune drugs hover nearby, their best placement still unsettled. Hering's team aims the update at everyday treatment choices.
pmc-13518863:
Reza Tadayonnejad leads an eight-author proof-of-concept study in 2026 on magnetic brain stimulation for impulsivity in borderline personality disorder. Impulsivity and emotional instability define the illness, treatment options are few, and imaging points to faulty wiring between frontal control areas and the amygdala, an emotion hub.

Eleven people had brain scans to locate personal frontal targets most strongly connected to each amygdala. After a task battery, each got one session of patterned pulses, then repeated the tasks. Hitting the right-side target sharply cut impulsivity, while left or both-side stimulation did not. Emotional reactivity stayed unchanged, and nobody had serious side effects. A single session is only a start, the authors caution.
pmc-13519763:
Liz Cuperus and colleagues tested whether hair samples can track long-term use of an inhaled asthma drug. Published in 2026, the study drew on COPD patients at ten hospitals in the Netherlands within the TRICOLON trial, pairing hair samples with data from digital inhalers. Each hair sample was cut into three one-centimeter segments, each standing for one month of growth.

Of 96 patients who gave hair, 49 had usable hair and inhaler data. Within-person drug levels stayed steady across segments, yet the link between hair levels and recorded inhalations was only a weak trend over three months. Dark hair and lower body weight carried higher drug levels, though neither changed the link itself. The authors judge hair testing promising but not yet ready to replace digital tracking.
pmc-13520263:
Carlos García-Porrúa leads a five-author narrative review in 2026 on using X-ray progression to monitor psoriatic arthritis, a chronic inflammatory disease that erodes joints. Scoring visible structural damage is the standard way to judge whether treatment truly modifies the disease, since damage predicts shorter survival.

Clinicians most often adapt two rheumatoid arthritis scoring systems to psoriatic hands and feet, the review finds. Faster damage clusters with heavier disease activity plus factors such as overweight and smoking. Checking damage at six months may already reveal progression in highly active disease. Newer approved drugs show varying ability to halt the damage. García-Porrúa and colleagues note agreed definitions of progression are still missing and no validated biomarker yet guides drug choice.
pmc-13520363:
Ying Li and colleagues catalogue in 2026 the WRKY control-gene family in apricot and single out one member for salt tolerance testing. Salty soil limits apricot growth and yield, while WRKY genes help plants handle stress.

Genome scanning found 58 family members, mapped by relatedness, chromosome position and structure. Candidate PaWRKY57 was then overproduced in tobacco as a test plant. Transformed plants germinated better in salt, grew more strongly, and showed less cell damage with stronger protective enzymes. Interaction predictions link the gene to stress signalling partners. Breeders gain a shortlist for developing hardier apricot varieties.
pmc-13520463:
Shaowen Zhang and colleagues test in 2026 whether a neck nerve block before chest surgery reduces sore throat after placement of a double-lumen breathing tube. Sore throat is among the most common complaints after this type of intubation.

One hundred twenty patients were randomised, with half receiving an ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block using a small dose of ropivacaine and half receiving no block. Sore throat rates at one, six and twenty-four hours were far lower with the block, and pain scores and severity grades also favoured the block. Hoarseness, cough, lung complications and inflammation markers were tracked as secondary measures.
pmc-13520563:
Sanjay Kalra and colleagues survey in 2026 how general physicians across India understand and handle fluid and salt losses in illnesses without diarrhoea, such as fever. Dehydration in those illnesses is common, yet oral rehydration habits outside diarrhoea care are rarely studied.

Responses came from 1,333 verified physicians, split almost evenly between modern medicine and traditional AYUSH training. Fever was the most recognised cause, with older patients seen as most vulnerable. Most respondents agreed that fluid deficits weaken immunity and delay recovery by about five days. Ready-to-drink balanced solutions were viewed very favourably, while taste ranked as a key driver of patient compliance.
pmc-13521963:
Shinsuke Sasada leads the 2026 annual report of Japan's national breast cancer registry for patients registered in 2023, covering 107,372 patients at 1,317 institutions. Just under half of tumours were stage I at diagnosis, with stage II near one third.

Hormone receptor positivity dominated the case mix, while HER2 positivity sat near one eighth. Among patients without distant spread, breast-conserving surgery covered about four in ten, sentinel node sampling about three quarters, and reconstruction only a small share. A focused section details drug treatment for very small node-negative cancers by subtype, showing endocrine therapy near universal in hormone-sensitive disease.
pmc-13522463:
Hsing-Hui Liu and colleagues use Taiwanese health databases in a 2026 cohort study of acid-blocking medicines and later dementia. Nearly two and a half million adults aged forty or older without dementia at the start were followed for new dementia diagnoses. Cumulative exposure to proton pump inhibitors, drugs that reduce stomach acid, was calculated from prescription records.

About five to six percent of participants developed dementia during follow-up. Higher cumulative use of the acid-blocking drugs was linked to higher dementia risk in a stepwise pattern, with the strongest link in people under sixty-five. The authors stress that the design shows an association rather than proof of cause, and that possible biological pathways still need clarification before prescribing advice changes.
pmc-13523263:
Maryam Amini-Pozveh and colleagues study whether denture base color matching affects satisfaction in a 2026 clinical study. Eighty-eight patients without teeth who were receiving complete dentures took part. A dentist selected the closest gum color match from a shade guide, patients independently chose their preferred base color, and all dentures were then made in one standard shade. Satisfaction was rated at delivery and one week later.

Satisfaction showed no link with age, sex, education, or the color patients chose themselves. Satisfaction did correlate positively with the dentist's initial color selection, and the relationship grew stronger at the follow-up visit. The authors interpret the pattern as evidence that a professionally judged match between denture base and natural gum tissue supports patient satisfaction.
pmc-13524963:
Hiroto Funahashi and colleagues ask, in a 2026 computed tomography simulation study, where bone removal concentrates when the hip socket is reamed for total hip replacement in osteoarthritis. Surgeons ream the acetabulum to seat a cup, and knowing direction-specific patterns could refine technique, especially in mildly shallow sockets from developmental dysplasia.

Preoperative scans from 118 female hips treated in 2021–2024 fed a simulation of cup placement at standard angles. Reamed area was measured at twelve clock-face positions. The smallest removal sat at one o'clock and the largest at eight o'clock, a posterior concentration clear across comparisons. The pattern was strongest in mild dysplasia, with notably small removal toward the upper front and large removal at eight and nine o'clock. The authors offer the map as anatomical guidance.
pmc-13525963:
Ann-Christin Eder and colleagues report a 2026 first-in-human imaging study of a radioactive tracer targeting EphA2, a receptor overproduced in pancreatic cancer and linked with poor prognosis. No suitable tracer for clinical scans had existed. The bicyclic peptide tracer, labeled with gallium-68, was tested in patients with confirmed pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Seven patients, five after chemotherapy and two at first staging, underwent PET and CT imaging at several time points after injection. No adverse events occurred, kidneys took the highest absorbed dose, and overall radiation exposure was modest. Tumor uptake was rapid, within fifteen minutes, with mainly kidney excretion. Of forty-five lesions, the new scan flagged thirty-six and found eleven that standard imaging missed, while missing nine that standard imaging caught. The authors support further study.
pmc-13527663:
Cielita Lopez-Lennon and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, which motor and nonmotor factors track with daily walking activity in people with Parkinson disease. Falling step counts can flag emerging disability that clinic visits miss. Multiday activity monitoring captures real-world movement, yet influences from disease severity and nonmotor symptoms were unclear.

Mean daily steps were computed over seven days in 198 participants with mild to moderate disease, and standard rating scales captured motor severity in both medication states plus nonmotor complaints. Median daily steps were about 5,180. Worse off-medication motor scores linked modestly with fewer steps, while on-medication scores showed no link. One nonmotor complaint stood out, where lightheadedness on standing was tied to roughly two thousand fewer daily steps. The authors urge autonomic screening in disability assessments.
pmc-13527963:
Zhening Miao and eight colleagues report a 2026 genetic survey of water-saving, drought-resistant rice lines. Such rice matters where water is scarce. Two diseases, blast and bacterial blight, threaten its yields. The team genotyped 47 core parent lines for eleven blast resistance genes and four blight resistance genes.

One blast gene, Ptr, appeared in nearly every line. Broad-acting genes such as Pigm were absent, and Pi9 was uncommon. Blight resistance genes showed up in only about a third of lines, mostly in restorer lines. The recessive gene xa5 was missing entirely. More resistance genes generally meant stronger disease scores in the tests. The authors offer the map as a guide for choosing parents and stacking genes in breeding.
pmc-13528063:
Anjali Yadav and four colleagues report a 2026 case of yoga used to support male fertility care. The patient was a 30-year-old Indian man with severe low sperm count. He and his partner had faced four years of infertility. His job as an architectural researcher meant heavy travel and poor routines. Stress levels were high. He followed a supervised yoga program for six months, five days a week.

Sessions mixed breathing work, meditation, and set postures. Afterward his sperm count and movement improved. Abnormal shapes fell, and sperm DNA damage dropped. Oxidative stress in semen eased as well. Quality of life rose across physical, mental, social, and environmental areas. Doctors then advised intrauterine insemination. The authors present yoga as a helpful add-on, while noting one case proves little on its own.
pmc-13528163:
Sathya Jeganathan and four colleagues follow kangaroo mother care at home after intensive care discharge in South India in a 2026 study. The method keeps small babies skin-to-skin for warmth and bonding. Four hundred twenty mother-baby pairs enrolled at discharge. Practice was checked two months later. Two babies had died and twelve families were lost.

A quarter of families never practiced the method at home. Only about nineteen percent practiced it well. Heavier babies, at least one and a half kilos, were cared for this way more often. Babies born at term got it less. Mothers over forty-five kilos also practiced less. Doing the care right before discharge tripled the odds of keeping it up. Father support mattered too. The authors say discharge coaching and family buy-in need work.
pmc-13529163:
Yang and colleagues applied data mining to Traditional Chinese Medicine literature on acupoint sticking therapy, where medicated plasters are applied to body points, for sudden asthma attacks. Their 2026 computational study aimed to replace practitioner habit with evidence-based rules for choosing points. They analyzed 40 published studies covering 2,107 patients using pattern-finding methods that expose hidden groupings and frequent combinations.

Yang found two dominant, clinically distinct patient patterns in the literature. For breathlessness with chills and clear sputum, a cold-type pattern, the strongest point combination paired two back points with a kidney-related point. For breathlessness with yellow sputum and fever, a heat-type pattern, the third point switched to one on the spine linked to clearing heat. The authors argue that turning accumulated clinical experience into quantified, pattern-specific rules gives a foundation for properly designed trials of personalized treatment.
pmc-13529663:
Feifei Qin and three colleagues sequence the genome of a fungus that lives inside a Chinese grass in a 2026 study. The fungus, Alternaria alternata strain Y-2, dwells in Leymus chinensis without causing disease. The draft genome spans about 34.4 million bases. Its GC share is fifty-one percent. Gene prediction found 12,724 protein-coding genes.

A completeness check scored the assembly at 98.9 percent. Nearly all genes matched known records. The team counted 448 genes for carbohydrate-cutting enzymes. Those tools suit breaking down plant fiber. Twenty-one clusters for making special metabolites also appeared. Family trees confirmed the strain's identity. The authors say this is the first genome for this fungus from this host. It should help explain how quiet tenants aid plant stress defense.
pmc-13530163:
Wang and colleagues built purely inorganic cages whose light response can be tuned by planned distortion, in a 2026 materials study. The cages are phosphorus and sulfur or selenium clusters with the lowest symmetry allowed, grown as pure left- or right-handed crystals. Materials that combine handedness with frequency-doubling light output are wanted for polarization-based photonics, but sturdy inorganic examples that pass infrared light widely are rare.

Wang created a controlled series by swapping single atoms in the cages. The series showed a strong handedness effect in doubled light output, beating a standard crystal and withstanding laser damage well. Across the series, the handedness effect tracked the cage's distortion and its electric dipole, the separation of charge within the molecule. That gives builders a simple number that predicts performance. The work makes inorganic cages a tunable platform for infrared chiroptical devices.
pmc-13530563:
Uppstrom and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 02, a cadaver study of treating a type 3 oblique radial tear of the lateral meniscus. Such a tear severs the knee cushion's hoop fibers near its root. They compared two repairs against simply trimming the torn tissue away.

Eight fresh-frozen human knees were loaded with five hundred newtons while sensors tracked joint pressure, meniscus extrusion, and root forces at four bending angles. The tear raised average and peak pressures sharply and pushed the meniscus outward. It also cut the front root's force transmission by at least forty percent at every angle tested in this laboratory study. Both repairs, one anchored to the shin bone and one stitched to the capsule, restored pressures, extrusion, and root forces to intact levels. Trimming could not match that restoration in the comparisons reported.
pmc-13531863:
Aurore Deledalle and co-authors survey 1,570 French medical residents in 2026 about wanting an academic medicine career that mixes research, teaching, and patient care. Interest has faded lately, especially among women. A career theory lens shaped questions on learning experience, confidence, expectations, and research interest.

Overall intention ran low, with women lower than men. Research interest predicted intention most strongly, followed by hands-on research history and mentorship. Stress dragged confidence down, while satisfaction lifted expectations. Gender gaps traced mainly to unequal learning chances and research access, pointing mentors and programs toward fairer exposure.
pmc-13532863:
Pierre and colleagues report a 2026 study of how moving visual scenes change the vestibular system's role in balance.  The team tested 22 healthy young adults standing still, with and without optokinetic stimulation, a rotating visual pattern. Mild electrical stimulation of the inner ear let them measure the vestibular share of balance control.

Participants without the rotating pattern showed no measurable change in vestibular contribution across conditions. The design thus isolates the visual effect: any shift in the vestibular share can be credited to the moving scene rather than to the task itself. This matters for virtual reality balance training and for disorders where visual motion provokes dizziness.
pmc-13533063:
Öztürk, Işık, and Teke anchor a workhorse enzyme onto an unlikely support: the papery inner membrane of an onion. Acetylcholinesterase matters for biosensors that detect nerve agents and pesticides, but free enzymes are fragile and single-use. Their 2026 study adsorbed the enzyme onto the natural membrane, locked it with a cross-linker, and tuned enzyme dose, membrane amount, and contact time for maximum activity. The team confirmed the attachment with electron microscopy and infrared spectroscopy.

The immobilised enzyme shrugged off heat and acidity changes that cripple the free form. At a warm operating temperature it kept about four fifths of its activity where the free enzyme kept only half on the reported comparison. It survived reuse, holding over three fifths of its starting activity after ten consecutive cycles, and still delivered a useful share after a month on the shelf at room temperature.
pmc-13533363:
Thomas Mock and a large global team outline in 2026 the 100 Diatom Genomes Project. Diatoms are algae found in nearly all waters, and they fix about a fifth of global carbon each year. Genome data so far cover only a few model species, which limits study of their variety and uses.

One hundred species were chosen for genome and RNA sequencing, with strains checked for growth and clean DNA. So far 104 species passed checks and 20 finished assemblies are ready. Readers gain a shared base for tracing diatom evolution, ecology, and future uses in industry.
pmc-13533463:
Rola H Ali and colleagues test in 2026 whether a stain pattern can flag gene changes in gastrointestinal stromal tumours. Tumours with PDGFRA changes often sit in the stomach, look distinct, and need specific drugs. The team studied 117 tumours and had three pathologists score stains without knowing gene results.

A Golgi pattern, where stain gathers near the cell centre, appeared in most gene-changed tumours and few others. The stain test was sensitive yet could not tell the key drug-resistant variant apart. Readers learn the stain can guide triage, while gene sequencing still decides drug choice.
pmc-13534463:
Jioun Kim, Youngirl Jeon, and Kilho Eom analyse in 2026 how an unstable surface changes the single leg deadlift, a one-leg strength exercise. The move builds strength and balance, yet wobble may limit joint motion and loading. Thirty healthy men performed the move on flat ground and on a foam pad.

Ankle sway nearly doubled on the pad, while hip and knee motion fell by several degrees. Key hip and ankle muscles worked harder, and the rear thigh muscle rose in both phases. Coaches should weigh balance gains against reduced loading for strength goals.
pmc-13536763:
Jia-Wen Hu and Tao Shi test a liver-based score for predicting problems after emergency repair of a torn main artery in a 2026 study. The albumin-bilirubin score combines two routine blood measures of liver reserve. Records for 306 patients who had urgent repair were split by score after surgery, with matching to balance starting traits. Breathing support delays, brain problems, dialysis need, and early death were compared.

Patients with worse scores after surgery faced far higher rates of delayed breathing tube removal, dialysis need, and death within a month. The score also predicted repeat breathing support and brain problems, and it beat either blood measure alone. The authors propose the simple score as a handy aid for sorting risk and guiding care after this high-risk operation.
pmc-13536863:
Francesco De Giorgio and co-authors review heme, the iron-holding ring at the core of many proteins, as a driver of new blood vessel growth in a 2026 synthesis. Vessel growth demands large energy supplies, so heme handling may govern whether lining cells can sprout new branches. The review traces heme making, balance, and movement inside vessel lining cells, plus links to gene control and energy production.

Balanced heme supports the many lining cell jobs needed for sprouting, while disturbed balance can stall or distort growth. That dual role opens drug angles in both directions, damping excess vessels in eye disease and cancer or boosting growth where blood supply falls short, such as after stroke. The authors frame heme control as a broad lever for vessel medicine.
pmc-13538463:
Yuanyuan Li and colleagues built the first chromosome-level genome for a small Chinese donkey. Published in 2026, the study mapped the Taihang donkey, a small-sized breed under 110 cm from a land with over 4,000 years of donkey breeding. Large-donkey genomes existed, but small-donkey genomes were nearly absent, blocking breed contrasts.

Long-read and chromosome-linking data plus RNA reads yielded a 2.7-billion-letter genome across 32 chromosomes, five with no gaps. The build captured 99.2 percent of a standard gene set with a very low error rate. The genome supports study of how small donkeys differ, adjust, and were tamed, and aids care of China's rich donkey gene pool. Readers get a base for saving and wisely using these breeds.
pmc-13538563:
Prakash Purswani and colleagues released a detailed X-ray dataset on trapping gas in rock pores. Published in 2026, the dataset comes from lab floods of rock cores with carbon dioxide and salty water under deep-storage heat and pressure. Gas storage safety turns on how fluids move and get stuck in pore networks, yet fine direct readings were rare.

X-ray scans finer than a hair's width tracked fluid levels through draining and soaking-back runs, with flow and pressure logged throughout. The set gives raw and sorted 3D images of dry and fluid-filled cores, plus fluid-share numbers, shape measures, and link maps between phases. Paired crisp and noisy scans at left-behind gas levels support faster scan methods. The set serves model checks and image-sorting benchmarks for deep gas storage.
pmc-13540963:
Matteo Villa and colleagues report a surprise drug effect in 2026. The drug is palbociclib, used in breast cancer care. It normally brakes the cell cycle. The study found it also destroys beta-catenin. That signalling protein drives most colorectal cancers. A chemical library screen surfaced the effect.

Mechanism work showed how the trick works. The drug quiets a growth pathway in the cell. Another enzyme can then tag beta-catenin for disposal. Pairing the drug with a KRAS blocker killed tumors strongly. The pair worked in dishes and in animals. A second partner, blocking ERK5, also paired well. Normal cells were largely spared by that pairing.
pmc-13542263:
Kiarash Tajbakhsh's team ran a 2026 imaging study that reads thyroid tumours in 3D instead of relying only on flat tissue slices. Samples from 418 patients, set in tissue microarrays, were scanned with micro-CT, a high-resolution X-ray method suited to small samples. Computer analysis then pulled radiomics features, meaning patterns of shape and texture, from each tumour volume.

Those patterns split cancerous from non-cancerous thyroid tissue and told papillary carcinoma apart from follicular neoplasms. The features also flagged whether the BRAF V600E mutation, a common driver change in thyroid cancer, was present. A tool highlighted which visual traits drove each call. A small early look at TERT promoter mutations hinted at further patterns, though the authors stress that this early signal needs checking before use in care.
pmc-13543463:
Xiaoshuang Wang's team published a 2026 study of how young footballers recover after matches in congested weeks, when fixtures pile up, versus ordinary weeks. Nineteen male under-19 provincial players who started and played at least an hour in every match were tested before matches and at fifteen minutes, twenty-four hours, and forty-eight hours afterward. Measures covered jump height, pressure pain sensitivity, and self-rated muscle soreness, with no training or special recovery between tests.

Jump height itself changed similarly in model terms, yet direct contrasts showed it lagging in the congested week at both later time points. Pressure pain sensitivity stayed lower, meaning players hurt more easily, and soreness ratings were higher at every post-match check during congestion. The pattern says a crowded calendar stretches both muscle performance and pain recovery beyond two days, a warning for coaches scheduling youth players.
pmc-13543563:
Zhenkun Tan's team ran a 2026 randomised trial of computerised cognitive remediation therapy for community-dwelling older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Sixty-eight people finished the twelve-week study: one group got health teaching alone, the other added structured computer-based cognitive training. Two standard cognitive tests were given before and after, and blood levels of two brain-related proteins, GFAP and phosphorylated tau, were tracked as hard markers.

The therapy group gained far more on both cognitive tests, with gains in memory, language, and attention. Their GFAP levels, a marker linked to brain inflammation and injury, fell against controls, while the tau marker did not change. The size of the GFAP drop foretold who gained most, with a solid hit rate. Cognitive training may thus leave a clear blood signature, giving future trials a yardstick beyond test scores.
pmc-13544763:
Wei Fu and colleagues published a 2026 review of recent advances in allergen immunotherapy, the only treatment that can retrain the immune system rather than merely suppress allergy symptoms. The therapy now serves hay fever, asthma, food allergy, and eczema driven by IgE antibodies. The review covers the tolerance machinery, new vaccine designs, response biomarkers, disease-by-disease evidence, and combinations with modern biologic drugs.

Tolerance is built by regulatory T and B cells, calming innate lymphoid cells, and blocking antibodies such as IgG4. Newer vaccines use engineered or hypoallergenic allergens, virus-like particles, and peptide designs to gain safety and speed. Candidate blood and cell tests for predicting response are weighed critically. Pairing immunotherapy with anti-IgE or anti-interleukin biologics looks promising in severe asthma. Patient selection, treatment length, and extract standardisation remain the field's open problems.
pmc-13547363:
Rafał Topolnicki, Paweł Dłotko, and Maciej Matyka trained in 2026 a neural network to predict how fluid moves through the tiny pore spaces of materials like rock and filters. That calculation normally needs slow, mesh-heavy simulation. Their encoder-decoder network reads the solid geometry and outputs the velocity field directly. A custom penalty function nudges predictions to obey physics: no compression of the fluid, no flow inside solid, and consistent wrap-around at the edges.

Tuning the penalty weights one at a time showed what each rule contributes, and the best variant stayed accurate on unfamiliar geometries, porosities, and boundary setups. Used as a starting guess for a standard solver, the predictions sped up convergence in more than ninety percent of cases. The authors offer the network as a fast front end for porous flow work.
pmc-13547563:
Qiwen Dong and colleagues followed a lead from human genetics in 2026, testing whether losing a gene called PRDM15 produces autism-like changes in mice. Their earlier sequencing work had flagged the gene, a regulator of other genes, as a candidate risk factor. Mice lacking it were checked for behavior, brain structure, and cell-by-cell gene activity in the hippocampus, a region central to learning and social memory.

The mice groomed repetitively, interacted less socially, and forgot social partners, mirroring core autism features. Their hippocampi held fewer mature neurons in one key subregion, with stem cells piling up instead of maturing. Deleting the gene only in neural stem cells reproduced much of the picture. The authors name PRDM15 a regulator of hippocampal development with relevance to autism.
pmc-13548563:
Mohamed Mustaf Ahmed reviews how bias can creep into artificial intelligence tools that predict surgical risk, in a 2026 article on patient safety and fairness. Models range from classic calculators to machine learning systems trained on large surgical registries. When a model performs unevenly across racial or ethnic groups, the flaw may hurt one group's safety or widen gaps between groups, and registry data often record race poorly.

Some studies report lower sensitivity or more missed high-risk cases for particular subgroups, which could lead teams to underestimate danger for those patients. Fixes such as reweighting data or fairness-aware training show promise but remain barely tested in surgery, and they force trade-offs between accuracy within a group and equal error rates across groups. The author calls for diverse validation studies, transparent reporting, and governance built around equity.
pmc-13549163:
Macedo and five colleagues published this 2026 study testing whether the strength-duration test can screen intensive care patients for critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy. The test is a bedside measure of how much electrical charge a nerve-muscle unit needs to fire. The conditions are the nerve and muscle damage behind ICU-acquired weakness. Full electrodiagnostic testing is often unavailable at the bedside. In 60 ventilated patients the team compared the strength-duration test and a rival test against a reference test.

It discriminated reasonably, with an area under the curve of 0.8 at its best cutoff. It gave 73 percent sensitivity and 68 percent specificity for probable disease. The stimulus electrodiagnosis test managed an area of 0.7, making it the more balanced screener. Neither test replaces diagnosis or separates nerve from muscle damage. The authors position it as a bedside adjunct for flagging cases early, and call for multicentre validation before adoption.
pmc-13550463:
Luping Zhu and colleagues search the gene activity of nasal polyp tissue for players tied to stress granules, the droplets cells form under duress, in a 2026 transcriptomic study of chronic sinusitis. Long-lasting sinus inflammation with polyps often resists steroids and surgery, and stress granules appear within its tissue. Combining two public datasets with granule gene lists, the team applied machine learning, diagnostic testing, and expression checks.

Three genes survived every filter: ANG, CRYAB, and FBP1. Enrichment analysis tied them jointly to cell cycle pathways. Immune mapping found twenty-three cell types differing between patients and controls, and all three genes correlated positively with type-two helper T cells, the allergic inflammation drivers. Drug databases linked three existing compounds, including estradiol, to all three genes. The authors offer the trio as diagnostic leads for this stubborn sinus disease.
pmc-13551263:
In a 2026 study, Amy Sorge and seven colleagues examined sorafenib-like compounds that could rescue a last-resort antibiotic. Colistin is toxic and bacteria increasingly resist it, so the team built a library of analogues of sorafenib, a cancer drug previously found to boost colistin. They tested the new compounds against resistant Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, and Pseudomonas, plus MRSA on its own.

A lead compound called NDM-773 dropped the colistin dose needed against all three resistant species to very low levels. It also killed MRSA by itself at low concentration, with a very low rate of resistance mutations in the reported test. Toxicity to liver cells fell more than threefold compared with sorafenib, giving the compound favorable safety margins in both roles.
pmc-13551863:
Paulina Własiuk, with a large Polish team, published a 2026 study of antibody genes in a blood cancer. The cancer is chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The mutation state of one gene region, IGHV, predicts how the disease will run. The cohort held 4,251 newly diagnosed Polish patients. It is the largest national set of its kind. The team read over 4,300 gene rearrangements and paired them with chromosome data.

Most patients carried a single clone. A small share carried two, at times with clashing mutation states. Shared receptor patterns clustered in unmutated disease. They also clustered in patients with a TP53 mutation. Unmutated cases carried more high-risk chromosome changes. Mutated cases more often showed one mild deletion, which sharpens subtyping.
pmc-13551963:
Dan Cai, Xiaojing Zheng, Bo Zheng, and Hui Ye published a 2026 review of nursing care and melatonin in intensive care. ICU patients sleep badly, which harms recovery. Nurses use non-drug steps such as dim lights and clustered care to protect rhythm. The team searched five databases to February 2026 for randomized trials. They pooled melatonin, cortisol, and sleep outcomes and graded the proof.

Five trials qualified for the review. Nursing care tied to modestly higher melatonin than usual care. Yet no trial profiled melatonin over time. So the authors refuse to claim that rhythm was restored. Cortisol showed no firm gap between groups. Sleep results were mixed and hard to pool. Proof quality was low to very low, which the team stresses.
pmc-13552063:
Xiaoniu Guo and colleagues report a new gel electrolyte design for solid-state sodium batteries, publishing the work in 2026. Sodium batteries promise cheaper, safer large-scale storage than lithium, but gel electrolytes have struggled to stay stable and in close contact at high-voltage cathodes and reactive sodium anodes. The team built a two-phase polymer with step-like channels that guide solvent movement and give different flexibility where each electrode needs it.

A full cell pairing sodium with a phosphate cathode reached a high energy density on total cell mass, and a 4.5-volt pouch cell held nearly all its capacity after 100 cycles, with safety checks included. The design tackles the interface problems that have held gel sodium cells back. Readers get a concrete engineering route toward practical, high-energy sodium storage.
pmc-13552563:
Qing Dong and colleagues examined whether two-tracer PET/CT scans can grade gut and pancreas neuroendocrine tumours, publishing the study in 2026. These rare tumours range from slow-growing to aggressive, and grade guides treatment, so better imaging markers matter. The team reviewed 34 patients with 198 target lesions who had both a somatostatin-receptor tracer scan and a glucose tracer scan.

A new combined measure, the total lesion glycolysis ratio, separated lower from higher grades about as well as existing uptake ratios, but added little once those were known. Its edge faded further in cross-checks that held out one patient at a time. The authors call the ratio exploratory: dual-tracer imaging adds context for grading, while the new measure still needs outside validation before clinical use.
pmc-13553563:
Glenn J Jaffe heads the GOLDEN trial team in a 2026 test of sefaxersen, a drug meant to slow a blinding eye disease. The disease, called geographic atrophy, grows out of age-related macular degeneration and eats away central sight. Sefaxersen is a short strand of genetic code that lowers a part of the immune system called complement factor B. In all, 332 patients joined the masked, placebo-controlled trial.

Monthly shots under the skin cut blood levels of the target protein by well over half. Yet the treated eyes lost tissue at much the same pace as placebo eyes over forty-nine weeks. Side effects matched those in the placebo group, with infections among the most common complaints. Lowering the protein in blood, the trial shows, was not enough to slow the eye disease.
pmc-13555863:
Eshetie Alelign Tsega leads a five-author team measuring whether malaria patients in an Ethiopian district finish a fourteen-day cure in a 2026 study. The drug primaquine clears dormant liver forms of vivax malaria, but only when the full course is taken. Home visits reached 545 of 594 sampled patients treated at local health centres. Self-reports were checked against pill counts.

Barely half the patients stuck to the full course closely enough to count as adherent. Women adhered more often than men. Knowing that malaria can relapse, and having had malaria before, both raised adherence. Side effects cut adherence roughly in half. The authors call for counselling on relapse and side-effect support to lift completion rates in the district.
pmc-13555963:
Qiang Fang, Yan Li, and Yue Yin test whether factory-made fake behaviour data can train procrastination predictors for sports teaching in a 2026 study. Real behaviour records are scarce and private, hampers model building. Their base set covered 487 university athletes, blending motion sensors, training logs, and self-reports. A hybrid generator learned to mimic those sequences while keeping their statistical shape.

Identical prediction models trained on fake and real data performed nearly the same. The small gap between them missed statistical significance. Key relationships among behaviours survived the copying process well. Smoothing during generation, not extra information, likely explains the fake data's slight edge. The authors offer synthetic data as a privacy-safe supplement, within controlled settings only.
pmc-13556063:
Lingyu Jiang and nine colleagues charted in 2026 two decades of echinococcosis, a parasitic tapeworm disease, across Xinjiang in western China. The region carries a heavy, unevenly spread burden. Using case reports from 2005 to 2024, the team mapped clustering by county, tested what changed when free universal health examinations began in late 2016, and fitted a seasonal forecasting model.

Nearly twenty-four thousand cases were reported over the period. Incidence climbed until 2016, jumped at the screening policy's start as hidden cases surfaced, then fell steadily through 2024. Cases clustered in the Ili and Altay areas, and declines were larger among men and among adults, with little change in children under ten. The forecast model gives local programmes a short-term outlook for planning control work.
pmc-13557463:
Joselyn Rwebembera and colleagues tested a smartphone tool that spots strep throat in Ugandan children, publishing the prospective study in 2026. Prompt diagnosis of group A streptococcal throat infection matters because untreated cases can trigger rheumatic fever and lasting heart-valve damage, yet affordable point-of-care tests are scarce where the burden is highest. Children aged 5 to 15 with sore throat had short throat videos recorded on a phone.

An AI image model, trained on Ugandan and US data, read the videos and checked them against lab-grown cultures. The tuned model was tested on 82 children, and it caught every culture-confirmed case and mislabelled few others, reaching about 97 percent overall accuracy. The tool offers a fast, noninvasive way to guide antibiotics and prevent rheumatic heart disease in endemic settings.
pmc-13557863:
Kiyofumi Shimoji and eight colleagues tested in 2026 whether a blood index of oxidative stress foreshadows lung cancer in people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Scarred lungs raise cancer risk, yet the fibrosis itself hides early tumours on imaging. The team measured two blood quantities at diagnosis in 90 patients, one reflecting oxidant damage products and one reflecting antioxidant power, and combined them into a single index.

Fifteen patients developed lung cancer during follow-up. Their starting index values were clearly higher than those of patients who stayed cancer free, even though the oxidant measure alone did not differ. The index separated the groups well in accuracy testing and stayed independently linked to cancer after adjustment for antifibrotic treatment and lung wash findings. It did not predict death in general, which the authors read as specificity for cancer development.
pmc-13558763:
Yiren Wu and three colleagues surveyed in 2026 village cadres in Hainan, China, about how internet use shapes their green behaviour. These officials run grassroots rural rule, so their habits steer local care of the environment directly. Survey data from 298 cadres were analysed through a social cognitive lens. The team traced links among internet use, awareness of green policy, social networks, and two kinds of green behaviour, daily life and farm work.

Internet use tracked with stronger green behaviour, and the path ran partly through sharper policy awareness, which social networks boosted. Feeling that the local environment had worsened strengthened the internet's link with lifestyle behaviour but not with farm choices. Benefits clustered among farm-focused, small-scale, and better educated cadres. The authors advise pairing digital access with policy outreach when training rural officials.
pmc-13558963:
Michał Bonczar and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review with meta-analysis comparing surgical and conservative care for primary fractures of the medial epicondyle, the bony point on the inner elbow. These breaks are common in children and teenagers, often after a fall, and treatment choice has long been debated. The team searched seven major databases and pooled results from 65 studies published between 1982 and 2026.

Surgery produced a pooled union rate of 97 percent, while immobilization without surgery reached only 46 percent in the pooled estimate. Complications were also less frequent after surgery, at 21 percent against 36 percent for conservative care. Among the operations compared, screw fixation paired the highest healing rate with the fewest complications. The authors argue that these pooled figures give clinicians firmer ground for weighing healing, elbow function, and risk when they choose a treatment path.
pmc-13559463:
Peng Song and colleagues developed a way to predict ALK fusion status in non-small cell lung cancer from CT scans and clinical data, sparing some patients the limits of biopsy testing. Their 2026 retrospective multicenter study enrolled 722 patients, 291 of them ALK-positive. Radiomics, the extraction of many measurable features from tumor images, supplied over two thousand candidate features.

Feature selection narrowed the field, and three models were compared: clinical features alone, image features alone, and a combined model. The combined model won, reaching an area under the curve of 0.973 in the validation cohort. Knowing ALK status matters because it directs patients toward targeted drugs built for that gene change. The authors argue their noninvasive approach could help select patients for such therapy before treatment starts. Performance in the training cohort ran higher still, which they report alongside the more cautious validation figure.
pmc-13560863:
Schofield and co-authors set out a 2026 study protocol for HOPE-AO, a project on overprescribing of pain medicines in older adults with chronic pain. Pain is often missed and then poorly managed in this group, breeding both underreporting and excessive prescribing. The protocol covers qualitative interviews within a wider mixed methods programme.

One work package mines a national primary care database for prescribing patterns across the older population in the United Kingdom. The qualitative package, detailed here by Schofield, will interview patients and health professionals about experiences, perceptions, and needs around pain prescribing. A discrete choice experiment adds evidence on what trade-offs people accept in pain care decisions. Findings will feed a jointly designed intervention to be tested in a later research programme, the authors state.
pmc-13562563:
Hafsa Matich and two colleagues build an automated tool that maps cracks, pixel by pixel, in earthen heritage buildings. Mud and clay structures crack as they age, and hairline fractures can warn of deeper structural trouble. Hand inspection is slow and uneven. The 2026 framework cleans high-resolution images, traces crack skeletons, and runs a lightweight learning model tuned for fine, thin damage. A purpose-built app lets inspectors upload photos or shoot them live through a camera on site.

Field tests in real time showed high accuracy and steady performance in both controlled and real settings. Beyond detection, the system reports each crack's width, average width, direction, and severity grade. Those numbers turn a photograph into evidence a conservation team can rank and act on. The authors pitch the tool as a scalable aid for heritage managers who must decide which walls need attention first.
pmc-13563963:
Łukasz Nowak leads a 2026 systematic review, prepared with European urology groups, comparing two kidney stone operations in older patients. Eight studies with 849 patients compared a flexible scope passed up the urinary tract against a procedure that reaches the kidney through a small opening in the back.

The back-entry procedure left more patients fully stone-free at the end. The scope procedure carried lower odds of overall and minor complications in the pooled results. Subgroup checks used two age cutoffs for defining older patients. Older adults and their surgeons get a clear trade-off between complete stone clearance and a gentler recovery profile.
pmc-13564963:
Tahniat Afsari and colleagues review a new kind of medical machine: micro- and nanorobots that swim, push, and squeeze through the body instead of drifting passively like ordinary drug carriers. Because their motion creates forces, these tiny robots can also trigger cells' mechanical sensors, changing how cells behave and tissues remodel. This 2026 review asks how propulsion, biology, and artificial intelligence can be designed together.

Rather than sorting robots only by how they move, the authors propose linking each propulsion pattern to the biological response it produces, a principle they call force-to-function coupling. AI adds prediction, image-guided steering, and closed-loop control under the body's uncertainty. The review closes with the translation hurdles, from safety to control, that stand between these machines and precision nanomedicine in patients.
pmc-13569263:
Mart Pothast and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a body-based model that predicts ferritin, the iron storage marker, in blood donors so donation spacing can be set before iron runs low. Inputs include starting ferritin and hemoglobin, donation gaps and volume, plus donor height and weight, tuned on earlier studies and checked on new Dutch donors from 2021.

Predictions after five donations landed within measurement uncertainty about seventy-one percent of the time, with slight underestimation and accuracy varying by sex and age. Starting ferritin and weight mattered most, and the team produced tables of sensible donation frequency. Blood services get a proactive alternative to reacting after donors become iron deficient.
pmc-13570863:
Maria Aleshin and colleagues published this 2026 study on the leftover burden of hidradenitis suppurativa, a painful chronic skin disease, in patients treated with adalimumab. Until recently it was the only approved biologic drug for moderate to severe cases in the United States.

Using insurance claims, the team followed more than two thousand adults who started the drug between 2015 and 2018. About six in ten stopped treatment, and only a small share switched to another biologic. Half had quit within a year. Women, younger patients, and those on Medicaid stopped more often. Visits and procedures fell during treatment, yet patients still needed antibiotics and surgery, showing relief remained incomplete.
pmc-13572363:
Jieying Sui, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 survey study of strain linked to feeling unable to be oneself. The work looks at how that strain ties to distress among students in China. Two inner factors get close attention: how clear a person's sense of self is, and how much a person hides feelings.

The team surveyed 5,202 full-time students at public and private schools across Henan Province in March and April 2025. Set scales measured strain, clarity of self, hidden feelings, and distress. Strain went with higher distress. Low clarity of self and hidden feelings each carried part of that link, and a chain ran from strain to low clarity, then to hidden feelings, then to distress. The model accounted for 41 percent of the spread in distress scores.
pmc-13572463:
Habtu Debash, with four colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of malaria drug performance in northeast Ethiopia. Two parasite species cause most cases there, and health teams must watch whether first-line drugs still work. The team also tracked how fast the sex forms of the parasite, which pass malaria to mosquitoes, clear after treatment.

From November 2024 to January 2026, 159 patients with mild malaria were followed for 28 days. One species was treated with artemether-lumefantrine and the other with chloroquine, and some patients got a low dose of primaquine as well. Cure rates were 88.9 and 97.4 percent for the two species. Fever and parasites cleared faster in the second species. Primaquine cut sex-form clearance time in one species from eleven days to seven, and from seven to four in the other. Side effects stayed mild.
pmc-13572563:
Enrique Díaz Cantón offers a 2026 perspective on where artificial intelligence meets molecular biology by 2035. Tools such as AlphaFold can now predict a protein's still shape with fine precision. Yet proteins move, bend, and reshape when a drug binds, and that motion drives how they work.

The essay argues that world models, systems that learn the rules of how things change over time, are the next step. Applied to molecules, they could trace how a protein flexes along a path, not just where it rests. That skill could aid cancer drug design, above all for proteins long called undruggable, such as shapeless ones with no fixed form. The piece maps gains and hard problems on the road to 2035. It frames motion, not shape alone, as the field's next frontier.
pmc-13573263:
Sanjay R. Kalliat, M. Alejandro Valdes-Pena and Joshua G. Pierce published this 2026 chemistry study expanding a family of candidate antibiotics, pyrrolidine-2,3-dione monomers, against Staphylococcus aureus. This bacterium readily develops drug resistance and shelters in biofilms, slimy surface communities that shrug off standard treatment. The team built a new wave of the compounds through a multicomponent reaction and tested them against three S. aureus strains, including for biofilm killing.

Adding a trifluoromethyl group at a key position on the scaffold improved the compounds' profile over earlier versions. The most potent analogue, compound 18, stopped bacterial growth at 2 micrograms per millilitre against all three strains tested. Biofilm activity varied more. Three compounds cleared established biofilms at 32 micrograms per millilitre. Two achieved a clearance-to-inhibition ratio of 4, a performance the authors call uncommon among approved drugs. They note testing against Gram-negative bacteria and for cell toxicity is still to come.
pmc-13573363:
Konstantinos Triantafyllias and a large consortium team set out a 2026 protocol for a review that will define lung disease linked to muscle inflammation diseases. These autoimmune diseases, grouped as idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, can scar the lungs, with courses from slow to fast and deadly. No shared name or set of criteria exists, which blocks fair comparison across studies.

The review will search five databases for studies to June 30, 2025, that state a definition for the lung condition. Trials, cohorts, reviews, and guidelines all count, for adults and children alike. Screeners will pull out case definitions, test methods, lung patterns, and antibody profiles. Counts will sum how often each part appears, with a structured story where counts fail. The map will feed a consensus process to fix one standard definition.
pmc-13573463:
Saman Najafi, with six colleagues, presents a 2026 scoping review of extended cost-effectiveness analysis in health care. The extended method adds two lenses to standard value checks: who gains the health, and who is shielded from ruinous bills. That lens matters most where families pay much of the cost themselves.

Searches in October 2025 found 1,955 records, and 19 studies met the bar, spanning work from 2000 to 2025. Most came from low- and middle-income countries in Asia and Africa. Vaccine programs, taxes on harmful goods, public services, and mother-child care led the topics. Gains were most often told as bills avoided, disaster spending averted, and poverty cases averted, split by income band. The authors call for wider use and shared measures.
pmc-13574763:
Fırat Oğuz, with two colleagues, ran a 2026 study of how pulling the upper jaw forward shapes the chin bone in growing children. The treatment, a face mask braced on the chin, fixes a class III bite where the upper jaw sits too far back. Its side effects on the jaw joint of the chin, the symphysis, were the open question.

The records covered 35 growing patients with that bite pattern. Twenty wore a Petit-type face mask, while 15 matched patients went untreated as controls. Length and angle measures of the symphysis came from side head X-rays taken before and after the period. The chin brace is the load path of interest, since mask force passes through it to the upper jaw. Any change in chin shape would matter for later bite and face balance. The authors frame the read as a safety check on a common early treatment.
pmc-13577563:
Hsiang-An Lee and three colleagues review surgery tactics for knee replacement in patients whose thigh bone bows sideways, in a 2026 systematic review. This bowing is common in Asian patients and can throw off the alignment of an artificial knee. The review gathered studies from four databases up to August 2025 on techniques and their X-ray outcomes.

Thirteen studies made the final set. Setting the cutting angle for each patient beat using one fixed angle for restoring leg alignment. Shifting the rod entry point sideways let the guide rod sit straighter and improved component placement. Cutting inside the joint worked as a fallback, limited by deformity severity and technical difficulty. Computer guidance improved accuracy and cut outliers, while custom-made guides showed no clear edge. The authors stress a full-length standing leg scan before planning.
pmc-13577863:
Aaron C Tan, Benjamin Y Kong, and Molly S C Li survey rare gene fusions involving ALK in lung cancer in a 2026 commentary. ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer responds well to targeted pills, with the newest drug holding disease back for a median of over seven years in first-line use. The classic partner gene is EML4, yet wider sequencing keeps finding rare and unusual partners.

The authors gather recent case reports: a complex inversion inside ALK itself that standard tests missed but a blood-based sequencing test caught, plus three new partner genes. All four patients responded to alectinib, a sign that rare fusions can still be actionable. The piece compares detection methods, noting that tissue staining and older targeted tests can miss odd rearrangements, while RNA-based sequencing finds more at higher cost and difficulty.
pmc-13578563:
Dandan Zhang and colleagues pair AI with a pocket ultrasound probe to screen baby hips, in a 2026 study. A loose hip socket in infancy, if missed, can lead to lasting gait trouble, yet expert scanners and big machines are scarce in poor or remote areas. Their system spots six landmarks in hip images and clips, then measures the two angles doctors use to grade the socket.

Training used close to twelve hundred still images and about five hundred video clips. Against expert hand measures, the system missed by about a degree on the main angle in still mode. A junior doctor using the handheld tool matched expert work closely as well. The authors pitch the kit for wide screening where specialists are few.
pmc-13578763:
Hongchun Feng, Lin Hu, and Kedong Yue test whether fine plastic fibers toughen dam concrete against weather cycles and hammer blows, in a 2026 study. Dam concrete swings between wet and dry states and takes impact loads, a pairing that grows cracks over time. Blocks of plain concrete and fiber laced concrete went through up to one hundred twenty soak and dry rounds, then took hits in a pressure bar rig.

Both types weakened as cycles rose, losing peak strength and toughness. The fiber blocks always degraded less, held higher peak stress, and soaked up more hit energy. Under the microscope, fibers bridged cracks and spread stress, turning sudden brittle shattering into slow, ductile failure. The authors back the fiber mix for harsh water project settings.
pmc-13584463:
Jiaxin Gao and colleagues test a 12-week Tai Chi program in older adults who are starting to grow frail. Prefrailty is an early, still reversible stage of frailty that raises fall risk. Their 2026 trial enrolled 68 prefrail adults and split them between Tai Chi plus health lessons and health lessons alone, with 64 people finishing the study.

The Tai Chi group practiced a 24-form routine three times a week. By the end, they rose from a chair and walked a short course faster, scored higher on balance and body-performance tests, and swayed less while standing still, with eyes open or closed. Walking speed and overall gait quality also improved. The authors say the pattern fits Tai Chi as a gentle way to protect balance, while asking for bigger trials.
pmc-13586363:
Bai-hui Chen and colleagues trace how a common anesthetic can leave a lasting mark on the young brain. Sevoflurane is widely used in children's surgery, yet early exposure has been tied to later learning problems. Their 2026 mouse study found that the first three weeks of life form a tender window. The harm was pinned on a protein called Arc. Arc normally surges in that window to help prune spare connections in the hippocampus, a memory center.

The gas blocked that surge by speeding the protein's destruction. Young brains then kept too many connections at first, while cleaner cells called microglia pruned badly. Later, those same cells overcorrected, eating too many connections and leaving adults with thinking deficits. Restoring Arc only during the tender window reset the whole path and saved adult thinking, which names a timed target for protecting children under anesthesia.
pmc-13587363:
Junjie Ma and colleagues review a missing second signal that lets tumors escape killer T cells. A T cell needs two inputs to attack: sight of its target, and a co-stimulatory push, most famously through the CD28 switch. Without that push, tumor-hunting cells may spot their target yet fail to multiply, survive, or keep killing. Tumors exploit the gap by hiding the push-giving molecules and raising brake signals instead.

The 2026 review follows the damage through three failure modes: cells that go limp, cells that die off early, and cells worn into exhaustion under constant attack signals. It also weighs the fixes, from standard brake-release drugs to newer co-stimulatory triggers, engineered T cells, and multi-armed antibodies, many still early in testing. The authors urge matching the fix to the stage where activation stalls.
pmc-13588463:
Nithye Parvathy and colleagues audit eight years of skin amyloidosis cases to test how lab staining helps the diagnosis. Primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis deposits misfolded protein only in the skin, in four forms ranging from itchy bumps to flat patches and nodules. Their 2026 review covered 42 cases from 2017 to 2024, running a panel of stains that mark keratin, antibody light chains, and an inflammation protein.

The lichen form made up half the cases, and the upper back was a favored site. A keratin stain lit up in about two thirds of the lichen, macular, and color-change forms. That staining confirms their amyloid comes from skin cells, and it can reveal deposits too small for routine checks. Every nodular case showed light chain restriction, a flag that pushes doctors to rule out body-wide amyloidosis. The authors back the keratin stain as a routine step.
pmc-13592563:
Azura Mohd Affandi leads a large team of clinicians arguing that alopecia areata deserves far more attention in Malaysia. The immune driven disease strips hair in patches without scarring, and many dismiss it as cosmetic. Local studies are few and mostly backward looking, the authors note, with uneven severity scoring, heavy reliance on older therapies, and many patients lost to follow up. Newer immune drugs remain hard to reach on cost grounds.

Their viewpoint sets five priorities. They want a national registry and stronger local data, standard severity tools, and mental health support inside care pathways. They also want guidance written for local practice and wider awareness among public and policymakers. Together, they argue, the steps would speed diagnosis, fair access, and whole person care for adults and children.
pmc-13592663:
Sorasak Suwan and five colleagues build and test a community based service model for stroke rehabilitation in rural Thailand. Most support for occupation based practice comes from hospitals, not village centers. Their model drew on occupation frameworks and stroke care principles, then ran for fourteen sessions over seven weeks with seven stroke survivors at the Doi Lor center in Chiang Mai. Performance, goal, and quality of life scales were paired with an interview of the treating therapist.

Survivors improved on daily occupation performance and satisfaction, hit higher goal levels, and reported better quality of life. The therapist called the model practical, said it sharpened client centered results, and felt more confident using it. Suwan and the team present the model as a workable base for long term rural stroke services.
pmc-13593363:
Zhiyan Wang and three colleagues test whether people can learn to raise or lower a brain chemical on purpose. Neurofeedback usually trains electrical rhythms; here the target was glutamate plus its partner glutamine in the visual cortex, read live by a spectroscopic scanner method. Thirty volunteers used self chosen mental strategies across thirty trials. Half saw true feedback shown as a green or red disk, while half saw random feedback.

The true feedback group learned to push the chemical level in the asked direction over the session. The random feedback group showed no such shift. Wang and the team say chemical level neurofeedback works in principle and could sit beside rhythm based training for disorders tied to this transmitter system.
pmc-13594263:
Johanna E. Reinhard and co-authors used a citizen science setup along a lakeside road to ask when during the night streetlights pull in the most insects, and whether gentler lights help. Volunteers and traps compared old sodium lamps with tailored, shielded LED lights across five slices of the night.

Insect attraction peaked in the late evening and around midnight, and road lights mirrored that rhythm closely, while the mix of species caught also shifted through the night. The shielded LEDs drew fewer insects overall, with the strongest benefit exactly at peak activity hours, though they helped little at twilight and late at night. Because the effect of a light depends on the hour, the authors say towns can time and tune lighting changes to the periods when insects are most active.
pmc-13594463:
Ting Liu and colleagues tracked how COVID-19 reshapes heart nerve control in hamsters over two months. Nerve-control trouble sits at the heart of long COVID, yet how it builds during and after infection is little known. Their 2026 study fitted hamsters with telemetry implants, recorded heart and breathing signals for 56 days after infection, and tested two early treatments.

Nerve control moved in three phases. First came a surge of calming-nerve dominance in days one to four, then a broad slump in days seven to 14, then rising sympathetic and calming inputs from day 28 onward. Early blockade of immune signalling or mitochondrial oxidative stress suppressed the late remodelling. Liu and colleagues frame early immune or stress blockade as a possible route to prevent long-COVID nerve trouble.
pmc-13601363:
Guangju Wang and co-authors study in 2026 how long, mild heat affects reproduction in broiler breeder hens, the parent birds behind meat chickens. Heat stress is a growing problem for poultry farms, but most earlier work used short, sharp heat rather than weeks of moderate warmth.

The team kept one hundred forty-four hens at thirty-two degrees and measured laying, hormones, and organs. Heated hens laid fewer and lighter eggs, and their wombs and young egg follicles weighed less. Blood levels of thyroid hormone and cholesterol fell, while liver fat rose. Brain and blood levels of three reproductive hormones were also suppressed. The authors conclude that steady mild heat weakens the hormone chain that drives egg production, not just appetite.
pmc-13613163:
Borys Fylenko, Ivan Starchenko, and Nataliia Roiko review the health harms linked with vaping, the use of electronic cigarettes that are often sold as a safer choice than smoking. Their short review gathers recent studies on what is in vape aerosol and what it does inside the body. The mix includes nicotine, flavourings, and base fluids, plus breakdown products formed when the liquid is heated, such as formaldehyde and acrolein.

The authors trace effects across the lungs, heart and blood vessels, immune system, and nerves. They discuss a severe lung injury tied to vaping, scarring of the small airways, and raised risks of cancer and heart and brain disease. Young people whose bodies are still developing appear especially at risk. The review gives readers a plain summary of why vaping is not the harmless habit its marketing suggests.
pmc-13614063:
Scovian Lillian profiles malaria researcher Abdoulaye Djimdé of Mali in a 2026 article. Djimdé cracked parts of the malaria parasite's genome while working in his home country. He has since come to advise the United Nations. Djimdé spent decades studying how the parasite resists drugs, working inside the communities where the disease strikes hardest. In March he joined the UN Secretary-General's Scientific Advisory Board.

Lillian describes his work at the Malaria Research and Training Center in Bamako, where he reviews genomic data with younger colleagues. Djimdé argues that African scientific voices belong in the rooms where global science policy is set, since the board guides leaders on science for development. Readers meet a researcher whose career links village-level fieldwork in Mali with the highest level of global advice.
pmc-13614863:
Joseph Jackson and colleagues report a 2026 study of lab-made antimicrobial peptides that resist enzymes, tested as a way to stop bacteria growing in stored human platelet concentrates. Platelets for transfusion are kept at room temperature, about 22 degrees, which limits shelf life to five to seven days and lets any stray bacteria multiply fast. Current sterilising steps using chemicals or ultraviolet light cut infection risk but can damage platelet quality.

The team treated platelet units outside the body with peptides built to survive the enzymes that normally chew such molecules up. The goal is a pre-storage treatment that guards against both known and new germs without weakening the product. Even with strict safety steps, infected transfusions still harm patients, so a gentler shield would be welcome news for blood services.
pmc-13616363:
Tae Young Choi and colleagues watch, live, how unevenly lithium fills a graphite battery anode during charging, and how that unevenness sets the stage for harmful lithium plating on the surface. Standard probes average the whole electrode, hiding local trouble. Combining a microscope view during operation, X-ray diffraction, colour analysis, and simulation, the team followed filling from single particles to the full electrode sheet.

Denser electrodes and faster charging choked ion flow, building steep filling gradients through the sheet's thickness that later spread sideways, so neighbouring zones advanced through the filling stages at wildly different speeds. Plating risk grows where local filling races ahead. Battery designers can use these pictures to balance charging speed against electrode density before plating eats the cell's life, rather than after failure shows up in the field.
pmc-13617263:
Alexander Muacevic and seven colleagues review a quiet shift in psychiatric care: patients increasingly consult large language models about their mental health without telling their clinician. The authors call this the parallel consultation. Cost, scarce appointments, and stigma push patients toward chatbots, which many find validating and non-judgmental compared with human care.

The review gathers early evidence on the risks this creates for clinical decisions. Patients may arrive with chatbot-made self-diagnoses that reshape how they describe symptoms, shift trust away from the clinician, or weaken treatment adherence. Reports also link daily chatbot use with delusional thinking in an emerging pattern dubbed AI-associated psychosis, and chatbot flaws include hallucination, flattery, and bias. The authors urge screening for AI use at intake, clinician training on these tools, and proper prospective studies.
pmc-13617963:
Bruno Grassi, writing alone, revisits the lactate paradox of altitude physiology thirty-five years on, in a review dedicated to the memory of Paolo Cerretelli. The paradox: at altitude, blood lactate at a given hard pace first runs higher than at sea level, yet after acclimatization it falls, and peak lactate drops steadily with height. That pattern seemed impossible if lactate simply meant oxygen shortage.

Modern lactate shuttle research reframes the story. Lactate builds when sugar burning outruns oxygen-based energy production, and the body deliberately circulates lactate for other uses. Fresh hypoxia speeds sugar burning through adrenaline-like stimulation and deepens cell-level oxygen lack. During acclimatization that stimulation fades, oxygen demand drops, and production and use of lactate couple more tightly, so levels fall. Grassi calls the adaptation series remarkable even under the radically changed interpretation, and a fitting legacy for Cerretelli's field.
pmc-13618063:
Zhihao Huang and seven colleagues probe how sodium steers nitrogen chemistry when coal and biomass are heated together. It is a carbon-cutting fuel strategy whose nitrogen oxide emissions depend on what the fuel nitrogen becomes. They pyrolyzed sawdust and lignite, separately and blended, in acid-washed and sodium-loaded forms at five hundred and eight hundred degrees. They tracked nitrogen gases with infrared analysis and nitrogen in the remaining char with spectroscopy.

Temperature split the pathways: at the lower heat, fragile biomass nitrogen escaped as ammonia while coal nitrogen stayed stable. At the higher heat, nitrogen broke open into hydrogen cyanide and coal kept nitrogen locked in its char. Sodium pushed gas release from biomass at low temperature but blocked ring opening at high temperature. During co-pyrolysis it suppressed volatile nitrogen precursors, stabilizing nitrogen in the char. The authors suggest managing alkali metals to control these precursors.
pmc-13618363:
Dan Niu and three colleagues review what happened when a Chinese hospital made CYP2C19 genotyping routine for heart patients receiving stents. The gene shapes how well clopidogrel, a blood-thinning staple after percutaneous coronary intervention, works, and doctors can switch patients to ticagrelor instead. The retrospective study covered three hundred sixty-four adults treated during 2023, all of them genotyped under the hospital's policy.

Prescribing flipped dramatically once results landed. Before testing, three quarters of patients were on ticagrelor and a quarter on clopidogrel; afterward the proportions nearly reversed, with over two hundred fifty patients switching one way and seventy the other. About half the cohort were intermediate metabolizers and about one in seven poor metabolizers. Clinical outcome data were sparse and incomplete, so the authors explicitly refuse causal claims and label event comparisons exploratory only.
pmc-13618563:
Thi Thanh Ngoc Nguyen and five colleagues test a toothpaste with two percent zinc citrate in a randomized trial of orthodontic patients, whose fixed braces trap plaque and inflame gums. One hundred two patients with plaque-induced gingivitis used either the zinc toothpaste or a conventional one. Gum and plaque indices were scored at the start, one week, and four weeks, and plaque samples were analyzed for key bacterial species.

Week-four snapshots favored the zinc paste, with lower gum inflammation, less plaque, and lower loads of three bacterial species. The more rigorous longitudinal analysis, however, found no significant treatment-by-time interaction for the clinical scores or the measurable bacteria. Both groups simply improved over the four weeks, likely from trial attention to brushing. The authors conclude honestly that the zinc citrate toothpaste showed no additional clinical or microbiological effect attributable to it during the study period.
pmc-13618963:
Md Hafizul Islam and seven colleagues analyze what Bangladeshis eat across the life cycle and whether diets deliver enough micronutrients. Combining two nationally representative surveys covering sixteen thousand people, they estimated usual intakes of energy, thirteen food groups, and eleven micronutrients. Adequacy was expressed as each nutrient's probability of meeting requirements, averaged across the set.

Cereals dominated plates, while fruits, leafy vegetables, pulses, milk, and nuts were eaten sparingly. Adequacy ran low for calcium, riboflavin, vitamin B12, folate, zinc, and vitamin A; only niacin and vitamin B6 looked comfortable. Median adequacy was low in every age and physiological group. Women fared worse than men, adolescents worse than young children; those under two fared worse than women of reproductive age, and members of large families worse than small ones. The authors urge policy to make nutrient-dense foods, especially pulses, fruits, nuts, leafy greens, and dairy, cheaper and easier to get.
pmc-13619063:
Kei Saito and eleven colleagues trace one patient's Felty syndrome as it slowly became an aggressive T-cell disease, confirmed at autopsy. Felty syndrome, a rheumatoid arthritis complication marked by low white counts and enlarged spleen, overlaps biologically with clonal disorders of cytotoxic T cells, yet such aggressive progression is rarely documented. Serial immune profiling and molecular testing across the patient's final years let the team follow the disease's course.

An unusual gamma-delta T-cell pool expanded, the T-cell receptor rearranged into a single clone, and the same two gene mutations, in STAT3 and TET2, persisted across samples. That proved the later malignancy grew from the earlier condition rather than arising separately. A complex chromosome pattern marked the final phase. The authors present clinicopathological evidence that Felty-associated clonal disease can evolve over years, which argues for molecular monitoring when counts and spleen signs change in such patients.
pmc-13619563:
Jingyi Xu and eleven colleagues studied what makes Mengding bud yellow tea taste the way it does, in a 2026 paper. This prized Chinese tea is known for a mellow, savory-sweet flavor built by a traditional method of repeated yellowing and frying steps. The team paired trained taste evaluation with chemical profiling across the processing stages.

Taste quality improved step by step, and the yellowing stage did the most to raise savory and sweet notes. Chemical analysis flagged 156 compounds that changed during processing, with a theanine-related compound emerging as a likely taste contributor. Comparison with green tea found nineteen marker compounds that set the yellow tea apart. Pathways for building amino acids and flavonoids stood out as well. The authors frame the results as guidance for protecting and refining a heritage craft.
pmc-13620163:
Seol Ah Park and four colleagues built a method for reading the geography of cancer and immune cells inside tumor tissue, in a 2026 paper. Where immune cells sit relative to malignant cells shapes how a tumor behaves, yet tumor borders are often fuzzy. Their framework uses topological data analysis, a branch of mathematics that finds persistent shapes in data, to draw the malignant region objectively.
